abstract: Same-sex sexual behaviour is widespread in animals 1 , 2 , yet to our knowledge observations of such behaviour between individuals of different taxonomic families remain rare. In a grazing area on an Ethiopian plateau (Debre Libanos, Oromia), Achille, a bull (Bos taurus/indicus), and Patroclo, a male donkey (Equus asinus), actively engaged in reciprocal socio-sexual interactions, thus forming an unusual association. Although interpreting this behaviour is challenging, the mounting attempts, taken together with the repeated and mutual affiliative interactions between the two animals, may signal the quality of their relationship. The interactions must have reproductive opportunity costs, in time and energy diverted away from potentially functional reproductive activities, and it would seem that these costs are outweighed by the strength of the animals' social bond 3 .

abstract: Army ant raids by Eciton burchellii parvispinum are iconic spectacles of Neotropical forests, driving ant-following birds and intense predation on leaf-litter arthropods 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 . However, whether these terrestrial predators influence energy flows across ecosystem boundaries remains unknown. Apart from isolated natural history anecdotes, evidence for such interactions is lacking despite recognition that cross-ecosystem subsidies strongly affect food-web dynamics 5 , 6 , 7 . Here, we report a previously undescribed cross-ecosystem interaction in the mangroves of Yucatán, Mexico, where army ant raids trigger localized feeding aggregations among aquatic vertebrates. Stomach-content analyses of fishes attending raids at four independent Eciton colonies, complemented by observations across six colonies, show that prey escaping army ant predation can become a substantial terrestrial subsidy for resident fishes. This pulse was associated with marked shifts in fish diet and recurrent higher-order predator aggregations, revealing a pathway through which terrestrial predator effects can extend across ecosystem boundaries.

title: Fungal-bacterial interactions.

author_details.name: Uehling J
author_details.affiliation: Department of Botany and Plant Pathology, Oregon State University, Corvallis, OR 97331, USA. Electronic address: jessie.uehling@oregonstate.edu.

author_details.affiliation: Department of Botany and Plant Pathology, Oregon State University, Corvallis, OR 97331, USA.

abstract: The study of fungal-bacterial interactions is an emerging field of biology with relevance for environmental health, medicine, and agriculture, among other sectors. The frequent co-occurrence of fungi and bacteria in many habitats has facilitated the evolution of their symbioses. Both groups are key players in host-associated microbiomes and in nutrient cycling, and these roles often intersect in dynamic ways. Interactions between fungi and bacteria can be mutualistic, commensal, or pathogenic, and they can vary in a context-dependent manner. In mutualistic interactions, fungi and bacteria can exchange nutrients, ameliorate each other's stress, enhance growth, enable dispersal, and facilitate novel niche exploration via metabolite exchange. In contrast, antagonistic interactions frequently involve competition for limited nutrients, such as iron, and active chemical warfare with secreted and bioactive compounds. Bacteria associated with fungi can occur inside of fungal cells (endosymbiotic) or on the surface of fungal hyphae (exosymbiotic). Endosymbiotic bacteria can be further differentiated into facultative symbionts, which retain the ability to enter fungal hyphae but also live independently, and obligate endosymbionts, which are always intracellular and not capable of independent life outside of hyphae. Whereas free-living bacteria can be pathogenic or mutualistic, endosymbiotic bacteria are often regarded as commensals or mutualists, although some can exhibit parasitic attributes in some conditions. A combination of molecular genetics, genomics, and microscopy has been used to study free-living bacteria. In addition to these approaches, fluorescence and electron microscopy have been used as the gold standards to study and differentiate endosymbiotic bacteria based on their intracellular location. More recently, researchers have started using systems-biology approaches to study fungal-bacterial interactions including high-throughput -omics assays. These methods produce expansive datasets that are ideally suited to artificial intelligence (AI)-based approaches to tackle long-standing questions about the basic biology and evolution of fungal-bacterial interactions. In this primer we give an overview of fungal-bacterial interactions, including their diversity, community structure, and symbiotic evolution. We highlight two research systems in particular: the intracellular endosymbionts of Mucoromycota fungi and the free-living bacteria associated with edible fungi. We focus on these systems because fungi remain understudied relative to other groups, and only a handful of fungal taxa with their bacterial symbionts are backed by large enough data sets to explore these concepts in detail. Our aim here is not to be comprehensive, but instead to use the most well-understood systems to illustrate emerging principles. We then discuss advances in using AI to infer new aspects of microbial biology and provide suggestions for how these technologies could advance research on fungal-bacterial interactions utilizing existing genomic datasets.

title: Hippocampal-prefrontal cortical interactions and neural representations of memory.

author_details.name: Morales-Rodriguez D
author_details.affiliation: UCSF-UC Berkeley Graduate Program in Bioengineering, University of California, San Francisco, San Francisco, CA 94158, USA; Medical Scientist Training Program, University of California, San Francisco, San Francisco, CA 94143, USA.

Electronic address: Loren.Frank@ucsf.edu.

abstract: The ability to store memories and access past experiences when making decisions in the present is fundamental to cognition. The hippocampus is critical for these processes and has been a primary site of investigation in the learning and memory field for the last several decades. However, it is also clear that the hippocampus must work in concert with cortical brain regions to store and recall memories. Findings that demonstrate the necessity of hippocampal-medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) communication in these processes, as well as findings that link the mPFC to memory storage, retrieval, and decision-making, have contributed to this growing area of study. Here, we review our current understanding of three questions related to this communication. What information is represented in the hippocampus and the mPFC? What are the underlying neural activity patterns and brain states that facilitate communication of those representations? What impact do these patterns have on the ability to learn and remember in new and familiar settings? We highlight evidence for bidirectional communication both during and after experience, and we discuss areas of active investigation to further uncover the role of bidirectional hippocampal-cortical interactions in the formation and maintenance of neural representations of memory.

abstract: The hypothalamus is a highly heterogeneous brain region that regulates fundamental physiological processes and behaviors, including innate social behaviors such as aggression, mating, and parenting 1 . Distinct cell types within hypothalamic nuclei have been linked to social behaviors, a principle established most clearly in mice, where manipulation of defined hypothalamic neuronal subtypes can initiate or suppress behaviors including attack, mounting, and parenting 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 . Whether hypothalamic cell types are modified as a result of selection during the evolution of social behavior remains unknown. Silver foxes (Vulpes vulpes) have been selectively bred for tame or aggressive behaviors and we have studied whether there are differences relating to these behaviors in the cellular makeup of the hypothalamus. We report here that tame foxes have fewer estrogen receptor-expressing neurons in the ventrolateral subdivision of the ventromedial hypothalamus (VMHvl) than aggressive foxes, and that this reduction is specific to a neuronal subtype linked to aggressive states in mice 5 . We have thus identified a candidate hypothalamic neuronal subtype associated with selection on social behavior during animal domestication.

title: Capturing the Attentional Trade-off between Speech Planning and Comprehension.

author_details.name: Hustá C
author_details.affiliation: Max Planck Institute for Psycholinguistics, Nijmegen, The Netherlands.

author_details.name: Meyer A
author_details.affiliation: Max Planck Institute for Psycholinguistics, Nijmegen, The Netherlands.; Donders Institute for Brain, Cognition, and Behaviour, Nijmegen, The Netherlands.

abstract: In conversation, future speakers often plan speech simultaneously with comprehension, which means that they must divide attentional resources between these processes. In this EEG study, we used responses to linguistic attention probes (i.e., syllable "BA" presented during spoken sentences) to track temporal variations in attention to comprehension. Participants were asked to listen to prerecorded sentences with expected or unexpected sentence-final words. Each sentence was presented twice, once with and once without the attention probe starting 100 msec after the target word onset. Participants saw a picture 50 msec before the target word. Depending on the test block (picture naming or button press), participants either named the picture or pressed the space bar, both after an 850-msec delay. The probes elicited a negative potential approximately 100 msec after probe onset (i.e., an attention probe effect) in all probe conditions. Unexpectedly, neither word expectancy nor speech planning influenced the timing or strength of the attention probe effect. This indicates that expectancy of words in Dutch does not affect the allocation of attention toward these words 100 msec after their onset (i.e., the time of the probe presentation). Interestingly, engaging in speech planning does not seem to divert attentional resources away from comprehension at the moment of probe presentation. These findings imply that listeners are able to effectively distribute their attentional resources between comprehension and speech planning and carry out these processes at the same time. Considering these unexpected findings, using attention probes might not be the best approach to capture variations in temporal attention in dual-task paradigms.

title: Exploring Neural Mechanisms Underlying Error-related Impairments in Active Working Memory Suggests an Adaptive Shielding of Contents during Cognitive Control.

author_details.name: Choo Y
author_details.affiliation: University of Maryland.; University of Iowa.

author_details.name: Adam KCS
author_details.affiliation: Rice University, Houston, TX.

author_details.name: Wessel JR
author_details.affiliation: University of Iowa.

abstract: Goal-directed behavior relies on cognitive flexibility-the ability to rapidly adapt ongoing thoughts and behaviors while preserving task-relevant information. The performance monitoring system optimizes such behavior by detecting and evaluating errors, whereas the working memory (WM) system maintains relevant information and protects it from interference. We previously showed that motor errors impaired active WM maintenance (Error-Related Impairment of Active working Memory [ERIAM]; [Wessel, J. R., Jiang, J., & Stolley, J. J. Action errors impair active working memory maintenance. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 151, 1325-1340, 2022]). Here, we investigated the source of ERIAM by tracking the contralateral delay activity (CDA), a neural marker of visual WM maintenance, throughout the error-making process. Forty-two participants maintained visual information in WM while performing a flanker task during the delay period. Consistent with prior results, a significant ERIAM effect occurred. We observed the canonical CDA before flanker task onset, and this CDA declined after the flanker task began. Following the flanker response, however, we observed a sustained contralateral positivity (CDAp). Critically, CDA amplitudes did not differ between motor correct and error trials before the flanker task, ruling out a general performance deficit. The CDA was also unaffected immediately after flanker onset, ruling out a perceptual interference explanation. Neural differences emerged only after the flanker response, supporting a genuinely error-related origin of the ERIAM effect. Importantly, CDAp was larger following correct responses than errors, and greater CDAp modulation predicted a smaller ERIAM effect. On the basis of prior work, we interpret CDAp as reflecting disengagement from WM storage, suggesting a possible adaptive shielding strategy. These findings provide clear evidence regarding the timing of the ERIAM effect and suggestive evidence regarding potential mechanisms underlying error-related interference in active WM maintenance. Future work will help determine the functional significance of CDAp and its relationship to WM storage and cognitive control.

title: Neural Distinctions between Social and Nonsocial Reward Anticipation: An Examination of Activation Magnitude, Representational Patterns, Individual Differences, and Functional Connectivity.

author_details.affiliation: The University of Texas at Austin.

abstract: Prevailing theories emphasize a "common neural currency" for social and nonsocial rewards, particularly during reward anticipation. However, direct comparisons of social and nonsocial reward anticipation remain limited, and clinical observations suggest that social reward processing can be selectively disrupted. The present fMRI study directly compared social and nonsocial reward anticipation to test differences in activation magnitude, functional connectivity, multivariate activity patterns, and modulation by individual differences in social reward motivation. Consistent with a "common neural currency" perspective, reward anticipation (collapsed across domains) was associated with increased activation in ventral striatum (VS), anterior insula (AI), dorsal ACC (DACC), and SMA. Furthermore, social reward anticipation did not significantly shape functional connectivity among ventral striatum, AI, DACC, and SMA. However, local activation patterns in AI and SMA reliably discriminated the anticipation of social versus monetary reward. Additional decoding emerged in TPJ, STS, and OFC-regions previously inconsistently linked to social reward anticipation or more commonly associated with later stages of reward processing. Moreover, individual differences in Need to Belong predicted greater ACC (including ventromedial PFC) engagement during social reward anticipation. These findings support the perspective that social and nonsocial reward anticipation share some neural circuitry but are dissociable when local activation patterns and social motivational priorities are considered. The current study recasts our understanding of ways in which social reward anticipation may be distinct and raises an expanded role for brain regions typically associated with reward and/or social processing.

title: Slow Oscillations Modulate Overnight Brain Changes in Working Memory Function.

author_details.name: Zhang J
author_details.affiliation: Massachusetts General Hospital, Harvard Medical School.; Athinoula A. Martinos Center for Biomedical Imaging.

author_details.name: Chen PC
author_details.affiliation: Royal Holloway, University of London.

author_details.affiliation: University of California, Irvine.

author_details.affiliation: Nathan S. Kline Institute for Psychiatric Research.; New York University Grossman School of Medicine.

abstract: Working memory (WM), the transient storage and manipulation of information, is a cognitive function that can improve with training. Accumulating evidence suggests that sleep, particularly slow oscillations (SOs) that occur during nonrapid eye movement sleep, supports this improvement. Yet, how sleep and SOs in particular relate to neural processes supporting WM remains poorly understood. In this study, we investigated how WM-related neural activity evolves across nocturnal sleep and how these changes relate to neural processing during SOs. Participants performed a WM task during fMRI before and after sleep, with simultaneous EEG-fMRI capturing neural activity during the first 2.5 hr of sleep. Our results showed significant overnight changes in WM-related activity, characterized by reduced recruitment of the dorsal precuneus during WM encoding/maintenance phases and frontal regions during the retrieval phase of WM. In addition, sleep increased item-specific reinstatement in a sensory processing region during WM. This pattern of results suggests a combined influence of sleep on enhancing sensory reinstatement while reducing potential top-down control (i.e., reduced parietal and frontal activity). Critically, SO-related activity was directly linked to overnight activity changes: Stronger SO activation in the premotor cortex and ventromedial pFC predicted greater overnight reductions in WM-related activity, and multivoxel analyses in the ventral attention network revealed a parallel relationship. These findings suggest that SOs play a critical role in WM function by facilitating the reorganization of WM-related processing.

title: Transformer Mechanisms Mimic Frontostriatal Gating Operations When Trained on Human Working Memory Tasks.

author_details.name: Soni A
author_details.affiliation: Brown University.

author_details.name: Traylor A
author_details.affiliation: Brown University.

author_details.name: Merullo J
author_details.affiliation: Brown University.

author_details.name: Frank MJ
author_details.affiliation: Brown University.

author_details.name: Pavlick E
author_details.affiliation: Brown University.

abstract: Working memory (WM) is thought to rely on sophisticated frontostriatal mechanisms for selective gating, supporting updating and readout of information to and from distinct memory "addresses" (neural populations). According to computational models, capacity limitations in WM arise due to challenges in "role addressability": learning to correctly bind items in memory to their respective roles and assigning credit to the corresponding gating operations. However, these conclusions are based on particular assumptions about biological neural networks, and it is unclear whether the principles generalize to other architectures. To address this question, we examine whether similar gating mechanisms emerge in Transformer neural network architectures, which have demonstrated success on tasks requiring executive function-the ability to represent, coordinate, and manage multiple subtasks-yet lack intentionally built-in gating mechanisms. We analyze the mechanisms that emerge within Transformers trained on human WM tasks explicitly designed to place demands on gating. We find that the Transformer's attention mechanism develops role-addressable input and output gating, but only when trained on task distributions that benefit from frontostriatal-like gating mechanisms. Moreover, these gating strategies support enhanced generalization and variable binding and increase the models' effective capacity to store and access multiple items in memory, resembling the constraints found in frontostriatal models. These results suggest that gating mechanisms serve a fundamental computational role in managing role addressability and binding and highlight opportunities for future research on computational similarities between modern artificial intelligence architectures and models of the human brain.

title: Visual Perspective Shapes Subjective Experience: Dissociable Parietal Contributions to the Constructive Nature of Memory.

author_details.name: St Jacques PL
author_details.affiliation: University of Alberta.

abstract: Subjective features of memory are often treated as secondary to the objective content of remembered events. However, growing evidence suggests that these features actively shape how memories are constructed, experienced, and used. Rather than treating visual perspective as a peripheral correlate of subjectivity, this review positions it as a key mechanism that shapes the memory. Because perspective can be flexibly controlled and reliably measured, it offers a unique window into how retrieval goals interact with mental simulation to produce vivid and emotionally resonant recollections. Drawing on behavioral and neuroimaging research, this review shows that visual perspective determines the spatial framing of memory and the emotional and sensory qualities of recollection. Focusing on the posterior parietal cortex, it outlines distinct roles for the angular gyrus (AG) and the precuneus in supporting perspective-dependent retrieval. The AG contributes to the selection and maintenance of a retrieval perspective, integrating perceptual and conceptual features into a coherent scene. In contrast, the precuneus supports spatial transformation and modulates the vividness, emotional tone, and embodied character of recollection, particularly when individuals recall events from a nondominant or shifted perspective. Together, these findings position visual perspective as a central mechanism in the construction of subjectivity. Understanding how perspective shapes the process of remembering provides insight into how memory supports emotion regulation, mental simulation, and the continuity of the self across time.

abstract: Coordination between central pattern generator (CPG) networks underlies coordination of related rhythmic behaviors (e.g., mastication, respiration). This includes individual neurons periodically expressing activity related to more than one behavior. Here, we investigated whether muscles involved in different behaviors respond broadly to dual-network activity, or are biased toward their primary network input. We used the pyloric ("fast": ∼1 Hz: filtering of food) and gastric mill ("slow": ∼0.1 Hz: chewing) networks in the crab, Cancer borealis. During the modulatory state elicited by the neuropeptide Gly 1 -SIFamide, the pyloric-only lateral posterior gastric (LPG) neuron switches to dual pyloric and gastric mill network participation, enabling its contributions to inter-network coordination. LPG innervates pyloric (p7) and gastric mill (gm3b,c) muscles. Using intracellular muscle fiber recordings, we found that p7 responded to single LPG stimuli whereas gm3 required bursts to generate measurable responses. Naturalistic or fixed-parameter dual-network stimulations elicited similar peak p7 amplitudes for both network components. In contrast, gm3 primarily responded to longer-duration, slower-frequency gastric mill bursts. There were reciprocal interactions between the p7 pyloric and gastric mill responses, whereas it was unidirectional in gm3. The inter-network influences in p7 are likely due to activity-dependent synaptic plasticity which we found occurring at multiple time scales, but this was difficult to assess in gm3. Thus, interactions at the motor network level can be translated to electrical responses of muscles. However, the activity of some, but not all, muscles may be tuned to a primary behavior, even for muscles innervated by the same motor neuron.

abstract: Pulmonary complications are a primary cause of morbidity and mortality in children with Down Syndrome resulting from Trisomy 21 (T21). We recently described congenital lung anomalies associated with T21, yet the underlying mechanisms remain elusive. Type I interferon (IFN-I) signaling is consistently hyperactivated in many T21 tissues. IFN-I is recognized as a key regulator of immune cell activation and differentiation, with an under-appreciated role in tissue development. In this study we examine the effects of over-activation and repression of IFN-I signaling in developing human lung tissues. Single-cell RNA sequencing indicates that IFN treatment of tissue explants largely recapitulates transcriptional changes associated with altered epithelial differentiation in T21 lungs. Lineage-specific cell co-culture experiments confirm that mesenchyme-driven IFN-I hyperactivation promotes epithelial bud remodeling, shifts progenitor cell identity, and suggests the induction of AT2-like programs. Our data show that IFN-I is necessary and sufficient to drive T21-related lung pathologies and provide a model system enabling therapeutic discovery.

abstract: Spatial transcriptomics maps gene expression within tissue sections, but dominant short-read approaches have limited ability to resolve full-length transcript structures such as alternative splicing. Long-read sequencing provides transcript-structure information, although its higher sequencing error rates can complicate spatial-barcode identification on high-density arrays. Here, we show a lab-made, high-density spatial transcriptomics system that uses a tri-part combinatorial barcode design to expand barcode capacity and facilitate spatial assignment of long reads. By splitting full-length complementary DNA generated from a single capture chip, the workflow combines high-depth short-read quantification with single-molecule long-read profiling within the same spatial coordinate system. In incompatible tomato–pepper grafts and mouse embryos, the approach identifies spatially localized unannotated isoforms and intron-retention events, and reveals regional differences in isoform usage that are not apparent from gene-level expression alone. Together, this system provides a framework for combining spatial gene-expression quantification with full-length transcript-structure analysis in the same tissue.

abstract: Left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) is a major cardiovascular complication of chronic kidney disease (CKD), yet its mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here we show that in preclinical experiments, CKD drives cardiomyocyte metabolic reprogramming characterized by enhanced glutaminolysis and impaired oxidative phosphorylation in male C57BL/6J mice. Integrated transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses identified early upregulation and activation of glutaminase 1 (GLS1) in CKD hearts, while serum-induced GLS1 activity was associated with LV hypertrophic remodeling in a multicenter peritoneal dialysis cohort. Human myocardial samples also showed increased GLS1 expression in CKD. Cardiomyocyte-specific deletion or pharmacological inhibition of GLS1 attenuated CKD-induced hypertrophy in these mouse models. Proteomic and mechanistic analyses further identified phosphate as a major regulator of GLS1 activity and expression. Excessive GLS1 activation increased ammonia production, disrupted mitochondrial respiratory protein expression and redox homeostasis, and reduced bioenergetic efficiency. These findings identify a phosphate–GLS1–glutaminolysis axis linking the uremic milieu to mitochondrial dysfunction and cardiac hypertrophy, and suggest GLS1 as a potential therapeutic target for CKD-associated LVH.

abstract: Protein phosphorylation cascades are essential for cell proliferation. Here, we identify protein arginine methyltransferase 1 (PRMT1) as a key stabilizer of phosphoproteins that is indispensable for hepatocyte proliferation during liver regeneration. PRMT1 is upregulated by epidermal growth factor (EGF) via receptor tyrosine kinase signaling and catalyzes the asymmetric dimethylation (ADMA) modification of SKP1 at the R81 residue. This methylation event disrupts FBXW7 recruitment to the SKP1-CUL1-F-box protein (SCF) E3 ubiquitin ligase complex, thereby preventing FBXW7-mediated ubiquitination. Since FBXW7 targets multiple pro-proliferative phosphoproteins, this mechanism prevents their degradation, ensuring the transduction of proliferative signals via phosphorylation cascades. Furthermore, in vivo administration of S-adenosylmethionine, the methyl donor for PRMT-catalyzed methylation, significantly accelerates liver regeneration in both mice and patients. Collectively, these findings establish PRMT1 as a central post-translational regulator of hepatocyte proliferation, highlighting its potential as a therapeutic target for liver diseases.

abstract: DNA damage is a central driver of the aging process. We previously found that the kinesin-13 KIF2C, shown to play a role in DNA repair, is repressed in aged cells. Here, we investigate whether increased KIF2C activity can counteract DNA damage and alleviate aging-related phenotypes. We demonstrate that a small-molecule agonist of KIF2C enhances DNA repair in two distinct genetic disorders characterized by pervasive DNA damage and accelerated aging: the Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome (HGPS) and the Down syndrome (DS). Mechanistically, the KIF2C agonist improves double-strand break (DSB) DNA repair in aged and patient-derived cells by restoring the assembly of nuclear envelope invaginations driven by cytoplasmic microtubules. Enhanced DSB DNA repair in HGPS and DS cells translates into amended nuclear structure and transcriptional signatures. Moreover, subcutaneous administration of the KIF2C agonist in progeria mice mitigates aging phenotypes and extends both health and lifespan. Our study discloses a geroprotective pharmacological approach that acts by hindering DSB DNA damage, and thus we demonstrate that enhanced genome stability can delay aging.

abstract: The accelerating global energy demand, coupled with diminishing fossil fuel reserves and growing carbon emissions, underscores the urgent need for sustainable energy solutions. Autotrophic microalgae are promising cell factories for converting CO 2 into renewable biofuels. However, conventional microalgal biofuels typically depend on energy-intensive or nutrient-deficient regimes that suppress microalgal proliferation, resulting in a critical trade-off between biomass growth and lipid biosynthesis. Here, we report a separable living interface with microalgae (SLIM) platform that employs extracellular-matrix-mimicking hydrogel scaffolds to spatially organize microalgae and dynamically reconfigure their microenvironment, enabling spatiotemporal switching between biomass accumulation or lipid induction. The SLIM platform supports high-density growth of microalgae while facilitating precision substrate-driven metabolic regulation, enabling low-carbon operation and improved lipid production (8.89 g L −1 ). This work establishes an engineered living material that overcomes essential bottlenecks in microalgal biofuel production and offers a generalizable blueprint for biohybrid systems in advanced biomanufacturing.

abstract: The ivory:mir-193 locus is a genetic hotspot underlying melanic wing pattern variation across Lepidoptera, acting as a master regulator of melanic scale fate. This includes the genus Heliconius , where aposematic mimicry is driven by three scale cell types: light Type I, dark-melanic Type II, and red Type III scales. We test functions of ivory:mir-193 in Heliconius using CRISPR-induced somatic mosaic knockouts of ivory and mir-193 across multiple pattern morphs. Knockouts convert Type II scales to Type I scales. Effects on Type III scales vary among and within individuals, indicating that ivory:mir-193 is permissive for Type III development. Using single-nucleus RNA-seq, we profile the transcriptional landscape of H. melpomene Δ78k mutants lacking mir-193 . Loss of mir-193 produces readthrough transcription, consistent with a model where mir-193 acts as a co-transcriptional terminator. These data show that miR-193 , a miRNA under the transcriptional control of the ivory host gene, mediate the diversification of wing patterns across Lepidoptera by modulating scale cell identity during pupal wing development.

abstract: Optical scattering in biological tissues fundamentally limits fluorescence imaging by disrupting spatial and angular information, thereby restricting volumetric visualization. Although hardware-intensive and computational approaches have advanced scattering microscopy, practical three-dimensional imaging through tissue remains constrained by instrumental complexity and axial ambiguity. Here, we present volumetric scattering microscopy (VSM), a scan-free, optical–computational framework for three-dimensional fluorescence imaging in scattering biological media. VSM captures angularly resolved speckle-encoded fluorescence using an aperture-segmented Fourier light-field configuration and reconstructs volumetric structure through adaptive feature-based descattering and joint sub-pupil alignment. This hybrid strategy preserves angular information embedded in scattered light without wavefront measurement or mechanical scanning, while maintaining the simplicity of a standard epi-fluorescence architecture. We demonstrate high-fidelity volumetric reconstruction across phantoms, engineered cellular systems, ex vivo tissues with volumetric muscle loss, and intact Xenopus embryos, achieving preserved spatial resolution, enhanced optical sectioning, and quantitative accuracy under strong scattering conditions. VSM supports large-field, robust volumetric imaging in both layered and fully embedded scattering environments. By transforming scattered light into a structured encoding resource, VSM establishes a scalable pathway toward routine three-dimensional fluorescence imaging in complex biological systems.

title: A Planar Switching Neuron Shares Logarithmic First-Spike Latency with Its Three-Dimensional Parent But Not Its Onset Mechanism
abstract: Can a reduced neuron model reproduce first-spike latency scaling while changing how a stimulus initiates sustained firing? We compare a piecewise-linear planar Neurosimilator with its three-dimensional parent. Both exhibit logarithmic latency dependence over the investigated input intervals, with different fitted coefficients. The mechanisms differ. In the parent, sustained spiking and a stable resting focus coexist in a spiking--rest bistability regime. An abrupt step accesses spiking, while slow stimulation can retain rest at the same final input. Its step-induced firing threshold is therefore an operational basin-access threshold below the saddle-node limit point, not a loss of equilibrium stability. In the planar model, the resting equilibrium instead reaches a switching boundary while its subthreshold eigenvalues remain negative. We derive the planar latency law from this boundary approach. The model generates repetitive excursions without an imposed reset and admits exact trajectories within six switching regions. Similar measured latency scaling thus coexists with different mechanisms of access to firing. Validating a reduced model's mechanism of excitability requires examination of stimulus protocol and attractor access alongside equilibrium structure and spike timing.
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures

title: Accurate automated photo-identification of Near Eastern and European fire salamanders
abstract: Photo-identification underpins non-invasive capture-recapture monitoring of amphibians, but manual identification becomes slow and error-prone as reference libraries grow. Focusing on the Near Eastern fire salamander (Salamandra infraimmaculata), we developed a pipeline based on zero-shot local-feature matching (SuperPoint and LightGlue) without species-specific training and evaluated it on $2{,}440$ field photographs from Haifa and Tel Dan in northern Israel. We isolated the yellow spot pattern, scored image similarity by the number of high-confidence keypoint matches, which reduced a confound whereby many-spotted individuals accumulate spurious matches, and assigned identities across the database by two-tier clustering. Pipeline-assisted expert review corrected misidentifications, reducing the number of identities by almost a quarter. On held-out individuals, the pipeline ranked the correct individual first for $95.2\%$ of queries and recovered identities with an ARI of $0.958$. Without modification, it reached $95.1\%$ and $91.7\%$ top-1 accuracy on two datasets of the European fire salamander (Salamandra salamandra) and recognised $93.7\%$ of recaptures in one of them, compared with $38$-$77\%$ for five established programs and $93.9\%$ for visual inspection. Zero-shot local-feature matching thus offers amphibian monitoring a re-identification tool that needs no training data, transfers between related species, scales to databases of over a thousand individuals, and can audit existing databases before capture-recapture analysis.

title: Cell lines that share a well are not independent observations in the Tahoe-100M drug screen
abstract: Pooled drug screens treat and sequence dozens of cancer cell lines together in one well. Tahoe-100M, the largest, is used to train and benchmark models that predict how unmeasured cell lines respond to drugs, and its benchmarks, reproducibility ceilings and statistical tests treat the cell lines of a well, and random halves of a well's cells, as independent observations of a drug's effect. Because the drug is applied to the well, this is harmless only if the lines of a well share nothing beyond the drug's reproducible effect. We tested this with pairs of untreated control wells on 13 plates, with replicate wells whose labels we checked, and with two plates that repeat each other well by well. In each test the cell lines of a well share a component of expression that a replicate well does not reproduce, also when the two wells occupy the same inferred position; where drugs are present, it cannot be told apart from an interaction of plate and drug, but in untreated wells it can. In replicate wells at different positions whose labels pass the check, about a third of what two halves of a well have in common (35%, 95% interval 22-58%, 9 compounds) is not reproduced by the replicate well. The well effect inflates results that take something from a well and judge it in the same well: retrained versions of two published models that take a measured response as input lose about a quarter to a third of their score when the input comes from a replicate well instead of the predicted well (22-43% under the control-well reference), halves of a well overstate how well the experiment reproduces, and a test across the lines of a well calls 5 of 13 plates significant when two untreated wells are compared. Many labels of strongly responding replicate wells, those of plate 13 above all, fail the label check. Evaluations, ceilings and tests on such data should treat the well as the experimental unit.

title: Comparative Strategies for Handling Imbalanced QSAR Regression: A Case Study on hERG Activity Prediction
abstract: Data imbalance frequently occurs in QSAR modeling, yet most studies focus on classification tasks, and few address regression tasks, as it is challenging to determine which regions of the data are sparse or dense. Data-level and algorithm-level imbalance-handling strategies can have different effects on model performance. In this study, we systematically compare various strategies across GCN and fingerprint-based machine learning models. To evaluate model performance more meaningfully, we partitioned the target region into several subregions based on both domain knowledge and data distribution. We focused on the region of greatest practical interest. Our results demonstrate that selecting models based on this interest-region metric leads to more reliable performance than using the total region metric. We also observed that different imbalance-handling strategies can have divergent effects depending on the model type. These findings highlight the importance of region-aware evaluation in regression QSAR modeling and provide practical guidance for selecting appropriate strategies for imbalanced datasets.

title: Do agents need to sleep?
abstract: LLM-based agents, which increasingly operate persistently across sessions and accumulate memory through interaction, already exhibit the familiar symptoms of unchecked plasticity: semantic drift, degraded retrieval precision, propagation of stored errors, and saturation of memory capacity. Drawing on the selectionist "ringing, resonance and renormalization" (RRR) account of sleep, we propose that each of its three phases maps onto an operation feasible in digital memory architectures. Engineers building stateful agents, meanwhile, are independently rediscovering the problems sleep evolved to solve: what to forget, and when to do the forgetting. From this we derive the falsifiable prediction that selectionist consolidation will outperform instructionist alternatives as memory stores grow large. The core claim concerns the nature of continuous learning itself: plasticity has a price, and for any system that learns continuously under finite capacity while coupled to its environment, that price is sleep.

title: From Tool State to Scientific Action: Auditing Decision Provenance in Biomedical Research Agents
abstract: A scientific agent can give the same verdict while reading and citing different evidence. BioAgent-DF tests this separation using paired reference and candidate values saved at the same scientific computation site. It restores or transplants those values at their original coordinates, then runs the agent on healthy hardware. Across eight SciFact batches, Qwen3.5-4B shows repeatable citation changes in three capture-claim combinations, and Gemma 3 4B IT shows repeatable read and citation changes in four. These seven combinations cover two claims. Full restoration recovers the reference evidence sets while verdicts remain unchanged. Verdict changes observed under the baseline prompt did not recur under the explicit-example prompt. Complementary tool and optimizer experiments distinguish recovery of numerical state, recovery of ranked lists, and restoration of an agent's visible history. These results show that an audit should track both the evidence an agent uses and its final answer. In hERG cardiac-safety assay allocation, silent numerical faults changed testing decisions while the fixed-budget shortlist kept the same number of compounds labeled as blockers. After the agent had used faulty values, restoring its earlier execution state and supplying certified scores recovered all 39 changed decisions, whereas replacing the prediction file recovered none; no incorrect action was committed. A streaming implementation of the arithmetic checks reduced the total time for forward execution and verification by 42.4% relative to the original FP64 implementation, with identical flags and recovery outputs.

title: Modeling Visual Cortex with Layerwise Multiscale Manifold Capacity Maximization
abstract: Task-optimized deep neural networks have risen to prominence as the most predictive phenomenological models of responses in primate visual cortex, but leave much to be desired from the perspective of biological plausibility. One such limitation is the reliance on precise credit assignment through global backpropagation of error signals. Recent work has shown that this weakness can be circumvented by requiring each subsequent stage to solve a distinct and increasingly complex task, allowing for layerwise local learning signals. We propose a novel strategy for crafting such intermediate losses that uses an efficient coding framework formulated in terms of manifold capacity, and which can be computed using a sequence of {canonical cortical computations}. In particular, we leverage the relationship between the multiscale nature of visual signals and the dilation of receptive field sizes in cascaded visual representations to modulate complexity, allowing for the reapplication of these common loss computations at each stage of the hierarchy. We evaluate our approach on its ability to predict neural datasets spanning three areas of the ventral stream hierarchy in macaques, as well as human psychophysical data on an object classification task. We find that our unsupervised layerwise model matches or exceeds the performance of competitive architecture-matched baselines on all evaluations considered.

title: Stand-In Effects and Pooling Amplification: Design-Based Tests of Whether Biological World Models Use Actions
abstract: Action-conditioned world models are increasingly trained on data from randomized experiments, and whether their predictions respond to actions is usually checked by replacing or removing the actions and measuring the loss in accuracy. We show that such diagnostics report action effects where there are none: under autocorrelated designs, future actions stand in for history the model does not see, and a better model learns the stand-in better. When the design law is known, a conditional randomization test written as an e-value is valid in finite samples whatever the model, provided the resampler conditions on the full state the design used; resampling from a simpler law reproduces the false effect. We identify a second failure, specific to world models: when many sites share one action sequence (cells in a microscope field, pixels in a frame), the natural pooled score turns small model errors along the action contrast into overwhelming evidence against a true effect. In a pixel world, its median log e-value fell from $-17.3$ to $-6832$ as frames grew from 64 to 4096 pixels, while the oracle's rose. Tempering the score by a design effect estimated on training data changes the bet, not the validity. Our own preregistered analysis of optogenetic ERK experiments failed in exactly this way; a tempered statistic, selected on synthetic data and registered before the data were obtained, then rejected the null on a never-opened field ($E\approx 1.1\times10^{10}$). Every analysis is preregistered, fixed in a dated protocol before it was run, or labelled exploratory, and every reported result is generated from hashed result files.
