title: Statistical mechanics of spontaneous behavior
abstract: Why do a few behaviors fill most of an animal's time? The usual answer is that these behaviors are started more often, because learning and reinforcement favor them. Here we show that how long a behavior lasts can, by itself, explain much of what is observed. We consider a system that runs until it meets a constraint, such as a wall, and then resets. The fraction of time it spends in each behavior then follows the Boltzmann law, and the partition function is the mean time between resets. The four laws of thermodynamics follow as theorems from four postulates, and critical points that act as bottlenecks become the most occupied states. In 47 multi-day recordings of fruit flies, the dominant behavior accounts for only $13\%$ of bout starts yet fills $49\%$ of the time, and its typical duration identifies the individual fly. These results lay the groundwork for a statistical mechanics of behavior.

title: The (Butter)fly Dream: Linear Separability of World-Model Rollouts in a Connectome-Constrained Visual Model
abstract: Zhuangzi dreamt he was a butterfly and, on waking, could not tell which was the dream. We ask a version of his question of a model of the fly brain: placed inside a world generated by a world model, can a fixed brain tell that the world is a dream? We treat it as a question about what a connectome-constrained model trained on one task makes available beyond that task: do its responses make the defects of a dream linearly decodable? The observer is a published model of the fly visual system trained only for optic-flow estimation; reality is the MPI-Sintel movie on the model's 721-column retina; dreams are continuations of five real frames by three small world models (a persistence random walk, an MDN-RNN and an RSSM) at three temperatures. The judge is a classifier two-sample test on temporal statistics of cell-type responses, with sequence-level cross-validation. In the trained observer's responses all nine dreams are separable from reality (AUC 0.85-0.99, mean over 50 trained models), in those of the same network before training much less so (0.58-0.75 for the learned world models; paired difference 0.20-0.37), equally on sequences the observer never saw, and in an order unrelated to pixel error. Because these AUCs are near ceiling, we add graded probes made of each window's own real frames with only their order broken. Swapping one adjacent pair of the 14 generated frames gives 0.73 on the trained responses against 0.54 before training and 0.56 for pixel statistics; the trained curve reaches 0.75 at 1.1 swapped pairs of seven, the pixel statistics at 4.7, and the untrained network not at all. A detection horizon, the test on the first k generated frames, orders the world models where the full-length AUC saturates.

title: A Unified World Model in Human Posterior Parietal Cortex
abstract: How does the brain understand the physical world, predict future events, and plan actions? Are these problems solved by a unified world model, as hypothesized by cognitive scientists and artificial intelligence researchers? Posterior parietal cortex has been implicated in all these functions, but whether the same neurons support each of them is unknown. We recorded from the superior parietal lobule (SPL) of two tetraplegic participants implanted with microelectrode arrays. SPL units preferentially engaged by intuitive physics, judging block-tower stability and viewing naturalistic physical events, also predicted whether moving objects would collide hundreds of milliseconds before contact, generalizing between different physical scenarios. These populations also encoded which hand action the participant intended to perform. These findings identify SPL as a substrate for physical world modeling.

title: An ecological origin of the asymmetry of human color discrimination: evidence from psychophysics, MEG, and deep neural networks
abstract: Hue is a powerful cue for object discrimination, but human color discrimination is anisotropic: hue thresholds are lower than chroma thresholds for orangish colors, but nearly equal for purplish colors. Here we show that this asymmetry reflects environmental color statistics rather than being a fixed consequence of cone-opponent architecture. Across fifteen image and reflectance databases, orangish hues accounted for 62.5% of chromatic samples, compared with 5.3% for purplish hues. We replicated the hue-chroma asymmetry psychophysically in 44 participants. Magnetoencephalography revealed a corresponding neural asymmetry, with superior decoding of orangish hue differences emerging around 250 ms after stimulus onset. Deep neural networks trained on naturalistic image datasets reproduced the human-like asymmetry without explicit color supervision. Critically, training on hue-inverted images reversed the asymmetry, producing greater hue sensitivity for purplish than for orangish colors. These results suggest that the geometry of color discrimination is shaped by ecological chromatic structure.
author_corresponding_institution: Department of Psychology, Justus-Liebig-University Giessen, Germany; Department of Experimental Psychology, University of Oxford, Oxford, UK

title: BMP4 Restricts Axonal Ramification and Bouton Density in Cholinergic Projections from the Basal Forebrain
abstract: Axonal projections and precise synapse formation are essential for the establishment of functional neural circuits, and their dysregulation contributes to various psychiatric and neurodegenerative disorders. Although numerous extracellular cues secreted from surrounding tissues regulate axon guidance and synapse formation, the mechanisms by which neurons locally regulate terminal patterning within their projection fields remain poorly understood. Bone morphogenetic protein 4 (BMP4) is a classical morphogen that is involved in early neural tube patterning during development. However, its postnatal function remains unclear. Previous in vitro studies using hippocampal glutamatergic neurons demonstrated that BMP4 can act locally on axons to suppress synapse formation, raising the possibility that BMP4 regulates terminal differentiation after target innervation. Here, we investigated the role of BMP4 in postnatal cholinergic circuit development using cholinergic neuron-specific Bmp4 conditional knockout (Bmp4 cKO) mice, with adult analyses performed in males. Basal forebrain cholinergic neurons project extensively throughout the neocortex and are essential for higher brain functions, including arousal and attention. Bmp4 cKO mice exhibited increased cholinergic axon terminals in the neocortex, hippocampus, and amygdala, as well as increased axonal ramification in the neocortex without affecting cytoarchitectonic organization or cholinergic neuron numbers in the basal forebrain. These findings demonstrate that BMP4 functions as a negative regulator of cholinergic terminal formation and axonal arborization, suggesting that BMP4 may act locally to restrict cholinergic axonal expansion during neural circuit maturation.

title: Cortical long-range dynamics track excitation-inhibition balance across cognitive states and organizational principles
abstract: A fundamental question in systems neuroscience is how the brain's excitation-inhibition (E/I) balance shapes the temporal structure of neural activity and whether we can non-invasively recover this relationship from neural scaling properties. We show that MRS-derived E/I balance is expressed in long-range temporal dynamics and constrained by cytoarchitecture. The laminar organisation of inhibitory circuits, spanning agranular to granular cortex, determines how faithfully regional dynamics reflect E/I balance. This neurochemical signature is state-dependent: its relationship with cortical dynamics reverses during task engagement, consistent with traversal of dynamical regimes around a critical point. It extends beyond fMRI to arousal-linked dynamics, indexed by pupil diameter and microsaccades, indicating a global mode of cortical state rather than a regionally isolated property. The imprint of E/I balance on long-range dynamics follows the sensory-association axis at rest, and is reconfigured during task engagement. These findings establish E/I balance as a neurochemical quantity with structured, scalable signatures across the temporal and spatial organization of the human cortex.

title: DNA polymerase kappa supports repair-associated DNA synthesis and genome maintenance in postmitotic neurons
abstract: Postmitotic neurons depend on continuous DNA repair to preserve genome integrity, yet the polymerases supporting repair-associated DNA synthesis remain poorly defined. Here, we identify DNA polymerase kappa (POLK), a Y-family translesion synthesis polymerase studied predominantly in proliferating cells, as a regulator of DNA synthesis and genome maintenance in postmitotic neurons. Using primary mouse cortical neurons and human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived forebrain neurons, we show that POLK localizes near newly synthesized DNA and repair-associated proteins, including ubiquitinated PCNA. POLK depletion reduces DNA synthesis in both mouse and human neurons and promotes nuclear and organelle remodeling, p21-associated senescence-like stress, inflammatory responses, and increased p38 MAPK immunoreactivity. In an Alzheimer's disease-risk genetic background, POLK depletion also increases cytoplasmic double-stranded DNA and tau phosphorylation. Conversely, POLK overexpression enhances neuronal DNA synthesis while reducing DNA damage-associated signals, p38 MAPK immunoreactivity, cytoplasmic DNA, and Alzheimer's disease-relevant phenotypes. These findings uncover a role for POLK in postmitotic neuronal genome maintenance, linking specialized DNA polymerase function to neuronal stress and vulnerability relevant to aging and neurodegeneration.
author_corresponding_institution: Penn State University College of Medicine

title: Differential Glutamatergic Inputs to Semilunar Granule Cells and Granule Cells Underscore Dentate Gyrus Projection Neuron Diversity
abstract: Semilunar Granule Cells (SGCs) are sparse dentate gyrus projection neurons whose role in the dentate circuit, including pathway-specific inputs, remains unknown. We report that SGCs receive more frequent spontaneous excitatory synaptic inputs than granule cells (GCs). Dual GC-SGC recordings identified that SGCs receive stronger medial entorhinal cortex and associational synaptic drive but lack short-term facilitation of lateral entorhinal cortex inputs observed in GCs. Consistently, the probability of firing in response to medial perforant path input was greater in SGCs than in GCs. Additionally, the dendritic spine density on proximal and middle dendrites was higher in SGCs than GCs. However, the strength of commissural and supramammillary nuclear inputs and dendritic input integration, examined in passive morphometric simulations, did not differ between cell types. Activity-dependent labeling identified an overrepresentation of SGCs among neuronal ensembles in both mice trained in a spatial memory task and task-naive controls. The divergence of modality-specific entorhinal inputs to SGCs and GCs identified here can enable parallel processing of information streams and expand the computational capacity of the dentate gyrus.

title: Differential Survival of Retinal Ganglion Cell Types Following Branch Retinal Vein Occlusion
abstract: Background. Branch retinal vein occlusion (BRVO) is a common cause of retinal ischemia, rapidly inducing neuronal death and often producing irreversible vison loss. Interventions such as thrombolysis restore perfusion but cannot recover neurons already lost, and most patients retain permanent visual deficits. Identifying which neuronal populations die, and how rapidly, may therefore reveal timing windows and targets for neuroprotective treatment. Aims. To determine the timing of pathology, we evaluated vascular changes and neuronal degeneration in a photocoagulation-induced mouse model of BRVO. To determine differences in retinal ganglion cells (RGC) type susceptibility, we tracked the survival of RGC subpopulations using immunofluorescence markers. Methods. BRVO was induced by retro-orbital injection of Rose Bengal and FITC dextran followed by targeted photocoagulation of a branch vein. Obstruction was confirmed by fluorescein angiography and vascular damage was viewed by optical coherence tomography angiography. Cell survival was quantified by immunostaining at 3, 7, and 14 days using RNA Binding Protein with Multiple Splicing (RBPMS, pan RGC). RGC subtype markers for intrinsically photosensitive RGCs (TBR2),  RGCs (SPP1), ON OFF direction-selective RGCs (CART), and F RGCs (FOXP2) were used to examine differences in survival across RGC types. Results. Occlusion selectively disrupted the superficial and intermediate capillary plexus, sparing the deep plexuses. All examined neuronal populations were significantly depleted, but with markedly different magnitude and timing.  RGCs and F RGCs were the most vulnerable subtypes, both approaching complete loss by one week, whereas intrinsically photosensitive RGCs were the most resistant. Conclusion.  RGCs, typically resilient in glaucoma, trauma, and excitotoxicity, were markedly vulnerable in BRVO, indicating that RGC subtype susceptibility is insult-specific.
author_corresponding_institution: John F. Hardesty, MD, Department of Ophthalmology and Visual Sciences, Washington University School of Medicine, St. Louis, MO, USA

title: Human iEEG recordings during audiovisual speech violations support and extend predictive routing models
abstract: Rather than constantly reconstructing the world solely through sensory input, predictive processing theories posit that the brain utilizes predictions maintained as internal representations to guide sensory processing. An emerging model, predictive routing, proposes that an interplay between neuronal gamma (40-150 Hz) and alpha-beta (10-30 Hz) rhythms implements a dynamic mechanism for predictive processing. Namely, predictions enhance alpha-beta oscillations that suppress gamma activity during the processing of predicted inputs. While this model is supported by animal studies, its validity has not been fully explored within the human brain. The present study addresses this by leveraging human intracranial EEG (iEEG) recordings across superior temporal and prefrontal/premotor areas of seven presurgical epilepsy patients during an audiovisual speech paradigm. We calculated iEEG power in the theta, alpha-beta, and high gamma bands during simple auditory deviance, multisensory integration, and a condition where an incongruent visual cue (lip movements) clashed with an auditory stimulus (a syllable), creating audiovisual incongruence that can elicit the McGurk illusion. Results revealed increased high-gamma and decreased alpha-beta power in the superior temporal cortex in response to auditory deviance and the McGurk condition, while frontal areas, despite reflecting a similar decrease in alpha-beta power, did not present this high gamma prediction error signal. Instead, the theta band revealed a strong prediction error signal in the McGurk condition, consistent with theories on the role of theta in reorganizing cortical networks. These results both support and extend existing predictive routing models for human-specific forms of predictive processing.

title: Impaired formation and updating of internal predictive models in a rat model of Fragile X Syndrome
abstract: Predictive coding frameworks propose that perception emerges from a continuous comparison of incoming sensory signals with internally generated predictions, with mismatches between the two computed as prediction errors. Disruptions to the balance between these top-down predictions and bottom-up sensory signals are theorized to contribute to sensory abnormalities in neuropsychiatric conditions like autism spectrum disorders. However, disambiguating bottom-up from top-down contributions to sensory processing remains a difficult challenge, particularly in animal models. Here we develop a probabilistic oddball detection task in which rats must track local statistics within a trial to detect a deviant stimulus, as well as global statistics across trials to anticipate when a deviant will occur. This design enables formation of experimentally specified internal models of deviant expectation that can be quantitatively derived from behavior and manipulated independently of local stimulus statistics. We used this task to characterize sensory predictive behavior in a Fmr1 KO rat model of Fragile X Syndrome, the most common monogenic cause of autism. Male Fmr1 KO rats detected deviant stimuli at wildtype levels but exhibited reduced anticipation of deviant occurrence based on cross-trial statistics and failed to adapt their behavior when these statistics changed. Computational modeling revealed that these behavioral deficits reflected an overweighting of immediate sensory evidence and temporal response pressure at the expense of learned predictive expectations, consistent with imprecise internal models skewed towards sensory immediacy. These findings provide evidence for disrupted predictive processing in Fragile X Syndrome, consistent with active inference accounts of autism, and highlight the utility of this probabilistic oddball task design for interrogating predictive coding and perceptual impairments in neuropsychiatric conditions.

title: Increased CA3 burst activity in Doc2α and Syt7 knockout mice
abstract: The hippocampal CA3 subfield is central to associative learning and memory consolidation. CA3 pyramidal neurons execute these functions by generating hypersynchronous bursts that feed forward to the CA1. Extensive recurrent collateral connections within CA3 are crucial for the generation of this burst activity. Double C2 domain-containing protein  (Doc2) and synaptotagmin 7 (Syt7) are high-affinity calcium sensors implicated in asynchronous release (AR) of neurotransmitter and in the exocytosis of dense-core vesicles (DCVs). Additionally, Doc2 is a sensor for miniature neurotransmission, whereas Syt7 is involved in synaptic facilitation and SV replenishment. Both Doc2 and Syt7 are expressed in the hippocampus, but their potential roles in spontaneously bursting networks, like CA3, remain unanswered. Using whole-cell recordings at near physiological conditions (33-34 {degrees}C and 1.2 mM Ca2+) in acute hippocampal slices obtained from juvenile (P15-21) KO mice lacking Doc2, Syt7, or both proteins, we report no changes in spontaneous inhibitory or excitatory postsynaptic current frequency or amplitude in CA1 pyramidal neurons. However, there was a marked increase in burst activity, originating in CA3, in all three KO conditions; this was not due to changes in AR or the intrinsic properties of CA3 pyramidal neurons. We propose that this novel burst phenotype in Doc2- and Syt7-KO mice is unrelated to changes in neurotransmitter release but might be mediated by changes in neuropeptide release from DCVs in the CA3 subfield, or along upstream pathways. Regardless of the underlying mechanisms, this work reveals that both Doc2 and Syt7 act to regulate network activity.

title: Infection-related images reduce cortical edge metastability: a specification-curve analysis of a block-design fMRI study
abstract: Cues of infection evoke disgust, attentional capture, withdrawal and shifts in social orientation, a set of responses attributed to the behavioral immune system. Responses this varied have to be coordinated, as the effects of inflammation are, so they should be visible in whole-cortex coupling. We predicted that infection-related images hold cortical dynamics in a narrower repertoire, reducing cortical edge metastability, the temporal variability of mean cofluctuation across parcel pairs. In two fMRI runs, 44 adults viewed alternating 18-s blocks of infection-related and neutral images; the primary test was specified before we looked at the data. That test gave Cohen's d = -0.31 (permutation p = .042), and 263 of 480 specifications were significant, all negative (joint p < .001). With global signal regression, the synchrony-based reduction survived removal of the stimulus-locked response, detrending, and motion, white-matter and cerebrospinal-fluid regression (d = -0.47), recurred in the second run (d = -0.44), and was smaller on strictly alternating blocks (d = -0.36). Without global signal regression, the pre-specified effect did not survive white-matter and cerebrospinal-fluid regression. Individual-difference predictions were not supported, and participants' contrasts did not replicate across runs. Infection-related images reduce the variability of residual global cofluctuation at the group level; whether this is specific to pathogen cues remains open.

title: Longitudinal persistence of EEG brain fingerprints: phase and complex coherency geometry across sessions and functional states
abstract: Sensor-level EEG coherency can distinguish individuals, although its phase and magnitude patterns may reflect neural activity, source mixing, and recording geometry. We evaluated two geometric representations of complex coherency - unit phasors and full complex coherency - alongside triangle holonomies and magnitude-only descriptors. Using direct enrollment-probe matching without a trained identity classifier, we analyzed three independent longitudinal cohorts: RestCog (N = 60; approximately one month), L-FAME (N = 44; six weeks), and Dortmund (N = 206; approximately five years). In eyes-closed rest-to-rest matching, alpha phasors identified 81.67% of participants in RestCog (AUC 0.9473) and 79.55% in L-FAME (AUC 0.9735); full complex coherency identified 78.33% and 84.09%, respectively. After five years in Dortmund, fixed row-standardized alpha-beta fusion yielded 77.67% rank-1 identification (AUC 0.9744) for phasors and 70.39% (AUC 0.9527) for full coherency. Changes in functional state exposed different strengths: full coherency preserved higher rank-1 accuracy in some monthly RestCog rest-to-task comparisons, whereas alpha phasors retained higher verification AUC. Switching between eyes-closed and eyes-open recordings in Dortmund substantially weakened identification with both representations. Triangle holonomies also retained individual information across visits. An exact factorization of complex cosine shows how magnitude-pattern alignment and magnitude-weighted phase agreement contribute to full-coherency matching. Together, the results establish longitudinally discriminative structure in measured scalp EEG coherency over weeks to years, while distinguishing persistence across visits from robustness to changes in recording state.

title: Molecular MRI of Neuroinflammation in Alzheimer's Disease using a Folate-targeted Nanoprobe
abstract: Background: Neuroinflammation, driven by activated microglia, plays a central role in the pathogenesis of Alzheimer's disease (AD). Non-invasive imaging of neuroinflammation holds promise for advancing our understanding of disease mechanisms and evaluating anti-inflammatory therapeutic strategies. The folate receptor (FR), specifically its {beta} isoform, has been identified as a marker of pro-inflammatory myeloid cells in peripheral inflammatory diseases; however, its association with AD neuroinflammation remains unknown. In this work, we first determined FR expression in microglia in mouse models of AD and subsequently evaluated molecular MRI (mMRI) using a folate-targeted nanoprobe for in vivo imaging of the folate receptor expression. Methods and results: Microglial activation and FR expression in APP/PS1 and P301S transgenic mouse models of AD was measured using flow cytometry. A FR-targeted nanoprobe for mMRI was prepared by functionalizing high T1-relaxivity liposomal gadolinium nanoparticle with folic acid. Following intravenous injection, localization of the nanoprobe in the brains of aged transgenic and wild-type mice was measured using T1-weighted MRI. Post-mortem microscopy measured nanoprobe localization relative to microglia and amyloid pathology. In both mouse models, FR{beta} was significantly (p < 0.05) upregulated in pro-inflammatory microglia expressing TNF and IL-1{beta}. The folate-targeted nanoprobe demonstrated MR signal enhancement in the cortical and hippocampal regions of transgenic mice but not in wild type mice; non-targeted nanoprobe control did not demonstrate signal enhancement in brain of transgenic mice. Microscopy confirmed colocalization of FR-targeted nanoprobe with IBA1-positive microglia/macrophages and amyloid plaques. Conclusions: Pro-inflammatory microglia exhibit elevated levels of FR, and its measurement by non-invasive mMRI is a promising marker of neuroinflammation in AD.
author_corresponding_institution: Texas Children's Hospital / Baylor College of Medicine

title: NeuroGraphBench: Interacting with Drosophila Connectomes at Scale for Exploring the Functional Logic of Neural Circuits
abstract: Drosophila connectomic datasets provide increasingly comprehensive maps of neuronal morphology and synaptic connectivity, offering an unprecedented opportunity to explore the structural organization of its neural circuits. This calls for designing automated tools to interact with connectomic datasets at scale for efficiently exploring structural features embedded in the vast amounts of data. Yet the central challenge remains the understanding of the functional logic of neural circuits. In order to formulate a connectome-grounded hypothesis for what a circuit computes, it is critical to (i) characterize the objects in the natural environment in which brain circuits operate, and (ii) formulate how brain circuits represent and process the defined objects. To develop and demonstrate a methodology for these requirements, we focus on the Drosophila looming-evoked escape pathway. We modeled the trajectory of looming objects that are on a collision course (direct-hits) or pass by the fly (near-misses): their projected images on the retina can be characterized by the subtended solid angle and center elevation. By analyzing the sub-neuronal structure and retinotopic organization of the looming pathway embedded in connectomic datasets, we devised a pathway abstraction, and mapped its structural elements into a connectome-grounded functional model. We demonstrate that (i) the expanding boundary of a looming object activates an annulus of LPLC2 neurons, and (ii) the Giant Fiber reads out this population code through its two dendritic branches, modeled as separate units whose outputs are combined to drive its axon. It is this functional separation of the dendritic branches that gives the model access to the center elevation, separating direct-hits from near-misses well before the solid angle of the two trajectories diverge. To accelerate the connectomic analysis step, we developed a Python toolset with an agentic, code-free workspace interface called NeuroGraphBench (NGB). NGB provides four composable morphology-analysis primitives and an AI Agent that composes them to interactively respond to natural-language queries aided by visualization on an interactive 3D canvas. Thus, NGB automates tedious and repetitive tasks to enable faster and scalable connectomic exploration, keeping human reasoning, instead of writing code, at the center of an open-ended research inquiry.

title: Neuronal and glial transcriptional states vary with proximity to tangle-bearing neurons in the human entorhinal cortex
abstract: More neurons die in Alzheimer's disease than form tangles, and tangle-bearing neurons can persist for decades, so tangles alone cannot explain degeneration. We combined 6,000-plex spatial transcriptomics with PHF1 immunofluorescence (167,176 cells; 9 donors) and imaging mass cytometry (170,195 cells; 62 donors), measuring each cell's distance to the nearest tangle. Tangle-bearing layer 2-3 excitatory neurons were enriched late along a trajectory of increasing microtubule-associated, synaptic and V-ATPase expression, with elevated p62 and K48-ubiquitin. Tangle-free neurons shared more of this state the closer they lay to a tangle, including higher chaperone and autophagy scores, p62 and nuclear size. Nearby glia had higher disease-associated scores, with astrocytes expressing less GFAP. Excitatory, but not inhibitory, neuron loss was greatest in subtypes closest to tangles and cortical depths richest in phosphorylated tau. Selective neuronal vulnerability may reflect not only a neuron's susceptibility to forming a tangle but also where it lies relative to one.

title: Phenotypic screening in Parkinson's iPSC-dopamine neurons identifies the FASN-SREBP1 axis as a potential therapeutic target
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) remains highly challenging to model in vitro, particularly when seeking robust functional phenotypes for target discovery. Patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cell dopaminergic neurons (iPSC-DANs) offer a promising platform to address this challenge. Because calcium dyshomeostasis is well-described in PD pathophysiology, it offers a platform for phenotypic screening. We have previously shown that GBA-N370S iPSC-DANs display impaired intracellular calcium release. Here, we used this disease-relevant phenotype to undertake a 4,108-compound phenotypic screen in GBA-N370S (GBA-NS) iPSC-DANs. This screen identified fatty acid synthase (FASN) as the most enriched protein target. The ability of compounds to rescue calcium release correlated with biochemical potency against FASN across multiple chemical series. We confirmed that FASN knockdown increased intracellular calcium release, supporting an on-target effect. Untargeted lipidomics demonstrated broad remodelling of the neuronal lipidome after FASN inhibition, confirming target engagement. FASN inhibition also increased active a-glucocerebrosidase (GCase), reduced extracellular a-synuclein release and ER stress, and altered RASGRF1 expression. Mechanistically, FASN inhibition activated sterol regulatory element-binding protein 1 (SREBP1), and SREBP1 overexpression alone was sufficient to increase intracellular calcium release, identifying a FASN-SREBP1-calcium homeostasis axis in human neurons. Finally, the FASN inhibitor BI 99179 achieved brain exposure and reduced brain fatty acid levels while inducing an SRE-associated transcriptional response in a Parkinson's mouse model, providing evidence of in vivo target engagement. These findings establish patient iPSC-neuron functional screening as a tractable discovery platform to identify targets which can be taken in vivo and nominate the FASN-SREBP1 axis as a candidate therapeutic pathway in PD.
author_corresponding_institution: Oxford Parkinson's Disease Centre and Department of Physiology, Anatomy and Genetics, University of Oxford; South Park Road, Oxford, OX1 3QU, UK; Kavli Institut

title: Policy regularization as a unifying theory of the striatal division of labor in learning
abstract: Learning novel behaviors requires balancing previously learned actions with the ability to flexibly adapt to changing reward contingencies. This trade-off is well documented in the division of labor between dorsolateral striatum (DLS), which promotes selection of cached, history-dependent actions, and dorsomedial striatum (DMS), which supports flexible learning as reward contingencies change. Here, we propose policy regularization as a general computational principle for understanding this division. Capacity-limited agents face a fundamental trade-off between maximizing reward and minimizing the cost of deviating from a default policy that caches frequently used action transitions. We formalize this trade-off as a KL-regularized reward objective in which a flexible controller (DMS) incurs a cost for diverging from a history-dependent default (DLS). The resulting optimal policy is a combination of a reward-driven action value, continuously updated by DMS, and a default policy conditioned on action history, cached by DLS. In practice, DLS consolidates the action transitions shaped by DMS's reward-driven value learning, so DLS preserves behaviors that were once optimal even when reward contingencies change, producing robust but inflexible action selection and effectively "regularizing" DMS-driven learning. We show that a single model, with a single set of learning and lesion parameters, shared across paradigms, provides a unifying explanation for the functional organization of the striatum, reproducing canonical DLS-DMS dissociations in outcome devaluation, serial spatial reversal, skilled action sequencing, and motor sequence execution tasks.

title: Representations of semantic relations in the human cerebral cortex
abstract: An essential aspect of human cognition is the ability to explicitly think about semantic relations between concepts. Neuroimaging studies have found that individual concepts are encoded by distributed patterns of cortical activity, but it is unclear how representations of semantic relations compare to concept representations in the brain. Some theoretical models suggest that relation representations are embedded within concept representations, while others suggest that relation representations are independent of any specific concept pair. We designed a study to compare how semantic relations and concepts are encoded across the cerebral cortex. To characterize how relations are encoded across cortex, fMRI was used to record brain activity while six participants each answered over one thousand questions about different semantic relations. We find that representations of relations are distinct from their relata. Our results further suggest that relations and concepts are represented in similar cortical regions, and that, within these regions, each location is preferentially selective for specific relations. Overall, these results suggest that in the human cerebral cortex, relations and concepts have distinct representations that share a common functional organization.

title: Sleep Renormalizes Negative Emotional Generalization
abstract: Overgeneralization of negative experiences co-occurs with sleep disruption and characterizes anxiety and posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD). A strategically-designed behavioral paradigm tested whether sleep shifts emotional generalization away from negative and toward positive representations. Participants learned positive, negative, or neutral face-outcome associations, then completed immediate and delayed generalization testing with morphed faces after sleep or wakefulness. Sleep selectively enhanced positive generalization, whereas wakefulness favored negative generalization. To uncover the underlying neural mechanisms, individual variability in generalization was examined using fMRI and high-density EEG. Amygdala and limbic activity during outcome-processing predicted both stronger immediate negative generalization and a sleep-specific shift toward positive generalization. Additionally, sleep-spindle activity positively correlated with post-sleep increases in positive generalization and reductions in negative generalization. Together, these findings identify a neural mechanism through which sleep reduces negative bias while strengthening positive representations, highlighting a pathway by which sleep may protect against maladaptive generalization associated with anxiety and PTSD.

title: Superior Frontal Gyrus Cortical Thickness Mediates the Association Between Openness to Experience and Theory of Mind: Evidence from the Human Connectome Project
abstract: Background: Theory of mind (ToM), the capacity to infer the mental states of others, varies considerably across healthy adults. Openness to experience has been linked both to social-cognitive abilities and to thinner prefrontal cortex, but whether cortical structure statistically accounts for the association between openness and ToM is unknown. We tested whether bilateral superior frontal gyrus (SFG) cortical thickness mediates this association. Methods: Data from 1,049 healthy young adults with complete data were drawn from the Human Connectome Project. ToM was indexed by accuracy on the Heider-Simmel social animation task, openness by the NEO Five-Factor Inventory, and SFG thickness by FreeSurfer. Models adjusted for age, sex, intracranial volume and fluid intelligence; indirect effects were tested with 5,000 bootstrap resamples, and Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction was applied. Results: Openness showed a positive total effect on ToM accuracy (beta = .081, p = .009). Higher openness was associated with thinner left and right SFG (beta = -.085 and -.084), and thinner SFG with higher ToM accuracy (beta = -.082 and -.075). Indirect effects were significant (left: .0069, 95% CI [.0010, .0158]; right: .0063, 95% CI [.0007, .0146]), accounting for approximately 8.5% and 7.8% of the total effect, and remained significant after rank-based normalisation of the ceiling-affected ToM scores. Conclusions: SFG cortical thickness partially and statistically mediates the association between openness to experience and social cognition. Because the data are cross-sectional and effects are small, the findings do not establish a causal mechanism, neural efficiency or synaptic pruning, but they identify a candidate structural pathway for longitudinal testing.

title: The ViRA-L (Visual Recognition Assessment-Leuven): Development, Validation, and Age Stratified Normative Characterization of a Multi-Category Visual Recognition Battery
abstract: Objective: To develop and validate the Visual Recognition Assessment-Leuven (ViRA-L), a recognition-memory battery assessing ten visual categories within a matched task structure, and provide age-stratified normative data. Method: Healthy Dutch-speaking adults completed a visual recognition task for ten categories. Each category included six targets, 18 Learning trials, and 30 Novel trials requiring recognition across appearance changes. After exclusions, 417 participants remained. We evaluated reliability, score distributions, task effects, demographic associations, and category-specific norms. Results: Battery-level internal consistency was good (Cronbach's  = .879; omega total = .901), with lower category-level estimates, broad score dispersion, and minimal floor and ceiling effects. Novel and difficult trials produced lower accuracy and slower responses. Age was the clearest demographic correlate of accuracy; gender and education showed no independent overall associations. Age effects varied by category and were larger in Novel than Learning trials. Model-based differences between ages 50 and 85 were largest for Pseudowords and Hands and smallest for Houses. Conclusions: The ViRA-L supports comparison of recognition-memory profiles under matched procedures. Category-dependent age associations support age-sensitive, category-specific interpretation. The battery provides a foundation for neuropsychological research; further validation is required for clinical diagnostic use.

title: The human-specific gene FRMPD2B couples postnatal experience to the expansion of cortical connectivity
abstract: The human neocortex is characterized by its uniquely prolonged postnatal developmental period during which experience sculpts neuronal circuits, a process essential to human cognitive abilities. Yet whether human-specific genetic innovations have shaped the activity-dependent mechanisms regulating circuit assembly remains unknown. Here, we identify the human-specific gene FRMPD2B as an activity- and experience-regulated modifier of cortical connectivity. FRMPD2B is primarily expressed in cortico-cortical projection neurons postnatally and throughout childhood. It promotes dendritic, axonal and synaptic development, and is required for proper morphogenesis in xenotransplanted human cortical neurons. FRMPD2B expression is bidirectionally regulated by neuronal activity and experience. This activity-responsiveness was gained after FRMPD2B arose through partial gene duplication, when a retrotransposon insertion remodeled its promoter. Our findings highlight how a series of genetic innovations have led to the emergence of a human-specific activity-regulated developmental program through which postnatal experience drives cortical connectivity expansion, linking genome evolution to human brain plasticity.

title: The nucleus accumbens dorsomedial column: distinct anterior-posterior inputs and activation inversely associated with opioid relapse
abstract: Anatomical studies suggest that a dorsomedial region of nucleus accumbens (dmACB) forms a basal ganglia-like closed-loop circuit with medial ventral pallidum (mVP), lateral hypothalamic area (LHA), and paraventricular thalamic nucleus (PVT). The topographic organization of the circuit is unknown. We first used anterograde (Phaseolus vulgaris leucoagglutinin, PHAL) and retrograde (cholera-toxin B, CTB) tracers to map this organization. We then used immunoreactivity for Fos phosphorylated at serine 32 (pSer32-Fos-ir) as a proxy for the activation marker Fos (thus, we refer to pSer32-Fos hereafter as 'Fos') to determine whether the time-dependent increase (incubation) of oxycodone seeking after electric barrier-induced abstinence is associated with dmACB activation. In Experiment 1, we injected rats with PHAL into the anterior PVT (aPVT) and CTB into either the mVP or the anterior LHA (LHAa) to determine the distribution of their connections within the dmACB. We also injected CTB into anterior and posterior dmACB to identify afferent inputs. In Experiment 2, we trained rats to self-administer oxycodone for two weeks and counted Fos-labeled cells in anterior and posterior dmACB, the surrounding ACB, and dorsal striatum regions after drug-seeking tests on either abstinence day 1 or day 15 following electric barrier-induced abstinence. PHAL-labeled aPVT axons and CTB-labeled mVP and LHA neurons were confined to dmACB, forming a longitudinal column along the anterior-posterior axis of ACB. Inputs to anterior and posterior dmACB came from different cortical and subcortical regions. dmACB Fos+ cell counts were higher after oxycodone-seeking tests on day 1 than on day 15 and were negatively correlated with oxycodone seeking. These results characterize a connection-defined dmACB circuit and show that incubation of opioid-seeking is unexpectedly associated with reduced dmACB activation.
author_corresponding_institution: The University of Texas at El Paso

title: Variability and Landmark Quality in Anatomical Co-Registration in Neuronavigation for Brain Stimulation
abstract: Accurate neuronavigation depends not only on the technical performance of the tracking system but also on the reproducibility with which anatomical landmarks are physically localized. We quantified operator- and landmark-specific variability in repeated facial and cranial landmark localization in 19,630 measurements from 16 participants, four operators, and 13 landmarks under marked and unmarked conditions. Within-operator precision, inter-operator agreement, and marked-unmarked displacement were analyzed separately. Median within-operator precision was 1.60 mm and median inter-operator distance was 2.91 mm, with substantial differences across both operators and landmarks. The left medial canthus showed the greatest within-operator precision (1.43 mm), whereas the pronasale showed the closest inter-operator agreement (2.05 mm). Marking the positions before the procedure did not significantly improve within-operator precision overall but reduced inter-operator distances by 29.2%, which indicates convergence on a shared spatial reference rather than improved intrinsic repeatability. Between-operator differences also contained systematic directional components; signed offsets approached 1.5 mm. Exploratory analyses did not suggest general left--right difference in precision, although the approach side produced systematic spatial shifts for midline landmarks despite comparable repeatability. These findings demonstrate that anatomical landmark localization is both operator- and landmark-specific. Standardized landmark definitions, operator calibration, consistent pointer approach, and the use of multiple well-defined registration features should therefore be considered integral components of neuronavigation quality control.

abstract: Whether human-associated environments drive adaptive genome evolution in gut commensal bacteria remains largely unknown. Here, we investigate how genomic adaptation in gut bacteria differs between industrialized and non-industrialized human populations. We generated a collection of isolate genomes spanning diverse host geographies, lifestyles, species, and strains. We first found that, compared with metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs), paired isolate genomes recover more functional elements and signals of horizontal gene transfer (HGT). Leveraging isolate genomes from multiple species, we find that strains from industrialized hosts experience an expansion of proteome size and harbor greater pangenome fluidity, driven by recent HGT events. Gene- and variant-level analyses reveal convergent patterns of lifestyle-specific adaptation in functions that are critical for ecological adaptation, such as the stress response, cell-envelope remodeling, and central metabolism. Our results demonstrate that industrialization drives convergent genome evolution in gut bacteria, providing a framework for understanding the mechanisms of microbial adaptation to rapidly changing human environments.

abstract: When subject to damage or stress, cells develop responses in order to maintain tissue homeostasis. Two such responses are ferroptosis and cellular senescence, but how cells decide between these outcomes remains unclear. Here, we show that senescent cells increase import and membrane levels of multiple polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs), but a specific intermediate PUFA, dihomo-gamma-linolenic acid (DGLA, 20:3ω-6), is reduced. Exogenous repletion of DGLA instead results in cell death by ferroptosis. Senescent cells manifest additional features associated with ferroptosis, including labile iron and expression of lipoxygenases as well as low-level membrane peroxidation. Oral DGLA supplementation lowers markers of senescence in aged mice and improves age-related functional outcomes. Finally, obese humans with lowered DGLA desaturation rates have lower markers of adipose tissue senescence. Together, our data implicate shifts in PUFA metabolism as a driver of decisions between senescence and ferroptosis.

abstract: Understanding how industrialization reshapes the human metaorganism requires integrating microbiome ecology with host physiology across globally diverse populations. Here, we generate multivariate data from the Global Microbiome Conservancy cohort, including gut microbiome, immunoglobulin A (IgA) sequencing, host genotyping, diet, lifestyle, and fecal biomarker profiles, to investigate host-microbiome interactions across gradients of industrialization and geography. We show that industrialization is associated with homogenized microbial compositions, reduced microbial diversity, and lower community stability, independent of host confounders. We further show that industrialization is linked to elevated markers of gut stress, increased IgA secretion, and altered patterns of IgA-bacteria interactions. Finally, we show that microbiome-based disease predictors trained on industrialized populations are uninformative in less industrialized cohorts, highlighting limited cross-population transferability. Together, our results reveal coordinated restructuring of the microbial ecosystem and host physiology and emphasize the need for inclusive, globally representative data to improve translational microbiome applications across diverse human populations.

abstract: The Altiplano Cundiboyacense in the eastern Colombian Andes preserves one of the Americas' most continuous archaeological sequences, recording cultural and demographic change. We generated genome-wide data from 212 individuals spanning over 7,000 years, including early-middle and middle Holocene hunter-gatherers, initial late Holocene groups with mixed economies and the earliest isotopic evidence of maize consumption, and increasingly sedentary Herrera and Muisca populations. Individuals predating the Herrera Period form a lineage that persisted for five millennia, structured by drift in small groups without external gene flow. Two individuals dating ∼2,800 years before present (BP) retain autochthonous ancestry while showing isotopic signatures consistent with maize consumption, decoupling subsistence change from population replacement. The emergence of Herrera culture ∼2,200 BP coincided with a sharp genetic break by ∼2,000 BP, which reflects migration by people descended from admixture ∼4,000 BP between groups with Chibchan- and Amazonian-Andean-related ancestries. Herrera and Muisca Period individuals show north-south genetic substructure paralleling archaeological differentiation.

abstract: Acute liver injury caused by drug toxicity or immune activation remains a major clinical challenge with limited mechanistic understanding and few effective therapies. Here, we identify a previously unrecognized form of regulated cell death driven by palmitoylation of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-resident enzyme trans-2,3-enoyl-coenzyme A (CoA) reductase (TECR). We show that multi-site palmitoylation of TECR, redundantly catalyzed by the palmitoyl acyltransferases ZDHHC5 and ZDHHC2 and dynamically reversed by the depalmitoylase ABHD10, activates PERK-dependent ER stress signaling to trigger cell death. This cell death pathway is a TECR-dependent, palmitoylation-induced, ER stress-mediated necrotic cell death program (TPNCD). TPNCD contributes to liver injury in mouse models of acetaminophen- and concanavalin A-induced hepatotoxicity and is attenuated by hepatocyte-specific TECR ablation or by pharmacological inhibition of palmitoylation or ER stress signaling. Together, these findings establish TPNCD as a distinct, necrotic cell death pathway underlying acute liver injury and highlight new therapeutic entry points for hepatoprotection.

abstract: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) remains highly lethal, with treatment failure and relapse driven by dynamic cellular states and evolving interactions within the leukemic ecosystem. In this study, we built a comprehensive atlas of leukemia and its microenvironment (CALM) by integrating single-cell profiling from 73 AML samples and 9 healthy donors, bulk RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) from 87 newly diagnosed patients, and 4 paired bone marrow and peripheral blood single-cell data. All datasets were linked to clinical, cytogenetic, molecular, and treatment-response annotations. Immune analysis revealed diverse T cell distribution across disease status, where patients with persistent disease exhibited greater clonal expansion. Machine learning modeling on conventional T cells identified a T-cell signature pertinent to AML and outcomes, which were validated in two cohorts. CALM is a publicly accessible and interactive portal (calm.mdanderson.org) for exploring cellular compartments, cell-cell interactions, and longitudinal transcriptional and clonal dynamics to enable hypothesis generation, biomarker discovery, and target validation.

abstract: Obesity is a well-established risk factor for increased incidence and mortality in multiple cancers, including breast cancer. However, the key molecular mechanisms linking obesity to breast cancer progression remain incompletely understood. In this study, using several high-fat diet-induced obesity models, we demonstrate that obesity promotes breast cancer lung metastasis through elevated levels of adipocyte-derived circulating FABP4. Mechanistically, circulating FABP4 directly binds to a subset of breast cancer cells via the membrane lipid PIP2. This FABP4/PIP2 interaction activates PKC signaling and enhances mitochondrial ROS production, driving cancer cell migration. Genetic deletion of FABP4, either globally or specifically in adipocytes, markedly reduces obesity-associated metastasis. Moreover, therapeutic targeting of circulating FABP4 using a distinctive neutralizing monoclonal antibody significantly suppresses breast cancer metastasis in multiple preclinical models. Together, these findings identify the FABP4/PIP2 axis as a key mechanism underlying obesity-driven breast cancer and highlight it as a promising therapeutic target for treating metastatic breast cancer.

abstract: The protective adaptation of innate immune defenses against respiratory pathogens has been linked to previous exposure to immune stimuli; however, the underlying mechanisms of these adaptations are not yet fully understood. Here, we show that pre-exposure to a low dose of non-specific immune stimuli or infection protects against subsequent lethal methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) challenge. This enhanced protection concurs with increased alveolar macrophages (AMs) resulting from a self-renewal process in the lungs. Importantly, these AMs are programmed to acquire neutrophil-released antimicrobial enzymes from the extracellular space to clear MRSA, prevent tissue damage, and rapidly restore lung homeostasis. AM function depends on differential gene expression, including expression of the efferocytosis receptor Mer proto-oncogene tyrosine kinase (MerTK) and the anti-apoptotic regulator Bcl-xL. Thus, our data highlight that AMs acquire neutrophil enzymes as an integral component of innate immune adaptation.

abstract: During organ development cells undergo significant morphological and positional changes. Yet by the end of organogenesis, internal organ structure is typically reliably defined. It remains an open question how the internal structure of an organ emerges, particularly in the presence of dynamic boundary constraints. Here, we utilize live imaging and morphological measures of the developing zebrafish to unravel how early muscle organization materializes. We observed that myocytes undergo an ordered chiral twist according to their position within the myotome. Cell movement undergoes a rapid speed reduction once the cells span the myotome segment. Biophysical perturbation reveals cells are mechanically plastic and can adapt to changes in boundaries and environment. Combining these results, we propose that the early myotome may be undergoing a structural transition from a fluid-like to a solid-like state, which resembles a frozen system. Cell shape plasticity combined with structural changes in the material behavior could be a general mechanism for organ morphogenesis in dense tissues.

abstract: It is poorly understood when owls (Strigiformes) became nocturnal, which impedes considerations of the evolutionary reasons behind this distinctive behavior. 1 , 2 Here, we report an extraordinary owl skeleton from the middle Eocene of Germany, which preserves remains of an iridescent cockroach as stomach contents-the first identifiable insect remains ever found as the last meal of a fossil bird. Because iridescence is correlated with diurnal habits in cockroaches, 3 the fossil provides the strongest evidence to date for diurnality in archaic Strigiformes. Further support for a diurnal ecology comes from the absence of barred flight feathers as well as the lack of frayed leading edges of the primaries; the presence of these features is associated with nocturnality in extant owls. 4 , 5 The humerus is much stouter than in extant owls, indicating that the wings were less adapted to silent flight. Conversely, a slenderer humerus suggests that late Eocene owls had shifted toward a nocturnal ecology. This timeframe rules out previously suggested factors for nocturnality in owls 2 and constrains the origin of an ecological hallmark of these birds.

abstract: Forgetting is an active and essential process for adapting to constantly changing environments, yet the molecular and circuit mechanisms underlying selective forgetting remain poorly understood. Our previous studies in the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans suggested that non-cell-autonomous neurosecretory signals accelerate forgetting of olfactory memory for diacetyl, an attractive odorant, by erasing its memory trace, which can be detected as changes in odor-evoked Ca 2+ responses in sensory neurons. However, the identity of the forgetting signal, the circuit through which it acts to erase the sensory memory trace, and the time window in which forgetting occurs have remained elusive. Here, we identify a neuropeptidergic-glutamatergic circuit in C. elegans that drives the selective forgetting of olfactory memory. Our genetic and imaging analyses revealed that the gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH)-related neuropeptide NLP-47, secreted from AWC neurons, acts on its receptor GNRR-1 in AIZ interneurons. Glutamatergic neurotransmission from AIZ interneurons then erases the sensory memory trace in AWA neurons via GLR-4, an AMPA-type receptor expressed in AWA. Optogenetic silencing of AWC and AIZ showed that this circuit acts during the recovery phase following conditioning, defining a critical temporal window for active forgetting. This neuropeptidergic-glutamatergic pathway selectively promotes forgetting of a specific odorant memory without affecting another formed simultaneously. Together, our findings demonstrate that neuropeptidergic signaling promotes selective forgetting via a glutamatergic circuit, highlighting that active forgetting is regulated within a critical temporal window and with remarkable specificity.

abstract: Natural variation at the earliness locus, or potato CDF1, enabled cultivated potato to overcome strict photoperiodic control of wild andigena landraces and tuberize under long days. Yet long-day conditions (LDs) are often associated with warm temperatures, which strongly suppress tuberization at night. With the rising ambient temperatures due to global warming, uncovering genetic factors that enable tuber formation under elevated temperatures has become a priority for breeding new cultivars with improved heat tolerance. Here we report that heat-resilient tuberization in potato can be unlocked by inactivating the photoreceptor phytochrome F (phyF) and optimized by exploiting its haploinsufficiency. Knockdown of phyF activates the SELF-PRUNING 6A (SP6A) tuberization-inducing signal and facilitates tuber formation under heat-stress conditions. Unexpectedly, loss of function of both SP6A and phyF still leads to early tuberization and heat escape, although it reduces the resilience of phyF mutants. Intriguingly, we show that haplotype-specific phyF editing in the 5' UTR or exonic regions leads to haploinsufficiency phenotypes enabling tuberization under heat-stress conditions, without other phytochrome-related penalties. Our results suggest that derepressing SP6A by a reduction of phyF dosage provides a key to unlock heat-resilient tuberization and highlight haploinsufficiency as a strategy for generating dominant alleles to enable rapid improvement of crops.

title: Breathing may be primarily driven by the unceasing rotation of residual gravitational ischemia in the brain-'skull-trapped' regions of reduced oxygen tension.
abstract: The 'top half' of the brain sits on the 'bottom half' of the brain as a weight burden. Within the somewhat spherically shaped cranial vault, gravitational compression of the 'bottom half' of the brain against the inside of the skull, in theory, may generate ischemia, with underlying brain regions experiencing decreased blood flow and decreased oxygen tension. Some questions remain as to whether gravity is involved in the causation of breathing in humans. Is 'gravitational ischemia in the brain' a principle driver of breathing, underlying even the well-studied brainstem neuro-synchronization and automaticity mechanisms of breathing? Relevant reports from the general scientific literature were identified. A focused topical analysis of their intertwined concepts, together with their cumulative aggregate data, was done to explore the current status of this topic, as well as some possible directions for future research. One potentially testable hypothesis suggests that gravity may be a principle underlying driver for breathing, in humans, possibly working through glial cells (astrocytes), scattered throughout the brain, continuously sensing gravitationally-induced regional hypoxia in different regions of the brain, at different times, generated during different head positions, never completely resolved, and leading to a continuous repetitive triggering of the already well-established breathing automaticity mechanisms. Its position within the existing breathing neuro-circuit cascade would be at the very beginning. A second hypothesis explores the inverse of 'gravitational ischemia' in the brain, occurring in astronauts during long-duration spaceflight, and called 'gravity-opposition physiology'. This second hypothesis may potentially provide a framework for understanding Spaceflight Associated Neuro-Ocular Syndrome.

title: Neural correlates of perceptual biases in duration perception.

author_details.name: Shirzhiyan Z
author_details.affiliation: Computational Neuroscience, Institute of Medical Technology, Brandenburg University of Technology Cottbus-Senftenberg, Cottbus, Brandenburg, Germany.

abstract: How we perceive a current event depends not only on its immediate context, but also on how our internal expectations are shaped by prior experience. In time perception, these expectations manifest as systematic biases, namely sequential dependence, where the current percept is influenced by the previous stimulus, and central tendency, the overestimation of short durations and underestimation of long ones. Both perceptual biases, corresponding to individual beliefs about stimulus generation, can vary substantially between participants. However, the neural responses related to inter-individual differences in these biases remain poorly understood. Here, we investigate this question in a duration reproduction task. Our EEG results show that in the frontocentral region, the Contingent Negative Variation (CNV) while experiencing the current stimulus depends on the previous stimulus regardless of sequential dependence. In contrast, in the right parietal region, the slow potential was not influenced by previous duration but associated with inter-individual differences in sequential dependence. Stimulus-offset evoked P2 amplitude was associated with both central tendency and sequential dependence and P2 amplitude varied with previous stimulus duration depending on individual sequential dependence. A Bayesian model of time perception reproduced the observed neural dynamics of the frontocentral CNV and its dependence on previous stimulus duration, suggesting that individual internal time estimates and expectations of stimulus offset are reflected in EEG responses. Our results demonstrate that both forms of perceptual bias are reflected in neural activity while experiencing the ongoing stimulus, suggesting that neural processes related to perceptual biases directly affect the measurement of time.

abstract: Seizures in mesial temporal lobe epilepsy (MTLE) can spread to the insular cortex (IC) due to its connections with hippocampal and para-hippocampal areas. The contribution of specific cell types in the IC to ictogenesis remains however unclear. Therefore, we analyzed in the pilocarpine model of MTLE the effects of optogenetic activation of IC parvalbumin (PV)-positive interneurons on CA3 field activity. Light pulses were delivered at 0.5 Hz (300 s ON, 600 s OFF) in IC, between day 4 and 14 after status epilepticus in PV-ChR2 mice. During interictal periods, this procedure evoked CA3 field responses characterized by 5 Hz oscillations, which likely mirrored heightened inhibitory activity as suggested by a shift toward higher theta/beta ratio and a more negative spectral exponent. Analysis of ictal activity revealed that seizures occurred at higher rates during days of stimulation (day 4-14) compared to days with no stimulation (day 15-24) (p < 0.05). During the 300 s optogenetic stimulation cycle, seizures occurred at high rates between 301 and 502 s after the end of stimulation (p < 0.05). Our findings suggest that during the interictal phase, the synchronized activation of PV-positive interneurons in the IC imposes a GABAergic drive that, through post-inhibitory rebound mechanisms, entrains the CA3 network into a 5 Hz resonant oscillation. During states of pathological hyperexcitability, this synchronized rebound activity reaches a threshold that converts a rhythmic oscillation into a seizure. Stimulation of the IC could bias the hippocampal network toward 5 Hz oscillatory states and promote ictogenesis via inhibitory-rebound synchronization.

abstract: The ability of the brain to undergo plastic changes throughout the lifespan of an organism is essential to optimize its interactions with its environment. Adaptation to sensory loss is observed as cross-modal recruitment of the cortical areas deprived of their own sensory inputs by the spared senses and as compensatory plasticity of the spared cortical areas. The former is thought to increase the cortical resource for processing information related to the spared modalities and the latter is thought to refine the spared senses. In animal models, synaptic and circuit-level plasticity have been observed in both the deprived primary sensory cortex and in the spared primary sensory cortices. In this study, we examined how the primary visual cortex (V1) adapts to cross-modal auditory deprivation initiated in adult mice of both sexes. To do this, we recorded the stimulus-evoked neural activity in V1 layer 2/3 (L2/3) using 2-photon calcium imaging and presented visual stimuli restricted to either the central or the peripheral visual field. We found that adult-onset deafening intensified the attenuation of stimulus-evoked responses to a range of stimuli, largely in the medial V1 representing the peripheral monocular visual field, without affecting the population decoding capability. Furthermore, adult-onset deaf mice exhibited selective behavioral improvement on peripheral visual acuity for detecting static gratings, without changes in contrast sensitivity for detecting moving gratings. Our findings suggest enhancement of neural attenuation may support compensatory plasticity in adult V1, which may benefit the stimulus encoding efficiency to improve detection of fine peripheral visual features. Significance Statement Losing a sensory modality leads to widespread brain adaptation to enhance the remaining senses. In addition to cross-modal recruitment, which repurposes the deprived brain areas to process the spared senses, there is functional refinement of the spared sensory areas referred to as compensatory plasticity. While plasticity is prominent for early-onset sensory loss, functional compensation is also observed after adult-onset sensory loss. Here, we report that adult-onset deafness in mice accentuates attenuation of visual cortical responses to visual stimuli, especially in the peripheral visual field, with indications of more efficient coding. Additionally, deafened adult mice show rather selective improvement on peripheral visual acuity. Our study suggests a mechanism of compensatory plasticity in the adult visual cortex, which may benefit visual function.

abstract: Hypothalamic circuits play a central role in coordinating feeding and energy balance, yet how these circuits adapt to dietary excess to regulate body weight remains poorly understood. Lateral hypothalamic area glutamatergic (LHA Vglut2 ) neurons critically mediate food intake and body weight, but how they adapt their function to acute overfeeding and whether such adaptation is sexually dimorphic are unknown. Here, we examined the impact of high-fat diet (HFD) on LHA Vglut2 neurons in mice. Whole-cell recordings revealed baseline sex differences in neuronal properties: female LHA Vglut2 neurons exhibited higher basal excitability and differential synaptic input compared to males. HFD feeding produced distinct forms of neuronal plasticity between sexes within 1 day. In males, HFD increased intrinsic excitability while excitatory synaptic input was decreased. In contrast, excitability of female LHA Vglut2 neurons remained unchanged, but inhibitory synaptic strength was selectively reduced. To test the causal relationship between enhanced LHA Vglut2 neuron excitability and weight gain during overfeeding, we expressed the depolarizing sodium channel NaChBac to chronically increase LHA Vglut2 neuron excitability. Chronic elevation of LHA Vglut2 neuron excitability suppressed body weight gain during acute HFD exposure in males, whereas females displayed significant weight loss during HFD exposure. Together, these results suggest that female mice may be protected from diet-induced obesity via sexually dimorphic LHA Vglut2 neurons. In males, overfeeding rapidly induces compensatory changes in LHA Vglut2 neuron excitability that may act to limit body weight gain. Further enhancement of LHA Vglut2 neuron excitability can suppress weight gain in an obesogenic environment for both males and females. Significance Statement Chronic overeating alters hypothalamic circuits that regulate feeding, but the time course of these adaptations and whether they differ between sexes is poorly understood. Here we show that overeating engages lateral hypothalamic glutamatergic neurons, which negatively regulate food intake and body weight, through sexually dimorphic mechanisms. In males but not females, overfeeding rapidly enhances excitability of lateral hypothalamic glutamatergic neurons. These sex-specific adaptations lead to distinct behavioral outcomes following chronic neuronal activation. Our findings reveal that hypothalamic circuits employ fundamentally different strategies across sexes to respond to dietary excess, providing insight into sex-dependent vulnerability to metabolic disorders.

abstract: There is an urgent global need for affordable, large-scale health screening to enhance preventive care in the ageing population. Using low-cost, non-invasive retinal photographs and leveraging large foundation models, we developed a deep learning-based biomarker, Retinal Mortality Equivalent (RetiME), that directly mapped retinal features to individual mortality risk. Trained on a European cohort and externally validated across three independent external cohorts spanning Southeast Asia, Eurasia and North America, RetiME showed robust associations with all-cause and cause-specific mortality and predicted the incidence of a wide range of systemic and ocular diseases. Crucially, beyond static risk estimation, RetiME re-timed mortality risk by reconstructing personalized lifespan trajectories that were associated with observed mortality outcomes (for example, age of death). Clustering of these trajectories revealed distinct mortality patterns, spanning cancer-predominant, cardiometabolic and neurodegenerative risks, reflecting diverse ageing pathways captured by RetiME. Interpretability analyses showed that RetiME captures diverse biological and retinal features underlying mortality risk. Genome-wide analyses further identified genetic loci associated with RetiME. Collectively, these findings support further evaluation of retinal imaging and trajectory modelling as one component of a comprehensive assessment of mortality risk.

abstract: Closely related prophages have been found in phylogenetically distant bacteria in the human gut, despite limited evidence of productive phage infections across broad host ranges. It remains enigmatic how the wide distribution of prophages could emerge. Here, we identify a previously unrecognized association between a distinct group of conjugative megaplasmids and prophage genomes. We describe two related but diverged groups of conjugative megaplasmids (>300 kilobases) in the human gut microbiome, which we named Hodors. Hodors encode conserved replication, partitioning, and type IV secretion systems, along with a complex surface-associated gene module. A subset of Hodors harbors complete, intact prophage genomes, and closely related prophages (≥95% nucleotide identity) were detected across phylogenetically distant lineages within the bacterial phylum Bacillota, including both Bacilli and Clostridia. We detected signatures consistent with extracellular particle formation and transcriptional activity of Hodor-associated prophages. Our findings suggest that conjugative megaplasmids could contribute to the movement of related prophage genomes between distantly related bacteria, potentially explaining the widespread occurrence of closely related prophages in phylogenetically distant gut bacteria and the apparent uncoupling between lysogenic and infective host ranges.

abstract: The antigenic diversity of Klebsiella pneumoniae surface polysaccharides, O- and K-antigen, represents a significant challenge for developing broadly-acting vaccines. Here we report the development of Kp-OMV4, a multivalent outer membrane vesicle (OMV) vaccine incorporating the four predominant K. pneumoniae O-antigen serotypes responsible for most invasive disease worldwide. Kp-OMV4 elicits robust humoral and cellular immune responses, generating high-titer antibodies against both surface polysaccharides and conserved outer membrane proteins. Vaccine-induced antibodies display complement-mediated bactericidal activity against hypervirulent and multidrug-resistant clinical strains. In a murine sepsis model, immunization confers protection against lethal challenge and significantly reduces post-infection bacterial burden. Importantly, immune sera broadly recognize diverse clinical isolates, including strains expressing O- and K-antigen serotypes not included in the vaccine, supporting potential for broad strain coverage. This study indicates that the multicomponent nature of OMVs can be leveraged to overcome bacterial antigenic diversity and enable the development of vaccines with broad strain coverage.

abstract: Bacteriophage Exclusion (BREX) systems protect bacterial genomes via sequence-specific DNA methylation while blocking phage replication through a poorly understood “restriction-without-cleavage” mechanism. Here, we present cryo-EM structures and functional characterization of the core BREX machinery from Escherichia coli . We determined the structures of the ATPase BrxC in its monomeric state and two ATPγS-bound dimeric conformations, showing that ATP binding, not hydrolysis, triggers dimerization. The conserved Arg328 couples dimer formation to ATP hydrolysis and is required for both phage restriction and host methylation; the R328A mutant supports assembly but abolishes defense. We further resolved the BrxBCZ ternary complex, revealing BrxB as a central scaffold bridging the BrxC dimer and BrxZ without direct BrxC–BrxZ contact. Biochemical assays show that BrxZ is a dual-function enzyme with alkaline phosphatase and metal-dependent nuclease activities. Thus, ATP drives BrxC assembly and inhibits BrxZ activities. Disruption of the BrxB–BrxC interface or the BrxC ATPase cycle selectively eliminates restriction while preserving methylation, establishing BrxBCZ as a restriction-specific structural core. Collectively, these findings delineate the structural basis for ATP-dependent coordination of BREX, revealing how energy metabolism is integrated into bacterial innate immunity.

abstract: Microbiomes are integral to the function and resilience of cnidarian holobionts, yet the spatial and functional integration of microbial communities within host tissues remains poorly understood. Here, we show that symbiosis with photosynthetic dinoflagellates induces adaptive, tissue-specific restructuring of the microbiome in the cnidarian model Aiptasia, fundamentally enhancing holobiont nitrogen assimilation and metabolic flexibility. Using laser microdissection, tissue-resolved metatranscriptomics, gnotobiotic hosts, and stable isotope tracing, we reveal that symbiosis profoundly restructures microbial communities across the epidermis and gastrodermis, enriching for taxa and pathways that support nitrogen assimilation in photosynthetically active tissues. Expression of microbial nitrite reductase is strongly upregulated in the symbiotic gastrodermis, and 15 N-tracer experiments demonstrate that bacterial assimilation of nitrite synergizes with algal symbionts to fuel the biosynthesis of essential amino acids. These findings show that symbiosis drives spatially compartmentalized microbiome adaptation within animal tissues, aligning microbial metabolism with host-algal nutrient exchanges to enhance holobiont functioning.

abstract: Powdery mildew is a devastating fungal disease of wheat. Aegilops caudata , a wild relative of common wheat, is highly resistant to powdery mildew. However, the presence of chromosomal structural variations and the absence of a reference genome for Ae. caudata have significantly hindered the cloning and breeding application of resistance genes from this species. Here, we report the cloning of powdery mildew resistance gene Pm7C from Ae. caudata by integrating map-based cloning, collinearity and Pm7C -direct donor transcriptome analysis. Pm7C encodes a nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat (NLR) protein containing two distinct LRR domains. The resistance function of Pm7C is validated by mutagenesis, gene silencing and transgenic assay. The coiled coil (CC) domain of Pm7C induces cell death and self-associates. Additionally, we develop a set of Pm7C introgression lines and a Pm7C- specific diagnostic molecular marker. Cloning of Pm7C will shed light on NLR protein-mediated disease resistance and accelerate its deployment in wheat breeding.

abstract: We use our eyes to evaluate objects around us. Models of economic choice emphasise the impact of sequential fixation on valuation and choice, with prefrontal and anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) encoding values of fixated items. Yet whether these regions also evaluate non-fixated peripheral information to guide choice remains unknown. Here we show that in a decision-making task involving four simultaneously presented cues, rhesus macaques use peripheral information to guide information sampling and choice, and that ACC neurons encode this peripheral information. This served two distinct purposes: subjects were more likely to fixate valuable peripheral cues, and more likely to choose valuable options whose cues were never even fixated. ACC, orbitofrontal cortex, dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, and ventromedial prefrontal cortex neurons all encoded cue value as they were fixated. ACC was unique, however, in also conducting parallel processing of peripheral cues, including cues never fixated, to guide information sampling and choice.
