title: El Agente Fármaco: A Scalable AI Scientist for Drug Discovery
abstract: Computational drug discovery offers a growing range of tools for proposing and evaluating molecules, but combining them and deciding what to do next still requires substantial expert effort. Here, we introduce El Agente Fármaco, an AI scientist that uses modern large language model (LLM) technology to turn discovery goals expressed in everyday language into complex, scalable computational screening workflows. The agentic harness selects scientific tools, reviews their results, and adjusts subsequent steps to the target and the user's objectives. Our approach centers on a shared scientific memory: Fármaco Atlas, which stores molecules, structures, and results together with their provenance -- a record of how they were obtained. The agent uses targeted database queries to retrieve the evidence needed for each decision. A single request can launch calculations for an entire collection of molecules, without requiring a separate LLM decision for every compound. This design limits the information the model must process as screening collections grow, while keeping the underlying results available for inspection and further analysis. The integrated tools support molecule generation, prediction of binding and molecular properties, and searches for compounds available for purchase. In a retrospective comparison with an expert-led campaign, the agent proposed chemically distinct candidates with competitive docking scores and higher calculated drug-likeness under explicitly imposed selection criteria. In a 22-task benchmark against plain tool calls and Codex, the agent achieved the highest observed mean model-judged score, with lower median cumulative token use and peak context. Fármaco provides a foundation for flexible, scalable drug discovery workflows that connect scientific reasoning with an enduring, traceable record of computational work.
comment: 63 pages, 13 figures, including Supporting Information

title: Evolved Spiking Neural Networks for EEG Seizure Detection: Calcium Dynamics and Delay Mechanics
abstract: Neuroevolution can discover compact network designs that are hard to specify by hand. The EONS framework evolves the topology, weights, thresholds and delays of neuromorphic spiking networks without gradients. We tested whether giving integrate-and-fire (IF) neurons an activity-dependent calcium current (Ca-IF neurons) improves evolved networks for EEG seizure detection, with calcium parameters fixed, shared across a network, or evolved for each neuron. On 10 held-out CHB-MIT patients never seen in training, per-neuron calcium raised the record-level Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) from 0.592 to 0.726 over 20 independent runs (p = 0.008) and lowered the false-alarm rate from 0.17 to 0.10. Fixed or per-network calcium gave no significant benefit. IF networks with evolved synaptic delays of 1-3 ticks gave a similar gain (p = 0.005), whereas axonal delays did not. On Siena, with unchanged settings, per-neuron calcium gained +0.096 MCC over IF in one patient-disjoint split (p = 0.011) and +0.059 in the other (p = 0.052). These results suggest that calcium and delays may make the evolutionary search more effective, and motivate testing on more data and in neuromorphic hardware.
comment: 16 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables, plus three supplementary tables and one supplementary figure

title: Fly Whiskers Meet LiDAR: Robust Navigation under Sensor Failure
abstract: We extend FLYNN, a leaky integrator recurrent network wired on the Drosophila melanogaster connectome, with a 32-ray 2D LiDAR interface that requires no learned fusion layer beyond a scalar input gain. A 270 degree frontal scan at 8 m range is injected as inverted proximity into the 37 BM Vib head-bristle neurons. Across 24 paired comparisons in a four- state vision matrix with LiDAR on or off, FLYNN-LiDAR has 17 significant wins, 5 nonsignificant comparisons, and 2 significant losses against three LiDAR-capable baselines. Both losses are to MobileNet with the left eye off. With full vision, FLYNN- LiDAR reaches 96.6% success. Under total vision loss, the scan raises success from 45.2% to 64.6%; the baselines reach 44.6% to 56.6% with the scan on. Under out of distribution textures, it is the only LiDAR-capable model whose success improves with the scan (44.2% to 58.4%); both CNNs score 0%, and SmallWorld declines from 26.8% to 7.4%. Under periodic vision dropout, FLYNN-LiDAR achieves 93.6% and 89.6% success at 25% and 50% duty with fewer collisions. Profiling the evaluated forward paths gives 3.93M multiply accumulate operations per step; EfficientNet and MobileNet require 4.60x and 2.94x as many. Final- state analysis shows near-linear sensory superposition (cosine 0.9955).

title: From FAIR to AI-FAIR Metadata-First Infrastructure for AI-Enabled Science
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) technologies and their capabilities have advanced rapidly over the past few years, leading to widespread interest and adoption in the biological and ecological sciences. However, the data infrastructure and computational resources that provide the foundation for AI workflows in ecology and biodiversity science remain fragmented. Moreover, the flow of value remains largely unidirectional: data move from collectors, through repositories and aggregators into models, and finally to research products or management actions. The derived value, such as corrected taxonomies, annotations, quality flags, and insights, rarely returns to source communities. We propose an extension of the original FAIR principles to address the needs of AI-ready infrastructure: the AI-FAIR metadata criteria, which place AI-enabled science in the context of a bidirectional Question-Data-Model triangle. This framework is designed to facilitate large-scale content-based analysis across diverse collections and ensure that the scientists generating the data benefit from the AI-enabled advances built on their data. Alongside these criteria, we introduce an agentic evaluation workflow that both rates existing datasets on the AI-FAIR and traditional FAIR criteria and provides actionable feedback where critical metadata is missing or incomplete. This modular dataset evaluation tool, paired with a domain-appropriate checklist, translates these principles into a reusable assessment of machine-learning readiness, AI-readiness for specified tasks, traceability, and ethical and CARE-aligned stewardship. Through this approach we aim to create a community-informed system to close the model data loop, so that AI also enriches data to further enable scientific discovery.
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, Code available at: https://github.com/FAIR4AI-Bio/evaluator

title: HistoTx: Early fusion of H&E images and spatial transcriptomics at varying spatial transcriptomics resolution with self-supervised learning
abstract: Spatial transcriptomics maps gene expression across tissue sections and, when integrated with whole slide images, jointly captures both morphological architecture and molecular activity to provide a rich, multimodal view of tissue biology. ML approaches combining spatial transcriptomics and WSIs typically learn a mapping from morphological features to molecular profiles via contrastive alignment or supervised fine-tuning of pathology foundation models. In both cases, transcriptomics serves as a training signal rather than a true input modality, leaving inference fundamentally image-driven. We propose an early-fusion vision transformer architecture in which transcript tokens are constructed at arbitrary spatial resolution, merged with image patch tokens, and jointly processed through a shared transformer stack for deep cross-modal interaction. Starting from a pretrained vision-only pathology foundation model, we train HistoTx by continuing self-supervised pretraining on paired image and spatial transcriptomics data and demonstrate that: 1) at inference with image only, performance remains on par with the baseline on most tasks while improving on tasks that inherently benefit from molecular knowledge, such as gene expression prediction; 2) when both modalities are available at inference, jointly providing image and transcript inputs outperforms either modality alone.
comment: Presented at 3rd Workshop on Multi-modal Foundation Models and Large Language Models for Life Sciences (ICML 2026)

title: Intrinsic network dynamics catalyze switching in functional connectivity states of the brain
abstract: Dynamic functional connectivity (dFC) reflects ongoing reconfiguration of large-scale brain networks, but the temporal organization and network processes underlying spontaneous state transitions remain poorly understood. We developed functional connectivity state switching (FCSS), a phase-coherence-based framework that tracks multiscale changes in dominant whole-brain connectivity configurations. In Human Connectome Project fMRI, FCSS was strongly evoked by cognitive state and condition switches, and distinct transition dynamics differentially predicted working-memory performance. During rest, spontaneous FCSS was characterized by progressive changes in network segregation, integration, and cross-network communication as connectivity approached a switching event. Critically, event-related analysis time-locked to spontaneous FCSS revealed opposing pre-switch dynamics: salience-network contribution increased while default-mode-network contribution decreased, suggesting coordinated engagement and disengagement of these networks before switching. This reciprocal reweighting may provide a network-level mechanism for spontaneous FC reconfiguration. Together, these findings identify both global reorganization and network-specific processes underlying spontaneous and task-evoked brain-state transitions in the human brain.
comment: 15 pages, 5 figures

title: One Mistake, Three Layers: Persistence Rules Under Depth Correlation
abstract: Probing frozen representations layer by layer is now standard practice, but reporting when a signal first becomes decodable requires a rule for reading a depth curve, and the obvious rule is wrong. On synthetic curves with known ground truth, requiring a probe score to exceed a null-calibrated threshold for three consecutive stages reports an onset nineteen stages early under transformer-like depth correlation, with every resample returning an onset. The failure follows from correlation between neighboring layers, a hazard known in neuroimaging but not, to our knowledge, checked for depth curves. We give an estimator whose error rate is calibrated rather than assumed. Null trajectories are built by permuting labels within each evaluation unit and holding each permutation fixed across depth, preserving the correlation structure the rule must survive; thresholds are per-layer order statistics; and the persistence requirement is calibrated rather than chosen. Applied to pocket information in a frozen co-folding trunk, stratifying 1,820 post-cutoff targets by protein-family and pocket familiarity, the five-stage rule fires on 4 to 7 per cent of null trajectories against a nominal 5 per cent and the three-stage rule on 12 to 17: the synthetic failure reproduces on real data. Pocket membership is decodable above threshold at all 48 blocks in all four regimes, so the onset cannot discriminate them; the pre-declared accumulation depth does, and is latest for familiar families with structurally novel pockets in every feature set. That regime is also the weakest, by a margin surviving controls for length, pocket measure and alignment depth. Separately, a widely used public co-folding checkpoint loads against its own code with 128 trunk parameters missing; those would be randomly initialized, and every representation extracted would be partly noise while appearing normal.

title: Prior Action Control Causally Alters Language-Model Plasticity
abstract: Two copies of one language model start from identical weights and receive the same rewards during training. For one copy the rewards depend on its own answers. The other copy is yoked: it receives the first copy's rewards no matter what it answers, a design taken from the learned-helplessness experiments of animal learning. We ask whether the copy whose rewards depended on its answers, the copy with control, later learns a new task faster, that is, whether control changes the model's plasticity. In Experiment 1, copies of Qwen3-0.6B generated their own answers in a two-turn game and afterwards learned a new task. The copies with control learned the new task faster in every pair, and the advantage held on different starting models as well as on the larger Qwen3-1.7B. Copies with no reward signal, trained only on the updates that every copy shared, learned about as fast as the yoked copies. The advantage is therefore mostly a benefit of control, not damage from lacking it. Control had also changed how the copies answered, so the twins practiced different answers. That practice could carry part of the advantage, and Experiment 2 removed the difference. Both copies of a pair trained on the same answers, fixed in advance, in the same order, and received the same number of rewards. Only one copy's rewards followed the answers, and that copy again learned a new task faster. The advantage of the copies with control over their yoked twins could be forecast before the new task began from each copy's weights. In sum, control over rewards during earlier training left models faster at learning a new task later on, and a conventional model evaluation need not show it.

title: ProteoCraft: Protein Design as Proposal-Verification Search
abstract: Protein-protein interactions underpin nearly all biological processes. Yet, designing proteins with desired interactions remains challenging due to the structural complexity governing molecular recognition. This study views protein design as a search optimization problem over a combinatorial sequence space under expensive structural evaluation. Toward this goal, we introduce a novel tree-based search framework, ProteoCraft, that employs approximate structural gradients from diffusion-based structure predictors as effective proposal policies to specify where the search should explore. Complete no-gradient inference of folding models separately assigns values to the resulting sequences, determining what is good. ProteoCraft allocates this verification budget through a coarse-to-fine paradigm: multi-site edits first explore distinct sequence basins, then verified promising states undergo strict single-site refinement. Across fourteen de novo binder-design settings spanning eight target proteins, five immune-relevant TCR-facing targets, and four localized CDR redesign tasks, ProteoCraft improves design quality and high-confidence yield. These improvements persist under independent AF2-IG and Rosetta-based interface evaluation. Prospective experimental validation further yielded an 82.9% binding hit rate for PD-L1 miniproteins, with a best measured KD of 0.879 nM, and confirmed binding of designed IFNAR2 VHH. Our code is available at https://github.com/smiles724/ProteoCraft_v1.

title: RangeFinder: Predicting Ligand Property Ranges from Protein Pockets
abstract: Identifying ligands for a protein target requires searching a vast chemical space for a comparatively small set of compatible molecules. Existing machine learning approaches primarily address this problem by generating candidate ligands or scoring individual protein-ligand pairs, but provide limited information about the broader chemical space compatible with a binding pocket. We introduce RangeFinder, an SE(3)-equivariant transformer pocket-level model, trained and evaluated on BioLiP2 data, that predicts ranges over nine physicochemical ligand properties directly from pocket structure, chemistry, and evolutionary context. Using an intersection-over-union objective and evaluation metric (range-IoU), RangeFinder achieves a range-IoU of $0.464 \pm 0.002$, outperforming all deployable baselines while requiring only $12.2$ ms per pocket. We also quantify our method's ability to reduce the ligand search space while retaining compatible binders; in this regard, RangeFinder achieves a Reduction-Recall F-Score of $0.543 \pm 0.011$ --- once again outperforming all deployable baselines. Ablation experiments indicate that RangeFinder's performance depends more strongly on the density and quality of ligand supervision than on any individual input modality or specialized training strategy. Together, these results position RangeFinder as an inexpensive and effective molecular filtering prior, with demonstrated potential in narrowing the ligand search space of target pockets before docking, generation, or synthesis. The code for this project can be found at: https://github.com/alannadels/RangeFinder.
comment: Accepted at the AI for Drug Discovery workshop --- NeurIPS 2026

title: Substrate hypergraph cycles: unique steady states and persistence for every enzyme assignment; oscillations enabled by enzyme sharing
abstract: We associate a directed substrate hypergraph with an enzymatic reaction system. The hypergraph records which substrates each composite reaction consumes and produces, and each composite reaction is realized by a Henri--Michaelis--Menten (HMM) module whose enzyme may be distinct, shared with other reactions, or absent. We call the hypergraph a cycle when it is strongly connected and every substrate is produced by exactly one reaction and consumed by exactly one reaction, each time with coefficient one; equivalently, its dual is a strongly connected ordinary directed graph. For a cycle, every HMM realization, under every enzyme assignment and for all positive rate constants, has exactly one positive steady state in each stoichiometric compatibility class that contains a strictly positive point, and no steady state on the boundary of such a class, and every trajectory in such a class is persistent. The interior dynamics, in contrast, depend on how enzymes are shared. When each enzyme catalyzes at most one reaction, every trajectory in such a class converges to its unique steady state. With enzyme sharing, convergence can fail even for the three-substrate transformation cycle $X_1\to X_2\to X_3\to X_1$: if two transformations share an enzyme and the third has its own enzyme or none, the steady state can undergo a supercritical Hopf bifurcation that produces a stable limit cycle. Thus the substrate structure controls existence, uniqueness, and persistence, while the pattern of enzyme sharing controls the interior dynamics. The results extend to weighted cycles, which allow higher stoichiometric coefficients, and to longer chains of intermediates.

title: The DynaCell Evaluation Suite for Dynamic 3D Virtual Staining of Live Cells
abstract: Understanding how cells respond to perturbations over time is central to cell biology and drug discovery. Live-cell imaging captures the dynamics of perturbation-induced phenotypes in individual cells. While fluorescence imaging can visualize specific molecular phenotypes, labeling and repeated illumination often affect cell health. Virtual staining offers an alternative by predicting these fluorescence images from images acquired without fluorescent labels. Although many virtual staining models have been developed, their performance on volumetric time-lapse data remains poorly characterized. We address this gap with an evaluation suite for 3D time-lapse virtual staining of live cells. The suite combines paired 3D time-lapse images acquired with and without fluorescent labels, a set of baseline models, and three metric tiers measuring pixel-level fidelity, organelle segmentation performance, and single-cell phenotype similarity. Using this evaluation suite, we study metric and model behavior across 3 cell types, 2 microscopes, 4 organelles, and 3 perturbation states. We find that regression baselines better predict the spatial localization of target organelles, whereas the generative baseline better captures the distribution of phenotypes across cells. These differences expose trade-offs between structural and phenotypic fidelity that are obscured by single-metric evaluation and suggest how virtual staining models can be developed for diverse downstream tasks such as localization, segmentation, tracking, and phenotypic profiling. We release the curated datasets, baseline checkpoints, and evaluation code as part of DynaCell, a broader framework for image-based profiling of cell-state dynamics.
comment: 64 pages: 10-page main text with 4 figures and 1 table, plus references and a 49-page appendix with 15 figures and 25 tables. Accepted at NeurIPS 2026, Track on Evaluations and Datasets

title: Visualization and Characterization of Gene Group Distribution Patterns Across Genomes
abstract: Genes of the same family often lie close together on a chromosome, yet how far apart family members sit, and whether their spacing follows any pattern, has rarely been measured consistently across genomes. We built an interactive web application that places the members of any of the 1,396 FlyBase gene groups on the banded ideogram of the fruit fly (Drosophila melanogaster) and lists each member's neighbours. While browsing it, we found strikingly symmetric gene sets in which consecutive members are almost evenly spaced. In the RAB GTPases, two 5.08 Mb spacings differ by only 634 bp. We also found that distances between neighbouring members fall into two populations: short-range (median 1.8 kb) and long-range (median 2.4 Mb). Although an arm-matched random control suggests that the even spacing (without a minimum-distance filter) as well as the long-range population arise largely by chance, the short-range population turns out to be a genuine clustering signal. We then extended the analysis to human and six other model organisms (mouse, zebrafish, Caenorhabditis elegans, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Arabidopsis thaliana and maize), and every genome showed the same two populations. The mixture curve of the two is nearly constant across chromosomes in some genomes (Type I: fly, maize, Arabidopsis, C. elegans) but varies across chromosomes in others (Type II: human, mouse, zebrafish, yeast). Thus, across eight eukaryotes, family members lie in two distance populations. The scale of the short-range population follows the spacing of genes in each genome, and the long-range population matches random placement in fly and is consistent with it in the other genomes. Our results also show that visual patterns such as even spacing must be tested against chance before they are interpreted. Our tool and approach give a simple way to explore and compare gene clustering across species.
comment: 33 pages, 15 figures, 6 tables, 4 supplementary figures

title: When Model Complexity Matters in Cross-Subject Naturalistic fMRI Prediction
abstract: Increasingly complex neural models predict blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) responses to naturalistic stimuli, but the predictive value of this added complexity remains unclear. We ask when pretrained stimulus representations help and how much downstream complexity is needed, with and without recent measured BOLD history. We compare linear diagnostic references and nonlinear predictors across HCP movie fMRI (154 subjects), BOLD Moments (10 subjects), and Algonauts 2025 (4 subjects). Under a shared offline protocol, models are fitted on training subjects and evaluated on held-out subjects viewing largely familiar stimuli, without refitting. Pretrained visual features generally improve prediction over raw pixels; for linear autoregression, this advantage becomes more pronounced over longer rollouts (recursive predictions without additional measured BOLD). Measured BOLD history provides substantial gains that generally diminish {as rollouts lengthen}. Nonlinear stimulus-only predictors can improve on linear readouts, whereas linear autoregression provides a strong history-conditioned baseline. Controls examine context length, regularization, fitting procedures, and model capacity. Regional response consistency across subjects is associated with held-out prediction accuracy, while less consistent regions tend to gain more from measured history. In paired simulations with fixed linear neural dynamics, slower hemodynamic responses generally sustain high temporal prediction correlations over longer rollouts, illustrating how the observation process can contribute to predictive persistence. Together, these findings support evaluating stimulus representations and downstream complexity separately, using history-conditioned linear prediction as a diagnostic reference under matched inputs and measurement availability.
comment: 43 pages

title: A multimodal dataset of EEG, eye-tracking, and physiological signals during naturalistic smartphone interactions
abstract: Smartphones have become pervasive tools for communication, information consumption, and digital interaction, yet the neurophysiological dynamics associated with naturalistic smartphone use remain insufficiently characterized. Here, we present a multimodal physiological dataset collected during ecologically valid smartphone interaction and a subsequent relaxation condition. Twenty-three participants engaged with their most frequently used smartphone application (primarily gaming or short form video) for ten minutes, followed by a five-minute passive viewing of a standardized nature video. Simultaneous recordings were obtained from electroencephalography (EEG; 64 channels), wearable eye-tracking, photoplethysmography (PPG), and galvanic skin response (GSR) sensors. Questionnaire-based assessments, including the smartphone addiction scale (SAS) and the mobile phone problematic use scale (MPPUS), are also collected to characterize individual differences in smartphone-related behavioral traits. All data streams are synchronized using transistor-transistor logic (TTL) trigger signals to ensure precise temporal alignment across modalities. The dataset is organized according to the Brain Imaging Data Structure (BIDS) specification and is publicly available on OpenNeuro (Accession Number: ds007537). This dataset enables the investigation of neural, ocular, and autonomic responses during smartphone interaction and supports multimodal analysis of diverse smartphone behaviors while preserving ecological validity.
author_corresponding_institution: Birla Institute of Technology and Science (BITS) - Pilani

title: Brief Peppermint Odour Exposure and Immediate Free Recall of a Visual Object Array: A Three-Arm Randomised Experiment
abstract: Background: Odours reach limbic and prefrontal targets through a uniquely direct pathway and are often claimed to enhance cognition, yet experimental evidence for specific essential oils is mixed and frequently confounded by expectancy. We tested whether a brief inhalation of peppermint or clove essential oil, compared with no odour, alters immediate free recall of a visual object array. Methods: Sixty healthy adults aged 18-50 years were randomly allocated to peppermint oil, clove oil or no odour (n = 20 each). After 30 s of inhalation (or none), participants studied a 4 x 4 array of 16 pictured items for 20 s and then wrote down every item they could recall, without time limit. Groups were compared with one-way and Welch ANOVA, Welch-corrected pairwise tests with Holm correction, Hedges' g with 95% confidence intervals and Bayes factors. Results: Recall differed across conditions (Welch F(2, 37.0) = 8.53, p < .001; omega2 = 0.14). Participants exposed to peppermint recalled more items (11.20 +/- 2.14) than those exposed to no odour (8.45 +/- 2.04; g = 1.29, 95% CI [0.61, 1.97], p(Holm) < .001, BF10 = 134). Clove (9.55 +/- 3.19) did not differ reliably from either no odour (g = 0.40, p(Holm) = .203) or peppermint (g = 0.60, p(Holm) = .127; BF10 = 1.29). Conclusions: A single brief exposure to peppermint oil was associated with substantially better immediate recall than no odour. Because the peppermint-clove contrast was inconclusive and no placebo odour was used, the data do not establish an odour-specific effect; general arousal and expectancy remain plausible contributors. Pre-registered, laboratory-based replications with placebo odours, blinding and arousal measures are required.

title: Dissection of the contribution of bushy cell delays to sound localization in juvenile and adult Mongolian gerbils
abstract: Sound sources along the azimuth generate interaural time differences in arrival (ITDs) at the ears. According to Jeffress hypothesis, ITDs are detected by coincidence-sensitive neurons of the medial superior olive (MSO) for which a differential axonal delay from each ear to the MSO compensates for the ITDs. The origin and development of these delays remain poorly understood. To this end, we made recordings from bushy cells (BCs), which project to both MSOs, in adult and in 2-4-week-old Mongolian gerbils of either sex. First spike latency revealed a frequency-dependent delay likely originating in the cochlea. Latencies were markedly larger for pure tone stimulation than for complex sounds. Combined with our published recordings from the MSO, we observed a developmental decrease in most delays, including the contralateral BC-to-MSO axonal delay. Unexpectedly, the ipsilateral BC-to-MSO axonal delay did not decrease. Anatomical brainstem reconstructions revealed that the inter-MSO distance was stable whereas the cochlear nucleus-to-MSO distance increased during development. Together, this indicated an increase in axonal propagation velocity, particularly for the contralateral projection. The variability in the averaged firing onset between BCs was found to be as large as the variance in bITDs, suggesting that BCs with matching firing onset are selected to converge onto the same MSO neuron. Together, our results indicate that the developmental speedup of ear-to-MSO delays contributes greatly to bringing the bITDs within their ecological range, but that the difference in path length is not overcome, keeping the ITD tuning biased to contralateral sound sources.

title: Divergent Pontine and Cerebellar Pathology in Preterm Infants With Necrotizing Enterocolitis
abstract: Importance: Preterm survivors of necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) face substantial neurodevelopmental impairment, but the regional biology and timing of associated brain abnormalities remain poorly defined. Objective: To define the regional, cellular, molecular, and temporal features of NEC-associated brain pathology. Design: Prospective multimodal clinical cohort study (2012-2024), complemented by postmortem tissue analyses. Setting: Level IV neonatal intensive care unit at Children's National Hospital, Washington, DC. Participants: Of 400 infants screened, 253 preterm infants born before 37 weeks' gestation (128 with NEC and 125 without NEC) were included across neuroimaging, plasma metabolomic, and postmortem cohorts. Exposures: Medical or surgical NEC (modified Bell stage [≥]II). Main Outcomes and Measures: Primary outcomes were term-equivalent magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) abnormalities and serial ultrasound hindbrain growth; secondary outcomes were postmortem histopathology, brain and intestinal transcriptomics, and plasma metabolomics. Results: Among 179 infants with term-equivalent MRI (89 NEC, 90 controls; 102 [57.0%] male; mean [SD] gestational age, 26.3 [2.2] weeks), NEC was associated with a higher prevalence of pontine abnormalities (12.4% vs 1.1%; adjusted prevalence ratio, 9.14; 95% CI, 1.16-71.92), alongside white matter, callosal, and cerebellar abnormalities. In postmortem tissue (n = 27), white matter pathology qualitatively resembled that of prematurity, whereas the hindbrain showed distinct regional phenotypes. The cerebellum exhibited external granular layer contraction (42% reduction; P = .04), while the pons showed neuronal injury with increased morphological apoptotic burden (P [≤] .05). Brain and intestinal transcriptomics (n = 14), complemented by plasma metabolomics (n = 29), revealed divergent inflammatory and metabolic signatures. The pons showed increased neuroinflammatory and reduced mitochondrial programs, whereas the cerebellum showed reduced metabolic and cell-cycle programs alongside circulating lysophospholipid depletion. Serial ultrasonography (n = 159), anchored to the cohort mean NEC onset age of 29 weeks' postmenstrual age, identified earlier cerebellar dimensional deficits (P = .015) and later pontine growth deceleration (P < .001). Conclusions and Relevance: In this cohort study, NEC-associated hindbrain pathology showed asynchronous growth patterns accompanied by distinct cellular and molecular phenotypes. These findings support investigation of regional vulnerability and stage-specific neuroprotection; individual injury timing and causal mechanisms remain unresolved.
author_corresponding_institution: Children's National Hospital; The George Washington University School of Medicine and Health Sciences

title: Dopaminergic reward signals shape foraging decisions through learned value expectations
abstract: A fundamental function of the nervous system is to direct animals towards life-sustaining resources and enable adaptive strategies for acquiring them. Foraging, the challenge of securing these resources from the environment, requires making decisions that balance local gains against costs, opening a window on value-based decision making in ecological context. Yet despite the centrality of foraging in life, the algorithms and neural mechanisms underlying foraging decisions are not well understood. We studied mice making stay-or-leave patch foraging decisions for water across poor- and rich-resource environments with dynamic local reward outcomes. We found that mice integrate immediate rewards, local reward history, and reward (i.e. value) expectations to guide foraging decisions, favoring greater time investment in rich-environment patches. Computational models revealed influence of a time-varying bias which mirrored the shape of a learned value function. Consistent with a reinforcement learning mechanism, dopamine in the ventral striatum signaled a temporal-difference reward prediction error, which could be used as a teaching signal to construct value functions, and calibrated optogenetic manipulation of dopamine to create fictive reward signals recapitulated the value-related decision bias. Taken together, our results shed new light on the neurocomputational basis of foraging, revealing a novel role for value expectations in dynamic environments. Further, they establish generalized function of biological reinforcement learning in ecological context, demonstrating a specific role for the canonical dopamine reward circuit in shaping temporally resolved value expectations to guide behavior and cognition. The unification of this framework with foraging opens a new avenue to elucidate principles of how animals learn and dynamically adjust cognitive strategies for real-world ecological problems.

title: EigenBrain maps cortical molecular architecture from functional, geometric, and structural eigenmodes
abstract: Neurotransmitter receptor and transporter distributions shape neural communication across the cortex and underpin mechanistic interpretations of brain function. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-derived eigenmodes, low-dimensional spatial patterns that capture the principal axes of cortical organization, are increasingly used to reconstruct brain maps and offer a potential route to approximating molecular topographies in large cohorts where direct measurements are unavailable. Yet whether the type of MRI data used to derive these eigenmodes determines which receptor and transporter distributions can be approximated, and which molecular systems are accessible through this approach at all, remains unknown. Using a spatial reconstruction framework applied to 23 molecular systems spanning neurotransmitter, metabolic, and pathological markers, we show that eight receptor and transporter maps, spanning serotonin, dopamine, histamine, cholinergic, and opioid markers, can be selectively approximated from functional eigenmodes but not structural or geometric ones. This selectivity also reveals that functional brain organization encodes a specific subset of neuromodulatory topographies that structural and geometric organization does not. To illustrate translational potential in clinical cohorts where molecular imaging is unavailable, we applied individual-level eigenmode decompositions of MRI data projected onto the eight validated molecular systems and detected cross-sectional differences in autism and longitudinal changes in schizophrenia. Together, these findings reveal a difference in how geometric, structural, and functional brain organization relate to molecular architecture, offering a method for approximating validated molecular profiles in population neuroimaging cohorts that lack direct molecular imaging.

title: Endothelin-1 from Tongue Glands Gates 1 Sodium Taste and Intake
abstract: Sodium is an essential nutrient. To survive sodium deficiency, animals dramatically increase their appetite for salt. However, whether and how sodium depletion impacts the taste of salt to drive sodium intake is unknown. Here we show that tongue gland-derived endothelin-1 (EDN1) regulates the amiloride-sensitive, sodium-selective salt taste. Edn1 is specifically expressed in the glands embedded within the tongue. Under normal conditions, EDN1 suppresses salt taste by acting on its receptor EDNRB on the projections of salt-sensing taste neurons innervating taste buds. When internal sodium levels drop, EDN1 expression decreases, lifting this inhibition and enhancing responses to salt. Applying EDN1 directly to the tongue, using a nonionic eutectic-based organogel (Neogel) delivery technology that we establish here, dampens the activity of the salt-sensing taste neurons and reduces salt intake and preference. Conversely, genetic deletion of Ednrb in taste neurons mimics the effects of sodium deficiency, enhancing salt-sensing neuron activity and increasing salt consumption. These findings reveal a peripheral mechanism that regulates salt taste and intake in response to internal sodium levels, highlighting a direct role of the taste pathway in maintaining nutrient homeostasis.

title: Expertise modifies neural responses to causal inference during language comprehension
abstract: Linguistic communication relies on shared common ground, yet different individuals in a community have specialized semantic knowledge. As a key example, physicians acquire rich knowledge about the causes of illness. An open question is whether such "causal expertise" influences the neural basis of language comprehension. Here we tested the hypothesis that when understanding everyday language like, "Holly used a grimy faucet during her overseas plane ride. Now she has the stomach flu," medical experts retrieve richer representations in semantic networks of the brain. Physicians (n=16) and age- and education-matched controls (n=16) undergoing fMRI read two-sentence vignettes that elicited implicit causal inferences about illness or object mechanics as well as control vignettes that did not elicit causal inferences. Vignettes were linguistically matched across conditions and were accessible to experts and non-experts alike. Across both groups, causal vignettes about illness engaged a temporoparietal semantic network previously implicated in thinking about animates, i.e., people and animals (precuneus and left temporoparietal junction), whereas causal vignettes about object mechanics engaged a semantic network associated with places and objects. Critically, physicians' responses in the animacy network were more robust and self-similar, suggesting the activation of richer semantic knowledge. Medical expertise effects were specific to biological inferences rather than mechanical or mental state inferences. By contrast, individually localized frontotemporal language and frontoparietal reasoning networks did not respond preferentially to causally connected sentences or show effects of expertise. Our findings suggest that causal expertise alters neural responses to causal inferences that unfold automatically during language comprehension.

title: Feedback reliability modulates learning-related dynamics of midfrontal error monitoring
abstract: Learning from feedback requires the brain to evaluate both performance outcomes and the reliability of the information used for learning. This study examined the dynamics of neural performance monitoring during deterministic (100% reliable) and probabilistic (75% reliable) associative learning using two within-subject tasks with different stimulus materials. Behavioral performance improved under both feedback regimes, but learning was consistently more successful under deterministic feedback. Error-related negativity, feedback-related negativity, and phase-locked midfrontal theta became progressively more pronounced across deterministic learning, particularly in the image-image task, whereas corresponding changes were attenuated under probabilistic feedback. Induced theta showed the opposite pattern, decreasing across deterministic learning while remaining comparatively stable under probabilistic learning. These opposing theta trajectories suggest that phase-locked and induced activity reflect distinct components of learning-related neural adaptation that may be obscured when total theta power is considered alone. Overall, the findings indicate that feedback reliability shapes the progressive tuning of midfrontal performance-monitoring responses during learning.

title: Head movement allocation in freely-moving macaques learning object-context sequences
abstract: Flexible learning and long-term memory are hallmark features of primate cognition that are shaped by interactions with changing environments. A comprehensive understanding of these brain-body-environment interactions requires minimal constraints on behavior, and environments rich with conditional cues that encourage diverse behavioral dynamics. In this study, we introduce a multi-level enclosure (Treehouse) that allows for independent control of spatially distributed touchscreens for studying cognition in freely moving macaques. To test flexible learning, two monkeys completed trials consisting of a regular sequence of conditional object choices (targets) across four distinct spatiotemporal contexts (screens). Both monkeys acquired numerous unique, conditional object-context sequences without detriment to new learning as memoranda accumulated. They also successfully recalled their correct choices after weeks without exposure. To assess how monkeys allocate movement during learning and memory-guided decision making, we tracked their head kinematics and used recurrent neural networks to decode different aspects of their engagement with the environment during the choice epoch of the task. One such model predicted the position of the object about to be touched, including on error trials, tracking overt gaze towards objects. Separate models decoded sequence corner, the ordinal step, and the individual screen stations the monkeys occupied, despite identical stimulus layouts and behavioral demands at each station. Head movements also showed efficiencies that the task did not require: under conditions of uncertainty, monkeys were biased in their initial search locations to the targets that were closest to reach, and across days they made smoother head movements as training progressed, with no change in accuracy. These results demonstrate the potential of immersive 3-D environments, in which body kinematics can shed light on animals' goals, and reveal that situated learning in primates can be rapid, capacious, durable, and flexible.

title: How Well Does Structural MRI Classify Autism? A Leakage-Free, Site-Aware and Externally Validated Machine-Learning Evaluation in Two ABIDE Cohorts
abstract: Background: Many studies report high accuracy for classifying autism spectrum disorder (ASD) from structural MRI, but small samples, single train-test splits, site effects and information leakage can inflate performance. We evaluated how well brain morphometry distinguishes autistic from typically developing (TD) individuals under rigorous, leakage-free validation. Methods: FreeSurfer-derived features (n = 280: regional thickness, area and volume; subcortical volumes; Yeo-network composites; asymmetry indices; global measures) from ABIDE II (804 participants; 341 ASD; 12 sites) were used to train logistic regression, linear support vector machine, random forest, XGBoost and multilayer perceptron classifiers. Confound regression (age, age2, sex, brain volume), site-wise centring and standardisation were learned within training folds only. Performance was assessed with nested 10-fold cross-validation, leave-one-site-out validation and external validation in ABIDE I (917 participants; 20 sites), and compared with full-pipeline permutation tests and a confound-only baseline. Results: Cross-validated discrimination was modest: the best model (regularised logistic regression on all features) reached an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.60 [0.56, 0.64], significantly above chance (permutation p = .002) but far from clinically useful and below a confound-only baseline using age, sex, brain volume and site (AUC 0.63); non-linear models did not perform better (AUC 0.45-0.60 across models and feature sets). Pooled leave-one-site-out AUCs were 0.54-0.61, with large between-site variation, and AUCs in the external ABIDE I cohort were 0.52-0.58. Age-stratified models did not exceed AUC 0.60. Across 300 random 80/20 splits in young adults, test-set AUCs ranged from 0.21 to 0.90, showing that single-split estimates such as 0.74 can arise by chance. Conclusions: Under leakage-free, site-aware and externally validated evaluation, structural MRI morphometry classifies autism only slightly better than chance. Reports of high accuracy should be interpreted with caution, and the heterogeneity of autism argues for stratification and normative approaches rather than binary diagnostic classifiers.

title: Human single-neuron correlates of somatosensation
abstract: Understanding the neural correlates of consciousness poses a central challenge in neuroscience, with longstanding debate over which cortical areas underlie subjective sensory perception. In the tactile domain, posterior parietal cortex (PPC) and primary somatosensory cortex (S1) are candidate cortical substrates for neural correlates of consciousness due to their crucial roles in somatosensory processing. Yet whether and how these regions contribute to conscious tactile perception remains unclear. Here, to address this issue, we leveraged chronic intracortical recordings to simultaneously monitor large ensembles of single neurons in grasp related cortical areas from three participants with tetraplegia while natural vibrotactile stimuli were delivered to a sensate region of the upper limb. We demonstrate that an orchestration of neural activity emerged across the grasp-related parietal-frontal network at near-threshold perception. Within this distributed network, we then focused on PPC and S1. While S1 responses closely tracked the amplitude of the physical stimulus, PPC activity covaried more strongly with awareness and confidence. This single-neuron evidence reveals PPC and S1 have complementary neural codes with PPC transforming physical stimulation into conscious perception whereas S1 is more sensitive to stimulus amplitude.

title: In vivo discovery of blood-brain barrier opening small molecules with FishNAP
abstract: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) maintains neural homeostasis by tightly regulating molecular exchange between the circulation and the brain, but it also restricts drug delivery and thereby limits treatment of neurological disorders. Pharmacological agents that transiently and safely increase BBB permeability could therefore improve brain drug delivery, yet their systematic discovery has been constrained by the limitations of existing approaches. Here we present FishNAP, a non-invasive, high-throughput zebrafish platform for real-time in vivo assessment of BBB permeability. Screening 2,320 FDA-approved small molecules identified seven that increased BBB permeability in zebrafish, with barrier integrity recovering within 24 hours in each case, indicating reversible modulation. Three of these compounds, Calcitriol, Lovastatin and Sunitinib, which act through distinct signaling pathways, also increased BBB permeability in adult mice through both tight junction disruption and increased transcytosis. FishNAP thus enables the identification of conserved modulators of BBB function with translational potential for brain drug delivery.

title: In-vivo MRI of noradrenergic and dopaminergic nuclei predicts future cognition and Alzheimers disease progression
abstract: Noradrenergic and dopaminergic nuclei modulate cognition, and post-mortem data indicate they are affected early in the neurodegenerative cascade of Alzheimers disease. We derived in-vivo locus coeruleus (LC) and substantia nigra-ventral tegmental area (SN-VTA) MRI integrity measures from 739 ADNI participants, examined MRI-histology correspondence in individuals with both in-vivo imaging and post-mortem data, and tested whether these measures reflect early MRI-indexed degeneration predicting later cognitive decline. LC and SN-VTA contrast predicted cognitive and behavioral function 10 years later, despite only weak associations with current function. LC- and SN-VTA-associated brain-wide atrophy patterns aligned with PET-derived norepinephrine-transporter and dopamine-receptor maps, respectively. A one-standard-deviation decrease in baseline LC contrast was associated with 84% higher five-year odds of MCI-to-AD progression, and predictive effects of the catecholaminergic nuclei were mediated by their corresponding atrophy patterns. The SN-VTA pattern was associated with less amyloid PET-related memory decline. Together, these findings establish LC and SN-VTA MRI contrast as markers of early neurodegeneration that forecast cognitive decline years before clinical onset.
author_corresponding_institution: Leonard Davis School of Gerontology, University of Southern California

title: Increased Beta-Band Input to Spinal Motor Neurons is Not Confined to the Responding Muscle During a Go/No-Go Task
abstract: During movement preparation and inhibition, the sensorimotor cortex shows alpha- and beta-band oscillations that are also expressed in the discharge of spinal motor neurons. Whether this oscillatory activity is confined to the motor neurons innervating the muscles involved in the prepared action is unknown. Here we combined electroencephalography with recordings of spinal motor neurons innervating the tibialis anterior. Participants held a submaximal dorsiflexion while performing a Go/No-Go task in which the instructed response was either a ballistic dorsiflexion or handgrip, making the tibialis anterior the responding or a non-responding muscle, respectively. Alpha- and beta-band power increased after the imperative cue in both cortical activity and motor neuron output, including when the tibialis anterior was not involved in the response. Because power modulations in motor neuron output can be confounded by the concurrent change in discharge rate, we assessed the oscillatory activity shared across motor neurons by calculating coherence between disjoint subsets, which is largely insensitive to discharge rate. We then used simulation-based inference to identify synaptic input modulations compatible with our observations. These analyses indicated that beta-band common input increased whether or not the tibialis anterior was involved in the response, whereas alpha-band input increased only when it was the responding muscle. The concurrent decrease in discharge rate and torque was attributed to reduced net excitatory drive, whereas alpha- and beta-band inputs accounted for the increase in synchronisation. These results demonstrate that cue-related oscillatory inputs reach spinal motor neurons more broadly than classically assumed, and shape motor neuron synchronisation.

title: LAMA2-related muscular dystrophy alters Schwann cell calcium homeostasis and increases peripheral nerve inflammation
abstract: LAMA2-related muscular dystrophy (LAMA2-RD) affects skeletal muscle and peripheral nerves, yet the consequences of LAMA2 deficiency on peripheral nerve integrity beyond early postnatal development remain incompletely understood. We investigated sciatic nerve architecture and molecular alterations across postnatal life in hypomorphic Lama2dy2J/dy2J mice. LAMA2 localizes around the abaxonal surface of myelinating Schwann cells in control nerves. LAMA2-deficient nerves exhibited patchy regions lacking myelinated axons from early postnatal stages into adulthood, including expanded Remak bundles along with axons completely lacking normal Schwann cell ensheathment. In adult nerves, myelin infolding and reduced myelin circularity revealed abnormalities in the architecture of myelin that had formed. Bulk sciatic nerve RNA sequencing identified altered calcium-signaling and immune-related transcriptional signatures. Complementary Fura Red measurements in primary nerve-derived Schwann cell cultures demonstrated decreased intracellular calcium in LAMA2-deficient samples, while ATP-evoked responses were preserved. Older LAMA2-deficient nerves also exhibited increased CD45+CD11b+ myeloid-cell infiltration. Together, these observations extend the characterization of LAMA2-associated neuropathy into adulthood and identify calcium homeostasis and neuroimmune responses as candidate processes relevant to persistent peripheral nerve pathology.

title: Mapping Endogenous Psychedelic Chemistry: Indolethylamine N-Methyltransferase (INMT) Localizes Proximal to the Golgi Apparatus of Human Neurons
abstract: N,N-dimethyltryptamine (DMT) is a serotonergic psychedelic with a history of ethnobotanical use and emerging clinical efficacy for neuropsychiatric disorders. Following Julius Axelrod's pioneering studies showing DMT production in human tissues, DMT has been proposed as an endogenous neuromodulator because it is a serotonin 2A receptor (5-HT2A R) agonist. However, the DMT-producing enzyme, indolethylamine N-methyltransferase (INMT), has not been characterized at the protein level in the human central nervous system. Here, we validated an anti-INMT antibody and used immunocytochemistry to show that INMT localizes in close proximity to other DMT biosynthetic enzymes near the cytosolic face of the cis-Golgi network in human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived neurons, with immunoreactivity observed across multiple neuronal Golgi phenotypes. Notably, both DMT-like and 5-HT2A R immunoreactivity also partially localized in close proximity to the Golgi apparatus. Our results establish the first protein-level characterization of INMT in human neurons and identify the cis-Golgi network as a candidate microdomain for psychedelic tryptamine biosynthesis. We propose that INMT catalytic activity at the cis-Golgi network creates an enriched region of membrane-permeable psychedelic tryptamines that can access an intracellular 5- HT2A R pool. These findings provide new tools and insights that can inform efforts to understand the mechanism of action of psychedelics under clinical investigation and to target endogenous tryptamines therapeutically.
author_corresponding_institution: Chemical Neurobiology Laboratory, Center for Genomic Medicine, Department of Neurology, Massachusetts General Hospital, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA.

title: Natural predator-associated chemosignals evoke distinct spatiotemporal patterns of risk assessment and vomeronasal population responses
abstract: Natural predator-associated chemosignals elicit diverse defensive behaviors, yet it remains unclear how complex natural cues shape the spatiotemporal organization of risk assessment and activate vomeronasal sensory neurons (VSNs) and downstream circuits in the mammalian accessory olfactory system. Here, we investigated odor-dependent behavioral organization and VSN sensory representations using three-dimensional behavioral tracking, integrative machine-learning analysis, volumetric calcium imaging, and whole-brain FosTRAP2 mapping. We developed a pose-based integrative machine-learning analysis pipeline (PIMAP) to identify behavioral signatures based on posture, spatial exploration, state transitions, and temporal dynamics. We found that common behavioral states were expressed in multiple odor conditions, but their expression rates, spatial positions, and temporal sequencing distinguished responses to snake, tortoise, lizard, and mouse fecal cues. Snake fecal cues elicited sustained direct investigation and distinct patterns of spatial exploration, behavioral transitions, and grooming in both two-chamber and multiple-choice assays. Volumetric calcium imaging in the vomeronasal epithelium revealed distinct patterns of VSN activation by different reptilian cues. Whole-brain microscopy of FosTRAP2 transgenic mice indicated potential differential activity patterns in AOS-associated circuits following snake and tortoise exposure. Furthermore, Trpc2 deletion altered snake-associated behavioral signatures, while odor-discriminative behavioral patterns remained detectable. Together, these findings show that reptilian predator cues activate distinct AOS components and bias exploration patterns towards threat assessment and vigilance.
author_corresponding_institution: University of Rochester School of Medicine and Dentistry

title: Nucleus accumbens acetylcholine dips track reward value and temporal costs to shape delay discounting
abstract: As an organism chooses between competing rewards, it must often integrate learned reward value with the changing costs associated with obtaining them. Yet, the brain mechanisms through which these factors jointly guide choice are not well understood. Previous studies have shown that dopamine signals in the nucleus accumbens (NAc) track reward value and are modulated by their associated delay costs. Our prior work further implicated NAc cholinergic interneurons by demonstrating that dopamine D2 receptors in these neurons influence choice under temporal, but not probabilistic, costs. However, whether NAc acetylcholine (ACh) dynamics track reward value and/or delay, and whether they contribute to adaptive choice, remains unknown. Using in vivo fiber photometry during a delay discounting task in which mice choose between a small, immediate reward and a larger, delayed reward, we reveal that cue-evoked ACh dips dynamically track relative reward magnitude and are diminished by increasing delays. Our data further show that optogenetically enhancing these dips attenuates the delay-dependent decline in choice of the larger, delayed reward. These findings identify a previously unrecognized role for NAc cue-evoked ACh dips in shaping adaptive choice as temporal costs increase.

title: Prolactin Receptor Long Isoform ΔS1 Expression is Reduced in the Dorsal Root Ganglia of Humans with Chronic Pain
abstract: Prolactin receptor (PRLR) isoforms, specifically the short (PRLR-S) and long (PRLR-L), are differentially expressed in pathological conditions and may be involved in the induction and maintenance of pain in females. PRLR sex-dependent actions are well studied in rodent models of chronic pain, but the translatability of these findings have only been assessed in electrophysiology studies that found consistent results with previous sex differences described in mice. To increase our understanding of the sexual dimorphic nature of prolactin actions on sensory neurons and our knowledge of how this body of work applies to the human nervous system, we characterized the expression of the short and long isoforms of PRLR with RNAscope in situ hybridization in human dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons. Based on data in mice, we hypothesized PRLR-S and PRLR-L would be equally expressed in human DRG neurons, with higher expression in females. To test this, we used DRG tissues recovered from male and female organ donors and cervix as a positive control. Our results demonstrated human DRG neurons express more PRLR-L, specifically transcript variant 6 ({Delta}S1), than PRLR-S in both sexes and that female donors had a higher expression of PRLR overall. In DRGs from female organ donors with a history of chronic pain we observed less PRLR-L expression, a finding consistent with previous studies in pain models in female mice. Expression for both PRLR isoforms in cervix was consistent with previous reports. An analysis of previously published RNA sequencing studies on human DRGs revealed that PRLR expression is confined mostly to TRPV1-positive nociceptors in humans, consistent with our RNAscope-based findings. We conclude that the PRLR-L ({Delta}S1) form is the major isoform expressed in human DRG neurons, that this expression is higher in females than in males, and that PRLR-L ({Delta}S1) expression is suppressed in chronic pain conditions in females.
author_corresponding_institution: The University of Texas at Dallas

title: Reconfiguration of default mode metabolic demands and network organization during acute stress
abstract: Psychosocial stress engages coordinated physiological and neural responses that enable adaptation to environmental challenges. Maladaptive stress responses and reduced resilience are major risk factors for psychiatric and neurodegenerative disorders. As the brain's metabolic response to stress remains largely unexplored, we used simultaneous [18F]FDG PET/MRI during performance of the Montreal Imaging Stress Task to assess cerebral glucose metabolism, BOLD activation and functional connectivity. Multimodal data analysis identified the posterior cingulate cortex (PCC) as hub of stress processing beyond cognitive input, with increased glucose metabolism and attenuated BOLD deactivations. This was accompanied by reduced PCC connectivity within the default mode network and increased influence onto frontoparietal and dorsal attention networks. Endocrine stress responsivity was further reflected in lower resilience sub scores, failure to downregulate anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) metabolism during stress, and an inverse relationship between ACC glucose metabolism and anterior insula functional connectivity. These results indicate that acute psychosocial stress does not merely increase overall energy demand but reconfigures the relationship between regional metabolism and large-scale network organization, which further differs with individual endocrine stress responsivity. Our findings unify the roles of stress and the DMN in brain disorders, providing a multimodal framework for assessment in patient populations.
author_corresponding_institution: Department of Psychiatry and Psychotherapy, Medical University of Vienna, Austria

title: Resource competition controls the length-dependence of synaptic protein synthesis
abstract: Synaptic plasticity is dependent on the availability of specific proteins at the synapse with distinct requirements for potentiation and depression. Specifically, experimental evidence suggests an upregulation of short proteins and a downregulation for long proteins during long-term depression (LTD). The mechanism of this length-dependent protein synthesis regulation is yet unknown. In this work, we propose an computational model of ribosomal regulation of protein synthesis than can reproduce the length-dependent shift in protein expression seen during ribosomal elevations. By analysing the model dynamics, we discover that this effect is due to a shift from initiation-restricted to elongation-restricted protein synthesis. This works offers a novel explanation for the loss of ribosomal control of protein synthesis due to saturation in pathological ribosome enriched conditions. This new theoretical model of ribosomal regulation of protein synthesis is capable of explaining length-dependent shifts in protein synthesis.

title: Revisiting the role of cAMP in Drosophila aversive olfactory memory formation
abstract: In aversive olfactory conditioning in Drosophila melanogaster, an odor (the conditioned stimulus, CS) is paired with an electric shock (the unconditioned stimulus, US). Rutabaga adenylyl cyclase, which synthesizes cAMP in Kenyon cells (KCs), has long been proposed to act as a coincidence detector, synergistically activated by calcium/calmodulin in response to odor-evoked KC activity and by Gs downstream of shock-evoked dopamine signaling. This framework implies that CS+ responsive KCs, which receive both CS and US signals, should be distinguishable from the remaining KCs by elevated cAMP levels, such that elevated cAMP would selectively mark these KCs for memory-related plasticity. However, our live imaging revealed that olfactory stimulation alone activates dopaminergic signaling and elevates cAMP broadly across KC axons, with only weak spatial correspondence to sparse local Ca2+ responses, such that CS+ responsive KCs could not be distinguished from the remaining KCs by bulk cAMP levels. This observation challenges a key prediction of the Rutabaga coincidence-detection model. Our findings instead suggest that cAMP concentrations do not selectively mark CS+ neurons. Rather, we propose that the compartmental population dynamics of cAMP across the {gamma} lobe represent a KC-intrinsic expression of valence, integrated across compartments from multiple dopaminergic inputs. Associative conditioning reshaped dopamine responses to the CS+ odor, with corresponding changes in this compartmental cAMP pattern. Simultaneous imaging of cAMP and acetylcholine (ACh) revealed that conditioning establishes an inverse relationship between this pattern and ACh release for the CS+ but not for the CS- odors; this relationship was absent in rutabaga mutants. Pharmacological elevation of cAMP suppressed ACh release from KCs. These findings suggest that cAMP-dependent suppression of ACh release from KCs may shift the valence of the CS+ odor toward a more aversive state in conditioned flies, thereby contributing to aversive olfactory memory formation.

title: Sex differences in fear extinction are conditional, not categorical
abstract: Threat memories are dynamic, and their behavioral expression can change with subsequent experience and the passage of time. Extinction training can reduce conditioned fear responses, yet these responses may re-emerge over time through spontaneous recovery. Although biological sex has been implicated as modulatory factor in fear and extinction memory processes, studies have reported inconsistent findings. Here, we investigated how differences in extinction training and the timing of memory assessment influence extinction memory in male and female mice. Using contextual fear conditioning, we assessed fear acquisition and threat retention, characterized within-session and across-session extinction during repeated training, and compared shorter (3-minute) and longer (6-minute) daily extinction sessions. We subsequently evaluated extinction memory retention and spontaneous recovery at a later time point. Estrous-cycle stage in females was monitored daily throughout the experimental protocol to examine its potential association with fear and extinction behavior. We found that males and females demonstrated comparable fear acquisition and threat memory, as well as similar extinction progression across days. During longer extinction sessions, but not shorter, males showed greater within-session reductions in freezing, whereas females exhibited modestly higher overall freezing. We found no significant sex difference in the magnitude of spontaneous recovery. There was no significant association between estrous-cycle stage and freezing behavior. Together, our findings suggest that sex-dependent differences in contextual fear extinction are not uniformly expressed, but rather depend on the experimental conditions under which extinction is assessed

title: Single-molecule bouncing at a liquid interface governs presynaptic enrichment
abstract: Many cellular processes rely on accumulating highly diffusive cytoplasmic proteins to a specific location within the cell. This spatial enrichment is generally thought to rely on locally immobilizing proteins or slowing diffusion through binding and molecular crowding. Paradoxically, cytoplasmic proteins that are enriched within nerve terminals remain highly diffusive, raising questions about the mechanisms that govern presynaptic enrichment. Here, using in vivo single-molecule microscopy, we tracked the diffusion of a model cytoplasmic protein, -Synuclein (-Syn), and synaptic vesicles (SVs), in motor neuron presynapses of live Drosophila larvae. We demonstrate that -Syn undergoes rapid and frequent "bouncing" events at a presynaptic interface, locally impeding escape from the presynapse. We measured escape probabilities at the interface, and show that impeding escape, without dramatically slowing diffusion, is sufficient to govern presynaptic enrichment. The interface is liquid-like and coincides with the boundary of the SV cluster, which is a necessary scaffold for the presynaptic enrichment of -Syn. Our results provide direct evidence of interfacial reflectivity at the interface of liquid-like compartments, and that this phenomenon can govern the subcellular enrichment of proteins and small organelles at the level of individual particles.
author_corresponding_institution: Clem Jones Centre for Ageing Dementia Research, Queensland Brain Institute, The University of Queensland, St Lucia, QLD, Australia

title: Spatial transcriptomics reveals organizational properties of the mouse spinal cord and alterations in neuropathic pain
abstract: The spinal cord integrates diverse somatosensory inputs and executes motor outputs through anatomically and functionally distinct circuits. Here, we employed spatially resolved single-cell transcriptomic profiling of the adult mouse spinal cord to gain insights into the organizational logic of the spinal cord. Our results reveal distinct spatial and laminar distributions of neuronal subtypes, including axial level and sex-specific differences. Many neuronal subtypes exhibit close spatial proximity, implicating regionally specific patterns of connectivity and circuit functions. Additionally, neuronal subtypes within the dorsal horn exhibit a wide range of predicted cell-cell communication motifs, as assessed by the spatial distribution of neuropeptide- and other ligand-receptor pairs. Finally, we identified several neuronal subtypes with altered transcriptomic and predicted cell-cell communications in a model of neuropathic pain. This spatially resolved cellular and molecular map of the spinal cord will facilitate the decoding of circuit mechanisms underlying somatosensory and motor functions in health and disease.
author_corresponding_institution: Department of Pharmacology, Vanderbilt University, Nashville, TN 37240, USA

title: Stimulus Sampling Shapes Estimated Perceptual Geometry in Psychophysical Scaling
abstract: We used simulations and mathematical analysis to investigate how simultaneous estimation of transducer nonlinearity and perceptual geometry affects bias in maximum likelihood difference scaling (MLDS). Uniform sampling in the stimulus domain disproportionately sampled slowly varying regions and inadequately sampled rapidly varying regions of nonlinear transducers, leading to biased estimates of transducer shape. These biases were substantially reduced when stimuli were sampled uniformly in response space, distributing observations more evenly across the transducer. Likelihood-surface analysis revealed substantial confounding between sampling-induced distortions and effects attributable to changes in perceptual geometry. Uniform stimulus-domain sampling produced a pronounced trade-off between the parameters governing transducer nonlinearity and perceptual geometry, which was substantially reduced under uniform response-space sampling. Although response-space sampling generally improved the local conditioning of the likelihood surface, parameter identifiability remained dependent on its intrinsic geometry and thus on the underlying transducer. These results show that stimulus sampling can influence whether departures from a Riemannian perceptual metric are detected, highlighting the importance of sampling designs that adequately represent perceptual space. More generally, they demonstrate how appropriate sampling can help disentangle the effects of nonlinear transduction from those of nonlinear contributions of perceptual differences to judgments.

title: The transformer as a candidate canonical cortical microcircuit
abstract: Neuroscience hypothesizes a canonical microcircuit subserving cortical computation across brain systems. In artificial intelligence, neural networks have become a universal computational substrate. Here, we leverage newly available large-scale data and mapping techniques to compare neural network motifs to the brain. We embedded a spectrum of candidate microcircuit architectures within a common spatial macrocircuit, measuring alignment with an extensive battery of cortical signatures. We find that one specific circuit type--the transformer--uniquely captures fine-grained unit-level circuit details, population-level functional maps and neuronal activity patterns, and systems-level wiring efficiency and behavioral demands. The key ingredient enabling the transformer's success is a learned multiplicative component making relational information available without extensive long-range wiring. These results suggest striking convergence between computational motifs in natural and artificial intelligence.

title: When touch leads vision: flexible sensory leadership during active texture exploration
abstract: Vision can sample objects remotely and over a broad field, whereas touch is restricted to contacted skin and is often spatially serial however might outperform vision in resolution by transforming spatial information to a temporal code. This raises the question on how multisensory exploration is coordinated. We recorded gaze and or touch location in exploration of 60 three-dimensional surfaces with locally varying textures during visual, haptic and bimodal exploration while participants performed a same/different task, judging whether a second texture matched the first. In bimodal exploration, gaze and touch became more spatially similar than during unimodal exploration, while touch changed less than vision between unimodal and bimodal contexts. A temporal overlap analysis further showed that touch preceded gaze on average during the first 5 s of bimodal exploration. We then increased visual discriminability of the textures using cast-shadow illumination. A psychophysical pilot confirmed improved texture discrimination, and a new participant group showed a strong shift towards vision-leading exploration. Thus, sensory leadership during active visuo-haptic exploration is not fixed: touch can lead vision when texture information is important, but the balance adapts when visual information becomes more diagnostic.

title: Behavioural and neurogenetic evidence for emotion primitives in the fruit fly Drosophila from an open field test.

abstract: Emotions are based on evolutionarily conserved building blocks ('emotion primitives') that are present across mammals. Whether these building blocks are found in insects is largely undefined. Here, we employ the open field test (OFT) in Drosophila and focus on wall-following and total walking activity as behavioural indicators of emotion-like states. Wildtype and transgenic flies were subjected to various conditions prior to behavioural testing. The results indicate that wall-following and total walking activity are independent measures that are modulated, with generally increased wall-following observed under aversive stimuli and decreased values under positive conditions, independent of the time of day. The effects of genetic manipulation of selected neuromodulatory systems support their role in modulating emotion-like states in Drosophila . Activation of reward-related neurons decreased wall-following while inhibition increased it. Moreover, treatment with ethanol or diazepam produced predictable changes in behaviour. Our findings suggest that Drosophila shares conserved core emotion-like building blocks with vertebrates, and show that wall-following and total walking activity in the OFT can serve as a reliable indicator of emotional valence and arousal in the fruit fly. This positions Drosophila as a powerful genetic model to dissect the neuronal and neurochemical substrates of emotion primitives.

title: Glycolipid MPIase is essential for the TAT (twin-arginine translocation) pathway.

abstract: TAT (twin-arginine translocation) is a preprotein translocation system dedicated to membrane translocation of prefolded proteins in plants and bacteria. The TAT translocon, consisting of the TatABC subunits, drives translocation using proton motive force. However, there have been no reports on the successful reconstitution of the TAT system. In this report, we show that MPIase, a glycolipid that has been known to catalyze membrane protein integration, is essential for the TAT system. Our findings in recombinant Escherichia coli demonstrate that overproducing TatABC increases MPIase levels, and that depleting MPIase results in TAT precursor accumulation in the cytosol. Furthermore, co-reconstitution of MPIase with TatABC revealed the translocation activities of TAT substrates in a proton motive force-dependent manner. This is the first successful reconstitution of the TAT system and will be advantageous for understanding its mechanisms.
