abstract: Macrophages are driven to form distinct functional phenotypes in response to different immunological stimuli, in a process widely referred to as macrophage polarization. Transcriptional regulators that guide macrophage polarization in response to a given trigger remain largely unknown. In this study, we interrogate the programmable landscape in macrophages to find regulatory panels that determine the precise polarization state that a macrophage is driven to. Toward this, we configure an integrative network analysis pipeline that utilizes macrophage transcriptomes in response to 28 distinct stimuli, reconstructs contextualized human gene regulatory networks, and identifies epicenters of perturbations in each case. We find that these contextualized regulatory networks form a spectrum of 13 distinct clusters, with M1 and M2 at the two ends. Using our computational pipeline, we identify combinatorial panels of epicentric regulatory factors (RFs) for each polarization state. We demonstrate that a set of three RFs, that is, CEBPB , NFE2L2 , and BCL3 , is sufficient to change the polarization destination from M1 to M2. siRNA knockdown of the 3-RF-set in THP1-derived M0 cells, despite exposure to an M1 stimulant, significantly attenuated the shift to M1 phenotype and instead increased the expression of M2 markers. Single knockdown of each RF also showed a similar trend. The siRNA-mediated knockdown of the 3-RF-set rendered the macrophages hyper-susceptible to Staphylococcus aureus infection, demonstrating the importance of these factors in modulating immune responses. Overall, our results provide insights into the transcriptional mechanisms underlying macrophage polarization and identify key RFs that may be targeted to modulate immune responses.

abstract: Few concepts are as central to evolution as is fitness, and yet the quantification of fitness is often ambiguous. In particular, high-throughput experiments to measure mutant fitness in microbes are increasingly common, but vary widely in their definitions of fitness, which makes their results difficult to compare. What are the consequences of these different fitness statistics, and is there a best way to quantify fitness in a given context? Here, we systematize the set of possible fitness statistics according to the following three choices: (1) the encoding of relative abundance (e.g., transforming by a log or logit function), (2) the time scale over which to measure the change in relative abundance, and (3) the choice of a reference subpopulation for calculating relative fitness in bulk competition experiments, such as those using DNA-barcoded mutants. We show that these different choices can lead to significantly different interpretations of mutant fitness in Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Escherichia coli , affecting the magnitude of fitness effects, the apparent presence of epistasis, and even the fitness ranking across mutants. This can confound predictions for evolutionary dynamics and gene functions. Altogether, our results demonstrate the importance of consistent fitness definitions for reproducible results across experiments.

abstract: In chickens and humans, classical class I molecules of the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) have a spectrum of correlated properties, including cell surface expression and peptide repertoire. Understanding the impact of these promiscuous generalists and fastidious specialists is of considerable interest. The promiscuous BF2 molecule from the chicken B21 haplotype, BF2*21:01, binds a wide range of peptides by remodelling the peptide-binding site, allowing co-variation of the anchor residues at peptide positions P 2 and P c-2 , and binding of an anchor residue at Pc. Using in vitro refolding assays with peptides and peptide libraries, determining thermostability and crystal structures, and analysing a chicken B21 cell line by immunopeptidomics, we found that BF2*21:01 will accommodate many possible combinations at P 2 and P c-2 , as well as several hydrophobic amino acids at P c . However, marked preferences for particular peptide lengths, particular amino acids at the three anchor residues, and particular combinations of amino acids at P 2 and P c-2 as well as at P 3 and P c-3 together lead to high frequencies of major peptides while still allowing the possibility of presenting a wide peptide repertoire. These simplifying principles may eventually allow predictions of pathogen peptides with stable binding for this iconic promiscuous class I molecule, as well as providing the data for more sophisticated peptide prediction methods.

abstract: Vagus nerve stimulation has shown promising neuroprotective and anti-inflammatory effects in progressive neurodegenerative disorders such as Parkinson’s disease. However, its invasive nature introduces procedural and device-related risks. Here we introduce a magnetoelectric particulate system for oral delivery and non-invasive vagus nerve stimulation through the gut. The system comprises a magneto-responsive nickel ferrite core and a piezoelectric barium titanate shell, conjugated with capsaicin to specifically target TRPV1 receptors, ensuring effective adherence to the stomach lining after oral administration. Upon magnetic field stimulation, the particles generate electrical pulses that activate vagal afferent fibres, engaging the nucleus tractus solitarius in the brainstem via the gut−brain axis. This activation enhances norepinephrine production in the locus coeruleus and dopamine synthesis in the substantia nigra. Vagal efferent activation triggers the cholinergic anti-inflammatory pathway, mitigating both neuroinflammation and systemic inflammation. This non-invasive approach demonstrates potential for alleviating motor symptoms and non-motor anxiety in Parkinson’s disease, offering valuable insights into its mechanisms and clinical applications.

abstract: The ER membrane complex (EMC) facilitates insertion of integral membrane proteins into the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) lipid bilayer. Recent years have seen significant progress in understanding the structural aspects of EMC, but the identity of EMC-client proteins and EMC’s functional roles throughout evolution remain less well understood. Here we delete the essential EMC3 subunit in the liver and adipose tissues of mice and examine the impact of EMC loss-of-function in a range of metabolic and lipid homeostasis models. The absence of EMC3 in either the liver or adipose tissues results in defective storage of triglycerides and perturbations in lipid droplet (LD) homeostasis. EMC-deficient adipose tissues have reduced ability to mediate fat storage in mice on a high-fat diet and are unable to support non-shivering thermogenesis. Proteomic analyses of EMC3-deficient tissues show reduced levels of FITM2, a key regulator of LD biogenesis and ER homeostasis, identifying FITM2 as an EMC client. Deletion of EMC3 in the Drosophila fat body reveals similar defects in LD homeostasis, which can be rescued by a FITM2 mutant whose biogenesis was EMC-independent. Together, our results indicate that the EMC plays a key evolutionarily conserved role in the biogenesis of machinery maintaining triglyceride storage in metazoans.

abstract: Aging-related cognitive decline, including impairments in spatial orientation and memory, has been linked to dysfunction within the hippocampus and medial entorhinal cortex (MEC). However, the cellular and molecular alterations underlying MEC aging remain poorly understood. Here, we show that old mice exhibit a reduced proportion of grid cells and decreased spatial stability. Transcriptomic profiling of the MEC using 10x Genomics Visium technology reveals 1664 differentially expressed genes between young and old mice. Among these, Bglap3 is identified as a marker gene for a subpopulation of layer III neurons that showed an age-associated reduction in cell number. Chemogenetic silencing of Bglap3 + neurons in young mice impairs spatial tuning of MEC neurons. Together, these findings elucidate cellular and molecular mechanisms contributing to age-related MEC dysfunction and suggest that the loss of Bglap3 + neurons may underlie spatial coding deficits in aging.

abstract: Spatiotemporal compartmentalization is a powerful cellular strategy for concentrating biomolecules, buffering noise, and creating local niches, that enable robust information-processing and reaction cascades. While compartments formed by coacervation are known to modulate catalytic activity, how reaction kinetics and interphase mass transfer between the coacervate and the surrounding phase jointly regulate catalysis within these dynamically evolving compartments remains poorly understood. Here we introduce synthetic coacervate-containing droplets (CCDs)—microfluidically generated arrays of single droplets containing single coacervates in equilibrium with the dilute phase—to investigate coupled reaction-diffusion dynamics under confinement. Using CCDs formed by complex coacervation of oppositely charged polyelectrolytes, we quantify guest molecular partitioning and enzymatic dephosphorylation reactions within single droplets. By integrating spatiotemporal imaging, bulk kinetics, and mathematical modeling, we quantitatively link enzymatic activity to dynamic molecular redistributions across phases, revealing how reaction-driven fluxes regulate enzymatic reactions within biphasic droplets and demonstrating the noise buffering capability of the coacervate phase.

abstract: Plants must continually balance growth with arrest, especially under stress. Auxin signaling acts as a central regulatory hub in this process, yet the mechanisms that dynamically tune auxin signaling in real time remain unknown. Here, we use the light-gated, Ca 2+ -permeable Channelrhodopsin 2 variant XXM2.0 to optogenetically impose defined Ca 2+ signatures on Arabidopsis root cells. Repetitive light activation triggers cytosolic Ca 2+ signals that in turn suppress membrane depolarization and Ca 2+ transients triggered by exogenous auxin. Moreover, prolonged optogenetic Ca 2+ stimulation affects auxin-responsive transcriptional reprogramming. As phenotypic output, reversible inhibition of root growth by suppressing cell division and elongation is observed. We further identify a candidate CaM7–CNGC14 module that likely mediates Ca 2+ -dependent gating of responsiveness to exogenous auxin as well as Ca 2+ -dependent root growth inhibition. Our study thus introduces a synthetic biology approach to decompose calcium–auxin crosstalk in plant cells, and demonstrates that optogenetically imposed cytosolic Ca 2+ signals act as dynamic regulators of auxin susceptibility in roots.

abstract: Chromosomal position is known to influence gene expression, yet its impact on the function of genetic circuits remains largely unexplored. Here, we expand the scope of positional effects by showing that circuit function can be reprogrammed solely through spatial positioning. Using bacteria as a living chassis, we engineer 219 spatially distinct genetic circuits of four different types—three regulatory cascade circuits and a toggle switch. We show that spatial positioning can not only modulate circuit performance but also switch circuits between different dynamics, giving rise to new operational modes as circuit complexity increases. A mathematical model parameterized from experimental data predicts three distinct functional regimes for the toggle switch and links chromosomal position to switch stability through noise. This reprogramming is fundamentally mediated by changes in gene expression noise, moving beyond simple Boolean (on/off) or analog (more/less) interpretations of gene regulation and towards stochastic and probabilistic principles for cellular computation.

abstract: Androgenetic alopecia affects over 1.5 billion individuals, causing progressive hair loss with psychological and quality-of-life burdens. Current pharmacological treatment for androgenetic alopecia faces challenges due to systemic side effects from oral medications or limited efficacy of topical applications. Herein we develop a comb-shaped bioelectronic system, named “Detangle”, for efficient androgenetic alopecia treatment during daily hair combing. This system features electronic teeth embedded with height-differentiated electrodes and integrated drug-loading modules, which generate an enhanced electric field penetrating up to ~9 times deeper into hair follicle regions than conventional external application. We show that the localized electric field synchronizes electro-stimulating hair follicles, and electro-delivering vascular endothelial growth factor A encoding plasmid and steroid 5-alpha-reductase 2 targeting siRNA into follicular cells to promote angiogenesis and suppress androgen synthesis. Through the synergistic regulation of cellular metabolism, the system significantly increases hair restoration efficacy in an androgenetic alopecia mouse model, improving the outcome from ~70% to nearly 100% within one month compared to conventional topical minoxidil treatment. The Detangle system proves safe and effective for deep tissue delivery in dermatology.

abstract: Repair of double-strand breaks via non-homologous end joining requires the synapsis of DNA ends. APLF is emerging as an important repair factor, capable of forming synaptic bridges in the presence of the Ku70/Ku80 heterodimer. However, only a single one-to-one interaction between Ku70/Ku80 and APLF has been reported to date, which is fundamentally insufficient for synapsis. Moreover, it remains unclear how APLF-mediated bridging of Ku70/Ku80 heterodimers is prevented in the absence of double-strand breaks. Using a combination of single-molecule techniques, including Mass Photometry, Atomic Force Microscopy, and Magnetic and Optical Tweezers, we demonstrate that APLF-mediated synapsis requires threading of at least two Ku70/Ku80 heterodimers per DNA end. We show that this requirement stems from the need for a simultaneous interaction of two poly(ADP-ribose) binding Zinc Fingers in APLF with threaded poly(ADP-ribosyl)ated Ku70/Ku80s on a single DNA. We further provide evidence that long non-coding RNA NIHCOLE cooperatively binds up to four Ku70/Ku80, consistent with a synapsis efficiency enhancement mechanism based on the bridging of two Kus70Ku80s bound on both sides of the break. Our results propose a model for the physiological significance of Ku70/Ku80 threading and a regulatory mechanism based on multivalency that restricts APLF-mediated bridging to DNA-bound Ku70/Ku80.

abstract: Due to the assumed plasticity of the immature brain, early-life brain alterations are thought to lead to better recoveries in comparison to the mature brain. Despite clinical needs, how neuronal networks and associated behaviors are affected by early-life brain stresses, such as pediatric concussions, have been overlooked. Here we provide first evidence in male mice that a single early-life concussion durably increases neuronal activity in the somatosensory cortex into adulthood, disrupting neuronal integration while the animal is performing sensory-related tasks. This represents a clinically relevant mechanism that was previously unappreciated for understanding impairment of sensory-related behavior performance. We also demonstrate that pharmacological modulation of the endocannabinoid system a year post-concussion is well-suited to rescue neuronal activity and plasticity, and normalizes sensory-related behavioral performance. These findings identify persistent alterations in cortical sensory processing following early-life concussion and demonstrate that neuronal and behavioral deficits remain amenable to pharmacological intervention long after injury.

abstract: Proper organ development requires the coordination of cell type-specific differentiation programs with general maturation processes through precise spatiotemporal gene regulation. In plants, where RNA polymerase pausing is not well established, alternative mechanisms must ensure this coordination. Here, using single-cell resolution transcriptomic and chromatin accessibility data, we reconstruct developmental trajectories of the Arabidopsis root ground tissue to investigate these mechanisms. We describe phased transcriptional landscapes governing the transition from stem cell to early differentiation, in which chromatin accessibility marks the activation of key developmental regulators. A major transcriptional switch in the late meristematic zone, underpinned by extensive chromatin remodeling, drives the transition from cell division to differentiation. Leveraging machine learning to examine integrated transcriptomic and chromatin accessibility trajectories, we identify GATA transcription factors (TFs) as central coordinators of this switch; a role we validate experimentally. We show that the GATA TFs sit at the tipping point of a feedback-driven bistable system that integrates inputs from auxin and cytokinin to balance proliferation and differentiation, ensuring temporal precision in root development at both the tissue and organ scales.

abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a heterogeneous neurodevelopmental condition. Although the gut microbiome has been implicated in ASD, prior studies have insufficiently addressed clinical heterogeneity. Here, we perform shotgun metagenomic sequencing on stool samples from 720 children with ASD (median age 8 years, 87% male) and 151 matched controls. Children with ASD are stratified into three severity groups using 14 symptom subscales covering core features and co-occurring psychopathologies. Microbiome composition is significantly associated with clinical severity and individual symptoms; however, the proportion of microbiome variance explained by these clinical factors is modest (R 2 = 0.0017–0.0065). Children with higher severity show reduced abundance of Lachnospiraceae bacterium AM48_27BH, a short-chain fatty acid producer, together with reduced predicted capacity of GABA-related modules (GABA synthesis II, putrescine degradation and GHB degradation), while NAD+ salvage pathways show trend-level associations with severity. Sensory atypicalities have the largest number of associated microbial markers and show trend-level links to reduced predicted capacity for degradation of excitatory neurotransmitters. These findings demonstrate that gut microbiome composition varies across the ASD severity spectrum and that different symptom domains differ in their relevance to microbiome alterations. Whether alterations in GABAergic metabolism contribute to clinical severity, and whether microbial features are preferentially linked to sensory atypicalities, remain to be tested in mechanistic and longitudinal studies.

abstract: Inositol-requiring enzyme 1α (IRE1α) and the downstream spliced form of X-Box Binding Protein 1 (XBP1s) have been identified as tumor promotors. However, how IRE1α–XBP1s signaling affects tumor progression in a non-cell autonomous manner remains unclear. Here we show that the hepatocyte IRE1α–XBP1s axis unexpectedly inhibits liver metastasis by confining local metainflammation. Genetic ablation of IRE1α or XBP1 in mouse hepatocytes exacerbates liver metastasis due to the accumulation of inflammatory monocytes (IMs). Mechanistically, a non-canonical Forkhead box O1 (FoxO1)-glutamine synthetase (GS) pathway endows the IRE1α- or XBP1-null hepatocytes with the metabolic activity to secrete glutamine, which is necessary and sufficient for IM fitness. Reintroduction of hepatocyte XBP1s or blockade of glutamine metabolism effectively reduces IMs and mitigates disease progression. Importantly, clinical patient survival with liver metastases positively correlates with hepatocyte XBP1s expression. Our study defines a paradigm of hepatocyte–IM interaction that can be leveraged to treat liver metastasis.

abstract: Neuromuscular compartments provide the functional substrate for finger-specific motor control, yet their in vivo three-dimensional (3D) architecture remains unresolved because of the absence of clear fascial landmarks for imaging. Here, we present a multimodal imaging framework combining ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to provide volumetric compartment segmentation and in vivo architectural reconstruction of the flexor digitorum superficialis. During isolated finger flexion, tissue movement directions estimated from dynamic ultrasound delineate compartment contours, which are mapped into a 3D MRI reference to generate volumetric compartment masks. Using these masks as constraints, tractography reconstructs 3D fiber trajectories and yields compartment-specific architectural measurements. In ten healthy individuals, compartment topology and fiber orientations were consistent with classic cadaveric anatomy, and estimated compartments accurately predicted surface electromyography amplitude distributions. This framework provides 3D fiber trajectories and quantitative parameters for finger-specific computational models, establishing a foundation for subject-specific neuromuscular digital twins and next-generation neuromuscular interfaces.

abstract: Evolutionary relationships among homologous enzymes can be leveraged to introduce large numbers of amino acid substitutions for improved functional properties. Here, we combine evolution-informed design (EVdesign) with rational design to engineer improved poly(ethylene terephthalate) (PET) hydrolases (PETases). Designs derived from multiple PETases reveal strong parent-dependent differences in success and performance, with Thermobifida fusca Tf Cut2 emerging as the most design-amenable scaffold. Increasing sequence diversification reduces the number of active enzymes but broadens performance variance, enabling discovery of high-performing outliers. Four rational mutations overcome a thermostability bottleneck in Tf Cut2 and this variant provides a robust scaffold for iterative EVdesign, which further improves activity. Overall, we experimentally test 603 designs from eight parent PETases. More than 400 variants containing 12-68 substitutions were able to depolymerize PET, nearly all outperforming their parent enzymes, and many approach benchmark LCC-ICCG performance in partial conversion assays. These results establish EVdesign as a robust strategy for generating diverse, high-activity enzymes.

abstract: GWAS have identified thousands of SNPs associated with different human phenotypes. Most SNPs are located in non-coding regions of the genome, where a small subset of causal SNPs is thought to contribute to risk by regulating transcription. However, identification of such causal variants remains challenging due to linkage disequilibrium, where blocks of SNPs are inherited together. Here, we perform a massively parallel reporter assay called SuRE in human neural stem cells to assess the transcriptional regulatory potential of 7.1 million SNPs. We identify 7,002 SNPs with regulatory potential (emVars) among the 484,057 SNPs with sufficiently high expression. These emVars are enriched in enhancers and often coincide with binding sites for transcription factors, such as ZBTB33, YY1, and ETS factors. We overlap SuRE data with eQTL data to pinpoint likely gene-regulatory variants. Additionally, combining SuRE data with GWAS for seven neuropsychiatric phenotypes identifies 187 emVars in risk loci containing 183,186 SNPs assessed by SuRE. In conclusion, our SuRE dataset provides a rich source to prioritize genetic variants that may be relevant for complex human phenotypes.

abstract: The hippocampus serves as a hub of cognition, and its subfields differ in their susceptibility to aging and neurological disorders. Here, we established normative references for hippocampal and subfield volumes using 3D T1-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans from 34,789 healthy individuals (range from 4 to 85 years), revealing varied peak ages (27.4-40.1 years) across subfields. We then mapped the hippocampus and its subfields across various neurological disorders (mild cognitive impairment, Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, cerebral small vessel disease, and multiple sclerosis) by deriving personalized deviation (centile) scores from these references in 3,521 patients. These centile scores captured disease-specific hippocampal abnormalities, supported disease classification, and were associated with cognitive performance, longitudinal cognitive outcomes, and disease progression across disorders. Finally, a personalized hippocampal health report was developed to facilitate clinical translation. These findings demonstrate the value of hippocampal and subfield normative references for personalized diagnosis, cognitive assessment, and prognostic evaluation across neurological diseases.

abstract: Schizophrenia spectrum disorders have substantial genetic liability, but their stable incidence and clinical heterogeneity leave open contributions from non-genetic mechanisms. Though autoimmune encephalitis demonstrates that anti-neural antibodies can cause psychosis, encephalitis antibodies are uncommon in schizophrenia. Here we show that multi-platform autoantigen profiling of cerebrospinal fluid and plasma detects rare, anti-neural autoantibodies in schizophrenia spectrum disorders. By antibody profiling the cerebrospinal fluid of 32 schizophrenia spectrum participants and 32 neuropsychiatrically unaffected controls by brain tissue immunostaining, immunoprecipitation–mass spectrometry, phage display immunoprecipitation sequencing, and plasma by complementary protein microarrays, we identify three autoantibodies, including to alpha-crystallin B. The anti-alpha-crystallin B antibody preferentially recognizes phosphorylated serine-45 and is absent from the cerebrospinal fluid of individuals with untreated multiple sclerosis, a disease with frequent antibodies to unphosphorylated alpha-crystallin B. These findings do not define autoimmune psychosis as a new disease but support broader autoantibody searches in psychotic disorders.

abstract: Low-digestible carbohydrates (LDCs), including dietary fibers and sugars that resist absorption, are generally considered beneficial for the gut microbiota. However, we show that acute overconsumption of certain LDCs, particularly low-digestible sugars (LDSs), such as arabinose, lactulose, and polyols commonly used as sugar substitutes, can compromise colonization resistance against the common foodborne pathogen Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium. LDS overconsumption results in elevated fecal pathogen loads, systemic dissemination, and colitis in infected mice. Mechanistic analysis of arabinose overconsumption revealed that rapid fermentation acidifies the intestinal environment, perturbs the microbiota, alters gut-luminal short-chain fatty acid levels and elevated amino acid availability, which can support pathogen growth. Additionally, this perturbation impacts virulence by broadening tissue tropism (e.g. expansion to small intestine) and selecting for invasive Salmonella . Unlike antibiotic perturbations, Salmonella colonization requires SPI-1 and SPI-2 Type-III-secretion systems, linking virulence to pathogen fitness. These findings reveal how dietary perturbations can impact the gut ecosystem in ways that not only compromise colonization resistance but also enhance pathogen virulence.

abstract: Bacterial conjugation drives horizontal gene transfer and accelerates the spread of antibiotic resistance. In F-plasmid systems, the bifunctional relaxase-helicase TraI initiates transfer by nicking plasmid DNA through its trans-esterase activity and subsequently unwinding the plasmid via its helicase domains. Previous evidence suggested that two TraI molecules act cooperatively, yet how their activities are spatially and temporally coordinated has remained unclear. Here, we report the cryo-EM structure of a functionally asymmetric TraI homodimer and show that dimerisation is mediated predominantly by single-stranded DNA. Trans-esterasedriven duplex melting at the origin of transfer by one TraI molecule enables helicase loading by a second TraI molecule onto the transfer strand of the intact plasmid. Although the trans-esterase domain is intrinsically active, the host factor IHF inhibits nicking until helicase loading occurs. These findings uncover a regulatory loop coupling strand nicking with helicase engagement, defining a unified mechanism for initiating conjugative DNA processing.

abstract: Protein-protein interactions (PPIs) in diseased tissues represent a promising class of potential drug targets. However, PPIs are typically identified in live cells, lysate, and genetically engineered model organisms, limiting their translational value to human disease. Here we describe MAP-IT, an optimized photocatalytic carbene-based proximity labeling method for direct PPI mapping in primary human tissue sections, which bypasses the need for model organisms in the initial discovery step. We use MAP-IT to profile PPIs in situ for cell surface and nuclear target proteins, identify and orthogonally validate new interactors of EGFR in colon cancer, and couple light-powered MAP-IT labeling with spatially patterned visible light irradiation guided by neural network image segmentation to map location-specific protein interactomes.

abstract: Numerous undescribed species face extinction before formal scientific recognition. Despite research advances, the exceptional bat diversity of the Neotropics remains overlooked, with accelerating habitat loss threatening unrecognized lineages with silent extinction, requiring urgent conservation prioritization. Here, we integrate molecular species delimitation, phylogenetic inference, ecological niche modelling, and spatial conservation analyses to identify 95 Neotropical bat lineages that may represent undescribed species within 45 complexes, revealing that at least one-fifth of the recognized taxa may harbor hidden diversity spanning the entire evolutionary spectrum. This overlooked diversity faces a countdown to extinction: 62% of complexes face imminent habitat loss, and most are projected to lose over 50% of their suitable habitat by 2070. At current description rates, formally recognizing this diversity would take decades, a timeframe these putative species cannot afford. We develop a Hidden Species Richness (HSR) Index that pinpoints ten hidden diversity hotspots where undescribed richness coincides with significant human threats and extreme climate vulnerability. These hotspots highlight regions where research efforts are most needed, transforming crises into priorities. This race against extinction requires immediate taxonomic attention to document this biodiversity before it vanishes.

abstract: Sexual maturation and fertility of the malaria-causing parasite, Plasmodium spp., are critical to transmission between hosts. This developmental process involves an intricate gene expression regulatory network that drives gametocyte commitment, development, and the production of male and female gametes. Here, we characterize the role of the CCCH-type zinc-finger protein Plasmodium falciparum Male Development 3 ( Pf MD3) in the formation of gametes. Genetic disruption of Pf MD3 reveals a male fertility defect that decreases infectivity to mosquitoes. Molecular characterization of Pf MD3 reveals its binding to mRNA transcripts is associated with male gamete development through a specific RNA sequence. Gametocyte proteins encoded by these Pf MD3-bound transcripts decrease significantly in Pf MD3 knockout parasites, suggesting that Pf MD3 impacts translation. In addition to RNA-binding, Pf MD3 also interacts with proteins involved in mRNA processing and nuclear export that influence translational regulation. This study establishes Pf MD3 as an RNA-binding protein that impacts lineage-specific translation and male gamete fertility.

abstract: An age-related neurovascular impairment in nitric oxide (NO)-mediated vasodilation and reciprocal Piezo1-dependent vascular vasoconstriction may precede the accumulation of soluble brain proteins such as amyloid-β (Aβ) and disruption of brain fluid homeostasis in Alzheimer’s disease (AD). Preclinical studies suggest that restoring these pathways can enhance neurofluid transport and improve cognitive outcomes. In this study (EudraCT 2021-000625-27), we investigated the effects of sublingual NO and Piezo1-targeted whole-body vibrations (WBV p ) in healthy adults ( n = 29) using multimodal neuroimaging and blood biomarker analysis. The combined intervention (NO+WBV p ) was associated with correlating changes in brain fluid dynamics and increased blood levels of soluble brain-derived proteins (Aβ 40&42 , GFAP). These effects increased with age and the magnitude of NO-induced hypotension. The interventions were well tolerated under controlled experimental conditions. Overall, the findings are consistent with transient redistribution of brain-derived proteins toward circulation, suggesting a potential non-invasive approach to increase neurofluidic solute efflux in humans. Pre-specified primary endpoints, changes in circulating brain-derived protein concentrations, brain fluid imaging and brain pulsation measures, were met. Secondary outcomes included physiological analyses.

title: Visual LLM-guided consensus spatial domain detection with L-STAR

abstract: Spatial transcriptomics measures gene activity while preserving the locations of cells within tissue. A key analysis step is to divide the tissue into spatial domains, but the performance of computational methods varies considerably across datasets, and no single method consistently performs best. Here we show that a large language model can compare spatial domain maps and identify the better-performing methods. We developed L-STAR, which visually compares and ranks candidate methods, then builds a consensus map from the highest-ranked results. Across datasets representing different tissues, species, and technologies, L-STAR matched expert annotations more closely than individual methods or consensus analysis using a fixed set of methods. Its rankings were reproducible and generally stable when image colors or presentation order changed. L-STAR also provided rationales for its comparisons and assigned biologically meaningful names to the detected domains. These findings show that large language models can make spatial transcriptomics analysis more adaptive, robust, and interpretable.

abstract: Capturing the fine details of behavior when animals perform complex tasks, such as prey pursuit and capture, in natural environments is a challenging endeavor. For birds of prey, commonly used tracking approaches, such as lightweight GPS and inertial measurement units, cannot simultaneously track the bird’s position and the fine details of body part motion or moving external objects. Here we designed a head-mounted, tetherless, 4π camera system which, combined with a high-resolution environmental scan, enabled detailed three-dimensional measurement of both head position and orientation in freely flying Harris’s hawks ( Parabuteo unicinctus ) performing aerial pursuit in the wild. This stable head-mounted imaging approach enabled reconstruction of flight trajectories in natural environments, detailed quantification of head motion, optic flow and target position, while the bird tracked and captured airborne targets.

abstract: De novo peptide sequencing enables peptide identification from fragmentation spectra without relying on sequence databases. However, incomplete spectra create ambiguity, making unambiguous identification challenging. Recent deep learning advances have produced numerous de novo models that predict sequences and refine peptide-spectrum matches under such conditions. Yet, their relative strengths, weaknesses and ability to handle spectrum ambiguity remain unclear. Here we benchmark eight state-of-the-art models on three publicly available proteomics datasets, comparing performance using established metrics and quantifying inter-model agreement. We assess post-processing approaches, including iterative refinement, rescoring and reranking, for their ability to improve identification accuracy, and perform an error analysis to identify common mispredictions and their causes. Model performance varied, with considerable overlap of correct identifications. Post-processing yielded no or only modest improvements. Most sequencing errors were model-independent and driven by limited fragment ion coverage, a limitation also observed in database searches with large search spaces.

A Bayesian Optimized Biquad Filter-Burg Model for Real-Time EEG Phase Estimation
abstract: Real-time phase estimation on stimulus-aligned transient EEG is critical for closed-loop neuromodulation systems targeting the theta-band, yet most real-time phase estimation methods have been developed and validated on resting-state, high-fidelity signals in the alpha band. Recent work has pursued deep learning architectures, while individualized classical bandpass filter tuning remains underexplored. This study characterizes the spectral and temporal properties of non-anticipative bandpass filtering and demonstrates the performance gains achieved through individualized tuning. We present a Bayesian-Optimized Biquad Filter-Burg (BOB) model evaluated on EEG recorded during peripheral vibrotactile stimulation of the left median nerve (theta, N=20 healthy subjects) and on resting-state recordings from the Max Planck Institute's LEMON dataset (alpha, N=20 healthy subjects). BOB was benchmarked against the Deep Dual-Branch Complex Neural Network (DBCNN), EEG Phase Prediction Network (EPN), Phastimate, and Phase Estimation with Autoregressive Padding (PEAP) under matched testing conditions: channel selection, individualized optimization, evaluation time points, and an offline reference phase obtained through zero-phase filtering and the Hilbert transform. Under these testing conditions, BOB achieved matched or better performance than these models at a fraction of the calibration time.
comment: 24 pages, 12 figures (9 main, 3 supplements)

title: Ablating Design Choices for Protein Ensemble Generators Across Structural Regimes
abstract: Generative models of protein conformational ensembles inherit much of their design from structure prediction for folded proteins. Ordered and disordered proteins, however, occupy distinct structural regimes, and we investigate how design choices hold up across them. Using a minimal C$α$ flow-matching model, we ablate choices of architecture, sequence conditioning, rigid-body alignment and training source, and evaluate each variant against experimental SAXS and NMR chemical-shift data partitioned into ordered, disordered, multi-domain and transitional proteins. Mixture-of-experts routing, a static pair representation and a disorder probe have no detectable effect, a smaller protein language model performs worse on ordered proteins but not on disordered ones, and alignment in the loss degrades agreement with SAXS. Replacing coarse-grained simulations of disordered proteins with fragment-assembled ensembles improves agreement with chemical shifts at a cost to SAXS, while an equal mixture of the two keeps most of the gain at a smaller cost. This points to the training data, rather than the architecture, as the main constraint.
comment: 13 pages, 2 figures

title: Curriculum unlearning in humans and neural networks
abstract: During learning, humans often benefit from curricula that teach simple rules before exceptions. However, we lack a computational explanation for this phenomenon. Here, using a canonical behavioural task and modelling with neural networks, we develop and test a theory for why simple-to-complex curricula succeed. We show that during learning, both humans and neural networks show simplicity biases, a tendency to learn simple rules that are underfit to the data. In neural networks this bias is accompanied by compression of neural representations. Simple-to-complex curricula help both types of learners overcome this compression, developing representations (and policy) with appropriate dimensionality for the task. We test and confirm a further prediction from this theory: learners that have been pre-exposed to simple tasks and with more compressed initial representations benefit more from curricula. These findings suggest that curricula help with ``unlearning'' of simple rules.

title: Empirical Bayes Flow Matching for Continuous Cryo-EM Heterogeneity
abstract: We address the problem of learning generative priors over high-dimensional latent variables from indirect, noisy observations, with a focus on continuous heterogeneity in cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM). In this setting, 3D atomic structures $x \in \mathbb{R}^{3N_a}$ are never directly observed and must be inferred from 2D projection images $y$ generated by a complex, non-linear forward operator. We propose Empirical Bayes Flow Matching (EB-FM), a method that learns a flow matching prior $p_θ(x)$ directly from observations using a Monte Carlo stochastic approximation Expectation-Maximization framework. EB-FM alternates between an E-step that performs approximate posterior sampling from $p_θ(x \mid y)$ via guided flow-based generation while maintaining persistent latent estimates through stochastic approximation, and an M-step that updates the flow model using these stabilized latent variables as training targets. This approach eliminates the need for pretraining on clean data and naturally accommodates non-linear forward models. We validate our method on controlled inverse problems using two-moons and MNIST data, and demonstrate its effectiveness on simulated cryo-EM data with known poses, showing that EB-FM can recover continuous distributions of protein conformations directly in atomic-coordinate space.

title: GINsim 3.1: Qualitative modelling and dynamical analysis of logical regulatory networks
abstract: GINsim is a software for the definition and dynamical analysis of qualitative (Boolean and multi-valued) models of biological regulatory networks. Building on its modular architecture, based on the MDDlib decision-diagram and bioLQM model-manipulation libraries, GINsim version 3.1 introduces new functionalities aimed at the analysis of large logical models: the symbolic computation of trap-spaces, the Booleanisation of multilevel models and the reversal of model dynamics. GINsim 3.1 also extends the estimation of attractor reachability (Monte Carlo and Avatar algorithms), the computation of stable states, as well as model reduction functionalities. Analyses can be applied to perturbed models, and scripted, in particular from the CoLoMoTo interactive notebook. We illustrate the main functionalities of GINsim on a reference multilevel model of regulatory network that control the mammalian cell cycle, including the computation of its stable states and cyclic attractor, the assessment of their reachability, and the identification of the regulatory circuits driving multistability and oscillations. GINsim is freely available under GPL-3.0 at https://ginsim.github.io/, runs on any platform supporting Java, and is interoperable with the other tools of the CoLoMoTo community. Its website provides installation instructions and reference documentation, as well as a repository of Boolean and multilevel logical models.

title: Predicting protein structures at any folding stage from sequence
abstract: Protein structure prediction has largely focused on native conformations, leaving the continuum of unfolded states, folding intermediates, and native structures difficult to access. We present FoldScape, a sequence-conditioned deep learning framework for generating protein conformational ensembles at specified folding fractions $Q$. Trained on approximately one million conformations from 10,000 protein sequences, FoldScape combines coarse-grained folding and all-atom mechanical-unfolding trajectories. It reconstructs three-dimensional $C_α$ chains through hierarchical sliding-window regressions of inter-residue distances, chain-level assembly, and a rectified-flow decoder. By conditioning on folding progress, FoldScape generates conformations from unfolded states through intermediates to native-state structures without protein-specific molecular dynamics at inference. In matched-sample comparisons, FoldScape achieves median conformational-space coverage of 0.989, 0.722, and 0.877 along radius of gyration, fraction of native contacts $Q$, and secondary-structure fraction, respectively, versus 0.05, 0.05, and 0.10 for seed-varied AlphaFold 3 ensembles. Coverage advantages are consistent across the evaluated proteins and robust to binning choices. Reconstruction accuracy remains approximately stable across the evaluated stages of a folding trajectory, and stride-one crop-and-superpose inference extends predictions to chains several times longer than the single-pass limit. Analyses of mechanical-unfolding trajectories show residue-resolved pathways, reproducible extension-conditioned observables across pulling velocities, and geometrically coherent segments in partially unfolded chains. FoldScape extends sequence-based structure prediction beyond a single folded endpoint to controllable conformational-ensemble generation across protein folding.

title: Trail systems self-organize through individual route optimization
abstract: As animals, including humans, walk, they compact the vegetation and ground beneath them, reducing the cost of movement for subsequent travelers. From this positive feedback emerge networks of trails which allow for efficient movement and store generational-scale information about the environment. Models simulating this process show how individuals following local cues produce trail systems with many of the features of real-world networks. However, little has been done to investigate walkers with more complete knowledge of their environment and the abilities to plan their behavior intelligently. Here we introduce a simple general model for trail formation, based on minimizing cost of movement by individuals. As in real environments, our simulations produce a striking variety of complex trail networks. We show that these trail systems optimally connect space according to the spatial needs of the walkers, that the geometry of those trail systems matches theoretical predictions and that the systems they generate may fall into multiple attracting states. As technological advances allow us to quantify trail systems across diverse habitats and species, our model provides a theoretical foundation for empirical research on animal trails and for understanding the emergence of human transportation networks, with implications for urban design.

title: iGC: Antibody Optimization via Reinforcement Learning over a Learned Somatic Hypermutation Prior
abstract: Antibody affinity maturation is a natural optimization process in which B cells acquire mutations through somatic hypermutation (SHM), undergo selection for improved antigen binding, and iteratively evolve toward higher affinity. Computationally modeling this process requires capturing both biologically plausible mutations and antigen-specific selection. However, existing mutation models do not directly optimize binding, while affinity optimization often neglects realistic mutation trajectories. We introduce iGC (in silico Germinal Centers), a two-stage reinforcement learning (RL) framework for antigen-specific antibody optimization. Stage 1 learns an SHM mutation prior from parent-child pairs in B-cell lineage trees and adapts it to a target affinity-maturation dataset. Stage 2 initializes an RL policy from this prior and optimizes antigen binding with Kullback-Leibler (KL) regularization toward the frozen prior. To prevent reward exploitation, including repetitive high-reward substitutions and structurally tolerated framework mutations, we introduce a Reward-Tax Meta-Gradient objective. RewardNet smooths the affinity landscape, while TaxNet penalizes reward overexploitation, jointly defining a learned meta-reward for policy optimization. We evaluate iGC on mutation prediction, SHM consistency, affinity optimization, and mutation diversity. The mutation prior more than doubles the strongest baseline in mutation-site prediction. Following RL optimization, iGC maintains SHM sequence structure. It also achieves a strong exploration-exploitation balance, yielding competitive reward-diversity products across candidate-selection cutoffs. These results demonstrate that iGC integrates biologically plausible mutation generation with antigen-specific affinity selection, providing an in silico framework for iterative antibody affinity maturation.
comment: 10 pages with supplementary documents

title: A Biologically Inspired Attention Model for Neural Signal Analysis
abstract: Understanding how the brain represents sensory information and triggers behavioural responses is a fundamental goal in neuroscience. Recent advances in neuronal recording techniques aim to progress towards this milestone, yet the resulting high-dimensional responses are challenging to interpret and link to relevant variables. Although existing machine learning models propose to do so, they often sacrifice interpretability for predictive power, effectively operating as black boxes. In this work, we introduce SPARKS, a biologically inspired model capable of high decoding accuracy and interpretable discovery within a single framework. SPARKS adapts the self-attention mechanism of large language models to extract information from the timing of single spikes and the sequence in which neurons fire using Hebbian learning. Trained with a criterion inspired by predictive coding to enforce temporal coherence, our model produces low-dimensional latent embeddings that are robust across sessions and animals. By directly capturing the underlying data distribution through a generative encoding-decoding framework, SPARKS matches or exceeds state-of-the-art decoders across diverse electrophysiology and calcium imaging datasets from the motor, visual and entorhinal cortices. Crucially, the Hebbian coefficients learned by the model are interpretable, allowing us to infer directed functional interactions and recover the known functional hierarchy of the mouse visual cortex. Overall, SPARKS unifies representation learning, high-performance decoding and model interpretability in a single framework by bridging neuroscience and AI, providing a powerful and versatile tool for dissecting neural computations and marking a step towards the next generation of biologically inspired intelligent systems.

title: A Comparison and Validation of BIDS Apps for Preprocessing of UCB-J PET data
abstract: Background Preprocessing of Positron Emission Tomography (PET) data can be performed in many different ways and often involves manual steps, resulting in reduced comparability across analyses and pipelines. Apps working on PET data organized according to the Brain Imaging Data Structure (BIDS) seek to automate preprocessing, enabling the application of standardized pipelines that increase comparability and reproducibility. In this study, two of these apps were validated against in-house software. Methods Data were acquired in-house from 14 subjects who received placebo in a randomized controlled clinical trial and underwent two PET measurements using the radioligand [11C]UCB-J. Preprocessing was performed with two BIDS Apps, PETPrep and PICNIC, as well as an in-house software. Arterial blood data were processed using Bloodstream, and [11C]UCB-J total distribution volume (VT) values were calculated using a 1-tissue compartment model using kinfitr. Results VT values for all 9 regions of interest were highly consistent across tools with estimates of Intraclass Correlation Coefficients for consistency ranging between 0.94 and >0.99, although bias between tools measured as signed Percentage Difference was present, ranging from 0.1% - 10.2% depending on the region. Tools performed similarly on test-retest metrics. We observed a negative test-retest bias in [11C]UCB-J VT of unknown origin. Conclusion BIDS Apps produce reliable and consistent results when compared both with each other and with an in-house software optimized for processing and analysis of our in-house data. Region-dependant bias between tools warrants caution for direct comparison of VT between tools. The usage of these apps could enable better comparability across publications

title: A Preventive Effect of Exercise in a Mouse Model of Essential Tremor
abstract: The effects of exercise have not been widely studied for potential benefits in essential tremor (ET), while this has been growing for other neurodegenerative disorders. This study examines the effects of two types of exercise [high-intensity interval training (HIIT) and resistance training (RT)] on mice that were subjected to harmaline injections to trigger tremor. We employed a repeated-measures design with three groups: a HIIT group, a RT group, and a sedentary (SED) control group. Each group received an injection before and after the intervention. Tremor kinetics (power within the 8-14 and 14-29 Hz bands) were assessed using accelerometry. Tremor kinematics were also assessed using high-speed video analysis, for validation. As potential signalling molecules from exercise, we also tested for blood lactate and BDNF in each group. Compared to pre-intervention measurements, we found a significant decrease in power within the 8-14 Hz band combined with an increase in the 14-29 Hz band, for the HIIT group, but not in the RT or SED groups. We also found a change in BDNF concentration for the HIIT group. These results suggest that the HIIT protocol may have helped the animal to shift tremor frequency to higher bands, thereby offering functional resistance to harmaline-induced tremor. This study supports high intensity aerobic physical exercise as a potential therapeutic/preventive intervention for ET, with translational implications for human studies.

title: A VTA-pontine GABA pathway biases locomotor direction via local and distal inhibition
abstract: Locomotor direction in mammals is implemented by descending circuits, yet how midbrain selection systems bias directional motor output remains unclear. Here we define a projection-defined inhibitory pathway from the ventral tegmental area to the oral pontine reticular nucleus (VTAPnO) whose activation is sufficient to drive backward locomotion. These TH- VTA neurons form monosynaptic GABAA synapses locally while projecting to PnO, establishing a dual local-projection inhibitory architecture. Somatic activation reliably induced backward locomotion, and selective stimulation of VTAPnO terminals reproduced the effect. Pathway recruitment produced a rapid transient increase in dopaminergic single-unit activity and frequency-dependent increases in dopaminergic population calcium signals in awake mice. During forced locomotion, chronically recorded VTAPnO neurons were preferentially engaged during reverse compared to forward rotations. Together, these findings reveal a projection-defined midbrain pathway that biases locomotor direction through coordinated local inhibition and distal engagement of a brainstem premotor node.
author_corresponding_institution: Leibniz Institute for Neurobiology, Magdeburg, Germany;  Aligning Science Across Parkinson's (ASAP) CRN, Chevy Chase, USA;Departamento de Anatomía, Escuela de M

title: A Whole-Mouse-Brain Model of Coupled Neural Masses: Analysis of Network Dynamics
abstract: Neural mass models coupled through empirical structural connectomes are widely used to simulate whole-brain activity, but the dynamics of the resulting large, delay-coupled networks are rarely analyzed directly. We present a dynamical systems analysis of 434 Jansen-Rit neural masses coupled by the Allen Mouse Brain Connectivity Atlas at the canonical single-node parameter values. Pseudo-arclength continuation of the network equilibria in the global coupling scale and in the baseline external input, with stability determined from the characteristic roots of the delayed linearization by Beyn's contour-integral method, indicates where the network must oscillate and where it can rest. Simulations show that the oscillatory regime is chaotic: the maximum Lyapunov exponent is positive for the empirical connectome, grows with network size and coupling scale, and is insensitive to the conduction delays, but it is suppressed when the arrangement of connection weights is flattened, shuffled, or rewired. The same weight modifications that suppress chaos drive the network toward full synchrony and abolish metastability, as measured by the Kuramoto order parameter. We discuss the consequences of these findings for fitting whole-brain neural mass models to empirical data.
author_corresponding_institution: University of Cincinnati College of Medicine

title: A domain-general basal ganglia mechanism for inhibitory control during language comprehension
abstract: Whether controlled language processing involves domain-general or language-specific neural circuits is subject of controversial debate. We tested whether the inhibitory control of linguistic activity shares a common neural process with motor inhibition in twenty humans undergoing intra- and extracranial neural field potential recordings and deep-brain stimulation. Engaging motor and linguistic inhibition simultaneously resulted in a significant behavioral cost, suggesting a shared underlying neural process. Indeed, neural decoders trained during motor inhibition were able to decode linguistic inhibition and vice versa. Depth-electrode recordings from the subthalamic nucleus (STN), a key basal ganglia area for inhibitory control, showed increased {beta}-band (13-30 Hz) activity during both linguistic and motor inhibition. Finally, disrupting the STN via deep-brain stimulation impaired behavioral and neural signatures of both linguistic and motor inhibition. Together, these findings show that the inhibitory control of language and movement share a domain-general mechanism implemented via the subthalamic nucleus of the basal ganglia.

title: A hypothalamo-septo-hippocampal circuit for REM sleep-dependent consolidation of social memory
abstract: REM sleep constitutes a critical window for memory consolidation, yet the brain circuits orchestrating this process remain incompletely defined. Here, we identify a lateral supramammillary nucleus (SuM)-medial septum (MS) projection as a REM sleep-specialized pathway essential for hippocampal memory consolidation. Fiber photometry and optrode recordings revealed that lateral SuM-MS projecting neurons were selectively active during REM sleep. REM-specific optogenetic silencing of this projection impaired consolidation of both social and contextual fear memories. Crucially, silencing of its downstream target, the MS-CA2 pathway, during REM sleep selectively disrupted social memory while sparing contextual fear memory. This functional dissection establishes a hypothalamo-septo-hippocampal circuit (lateral SuM-MS-CA2) dedicated to social memory processing, in parallel to the recently-described direct SuM-CA2 pathway. These results also position the SuM as a REM sleep-hub that routes information via parallel septal pathways to consolidate distinct memory modalities.
author_corresponding_institution: Chongqing Institute for Brain and Intelligence

title: A medial entorhinal connectome reveals compartmentalized microcircuit architecture
abstract: The medial entorhinal cortex (MEC) transforms multimodal inputs into spatial representations, but the synaptic architecture underlying its computations remains unclear. Here we generated a synapse-resolution connectomic dataset spanning all six layers of mouse MEC and the adjacent parasubiculum with serial electron microscopy, providing a continuous volume for mapping cellular organization and connectivity across layers and regions. We found that clustered pyramidal neurons in MEC layer II extended oblique apical dendrites with a dorsolateral bias and long-range myelinated axons within the layer. Exhaustive reconstruction of one cluster revealed a central exclusion core (ExC) that spatially partitioned basal dendritic architecture and synaptic connectivity. A spatially constrained growth model reproduced the position-dependent dendritic patterns. Within the ExC, pyramidal neurons formed a compact recurrent excitatory network and converged onto shared inhibitory partners. Basket cells (BC) and recurrent Martinotti cells provided perisomatic and apical-dendritic feedback, respectively. Dense, compact reciprocal connectivity between L2P neurons and BCs within the ExC, together with BC axonal bands extending beyond the ExC, suggests a potential circuit mechanism for generating temporally structured inhibitory output from the pyramidal-cell cluster along directionally extended axons. Together, these findings link cellular-scale geometry and synaptic wiring to emergent circuit dynamics that extend from dense computation within individual clusters to region-wide modulation, providing a connectomic foundation for understanding the circuit basis of spatial navigation.
author_corresponding_institution: Anhui Province Key Laboratory of Biomedical Imaging and Intelligent Processing, Institute of Artificial Intelligence, Hefei Comprehensive National Science Cente

title: A phase decoder for reconstructing missing muscle activity
abstract: Upper-limb assistive devices are commonly controlled with electromyographic (EMG) signals, but nerve injury, muscle loss, or practical limits on electrode placement can leave only a few usable signals, which constrains the decoding of intended movements. Here, we introduce a decoder that reconstructs missing muscle activations from sparse EMGs using a two-stage real-time approach: (1) estimating ongoing movement phase from available signals, and (2) retrieving corresponding muscle activations from a library of pre-recorded muscle activity templates. In proof-of-concept tests, neurologically intact participants (N=4) performed object-transfer tasks under simulated denervation conditions. The decoder accurately estimated movement phase (median root-mean-square error [RMSE] <0.17 of movement duration) and reconstructed missing muscle activations (RMSE 0.08-0.34; correlation up to 0.97) within ~2 ms, in a previously unseen participant. The results indicate that template based reconstruction could leverage sparse EMG for low latency control of assistive technology.

title: A single dose of the antipsychotic drug clozapine has long-term behavioral and functional effects in mice
abstract: Antipsychotic dosing regimens, commonly daily or via slow-release compounds, are designed to maintain steady-state plasma concentrations. They are guided by their plasma half-life, which is typically in the range of several hours. This schedule contrasts with the slow time course of therapeutic efficacy, which takes days to weeks to develop fully. This discrepancy led us to hypothesize that the effects of a single dose of an antipsychotic drug might be detectable well beyond the time window predicted by receptor occupancy. To test this, we administered a single dose of the antipsychotic drug clozapine to mice. We observed long-term behavioral effects and changes to cortical activity patterns up to several days after administration. Specifically, clozapine induced a decorrelation of activity in the dorsal cortex observable up to 9 days post administration. This effect was driven by a genetically and functionally distinct subset of layer 5 intratelencephalic neurons and was accompanied by an increase in the reliability of long-range inhibitory functional influence on a similar timescale. Thus, a single dose of clozapine triggers changes in the function of specific circuits that outlast the presence of the drug. If antipsychotic action depends on slower processes involving plasticity, longer dosing intervals may warrant further clinical exploration.
author_corresponding_institution: Friedrich Miescher Institute for Biomedical Research (FMI)

title: A vagal-to-sympathetic reflex controls lung vascular leak
abstract: Dynamic regulation of the vascular barrier is required for innate immunity, yet excessive leak endangers vulnerable organs like the lungs, where edema stiffens tissue and threatens breathing. Using a chemogenetic screen, we discover a vagal-to-sympathetic reflex that controls pulmonary vascular leak. The reflex originates in a previously-uncharacterized population of polymodal, alveolus-innervating vagal sensory neurons marked by Cysltr2. Stimulating CYSLTR2 neurons increases lung fluid within minutes, whereas sustained activation elicits perivascular edema and respiratory dysfunction. Silencing them during allergen challenge reduces leak and improves lung mechanics. Rather than acting locally, CYSLTR2 neurons relay centrally to sympathetic efferents to broadcast effects throughout lung vasculature. This pathway thus forms an axis of organ defense that can go awry in disease, suggesting new ways to control lung fluid balance.

title: ADRA2B genetic polymorphism modulates vagus nerve stimulation response
abstract: Introduction. Given interest in vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) as a potential therapy for Alzheimer's disease, due to its hypothesized influence on the noradrenergic (NA) system, there is a need to understand the pronounced individual differences in responsiveness to VNS in aging. We tested whether a genetic polymorphism related to NA signaling, the {Delta}301-303 deletion in the ADRA2B receptor, modulates transcutaneous auricular (taVNS) effects on task-related pupillary responses or pupil-linked cortical activity in noradrenergic projection territory. Methods. Forty-one adults (61% deletion carriers; ages 19-79) performed a visual oddball task during a sham-controlled single-blind crossover taVNS trial. Of these people, 25 (68% deletion carriers) also performed the same task with simultaneous fMRI. Results. ADRA2B genotype predicted the taVNS effect on oddball pupillary responses (t(37) = 3.03, p = .004, d = 0.84). Deletion carrier responses were more likely to increase, while non-carrier responses decreased. Carriers showed stronger spatial alignment between pupil-BOLD coupling and cortical norepinephrine transporter (NET) expression (t(22) = 2.82, p = .010, adjusted d = 1.21). This difference was selective to NET among 19 PET maps (all other p > .11). The individual effect of taVNS predicted NET alignment of pupil-BOLD coupling ({rho} = .45, p = .023). Conclusions. ADRA2B {Delta}301-303 deletion status, which is thought to increase NA availability, predicts the direction of the pupillary response to taVNS and how tightly pupil-linked BOLD activity aligns with cortical noradrenergic projection territory.

title: APP functions at the endomembrane system
abstract: INTRODUCTION: APP is a type I transmembrane protein, and its intracellular domain (AICD) interacts with FE65, X11, and mDAB1, et al., through the YENPTY motif. Accordingly, it has been proposed that the functions of APP are similar to Notch, which regulates gene expression through releasing NICD after combining with its ligands. However, the detailed underlying mechanisms of how FE65 is regulated by APP, as well as their target genes, remain unknown. METHODS: We overexpressed APP695 in N2a cells, and deleted/mutated APP in H4 cells by CRISPR-Cas9, respectively. The impacts of APP overexpression and ablation were detected by proteome comparison and immunoblotting. Thereafter, the subcellular localizations of APP and its binding protein FE65 were examined by immunofluorescence. RESULTS: APP overexpression not only resulted in its retention in Golgi apparatus (GA) and Endoplasmic reticulum (ER), but also induced FE65 clustering. In addition, it significantly reduced the protein level of ATF4 in N2a cells. On the contrary, knockdown of FE65 restored the protein level of ATF4. More importantly, APP overexpression also impaired autophagy. In contrast, knockout of APP rescued LC3 conversion. Of note, the APP Swedish mutant did not impact ER stress or the autophagic flux. Nevertheless, it facilitated the cleavage of APP-CTFs by gamma-secretase. DISCUSSION: The evidence presented in the current study demonstrates that APP is involved in stabilizing the endomembrane system and the subcellular transport of FE65. More importantly, the role of APP in regulating autophagy indicated that full-length APP could be considered a therapeutic target for preventing the development of AD.

title: Active vision modulates early cortical stages of visual processing: Evidence from MEG and eye-tracking
abstract: Vision is fundamentally active. Humans and other mammals make several saccadic eye movements per second. This feature of mammalian vision has received increasing interest across the last decades and many behavioural and neurophysiological studies have investigated how the visual system accounts for the effects of self-generated motion (efference copy) in perceptual processing. Still, it is often believed that, besides accounting for the efference copy and for the rhythmic modulation of activity due to perpetual saccade-fixation cycles, active vision does not further modulate neural processing of visual input obtained during periods of fixation. In contrast, using a gaze-contingent trans-saccadic change design with concurrent MEG and eye-tracking data recording from human participants, we find sequential history effects in visual cortices. Harnessing the preview effect, we show that primary visual and ventral occipital cortices respond differently when eye-movements bring objects into focus compared to when the same objects appear during steady fixation. Specifically, we find that sequential modulations of cortical processing across saccades, in the form of preview effects, are increased during active vision compared to steady-gaze control conditions. Our data also show that these sequential modulations cannot be explained by any type of adaptation alone. Our study, therefore, provides an update on the role of active vision in modulating cortical function.

title: Apolipoprotein E4 Exacerbates Aβ Oligomer-Induced Synaptotoxicity through Promoting Autophagic Degradation of Glutathione Peroxidase 4
abstract: Extensive synaptic loss and progressive neurodegeneration are defining pathological hallmarks of Alzheimer's disease (AD), primarily driven by soluble A{beta} oligomers and neurofibrillary tangles. The apolipoprotein E4 (APOE4) isoform further aggravates these pathological cascades, yet the precise molecular mechanisms underlying AD pathogenesis remain poorly elucidated. Store-operated calcium entry (SOCE) deficiency in neurons has been proven to exert a detrimental effect on dendritic spine integrity and function. Herein, we investigated whether SOCE dysregulation contributes to A{beta}O-induced synaptotoxicity and how APOE4 modulates this pathological process. In primary neuronal cultures, co-treatment with A{beta}O and APOE4 markedly reduced synapse density and impaired dendritic arbor complexity, compared with A{beta}O treatments combined with APOE3 or APOE2 isoforms. Consistently, neurons exposed to A{beta}O plus APOE4 exhibited significantly lower SOCE amplitudes than those treated with A{beta}O and APOE3. In line with SOCE suppression, the A{beta}O/APOE4 combination specifically downregulated stromal interaction molecule 1 (STIM1) protein expression, with no observable change in STIM2 levels. Mechanistically, A{beta}O/APOE4-mediated STIM1 reduction was dependent on p62-selective autophagic degradation. Notably, exogenous STIM1 overexpression effectively rescued the deficits in dendritic arbor complexity. Furthermore, STIM1 downregulation induced by A{beta}O and APOE4 initiated the autophagic degradation of glutathione peroxidase 4 (Gpx4). This autophagy activation was attributed to decreased Bcl2 expression and occurs independently of STING accumulation. Subsequent Gpx4 insufficiency further triggered excessive accumulation of reactive oxygen species and disrupted mitochondrial cristae morphology in neurons. Collectively, our findings uncover a previously unrecognized mechanism whereby APOE4 exacerbates A{beta}O-induced synaptotoxicity. Specifically, the combination facilitates p62-mediated selective autophagic degradation of STIM1, which suppresses Bcl2 expression and ultimately promotes robust Gpx4 autophagic degradation, driving neuronal synaptic damage.

title: Assessing reinforcement learning and vigor with an online decision-making battery
abstract: Reinforcement learning and vigor are two fundamental aspects of decision-making modulated by dopamine. Although vigor is highly relevant for mood disorders, it has been overlooked by previous batteries characterizing decision-making abilities. We developed a test battery with two RL tasks (RL/working memory, go/no-go task) and two vigor tasks (physical effort discounting, foraging task) and administered it to an online community sample (N = 162). We used computational modeling and factor analysis to identify two factors reflecting RL and vigor. The RL factor reflected participants' general decision-making ability, while vigor corresponded to a motivational propensity to obtain rewards. Both factors demonstrated moderately strong test-retest reliability (ICC(2,1) = .65 and .67, respectively) over a one-to-two-week interval. Moreover, both factors were meaningfully related to self-report scales. The RL and vigor factors were negatively and positively associated with mania, respectively, although further analyses revealed that vigor was not fully independent of RL. Neither factor was significantly associated with depression symptoms. Collectively, we present preliminary evidence that vigor may represent a separate factor from RL in line with the putative dopamine hypothesis, paving the way for future longitudinal assessments of RL and vigor in mood disorders.

title: Association between white-matter lesion volume and heart-rate variability: A comparison of T1w, T1w+T2w and T1w+FLAIR-based segmentations using FreeSurfer SAMSEG
abstract: Background Heart disease is a crucial risk factor for brain degeneration, but the specific mechanisms of this association are still under investigation. Notably, the development of white-matter lesions, a hallmark of cerebral small-vessel disease with connections to progressive neurodegeneration and cognitive decline, has been linked to cardiovascular disease. As such, measures of cardiovascular function such as heart-rate variability may represent accessible indicators of white-matter lesion burden. Methods This study used data from healthy adults drawn from the Leipzig Study for Mind-Body-Emotion Interactions (LEMON) dataset to examine heart function through measures of heart-rate variability, as well as their relationship to cerebral small-vessel disease as quantified through white-matter lesion volumes, using FreeSurfer SAMSEG. White-matter lesion volumes were segmented using 3-Tesla T1w+FLAIR, T1w+T2w or T1w images alone. Results Unadjusted exploratory results suggested that lower heart-rate variability was associated with higher lesion volume, a cerebral hallmark of hypertension. After controlling for the effect of age on lesion volume, low-frequency heart rate variability specifically was found to interact with age-related lesion volume. Moreover, we showed that the relationship between white-matter lesion volume and heart-rate variability is apparent using T1w+FLAIR or T1w+T2w based lesion estimates could be observed with T1w-based lesion estimation alone, opening new avenues for studying cerebral small-vessel disease. Discussion These results suggest heart rate variability as a factor in the translation between cardiovascular risk and white matter degeneration, as well as an accessible and non-invasive indicator of white-matter lesion burden and associated cognitive impairment in later life. The unique association between reduced low-frequency band heart-rate variability and age-related lesion burden may help to establish the link between autonomic control of cardiac function and brain health in aging.

title: Betrayal is worse than loss during cooperation
abstract: Cooperative behavior refers to activities that benefit another individual or benefit both the person performing the behavior and the recipient. Although both betrayal aversion and loss aversion (the financial detriment incurred from betrayal) are established determinants of cooperative behavior, their relative potency remains undetermined. Here, we investigated these effects by integrating computational modeling and event-related potential (ERP) techniques. In two tasks involving risk and cooperation, participants decided whether to take financial risks or to cooperate under possible betrayal. Our results showed that betrayal aversion had a stronger effect on reducing cooperation compared to loss aversion. Furthermore, ERP data demonstrated a temporal pattern consistent with sequential processing: betrayal was encoded early in decision-making, reflected by increased P3 with weaker betrayal aversion, whereas loss aversion manifested later, marked by increased LPP. By dissociating the contributions of betrayal and loss, our finding provides novel insights into the cognitive and neural mechanisms underlying cooperative behavior.

title: Biomarkers indicate altered outer retinal fluid homeostasis in the absence of Kv2.1/Kv8.2 channels.
abstract: Purpose: Photoreceptor Kv2.1/Kv8.2 voltage-gated potassium channels carry an outward potassium current, helping to set the resting membrane potential and to shape dim light responses. Because potassium flux in the outer retina influences extracellular osmolarity and fluid distribution, we hypothesized that Kv2.1/Kv8.2 channels also contribute to fluid homeostasis in this region of the retina. Methods: OCT imaging was performed in Kv8.2 heterozygous (Het) and knockout (KO) mice aged ~5 weeks under dark- and light-adapted conditions. Light-dark differences in the distance between the external limiting membrane (ELM) and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) ({Delta}ELM-RPE) were calculated to quantify light-evoked outer retinal expansion, a biomarker associated with changes in subretinal space (SRS) fluid handling. As a secondary outcome, outer nuclear layer (ONL) thickness was also measured under both lighting conditions. Retinal gene expression was assessed by RNA-seq and droplet digital RT-PCR. Retinal protein expression was determined by western blotting and immunolabeling. Results: {Delta}ELM-RPE was significantly reduced in Kv8.2 KO mice compared with Het controls, indicating altered light-evoked outer retinal dynamics compatible with changes in subretinal space fluid handling. ONL thickness exhibited a small but significant light-dark change that was different between genotypes. Transcriptomic analyses revealed upregulation of osmosensitive genes, including osmolyte transporters and aquaporins. AQP1 protein expression in photoreceptors increased. Conclusions: These findings are consistent with altered outer retinal fluid homeostasis following loss of Kv8.2 and support a model in which photoreceptor potassium efflux contributes to osmotic water movement into the subretinal space.

title: Brain mitovesicles undergo stage-specific remodelling during the progression of amyloid-β pathology
abstract: Mitochondrial dysfunction is an early feature of Alzheimer's disease that shows nonlinear changes as the disease progresses.
