However, how these changes are reflected in the mitochondrial material released by brain cells remains poorly understood. Mitovesicles are a recently described extracellular vesicle subpopulation of mitochondrial origin that provide a unique insight into mitochondrial alterations in the brain and could potentially show how nonlinear changes evolve across disease stages of amyloid-beta pathology. Here, we isolated forebrain-derived small extracellular vesicles and mitovesicles from wild-type and Amyloid precursor protein (App) knock-in (AppKI) mice, carrying familial AD mutations and progressively accumulating amyloid-beta plaques, at presymptomatic (2-month) and symptomatic (12-month) stages using high-resolution density gradient fractionation. Vesicle identity and composition were assessed by morphological, biophysical and quantitative proteomic analyses, and mitovesicle respiratory function was measured by extracellular flux analysis. We show that mitovesicles carry a distinct, predominantly mitochondrial inner membrane proteome that is remodelled by age and disease in a stage-specific manner. Compared with small extracellular vesicles, mitovesicle proteomic profiles captured disease progression more clearly, with symptomatic AppKI mice forming the most molecularly distinct group. At the presymptomatic stage, AppKI mitovesicles showed reduced mitochondrial protein representation, most notably of fatty acid {beta}-oxidation and lipid-metabolism proteins associated with astroglial and vascular signatures, preceding any detectable respiratory impairment. At the symptomatic stage this reversed: AppKI mitovesicles were enriched for oxidative phosphorylation, mitochondrial membrane and transporter proteins, yet showed reduced Complex IV-linked respiration, revealing a dissociation between mitochondrial cargo abundance and respiratory function. Selected cargo changes were not mirrored in whole-brain tissue, indicating selective remodelling of mitovesicle content. Comparison with mitovesicles from post-mortem human Alzheimer's disease frontotemporal cortex and hippocampus identified a conserved 62-protein mitovesicle core, dominated by oxidative phosphorylation subunits and mitochondrial carriers. In addition, 25 of these proteins were enriched in mitovesicles derived from Alzheimer's and AppKI forebrains, defining a conserved mitovesicular disease signature. Together, these findings establish forebrain-derived mitovesicles as a dynamically remodelled vesicle population that reflects progressive mitochondrial dysfunction in the Alzheimer's disease brain and provides a cross-species resource for future biomarker and mechanistic studies.
author_corresponding_institution: Department of Neurobiology, Care Sciences and Society, Division of Neurogeriatrics, Centre for Alzheimer Research, Karolinska Institutet

title: Brain-wide representations of olfactory behavior in C. elegans
abstract: Olfactory navigation emerges from dynamic interactions between sensory input, brain activity state and the animal's own movements. In C. elegans, a compact nervous system enables brain-wide imaging in behaving animals exposed to controlled olfactory environments, with an undulatory locomotion that reduces navigation to transitions among forward runs, reversals, and turns. Here, we used tracking microscopy to record and compare brain-wide neural activity in crawling worms navigating spatial odor gradients or isotropic environments, and in immobilized worms responding to temporal odor pulses. Across conditions, we identified strongly correlated brain-wide activity patterns spanning olfactory sensory neurons, interneurons, and premotor interneurons. Comparisons between navigation in odor gradients and exploration in isotropic environments revealed a compact functional circuit linking olfactory sensory neurons, interneurons, and premotor neurons. Comparisons between different odors distinguished sensory activity relationships associated with odor identity from a shared sensorimotor circuit for navigational movement. Comparisons between crawling and immobilized animals revealed profound differences in motor-state transitions and brain-wide correlation structure, further demonstrating the dependence of sensory representations and motor decision-making on behavioral context. Our findings reveal a functional organization linking olfactory sensory activity to navigational movement and show how this organization depends on behavioral state and environmental context.

title: BundleMorphometry: Spatially Resolved White Matter Bundle Shape Analysis Using Nonlinear Streamline-based Registration
abstract: Diffusion MRI tractometry quantifies microstructural properties along white matter (WM) bundles but does not directly measure their geometry, potentially overlooking localized morphological alterations. Here, we introduce BundleMorphometry, a framework for quantifying local WM bundle shape using the analytical Jacobian of nonlinear streamline-based registration. Individual subject bundles are registered to a reference atlas bundle using BundleWarp, a streamline-based nonlinear registration method. We derive the analytical Jacobian of the resulting deformation field and compute its log-determinant (log det J) to quantify local expansion and compression at each streamline point. To enable spatially resolved group comparisons, these measurements are projected onto the two-dimensional grid, capturing variations along and across each bundle. We evaluated BundleMorphometry using two clinical datasets comprising patients with glioma and Parkinson's disease (PD). In the glioma dataset, BundleMorphometry revealed spatially extensive deformation patterns in lesion-affected WM bundles that were not captured by displacement magnitude alone. Additionally, in a group analysis of the PD dataset (32 patients and 32 healthy controls), we identified significant localized morphological differences in the corpus callosum forceps major, mid-body and right spinothalamic tract, with distinct patterns of expansion and compression. These findings demonstrate the potential of BundleMorphometry to advance conventional tractometry by enabling spatially resolved analysis of bundle morphology.

title: CD40 ligand and IFN-γ induce proinflammatory activity and microglia-mediated neurodegeneration in human stem cell models
abstract: The cluster of differentiation 40 (CD40)/CD40 ligand (CD40L) co-stimulatory pathway plays a critical role in the activation and regulation of immune networks involving both adaptive and innate immune cells. Dysregulation of this pathway has been implicated in multiple autoimmune diseases, including multiple sclerosis (MS). MS is characterized by progressive neurodegeneration driven by compartmentalized neuroinflammation within the central nervous system (CNS), sustained low-grade T cell infiltration at the blood-brain barrier, and T cell reactivation at CNS border tissues. CD40L-expressing T cells can activate CD40-expressing microglia, which are a critical effector cell that contribute to neurodegeneration in MS. However, the consequence of this functional interaction in the brain remains poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that the combination of CD40L and interferon-gamma (IFN-{gamma}), a cytokine produced by activated T cells, induces a robust inflammatory response and cell death in human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSC)-derived microglia. Stimulation with CD40L elicited microglial clustering, morphological transformation, and robust release of proinflammatory cytokines including interleukin-12 (IL-12), tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-), and IL-6. Anti-CD40L antibody treatment reversed both cell death and inflammatory response and partially normalized the associated transcriptional changes. Furthermore, using an hiPSC-derived tri-culture system comprising neurons, astrocytes, and microglia, we demonstrated that CD40L and IFN-{gamma} trigger microglia-dependent neuronal dysregulation and death. Anti-CD40L treatment substantially attenuated neuronal injury. Finally, transcriptomic enrichment analysis identified CD40L-mediated microglial gene expression signatures that correlated with CD40 expression in primary progressive MS brain tissue but not in the normal-appearing white matter of healthy controls. Collectively, these findings support a role for the microglial CD40/T cell CD40L axis in MS pathology and suggest CD40L blockade as a potential therapeutic strategy warranting further investigation.
author_corresponding_institution: Neurology Research, Sanofi, Cambridge, MA, USA.

title: Caudate nucleus aging and its association with brain disorders
abstract: The caudate nucleus supports cognition and goal-directed behavior, undergoes age-associated changes, and is implicated in substance use, psychiatric, and neurodegenerative disorders. However, how aging alters its diverse cell types and how such changes relate to diseases remains poorly understood. To address these questions, we assembled single nucleus transcriptomic atlases of the caudate tissue, comprising 963,842 nuclei from 178 human donors, including controls and individuals with alcohol use disorder (AUD) or opioid use disorder (OUD), and 83,699 nuclei from six healthy rhesus macaques. We also curated 3,139 bulk RNA-seq profiles from the caudate and other brain regions spanning controls and multiple diagnostic groups, as well as paired RNA and chromatin accessibility profiles from 257,524 caudate nuclei across 161 control and AUD donors. These datasets enabled comparisons across age, species, brain regions, and diagnostic groups. We found shared glial aging features in humans and macaques, whereas neuronal changes were more divergent. Inferred neuron-to-neuron communication declined with age, with greater declines in AUD. Both transcriptional and chromatin accessibility profiles showed nonlinear age-associated patterns, with pronounced changes in later adulthood. In donors with AUD, age-associated changes appeared earlier, with altered trajectories in lipid metabolism, mitochondrial function, and neuronal signaling. Across comparisons involving AUD, OUD, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, and Alzheimer disease, mitochondrial function and fatty acid metabolism emerged as consensus features linking caudate aging to diseases, although the direction and extent of overlap varied by disorder and brain region. Together, these findings define cellular and regulatory features of primate caudate aging and reveal shared and context-dependent relationships between aging and brain disorders.

title: Cerebrovascular Structure-Flow Gradients Revealed by Volumetric Ultrasound Localization Microscopy
abstract: Characterizing the joint organization of microscale cerebrovascular structure and flow in vivo is challenging. Volumetric ultrasound localization microscopy (ULM) provides spatially resolved measures of microvascular structure and flow from the same acquisition, but how these features are jointly organized across brain networks remains unclear. Here, we characterized local vascular phenotypes from transcranial volumetric ULM in mice and examined whether they contained reproducible low-dimensional organization. Local measures of vascular structure and flow dynamics were summarized within corresponding brain regions across mice. Subject-specific vascular phenotype similarity matrices were combined into a group-consensus graph and analyzed using diffusion embedding. Two leading gradients, showing distinct spatial distributions across brain networks, were reproducibly recovered across subject and spatial scales. The principal gradient was associated with local vascular density and flow complexity, defining a vascular structure-related axis. The secondary gradient was associated with flow speed and acceleration, defining a flow-dynamics-related axis. These gradients provide a low-dimensional representation of the cerebrovascular structure and flow and provide a reference for studying coordinated vascular changes across disease, aging, and intervention.
author_corresponding_institution: Department of Bioengineering, Imperial College London

title: Cholinergic-dopaminergic synergy and antagonism shape prediction-error broadcasting
abstract: Cholinergic and dopaminergic pathways control reinforcement learning, yet how their basal forebrain and midbrain populations interact remains unresolved. We simultaneously monitored both systems using dual-cell-type optogenetic tagging and neurotransmitter measurements in mice engaged in psychometric learning. Their activity contributed synergistically to reward prediction-error signaling. However, punishment-inhibited dopaminergic neurons showed antagonistic interactions with cholinergic neurons as well. Optogenetic stimulation and channelrhodopsin-assisted circuit mapping revealed a cholinergic-to-dopaminergic disynaptic inhibitory pathway through basal forebrain GABAergic neurons consistent with this antagonism. Chemogenetic suppression of cholinergic activity reduced dopaminergic responses to reward-predicting stimuli, attenuated punishment-induced dopamine suppression, and impaired learning. These findings reveal how a common underlying circuit architecture can flexibly shape prediction-error signaling through synergistic and antagonistic interactions, with implications for adaptive learning and neuropsychiatric disease.
author_corresponding_institution: Division of Neurophysiology, Center for Brain Research, Medical University of Vienna

title: Chronic hypertension disrupts the blood-brain barrier in the ventral hippocampus in females but not males in a rat model of vascular cognitive impairment
abstract: Background: Chronic hypertension is a leading cause of cerebrovascular disease, ischemic stroke, and cognitive impairment. In addition, anxiety and hypertension often co-exist, however, little is known about the relationship between the two. Understanding how chronic hypertension impacts limbic brain regions such as the ventral hippocampus may provide insight into how cerebrovascular contributes to altered emotional behavior. Methods: An open field task was used to quantify locomotion, exploratory behavior, thigmotaxis, rearing and risk assessment behaviors in adult (7-month-old) male and female normotensive Wistar rats and spontaneously hypertensive rats (SHR; n=8/group). Blood-brain barrier (BBB) permeability was assessed by measuring extravasation of sodium fluorescein, 3 kDa Texas red dextran and 10 kDa cascade blue into the ventral hippocampus. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays were used to measure markers of vascular signaling, inflammation, and central nervous system-specific proteins indicative of neuroaxonal and glial injury in serum from separate groups of male and female SHR (n=6/group). Main effects and interactions between two independent variables (sex and hypertension) were determined using two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with Tukey's post-hoc tests. Circulating factors were compared using a Welch's t-test. Relationships between BBB permeability and anxiety-like behavior were determined using Pearson's correlations. Results: Chronic hypertension increased circulating inflammatory factors and BBB permeability in female but not male rats. BBB permeability did not differ by sex in male and female normotensive rats. There was an anxiolytic effect of chronic hypertension on exploratory-related anxiety-like behavior, including less thigmotaxis, lower latency to cross through the center of the arena, and increased unsupported rearing. Risk assessment behavior, quantified as stretch-attend posture, was increased in female SHR. BBB permeability in the ventral hippocampus was correlated with anxiety-like behavior in females, but not in males, suggesting sex-dependent mechanisms of hypertension-induced changes in emotional behavior. Conclusions: These findings implicate a role for chronic hypertension-induced BBB disruption in neuropsychiatric disorders in the female sex and advances our understanding of cerebrovascular vulnerability in deep limbic brain regions.

title: Circadian multimodal physiological, ocular and behavioural data from a 40-hour forced-desynchrony protocol
abstract: We present a multimodal dataset from twelve healthy adults (aged 19-30 years, 50% female) who completed a 40-hour ultra-short sleep-wake forced desynchrony protocol which scheduled 2 h 30 min of wakefulness in dim light and 1 h 15 min of sleep in darkness (2:1 wake:sleep ratio), with the protocol ending after the last wake period. This schedule compressed the typical 24-hour day into an ultradian 3 h 45 min cycle to decouple circadian and homeostatic influences on physiology and behaviour. During each wake interval, participants completed repeated assessments of visual psychophysics (chromatic temporal contrast sensitivity), pupillometry with silent-substitution stimuli, ocular structure (optical coherence tomography) and physiology (intraocular pressure), psychomotor vigilance, salivary hormones, and standardised questionnaires, alongside continuous actigraphy, electrocardiography, and recordings of core and peripheral temperature, blood pressure, and interstitial glucose. Two supplementary evening sessions under experimental light exposure and dim-light conditions provide comparison data on circadian phase (salivary melatonin concentration, dim-light melatonin onset). Data collected from one pilot participant and screenings of two excluded candidates are additionally included. This dataset supports reuse for investigating circadian dynamics across multiple domains beyond the retinal-function hypotheses of the original study.
author_corresponding_institution: Max Planck Institute for Biological Cybernetics; TUM School of Medicine & Health, Technical University of Munich; TUM Institute for Advanced Study (TUM-IAS), Te

title: Circuit regulation along an activity continuum shapes flexible and stable representations during learning
abstract: Learning requires neural representations to flexibly incorporate new information while progressively stabilizing to support enduring memories. How neural circuits balance these demands remains unclear. Here, we identify complementary mechanisms supporting representational flexibility and stability in the medial entorhinal cortex (MEC), a key component of the cognitive map for memory-guided navigation. Longitudinal calcium imaging in mice learning novel virtual environments revealed a persistent axis of excitatory neuronal activity associated with distinct representational dynamics. Low-activity neurons exhibited intermittent activation that varied with learning stages and greater learning-dependent representational refinement, flexibly shifting their encoding from landmarks toward reward locations. By contrast, high-activity neurons exhibited more persistent activation and maintained more stable spatial representations. Dopaminergic pre-reward ramping was associated with the emergence of reward encoding in low-activity neurons, whereas interactions with inhibitory interneurons contributed to the stability of high-activity neurons. Notably, interneurons exhibited activity changes opposing those of excitatory neurons during learning, and their transient activation upon novelty exposure delayed excitatory representational remodeling, stabilization, and behavioral learning, suggesting that inhibitory circuits gate learning-dependent representational dynamics. Together, these findings reveal how activity-dependent excitatory neuronal organization and circuit-level regulation enable complementary forms of representational flexibility and stability to coexist, facilitating the incorporation of novel experiences into stable, context-specific cognitive maps that support learning.
author_corresponding_institution: National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke

title: Closed-loop acoustic stimulation promotes local slow oscillation train initiation and persistence in elderly adults
abstract: Slow oscillations (SOs) during non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep support memory consolidation and metabolic waste clearance. Aging is associated with reduced SO amplitude and density and disrupted temporal organization, characterized by more isolated events and shorter SO trains. We investigated whether closed-loop acoustic stimulation (CLAS) could enhance the initiation and persistence of rhythmic SO activity in elderly adults. Twenty-seven participants underwent a baseline night followed by an experimental night, during which online-detected SOs were either stimulated using CLAS (STIM; n = 16) or left unstimulated (SHAM; n = 11). We quantified the proportions of isolated and consecutive SOs, train-initiation probability, and SO train length. Analyses assessed local effects around online-detected SOs and global effects across NREM sleep using offline detection. Locally, CLAS reduced the proportion of isolated SOs and increased the proportion of consecutive SOs, train-initiation probability, and mean train length. Global overnight effects were weaker but directionally consistent, primarily reflecting a shift toward longer SO trains. These changes occurred without a significant between-group difference in the change in SO density, and local effects remained significant after adjustment for SO density. Thus, CLAS promoted sustained rhythmic activity beyond changes in SO occurrence. These findings suggest that CLAS can modify the temporal organization of SOs in elderly adults, supporting its potential to mitigate age-related disruptions in SO dynamics. Temporal organization measures may complement conventional amplitude and density measures when evaluating CLAS effects. Further studies should establish whether these changes translate into cognitive benefits or improvements in other aspects of brain health.
author_corresponding_institution: Instituto Tecnologico de Buenos Aires (ITBA), Buenos Aires, Argentina

title: Cognitive reserve depends on cortical neurochemistry to predict memory after partner-inflicted brain injury
abstract: Memory problems are commonplace following brain injury (BI). However, it remains unclear why some report memory problems while others do not, especially following repeated neurotrauma. Cognitive reserve has been widely hypothesized to account for this variation, but testing this account has yielded inconsistent results and proven difficult, likely as it requires a sample spanning a wide range of BI burden with concurrent neuroimaging and cognitive measurement. Here, we combined a wide range of cognitive assessments with measures of neuronal health using magnetic resonance spectroscopy across three brain regions in 62 women who had experienced physical intimate partner violence. Partner-inflicted BI counts ranged from 0 to 420, yet we found that the number of BIs alone did not explain the variance in memory outcomes. Among a small subset with high BI exposure ([≥]10 BIs; n = 11), BI count explained 5% of the variance in delayed recall, the primary memory outcome, whereas cognitive reserve, inferred from a measure of premorbid functioning, explained almost half (unadjusted in-sample associations). In the full cohort, cognitive reserve predicted memory only among the most heavily injured participants. In a separate model, cognitive reserve predicted memory only when creatine-referenced total N-acetylaspartate, a marker of neuronal health, was lower in the posterior cingulate gyrus and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. Ultimately, our findings provide behavioral and neurochemical evidence consistent with the cognitive reserve hypothesis and shed new light on why, despite a high burden of neurotrauma, memory may remain resilient.

title: Common variation of cell abundances and gene expression in the human striatum
abstract: The cellular and molecular bases of inter-individual variation in the human brain are not yet understood, particularly beyond the neocortex. Here we describe cellular and gene-expression variation in the striatum and prefrontal cortex from single-nucleus RNA-seq analysis of 3.9 million nuclei from 178 adult brain donors. People with more astrocytes, microglia, or oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs) in any one brain region tended to have this property in all gray matter regions sampled. OPCs proportions declined by 40% across ages 30-80 in cortex and striatum. Age-associated gene-expression changes differed substantially across cell types. Donor age was predicted from RNA-expression patterns with a median absolute error of 6.6 years across cell types. Common genetic variants were associated with expression of nearly 10,000 genes; these effects were mostly cell-type-specific and distinguished striatal from cortical neurons. These open-access data provide a foundation for future studies of human brain variation and vulnerabilities.

title: ConfUSIus: an accessible and scalable toolkit for functional ultrasound imaging analysis
abstract: Functional ultrasound imaging (fUSI) maps brainwide hemodynamics at high resolution, yet analysis requires expert knowledge as pipelines remain fragmented across laboratories. We introduce ConfUSIus, an open-source Python package and graphical interface for accessible, scalable, and reproducible fUSI analysis. Its common data model unifies heterogeneous fUSI recordings across beamformed IQ processing, motion correction, registration, denoising, and statistical analysis. ConfUSIus lowers barriers and facilitates method development, comparison, and sharing.
author_corresponding_institution: UCL Institute of Ophthalmology, University College London

title: Cortical bursts provide spatio-temporal frames for the large-scale phase synchrony emerging across the birth transition
abstract: Structural corticocortical connectivity grows rapidly around birth, but how it establishes the large-scale neuronal interactions needed for lifelong neurocognitive performance remains unclear. Using repeated high-density EEG from 233 preterm-born infants recorded at 33-45 weeks postmenstrual age, we characterized the development of three phase-based interaction modes with distinct temporal relationships to cortical bursts: burst-based, burst-framed, and general phase-based connectivity. Burst-framed connectivity was quantified with a novel metric, nested phase-phase correlation. All three modes declined globally with age but differed spatially: burst-based connectivity became more confined, burst-framed connectivity reorganized towards sensorimotor-association connectivity, whereas general phase-based connectivity retained a stable modular organization. General phase-based connectivity was initially concentrated along burst-framed connections, but this coupling weakened with age. Its greater persistence around term age was associated with poorer neurocognitive outcomes, suggesting delayed network maturation. These findings suggest that bursting may transiently scaffold the maturation of large-scale corticocortical phase synchrony across the birth transition.

title: DPYD	 links glial lipids and myelination to sleep duration
abstract: The regulation of sleep is heritable and conserved across species1,2, but the governing genetic mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we investigate the role of DPYD--which encodes the pyrimidine catabolic enzyme, dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase--in sleep. Using a cross-species approach, we show that DPYD and its orthologs act specifically in glia to promote sleep through the regulation of brain lipids. In mouse and zebrafish, we find that DPYD orthologs are enriched in oligodendrocyte lineage cells, and their loss reduces myelination and sleep independent of DPYDs established role in uracil catabolism to {beta}-alanine. Genetic and pharmacological manipulations of myelin in zebrafish show that altering myelination is sufficient to perturb sleep duration. In Drosophila, which lack myelin, we find that the DPYD ortholog acts in ensheathing glia to promote sleep through formation of glial lipid droplets, a proposed evolutionary precursor to myelin. Furthermore, a human GWAS-identified sleep variant2 resides in a conserved cis-regulatory element that selectively contacts the promoter of DPYD within oligodendrocytes, connecting the human genetic association to oligodendrocyte-specific control of DPYD. Together, these results identify a deeply conserved role for glial lipids in sleep regulation and establish DPYD as a mechanistic link between myelin biology and sleep.

title: Detecting deception in event narratives: the analysis of response latencies and error rates to unexpected questions.
abstract: Deception is a central phenomenon in the study of human behaviour, and in forensic and investigative contexts it assumes significance due to its potential consequences. Although the unexpected questions technique has shown promising results, its application to the narration of a false autobiographical event remains underexplored. This study aims to fill this gap using the unexpected questions technique in an investigative interview setting. A total of 60 participants were randomly divided into two groups: the honest group was asked to describe their most recent day trip, while the deceptive group was asked to memorise a narrative describing a day trip. Both groups underwent an audio-recorded interview containing control, expected and unexpected questions. The results showed that both groups exhibited longer response latencies and higher error and inaccuracy rates in response to unexpected questions, but these indices were significantly higher in the deceptive group (p = .022 for response latency, uncorrected for multiple comparisons; p < .001 for error and inaccuracy rates). The findings suggest that longer response times and higher error and inaccuracy rates during unexpected questions may reflect not only the difficulty of the questions, but also additional cognitive demands faced by deceptive participants. Furthermore, these indicators were used to classify a subject as deceptive or honest using machine-learning algorithms. Within the sample, the model showed excellent cross-validated discriminatory performance (AUC = 0.967), suggesting that these indices may have diagnostic potential worthy of further investigation.

title: Development of appropriate sensorimotor recalibration for a de novo skill
abstract: Implicit adaptation operates automatically to ensure that well-learned movements remain exquisitely calibrated. A long-standing puzzle is how this process is applied when learning a new skill: Prior work has highlighted that implicit recalibration is inflexible, even when its operation results in maladaptive behavior given the sensorimotor mapping required for the new skill. Here, we revisited this problem, training participants for up to a month on a range of tasks with novel mappings, including mirror reversals and large rotations. Contrary to previous findings, implicit recalibration was flexibly reconfigured after prolonged training in a manner appropriate for each novel mapping. Training that emphasized feedforward planning rather than feedback control was sufficient to induce this reconfiguration. Learning involved reconfiguration of the sensory predictions and error correction policy for the new mapping, and participants were able to switch between mappings with minimal interference. These results demonstrate that implicit recalibration is reconfigured during skill acquisition, enabling flexible, context-specific adaptation.

title: Diagnose Harmonisation (DHARM): An open-source tool for the harmonisation and analysis of batch effects in MRI-derived measures.
abstract: Technical differences between scanners, acquisition protocols, machine hardware and processing pipelines can introduce systematic variation into MRI-derived measures. Numerous harmonisation methods have been developed to reduce these effects. However, validation of these methods is often performed using different criteria depending on the method itself, the datasets used and the study design. Consequently, determining whether harmonisation is required, selecting an appropriate method and establishing whether or not technical variation has been sufficiently removed without compromising biological signal remain challenging. In this manuscript, we introduce Diagnose Harmonisation (DHARM), an open-source Python toolbox for diagnosing batch effects, applying harmonisation and evaluating harmonisation performance in cross-sectional and repeated-measures settings. DHARM is user-friendly, comes with GUI-based and command-line interfaces, and has graphical reporting. It provides standardised reporting workflows combining complementary measures of batch-associated differences in feature location, scale, empirical distributions, covariance and multivariate structure, together with measures assessing preservation of biological covariate effects and repeated-measures consistency. The framework includes several established harmonisation approaches, but its evaluation workflow is method-agnostic: users can also supply data harmonised using external or newly developed methods and benchmark their outputs using the same common set of diagnostics. We demonstrate DHARM using multisite cross-sectional MRI measures from UK Biobank, Cam-CAN and OxBAC as well as travelling-heads data from the ON-Harmony dataset. Across the cross-sectional datasets, harmonisation substantially reduced additive batch effects, while residual differences in variance and empirical distributions varied between methods. Multivariate diagnostics further demonstrated that reduction of batch-associated structure can coexist with preservation or increased detectability of biologically relevant variation. In the repeated-measures example, harmonisation reduced batch-associated and within-subject variability, while broadly preserving subject-level and biological relationships. DHARM provides a reproducible framework for diagnosing batch effects, applying different harmonisation methods and evaluating harmonisation as a multi-criteria problem rather than relying on a single measure of success. By jointly characterising technical variation and preservation of biologically meaningful information, DHARM can support dataset- and objective-specific selection, benchmarking and validation of harmonisation strategies.

title: Differential effects of chronic hypertension and sex on vascular density along the septotemporal axis of the hippocampus in a rat model of VCID
abstract: Background: Chronic hypertension is a major modifiable risk factor for vascular contributions to cognitive impairment and dementia (VCID), yet vascular changes that precede cognitive dysfunction remain poorly understood. This is particularly relevant for the hippocampus, a deep brain structure critical to memory function, which differs along its septotemporal axis functionally and in its susceptibility to hypoxic/ischemic injury. The impacts of hypertension and sex on hippocampal vascularization remains unclear and could contribute to the development/progression of VCID. Methods: In this study, adult male and female Wistar and spontaneously hypertensive rats (SHR) were used at 5 months old, an age before memory impairments. Vascular density and morphometric parameters in dorsal and ventral hippocampus were quantified using high-resolution confocal microscopy and 3D vascular reconstruction. Results: In SHR, vascular density was increased in the dorsal hippocampus in males and across dorsal and ventral hippocampus in females compared to normotensive rats. Diameter and length of the microvasculature shifted to be smaller and longer during hypertension in males, but not females. Conclusions: These findings demonstrate chronic hypertension increases vascular density differentially by sex along the septotemporal axis of the hippocampus in mid adulthood that may increase vascular resistance and potentiate perfusion deficits or increase sites of blood-brain barrier disruption and contribute to VCID.

title: Direction-Dependent Encoding of Forward and Inverse Models in the Same Purkinje Cells
abstract: Saccadic eye movements are too fast to be guided by sensory feedback and therefore depend on precisely calibrated internal models. The cerebellum is widely thought to compute both forward and inverse models, yet how these two computations coexist in the same circuit remains unclear. We hypothesized that the same Purkinje cells (PCs) can serve as a forward model for saccades in one direction and as an inverse model for saccades in the opposite direction, because target neurons on either side of the cerebellar nuclei contribute differently to leftward and rightward saccades. To test this hypothesis, we recorded from PCs in the oculomotor vermis of macaque monkeys during repetitive saccade paradigms that induce adaptation and fatigue. Using the preferred error direction of each PC conveyed by increased complex spike (CS) activity (CS-on direction) as a proxy of the side of the cerebellar nuclei it projects to, we compared population activity for saccades directed against the CS-on direction (CS-on opposed) and along it (CS-on aligned). CS-on opposed saccades, (toward the PC's projection side) were accompanied by a precisely timed, sharp burst of simple spike (SS) activity at saccade onset that scaled with peak velocity, and CS error sensitivity was highest after the saccade. SS activity also changed systematically after adaptation, reflecting the altered kinematics of the adapted saccade. These properties are consistent with a forward model that estimates ongoing movement and updates itself based on post-movement error. In contrast, the CS-on aligned saccades, (away from the PC's projection side) were accompanied by broader SS modulation around saccade offset, and the CS error sensitivity was highest before the saccade. CSs around saccade onset encoded target location and initial eye position, and their occurrence was associated with reduced saccade amplitude. This reduction likely adjusts the motor command to the starting eye position, as expected for an inverse model that pre-programs the motor command before movement begins. Together, these findings provide neural evidence that the same PC population can contribute to both forward and inverse model computations, depending on saccade direction.
author_corresponding_institution: Hertie Institute for Clinical Brain Research

title: Disambiguation of two-tone images aligns object representations in the EEG
abstract: Electrophysiological responses to visual objects carry information about stimulus identity and semantic category, but it remains difficult to know whether such information represents conceptual knowledge or merely regularities in physical image features. Here, we presented two-tone images before and after disambiguation via corresponding photographs to seventeen healthy participants while recording EEG to dissociate the learned image concept from its physical properties. After disambiguation, EEG responses to learned two-tone images became more similar to the responses of their photo counterparts. This effect emerged approximately 100 ms after stimulus onset and peaked at 350 ms. However, we found no evidence for a generalization of the response pattern to the stimulus semantic category. Furthermore, alignment to the photo counterparts was only detectable after explicit visual disambiguation rather than spontaneous recognition. Together, these findings indicate that EEG can capture specific learned conceptual modulations of responses to visually degraded stimuli, while also showing that low-level visual properties dominate the representational structure.
author_corresponding_institution: Institute of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry, Kiel University

title: Dissociable norepinephrine and dopamine representations during strategic decision-making and reward learning
abstract: Adaptive decision-making in competitive environments requires learning from immediate reward outcomes while tracking longer-timescale information to adjust behavioural strategies and remain unpredictable against others. Dopamine (DA) and norepinephrine (NE) have long been implicated in reward-guided behaviours, but their contributions to strategic choice remain unclear. We trained mice to play a zero-sum matching pennies game against a computer opponent that exploited regularities in their choice and reward history, such that optimal performance required stochastic choice decoupled from immediate reward. We combined fibre photometry recordings, behavioural and neural modelling, and a within-subject multi-task design to determine how NE and DA contribute to strategic choice in the matching pennies game versus reward-guided behaviour in a two-armed bandit (2AB) task. DA responses were dominated by trial-by-trial reward outcomes and consistently tracked model-derived reward prediction errors (RPE) across tasks and behavioural states. In contrast, NE activity reflected salient task events, predicted upcoming choice switches, and tracked longer-timescale variables including model-inferred behavioural strategy and average reward rate. In addition, NE responses were selectively enhanced following rewarded switches when these outcomes were informative for deciding whether to stay in or switch from the current strategy; and this enhancement could not be explained by RPE. Incorporating pre-choice NE activity into a reinforcement-learning model to modulate choice generation improved model prediction in matching pennies but not in the 2AB task. Together, these findings reveal complementary neuromodulatory correlates of competitive decision-making across timescales: DA primarily guides learning from immediate outcomes through RPE, whereas NE additionally represents contextual information and choice stochasticity relevant for shaping long-term strategies.

title: Distinct medial septal GABAergic pathways differentially regulate spatial memory and network activity
abstract: Septal GABAergic projection neurons form distinct pathways to subregions of the hippocampal formation, including the hippocampus proper and the medial and lateral entorhinal cortices. Parvalbumin (PV+) and calbindin expressing (CB+) projections target different types of interneurons and thereby differentially regulate neuronal activity in the downstream area. Consistent with the idea of dissociable functional roles, inhibition of septal PV+ neurons impairs reference memory whereas inhibition of septal CB+ neurons impairs both reference and working memory. Here, we show that these functions are differentially supported by specific projection pathways: PV+ projections to the dorsal hippocampus and medial entorhinal cortex (MEC) support reference memory, whereas CB+ projections to the MEC support both reference and working memory. At the network level, septal PV+, but not CB+, neurons regulate theta oscillations. Together, these findings further define the roles of septal PV+ and CB+ pathways in orchestrating network activity and supporting specific forms of memory.
author_corresponding_institution: Department of Clinical Neurobiology at the Medical Faculty of Heidelberg University and German Cancer Research Center (DKFZ), Im Neuenheimer Feld 280

title: Distinct processing of visual motion by transcriptomic cell types in the superior colliculus
abstract: How the brain organizes visual processing across distinct neuron types is a fundamental yet unresolved question. Here we study how visual motion is processed by transcriptomically defined cell types in the superior colliculus (SC). We generated or identified transgenic mouse lines to target three transcriptomic types of neurons in the superficial SC, the Cbln4+, Vip+, and Grp+ neurons. We find that each of these cell types encodes distinct ranges of stimulus direction, speed, size, and spatial and temporal features. In response to ecologically relevant visual flows, the three cell types occupy partitional spaces in the encoding manifold. The three cell types also show unique morphology and connectivity, including their retinal and intracollicular input and projection patterns. Together, these results reveal a genetic logic for visual motion processing in the SC, where transcriptomic cell types are likely the basic computational units with their specific feature selectivity, morphology, and input-output connectivity.

title: Dog and Human Brains Represent Human Emotional Bodies with Asymmetric Encoding of Happiness and Anger
abstract: Dogs live in an environment rich in human emotional signals, yet most of what we know about their visual emotion perception comes from faces. Our study shifts this focus to the body, a central channel of emotional communication in dogs and a source of social information when they observe human emotional expressions. Here, we investigated how the brains of dogs and humans represent emotions conveyed by human bodies. Using fMRI, we examined 24 awake companion dogs and 40 humans viewing videos of bodily happiness, anger, and neutral actions, alongside phase-scrambled controls. Both dogs and humans showed occipito-temporal sensitivity to human bodies, with emotional modulation in the right caudal suprasylvian gyrus in dogs and the right extrastriate body area in humans. Multivariate response patterns also differentiated bodily happiness from anger in both dogs and humans. Emotion-specific RSA further showed a similar representational asymmetry: happiness showed consistent category-specific neural patterns, whereas anger showed no comparable category effect but could still be differentiated from happiness and neutral actions. Despite this shared representational asymmetry, the anatomical distribution differed, with happiness represented across more distributed regions in dogs, whereas anger differentiation involved a broader cortical network in humans. No corresponding effects were found for phase-scrambled controls. Together, these findings provide the first direct neural evidence of how the dog brain represents affective information conveyed by human bodies, while leaving open whether emotions expressed by conspecific bodies evoke similar neural representations. More broadly, our results suggest similar representational relationships between bodily emotions in dogs and humans, despite differences in the anatomical distribution of these effects, while highlighting the role of human bodily expressions in dogs' social cognition, and advancing our understanding of the neural basis of emotional communication across species.

title: Donor Aware Reanalysis of Neuronal Nuclei Supports STMN2 Depletion Associated with Nuclear TDP 43 loss in FTD and ALS
abstract: Background. Nuclear TDP-43 depletion is a central pathological feature of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD), but donor-to-donor variation can obscure transcriptomic associations in small postmortem cohorts. We reanalyzed public RNA-seq data from FACS-isolated NeuN-positive frontal-cortex neuronal nuclei to quantify gene-expression changes associated with nuclear TDP-43 loss while explicitly accounting for donor structure. Methods. The supplied GSE126542-derived matrix contained 62,754 genes across 12 libraries from seven donors, including five complete matched pairs. Source labels TDP-43 positive and TDP-43 negative were harmonized as nuclear TDP-43 retained and lost, respectively. After validation against featureCounts-assigned read counts, 44,225 genes with at least 10 total counts were analyzed using PyDESeq2. The primary model was ~ donor + nuclear_status; status-only and diagnosis-adjusted models were sensitivity analyses. The contrast was TDP-43 loss minus retained. Results. The donor-aware model identified 3,442 genes at false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.05: 1,865 lower and 1,577 higher in TDP-43-loss nuclei. STMN2 was consistently depleted (log2 fold change = -1.813, 95% Wald interval -2.229 to -1.396; FDR = 6.22e-15), corresponding to approximately 71.5% lower expression. Normalized STMN2 counts were lower in TDP-43-loss nuclei in all five complete donor pairs. TARDBP expression was also lower (log2 fold change = -0.606; FDR = 4.98e-6). In contrast, UNC13A whole-gene expression was modestly higher in the donor-aware model (log2 fold change = 0.372; FDR = 0.00622) and was not significant in either sensitivity model. Conclusions. Donor-aware analysis supports a robust association between nuclear TDP-43 loss and STMN2 depletion in this neuronal-nuclei cohort, alongside extensive but model-dependent transcriptomic variation. Whole-gene UNC13A expression cannot be used to infer UNC13A cryptic-exon inclusion or functional UNC13A depletion. No splice-junction, percent-spliced-in, isoform, or protein measurements were available; mechanistic claims therefore require junction-level and experimental validation.
author_corresponding_institution: Tongji Medical College of Huazhong University of Science and Technology,

title: Dyskinesia induced by a dopamine 2 receptor-like agonist, but not a dopamine 1 receptor-like agonist, is blocked by sub-anesthetic ketamine
abstract: L-DOPA remains the most effective symptomatic treatment for Parkinson's disease, but chronic administration is frequently complicated by L-DOPA-induced dyskinesia (LID). Our prior work has established that sub-anesthetic ketamine can reduced LID acutely and has a long-lasting neuroplastic effect. This study tested whether low-dose ketamine reduces dyskinesia induced specifically by dopamine D2R-like or D1R-like receptor activation. Male Sprague Dawley rats were primed with daily L-DOPA to establish dyskinesia and then challenged with quinpirole, a D2R-like receptor agonist, or SKF-81297, a D1R-like receptor agonist, to induce abnormal involuntary movements (AIMs). After stable AIM baselines were established, animals received agonist plus vehicle or agonist plus ketamine. Limb, axial, and orolingual AIMs were scored on the acute treatment day (D0) and after washout on D4 and D7. Quinpirole and SKF-81297 reliably produced stable total LAO AIM scores following L-DOPA priming. Ketamine significantly reduced only quinpirole-induced, but not SKF-81297-induced, total AIMs compared with vehicle on D0, demonstrating an acute anti-dyskinetic effect. This reduction persisted after washout, with ketamine-treated animals continuing to show significantly lower AIMs on D4 and D7. Time-course analyses further showed reduced AIMs expression across the post-quinpirole observation period on D0 and at multiple time points on D7. These findings demonstrate that ketamine suppresses quinpirole-induced dyskinesia in L-DOPA-primed male rats and suggest that D2R-like receptor-mediated or indirect pathway-related mechanisms, but not direct pathway-related mechanisms, may contribute to ketamine's anti-dyskinetic effects. Together, these results extend prior work on ketamine by linking its sustained anti-dyskinetic effects to dyskinesia driven by D2R-like receptor stimulation in vivo.

title: Electroencephalographic activity patterns distinguish interdigitated default and frontoparietal networks
abstract: The brain is comprised of distributed functional networks that operate on diverse time scales. Evidence from precision fMRI shows that canonical networks, including default (DN), frontoparietal control (FPCN), and dorsal attention (dATN), each fractionate into multiple finely interdigitated networks. However, as fMRI is blind to fast processes underlying neural communication, there remains a need to neurophysiologically characterize individual-level network fractionation. To address this need, we conducted a simultaneous EEG-fMRI study, including multiple sessions per individual, resting-state and task conditions, and carbon wire loop sensors for optimized artifact correction. Using precision network mapping, we discovered dissociable electrophysiological correlates of blood-oxygen-level-dependent activity for two networks within the boundaries of the canonical DN. One (DNa) related more positively with alpha and high-beta power, while another (DNb) related more negatively with theta and low-beta power. Univariate and machine learning analyses further revealed electrophysiological dissociations between networks within the canonical FPCN (FPCNa versus FPCNb) but not dATN. The network-specific electrophysiological activity patterns were reliable across sessions, only modestly variable between resting-state and demanding task conditions, and observable for neighboring nodes of different networks across multiple cortical zones. Our findings provide insight into rhythmic neural processes that fine-grained networks may engage to support divergent cognitive operations.

title: Embodied Dynamic Causal Modelling: Brain and Cardiac Effective Connectivity
abstract: Brain-body interactions underpin embodied inference and interoception, and are central to both general health and the pathophysiology of mental health disorders. These interactions are orchestrated across a hierarchy extending from the cortex, through the brainstem, to peripheral autonomic effectors. Existing methods either reduce this communication to scalar summaries or lack an invertible biophysical model, and so cannot resolve where in this extended architecture an observed effect originates. To address this, we introduce Embodied Dynamic Causal Modelling, an extension of the generative causal modelling framework that formalises hierarchical message passing across the full brain-body axis. We instantiate the framework for brain-heart interactions with the Brainstem Cardiac Network, a closed-loop neural mass model of brainstem autonomic circuitry and sinoatrial node dynamics. By incorporating five brainstem nuclei, a viscerosensory thalamic relay and the cardiac pacemaker, the network enables estimation of directed effective connectivity across the cortical-brainstem-cardiac axis. As an illustrative case study, representative of the experiments and extended physiological systems that Embodied DCM and the BCN can now interrogate, we applied the framework to simultaneously recorded electroencephalography and electrocardiography during an auditory Go/No-Go paradigm. A multimodal observation model permits joint inversion of electrophysiological and cardiac responses, so that neural and bodily measurements together constrain an account of central and peripheral dynamics. The case study shows how the framework can arbitrate between competing hypotheses about functional cytoarchitecture, distinguishing granular from agranular microcircuits within the viscero-sensorimotor hierarchy. It also shows how time-varying estimates of synaptic efficacy can be recovered alongside continuous latent neuronal dynamics, over extended windows spanning anticipation, target processing and motor inhibition. By linking neural and cardiac signals to a single generative architecture, this work moves the study of brain-heart interactions beyond correlation, providing a framework for testing theories of embodied inference and for identifying circuit-level disruptions in disorders of interoceptive and autonomic regulation.

title: Establishing an assay for visual desensitization in larval zebrafish for understanding synaptic plasticity
abstract: Synaptic plasticity, the ability of neurons to modify the strength of their connections, is essential for learning. Desensitization is a type of synaptic plasticity during which a behavioral response to a stimulus is reduced after repeated presentations of a weakened version of the stimulus which does not produce the behavioral response and thus is deemed a subthreshold stimulus. Here we explore whether the larval zebrafish escape response from visual threats, such as an expanding dark spot, can act as a potential model to study desensitization. We developed a novel experimental setup to investigate visual desensitization, exposing larvae to looming visual threats of varying contrast, and used high-speed cameras to verify rapid escape movements. First, we established stimuli which reliably acted as subthreshold and suprathreshold stimuli. Next, we quantified the response rate before and after desensitization and compared those data to control larvae who were not desensitized. We observed desensitized larvae reduced their response rate to threatening looming stimuli. By providing an opportunity to explore the plasticity mechanisms governing sensory-motor transformations and behavioral adaptation, this research contributes to our understanding of fundamental principles of learning and neural plasticity across vertebrates.

title: Evolution Shapes Cortical Interneuron Migration
abstract: The cerebral cortex comprises excitatory neurons and inhibitory interneurons originating from distinct forebrain regions. During migration, cortical interneurons (cINs) interact dynamically with neighbouring cells and their microenvironment, contributing to cortical architecture. However, how evolutionary changes in cIN migration shape species-specific cortical development remains unclear. Comparative analyses in mouse, ferret, and human models revealed a conserved migratory sequence but distinct behaviours: human cINs migrate slower, display increased leading-process branching, and exhibit more frequent homotypic repulsive interactions than their mouse and ferret counterparts. These features promote dispersed cortical invasion of cINs in humans and ferrets, contrasting with the stream-like migration observed in mice. Mechanistically, elevated expression of the cytosolic carboxypeptidase CCP1 in human cINs reduces microtubule glutamylation and doublecortin recruitment, thereby facilitating leading-process branching. These findings identify a CCP1-dependent mechanism regulating cIN dispersion and suggest that evolutionary changes in cIN migration contribute to divergent patterns of cortical morphogenesis across mammals.

title: Facing the waves of negative mood: Trait mindfulness moderates the links between physiology and emotion
abstract: Trait mindfulness is a dispositional ability characterized by awareness, non-judgment, and acceptance of internal and external experiences. Stress is associated with numerous psychological and physical health concerns including depression and anxiety. Mindfulness-based interventions (MBIs) have consistently been shown to reduce perceived stress and improve a variety of other health outcomes. However, the mechanisms through which mindfulness confers these benefits are not yet fully understood. This study aimed to examine (1) the relationship between trait mindfulness and changes in cortisol following a negative Mood Induction Procedure (MIP) and (2) whether trait mindfulness moderates the relationship between changes in cortisol and mood reactivity following a negative MIP. Participants were recruited from the Dallas-Fort Worth Metroplex (N = 25 participants) and completed a series of self-report questionnaires, negative and positive mood induction, and mood assessments. Participants provided salivary cortisol samples before and after negative MIPs. Results indicated that, following the negative MIP, sadness and anxiety were associated with greater reductions in cortisol. Trait mindfulness moderated these associations. Overall, these findings contribute to a broader understanding of emotional responses to negatively-valenced stressors and how they are mitigated by mindfulness. They suggest support for future applications of mindfulness-based interventions in high-stress populations.
author_corresponding_institution: The University of Texas at Dallas

title: Fast rate coding in heterogeneous spiking networks
abstract: A network of spiking neurons is said to operate in the rate coding regime if its dynamics can be accurately described by a continuous rate network. But how can discrete spike-based communication between neurons give rise to continuous rate-based dynamics? Computational studies showing that heterogeneous spiking networks can approximate the dynamics of recurrent neural networks (RNNs), a special case of rate network, assume that spikes are approximately Poisson or that network dynamics are slow. Here, we show that neither assumption is necessary: heterogeneous networks of non-Poisson neurons can produce fast rate-based dynamics. To demonstrate this, we show that signal transmission in feedforward networks of integrate-and-fire-type neurons can be described by a history-dependent rate network that is asymptotically exact as network size grows, even if heterogeneity persists, while linear-nonlinear rate networks fail. By providing a constructive model of fast rate coding in heterogeneous networks, this work lays the foundation for extending rate-based analyses of neural recordings beyond the assumption of slow dynamics or Poisson rate codes.

title: Functional ultrasound imaging in free-moving marmosets reveals that intra-call prosodic features modulate large-scale cortical dynamics
abstract: Vocal turn-taking relies on sequential structure and rhythmic timing, yet how primate brains integrate these features across timescales in naturalistic, free-moving contexts is unclear. We developed functional ultrasound imaging for free-moving marmosets, combining an exogenous marker-based workflow for robust registration from non-standard imaging planes with preprocessing pipeline optimized to reduce locomotion artifacts. We systematically perturbed sequential and rhythmic features of interactive phee calls across hierarchical timescales. Cortical networks showed selective sensitivity to intra-call structure: disrupting phrase sequences increased activity in auditory and para-insular cortices and strengthened inter-subject functional connectivity within this network. Rhythmic manipulations primarily affected core auditory cortex: shortening inter-phrase intervals enhanced responses, whereas lengthening intervals suppressed them. These findings establish a practical framework for free-moving primate neuroimaging and identify intra-call prosodic features as promising targets for mechanistic investigation.
author_corresponding_institution: Institute of Neuroscience, Center for Excellence in Brain Science and Intelligence Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences

title: GFRAL neurons remodel intestinal structure and type 2 immunity
abstract: The brain has emerged as a key regulator of immune functions, but the underlying neural mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here we show that brainstem GFRAL-expressing neurons prime type 2 immunity and shape intestinal epithelial structure in mice. Type 2 inflammation results in activation of GFRAL neurons and potentiation of their excitatory synaptic inputs. Enhancing GFRAL neuron excitability is sufficient to remodel intestinal type 2 immunity through a polysynaptic vagal brain-gut circuit, expanding tuft and goblet cell populations and increasing intestinal type 2 cytokine expression; while inhibiting GFRAL neurons leads to largely opposite changes. Accordingly, manipulating GFRAL neuron function reshapes intestinal structure and pathophysiology in food allergy, helminth infection and colitis models. Thus, GFRAL neurons orchestrate type 2 immune responses to facilitate recovery from intestinal diseases.
author_corresponding_institution: Westlake Laboratory of Life Sciences and Biomedicine

title: Glider compositionality and information capacity in an E/I-balanced neuronal automaton
abstract: In cellular automata, localized activity patterns called gliders propagate and interact to carry and transform information. Whether neuronal networks can harness this computational power remains unclear. Here, we demonstrate that a cortical network model with separate excitatory and inhibitory populations, graded cellular activity and uniform local connectivity spontaneously generates diverse, interacting gliders. An analytical reduction identifies the cellular conditions sustaining propagation of the dominant G-glider. Distinct gliders can assemble into growing structures that emit other glider types. Near excitation/inhibition balance, sparse glider dynamics coexist with high computational capacity, measured by input differentiation and generalization, with local capacity varying across space and time. Strong mutual inhibition between interneurons instead permits metastatic proliferation with low computational capacity. These findings connect cellular automata to neuronal information processing and identify interacting gliders as a candidate mechanism for dynamic plasticity: the reorganization of computation within an unchanged synaptic architecture.

title: Graph neural network approach for inferring neuronal connectivity
abstract: Understanding the connectivity of neuronal networks is essential for understanding brain function. Current anatomical mapping techniques, such as serial section microscopy and viral tracing, are resource-intensive and cannot capture the efficacy of connectivity. A complementary approach is to infer effective connectivity from single-neuron-resolution population activity. We developed a graph neural network (GNN)-based tool, CircuitGNN, that accurately infers neural effective connectivity from population activity. CircuitGNN accurately inferred the connectivity of several small circuits and detected both the strengthening and weakening of connections, such as those that occur during learning. CircuitGNN outperformed other methods when applied to simulated population activity generated by an invertebrate central pattern-generating circuit and a cortical microcircuit. CircuitGNN was evaluated on networks of varying size, recording duration, and proportion of hidden neurons. Although performance improved with longer recordings, CircuitGNN achieved high precision with recordings as short as 4 min, scaled to large circuits of up to ~750 neurons, and remained robust when 20% or 40% of neurons were hidden. These results establish CircuitGNN as an accurate and robust technique for inferring neural connectivity from activity.
author_corresponding_institution: McGovern Medical School at The University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston

title: Hierarchical Uncertainty Transformation During Multimodal Comprehension
abstract: Human communication requires combining information from different modalities even when each source is incomplete or ambiguous. Yet how uncertainty is coordinated as distinct semantic representations interact and converge remains unclear. Here we propose a hierarchical uncertainty transformation framework and test it across four gesture-speech experiments combining behavioral measures, information-theoretic modelling, and electroencephalography. Rather than being uniformly reduced as information accumulates, uncertainty changed its computational form across three interdependent levels: uncertainty within modality-specific semantic representations, bidirectional but asymmetric changes during cross-modal interaction, and uncertainty associated with multisensory convergence. These computational distinctions were accompanied by differentiated but temporally overlapping neural associations. Modality-specific uncertainty was expressed relatively early, whereas cross-modal transformation and convergence were most prominently associated with activity in the N400 range. Critically, both the neural expression and statistical coupling of these computational quantities varied with the semantic information available from gesture and speech. Together, these findings show that multimodal comprehension involves a context-dependent reorganization of uncertainty across interacting representations, providing a computational framework for understanding how coherent meaning emerges from heterogeneous and uncertain information.
author_corresponding_institution: Institute of Psychology, Chinese Academy of Sciences

title: Hmox1/CO regulates retina regeneration via modulation of Wnt/β-catenin signalling and induction of vaspb in zebrafish
abstract: Muller glia (MG) in the zebrafish retina retain a latent stem cell capacity that is absent in mammals, yet the injury responsive signals that drive this reprogramming remain incompletely defined. Here, we identify heme oxygenase-1 (Hmox1), the stress-inducible, rate-limiting enzyme of heme catabolism, as a previously unrecognized regulator of this process. Following injury, hmox1a is selectively and rapidly induced among the heme oxygenase gene family, localizing to photoreceptors with expression peaking during the MG proliferation window. Pharmacological inhibition and morpholino mediated knockdown of Hmox1 dysregulate the acute inflammatory response, impair Muller glia-derived progenitor cell (MGPC) proliferation, and produce lasting deficits in retinal lamination, establishing Hmox1 as a potentially non-redundant, early-acting node required for structural recovery. Exogenous delivery of carbon monoxide (CO), a bioactive Hmox1 metabolite, partially rescues each of these phenotypes, functionally implicating CO as a key downstream effector. Mechanistically, Hmox1/CO signalling stabilizes {beta}-catenin likely via transcriptional repression of the Wnt antagonist dkk1b. This stabilized {beta}-catenin is enriched at a predicted Tcf7l2 site in the promoter of vaspb, which encodes an actin binding protein and is newly identified here as an injury-induced Wnt target gene. Bioinformatic and functional analyses further implicate Nfe2l2a (Nrf2) as a candidate intermediary bridging Hmox1/CO to Wnt regulation, with putative antioxidant response elements identified within the dkk1b locus. Together, these findings outline a putative Hmox1[->]CO[->]Nrf2[->]dkk1b[->]{beta}-catenin[->]vaspb relay coupling redox biology to Wnt-dependent glial reprogramming. Notably, HO-1 is similarly induced in stressed mammalian retina, yet Wnt/{beta}-catenin activation fails to sustain regeneration, positioning the Hmox1/CO axis as a candidate target for future investigation in mammalian retina regeneration.
author_corresponding_institution: S. N. Pradhan Centre for Neurosciences, University of Calcutta, India

title: Human and mouse cerebellar inhibitory circuits in dystonic crisis and their modulation with therapeutic stimulation
abstract: Dystonia is a neurological movement disorder characterized by abnormal muscle contractions that, at their most severe, lead to a life-threatening condition - dystonic crisis. Yet, therapeutic options remain limited by our incomplete understanding of what neural circuits underly the condition. Although cerebellar nuclei neurons are implicated in the origin of baseline dystonic symptoms, it is unclear whether their activity drives dystonic crisis. To explore this role, we found that cerebellar abnormalities and neural inhibition were recurring targets in patients with dystonic crisis, implicating cerebellar inhibitory neurons in its development. We devised a mouse genetics approach to test whether inhibitory cerebellar nuclei neurons (iCNNs) induce dystonic crisis. Directional optogenetic modulation of iCNNs induced dystonic crises on-demand and alleviated spontaneous crises in mice that mimic spontaneous dystonic crises. To investigate whether iCNNs interact with other motor areas during dystonic crisis, we identified monosynaptic iCNN projections to the centrolateral nucleus of the thalamus (CL). Deep brain stimulation of the CL alleviated dystonic crises induced by iCNN photoactivation. Our data uncover a cell type-specific cerebellar origin of dystonic crisis and highlight its therapeutic potential.

title: Iconic Sound-Shape Correspondences in Aphasia
abstract: Purpose: To examine speech iconicity for shape in aphasia, we compared shape iconicity ratings from people with aphasia to those from neurologically intact individuals and evaluated how these ratings relate to phonological and semantic processing profiles in aphasia. Method: Twelve people with aphasia and twelve age- and gender-matched neurologically intact participants rated how rounded or pointed 50 auditory pseudowords sounded, using a 5 point scale. Ratings from participants with aphasia were compared to predicted shape iconicity ratings derived from reference ratings from prior work and to ratings from neurologically intact participants. For participants with aphasia, correlations between individual ratings and predicted ratings were related to measures of phonological and semantic processing. Results: Ratings from people with aphasia were significantly correlated with both the predicted ratings and the ratings from neurologically intact participants. Relative to ratings from neurologically intact people, ratings from people with aphasia had weaker correlations to predicted ratings. There were indications that greater language impairment was associated with greater disruption of iconicity ratings; in particular, deficits in phonological segmentation and semantic processing were associated with reduced sensitivity to shape iconicity. Conclusion: These findings suggest that sensitivity to shape iconicity is preserved to varying degrees in individuals with aphasia. Disruption of phonological and semantic processing appears to affect shape iconicity processing in aphasia.

title: Imipramine binds to amyloid-β and extends the survival of Alzheimer's disease patients
abstract: Background Apolipoprotein E (apoE) plays numerous roles in the pathogenic pathway to Alzheimer's disease (AD). We previously performed a high-throughput screen and identified the antidepressant imipramine as an inhibitor of the interaction between apoE and amyloid-{beta} (A{beta}). We also found that imipramine use to treat depression in AD patients was associated with better Mini-Mental State Exam (MMSE) scores. Here we studied the mechanisms by which imipramine inhibits the AD pathogenic pathway and investigated its effect on mortality in AD patients. Methods Nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy was used to characterize the interaction between imipramine and A{beta} monomers. Human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived AD cerebral organoids (COs) and transgenic AD rats treated with imipramine underwent neuropathological evaluation, while rat learning and memory were assessed in the Morris Water Maze. AD patient mortality in the National Alzheimer's Coordinating Center's database was analyzed by Kaplan-Meier and Cox proportional hazards models. Results Imipramine inhibits the apoE-A{beta} interaction by binding directly to A{beta} monomers. Imipramine reduces A{beta} accumulation and neuronal cell loss in AD COs. Imipramine-treated female AD rats had enhanced reference memory and increased hippocampal cellularity and cholinergic neurotransmission. AD patients prescribed imipramine had reduced all-cause mortality over 10 years relative to those prescribed other tricyclic antidepressants (TCA), non-TCA antidepressants, or no antidepressants. Conclusions The findings support the conclusions that: a) the mechanism by which apoE confers risk for AD is by catalyzing the polymerization of A{beta} into neurotoxic species, b) targeting apoE is a promising, underappreciated strategy for the prevention of AD, c) imipramine should be used more frequently to treat depression in AD clinical practice, and d) imipramine should be evaluated in prospective trials, particularly in APOE4 carriers, as a potential method to improve cognition and reduce mortality in AD.

title: Impact of acoustic property uncertainty on transcranial ultrasound simulation
abstract: Subject-specific simulations of wave propagation are commonly used to plan and report acoustic and thermal exposure during transcranial ultrasound (TUS) interventions. Their accuracy depends on acoustic and thermal tissue property assumptions, including sound speed, density, and attenuation. Reported property measurements vary widely across the literature, precluding consensus point estimates for simulation. How this property uncertainty affects estimated exposure has not been quantified. We compile literature-based bounds for seven acoustic and thermal properties of skull and brain tissue and assess their individual impact on simulated intensity and temperature rise using two independent simulation platforms (PRESTUS/k-Wave and BabelBrain). Variations in skull attenuation and absorption produced the largest outcome uncertainty: peak intensity in the brain varied roughly threefold across the reported range of skull attenuation alone, while absorption most strongly affected temperature rise within the skull. The direction of each parameter's effect was consistent across platforms and, with one exception, across skull thickness. This allowed bounds to be combined into setups that bracket transmission and temperature rise. Compared to these extremes, default property sets of three simulation toolboxes (k-Plan, BabelBrain, PRESTUS) yielded similar brain intensity but divergent skull heating, driven mainly by differing assumptions on skull absorption and heat capacity. These results indicate that uncertainty in skull acoustic properties is a major source of variability in TUS exposure estimates, and that refined measurements of these properties, together with explicit reporting of exposure uncertainty, are needed to support safe, effective, and reproducible transcranial ultrasound planning.

title: Integrated Characterization of Proximal and Distal Nerve Stumps in a Model of Chronic Motor Nerve Transection
abstract: Prolonged peripheral nerve discontinuity subjects the proximal stump to chronic axotomy and the distal stump to chronic denervation, resulting in pathological changes that may compromise regeneration following delayed repair. Although these changes have been investigated in both nerve stumps, much of the existing evidence derives from mixed sensorimotor nerve models, leaving the histopathological changes of chronic motor nerve injury incompletely understood. Addressing this gap requires a well-defined, reproducible model that maintains prolonged motor nerve discontinuity and enables concurrent characterization of both nerve stumps. This study aimed to establish a chronic motor nerve transection model and characterize the distinct structural and microenvironmental changes occurring in both nerve stumps. The buccal branch of the facial nerve was transected in Lewis rats, and the nerve ends were secured to adjacent muscle to prevent spontaneous reconnection. At 10 weeks post-injury (p.i.), proximal and distal stumps were compared with uninjured nerves using histological, immunofluorescence, and morphometric analyses. Persistent functional impairment was observed throughout the study period. The proximal stump exhibited traumatic neuroma formation, altered axonal morphology, and loss of myelin integrity, but largely preserved its underlying nerve architecture and microenvironment. In contrast, the distal stump exhibited reduced neurofilament expression, clusters of small-caliber myelinated axons, and increased myelinated axon density compared to both uninjured nerves and the proximal chronically injured segment. These changes were accompanied by endoneurial tube atrophy, increased collagen I deposition, vascular remodeling, and immune-cell accumulation, indicating extensive structural and microenvironmental remodeling. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that chronic motor nerve transection produces two distinct pathological compartments: a proximal stump characterized by persistent but disorganized regeneration-associated features and a distal stump characterized by pronounced degenerative and microenvironmental changes.
