This study establishes a reproducible model of chronic peripheral nerve injury and provides a foundation for investigating how these compartment-specific pathologies contribute to regenerative failure and for developing targeted therapeutic strategies to improve regeneration following delayed nerve repair.

title: Integrated metabolomics and proteomics from voxelated cortical hemispheres of adult rhesus monkeys
abstract: The spatial organization of molecular networks across cortex likely contributes to differences in local circuit vulnerability in aging and Alzheimer's disease; yet many existing molecular datasets sacrifice spatial structure, sampling only a handful of regions per brain. Here, we present a framework for generating spatially registered, paired metabolomic and proteomic maps across an entire cortical hemisphere of an adult rhesus monkey, at millimeter resolution. One hemisphere each from two animals was harvested under controlled conditions, approximately flattened, and hand dissected at different sampling resolutions (roughly 2.5 and 4 mm/side) into tissue voxels. Each voxel was split after homogenization and extraction to provide matched aliquots for targeted metabolomics and deep untargeted proteomics. To handle these high dimensional data, we developed PChclust, a principal component guided feature clustering algorithm. For cross omic integration, we developed a spatially regularized sparse canonical correlation analysis (sr-sCCA), which incorporates spatial neighborhood structure via graph Laplacian smoothing. We recover meaningful biology: Molecular similarity between neighboring voxels decayed with distance in both modalities, confirming that voxelation captures spatially organized biological variance. The sr-sCCA identified joint proteome-metabolome components with coherent cortical gradients that were conserved across animals. Pathway enrichment analysis recovered brain relevant ontologies and reconstructed complete metabolic circuits from single voxels.

title: Intrinsic fluctuations modulate thalamic gating during the emergence of human conscious perception
abstract: Human conscious perception is not determined solely by external sensory input but is also shaped by moment-to-moment fluctuations in intrinsic brain states. However, how these intrinsic states directly function after stimulus onset to shape the emergence of conscious perception remains unclear. We recorded sEEG activity in thalamus and five other consciousness-related cortical regions, while 32 patients (n= 2,023 recording sites) conscious percept a near-threshold visual stimulus. Preceding the extensively evoked consciousness-related activities, there are early activities (0-200ms after stimulus onset) exclusively appeared in high-order thalamus. These early activities inversely associated with stimulus strength, which reflected an intrinsic state that compensated for the stimulus-evoked response to reach the conscious threshold. These early activities were closer to the critical state in conscious trials, which enables more efficient information processing. These results suggest that intrinsic fluctuations in the high-order thalamus directly modulate thalamic gating during the emergence of conscious perception.
author_corresponding_institution: School of Psychology, Shanghai Jiao Tong University;State Key Laboratory of Cognitive Neuroscience and Learning and IDG/McGovern Institute for Brain Research, D

title: Learning complex temporal dependencies via local synaptic plasticity
abstract: The ability to extract and exploit temporal structure across diverse tasks is central to human cognition. Neuroscientists have typically relied on recurrent neural networks (RNNs) trained with backpropagation through time (BPTT) when modelling neural and behavioural processes such as decision-making and motor control. However, this algorithm has limited biological plausibility, hence the computational principles underlying efficient learning of temporal dependencies remain unresolved. Here, we investigate temporal predictive coding (tPC), a recently proposed framework that extends predictive coding to the temporal domain while preserving local Hebbian update rules. We analyse and extend tPC to establish its relationship with several influential computational models of learning in RNNs, including BPTT, reservoir computing, and eligibility propagation (e-prop). We first demonstrate structurally equivalent weight update rules between tPC and tBPTT1, a variant of BPTT in which gradients are propagated only one time step into the past. We then show that tPC can leverage reservoir dynamics to encode short-range temporal context, and simultaneously sculpt neural trajectories in state space to support downstream readout. We further demonstrate that hierarchical recurrent dynamics can facilitate learning of more complex temporal dependencies, while additionally conferring robustness to strong distractors. Finally, we show that tPC networks can be augmented with biologically inspired eligibility traces to solve temporally extended context-dependent tasks. Together, these results reveal that relatively simple recurrent networks governed by local plasticity can support temporal learning in more complex settings than previously appreciated.

title: Lesion-Derived Estimated Functional and Structural Connectomes Predict Post-Stroke Recovery Outcomes
abstract: Accurate prognosis after stroke remains challenging, limiting the ability to predict individual recovery. While advanced connectome MRI can provide further prognostically-useful information regarding affected brain networks, its impractical nature has given rise instead to lesion-based estimates of network disruptions. Here, we present a novel pipeline that leverages our recently developed connectome analysis tools to estimate structural disconnection (eSDC) and functional connectivity (eFC) directly from N=96 patient lesion masks for use in predicting motor, language, attention and memory outcomes at multiple timepoints after stroke. Our approach jointly leverages our Network Modification (NeMo) Tool, a database of white matter tractography results that estimates structural disconnectivity (eSDC), and the Krakencoder, a joint autoencoder that estimates functional connectomes (eFC) from the NeMo Tool's output. Models based on eSDC and eFC predicted almost all outcomes, particularly motor outcomes, significantly better than models that used patients' fMRI-based observed FC (oFC) and models based on only lesion information and covariates. Estimated connectome measures also i) retained meaningful inter-individual variability when compared to observed functional connectomes, ii) reflected population-level, stroke-related changes in functional connectomes, and iii) resulted in outcome prediction models with feature importances that aligned with expected networks of relevance to the given outcome. Feature importance analyses also identified distinct predictive signatures across both modality and outcome domain, indicating that eSDC and eFC capture non-redundant, biologically meaningful information about post-stroke network disruption. Together, these findings establish our lesion-based estimates of post-stroke structural and functional connectomes as a practical, information-rich alternative to advanced imaging in patients. This approach allows for probing an individual's affected neural circuitry underlying stroke impairment and recovery, paving the way toward more efficient, accessible, and personalized approaches to post-stroke prognosis and intervention.
author_corresponding_institution: Department of Radiology, Weill Cornell Medicine, New York, NY, USA

title: Long term survival of chronically demyelinated axons in the taiep rat
abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an inflammatory demyelinating disease of the CNS in which neuroaxonal loss underlies permanent neurological disability. Axon loss in MS has been attributed to several causes, including loss of trophic/metabolic support from the myelin sheath. However, the contribution of chronic demyelination to axonal demise has been difficult to ascertain, due largely to the lack of long-lived models and uncertainty about the location of the primary injury site in long fibre tracts in MS patients. Here, we examine chronically demyelinated axons using light and electron microscopy of spinal cord tracts of 1- to 24-month-old taiep rats, in which the gene that is mutated, Tubb4a p.A302T, is expressed highly in oligodendrocytes. We find that small diameter axons in the dorsal column can survive for many months following demyelination. This is associated with significantly increased densities of oligodendroglia, and supernumerary glial cell processes. We hypothesise that trophic and metabolic support, sufficient to support axon survival, can be achieved through close contact between axons and glia. While efforts to restore myelin in MS remain crucial to recovering normal neurological function, myelin per se might not be a prerequisite for axonal survival under all circumstances.

title: Mapping AMPA and NMDA receptors at mouse brain hippocampal synapses by cryo-ET
abstract: AMPA and NMDA receptors are fundamental to synaptic transmission through the detection of released neurotransmitter. These ion channels open in response to glutamate binding, resulting in depolarization of the postsynaptic membrane and influx of calcium. Receptor localization plays a key role in synaptic strength, and changes in receptor number and location underpin synaptic plasticity, learning and memory. Here we apply receptor subunit-specific antibody fragments and multiplexed gold nanoparticle conjugates, together with cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET), to elucidate the in-situ molecular organization of AMPA and NMDA receptors at hippocampal synapses in adult mouse brain tissue. AMPA receptors are predominantly found in densely packed liquid-like clusters, with interspersed NMDA receptors and adjacent NMDA receptor clusters. By direct localization of individual receptors, we provide molecular-resolution insight into the distribution of AMPA and NMDA receptors across the synapse, at peri and extrasynaptic sites, and within endocytosed vesicles. Visualization of multiple presynaptic vesicle fusion events suggests that receptors are near, but not always directly adjacent to, transmitter release sites. By mapping AMPA and NMDA receptors, and glutamate release sites, we provide receptor-resolution insight into the structure and function of brain hippocampal synapses.
author_corresponding_institution: Oregon Health & Science University | Howard Hughes Medical Institute

title: Mapping brain networks underlying abstract perceptual decision formation and its EEG signatures
abstract: Perceptual decisions have been proposed to involve a common mechanism of evidence accumulation operating across sensory modalities and motor contexts. In human EEG, the centroparietal positivity (CPP) tracks evidence accumulation in such a supramodal motor-independent manner, but its cortical sources are uncertain. Here we combined fMRI and EEG, acquired in separate sessions of the same supramodal change-detection paradigm, with individualized finite element head modeling to identify decision-related networks. A conjunction analysis across visual and auditory modalities and across motor and non-motor required tasks revealed consistent activation of bilateral postcentral, supramarginal, and superior parietal lobules, precentral gyrus, central operculum, middle frontal gyrus, and cerebellum. Forward modeling of fMRI-defined sources indicated that parietal-opercular regions were the dominant contributors to the response-locked and non-motor-required peak-locked CPP signal. These results implicate a network of brain areas in supramodal, motor-independent target-detection decisions, whose specific functional roles can be interrogated in more complex decision tasks in future.

title: Metabolic complexity in the human brain supports metastable network dynamics and declines in normative ageing
abstract: The adaptive capacity of the brain is tied to the complexity of its neural activity. While entropy of brain signals has been used to characterise this complexity in haemodynamic and electrophysiological systems, it remains unknown whether entropy contributes to the temporal dynamics of the metabolic signals of the brain (glucodynamics) and how metabolic entropy may relate to network organisation, brain ageing and cognitive decline. Here, we combined dynamic functional PET (fPET) with 18F-fluoroedeoxyglucose and simultaneously acquired functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) in 84 adults to investigate multiscale entropy (MSE) in the brain. We report that metabolic complexity measured with PET MSE represents non-linear, high-frequency complexity, whereas hemodynamic complexity reflects non-linearly constrained neurovascular phase dynamics. Greater metabolic complexity was associated with greater network metastability, particularly in unimodal and higher-order associative networks. Greater regional metabolic complexity also correlated with greater cortical thickness, cerebral metabolic rates of glucose (CMRglc) and cerebral blood flow, and was lower in older than younger adults. In contrast, global and network haemodynamic MSE was not significant associated with network dynamics. Higher global metabolic complexity was associated with better cognitive performance, and voxel-level derived MSE clusters were \associated with cognitive performance in both modalities, with varied cluster sizes and spatial locations. However, these associations were largely accounted for by age variance. We conclude that temporal complexity in cerebral glucose is associated with the dynamics of the underlying metabolic signals, enables metastable network states and declines in ageing. Entropy of metabolic brain signals offers promise as a neurobiologically grounded metric of brain ageing.

title: Multimodal characterization of putative pan-inhibitory viral constructs in macaque monkeys
abstract: Transgenic approaches and validated viral vector toolboxes have advanced our understanding of how inhibitory neurons shape cognition and motor control in mice and other rodents. However, such advances have been elusive in non-human primates (NHPs). While many studies demonstrate expression of reporter proteins, few studies have provided clear quantitative evidence of whether these viral constructs can be reliably used for assessment of in vivo and in vitro function in primates, which, in turn, has hindered widespread adoption by NHP researchers. Here, we characterize putative pan-inhibitory cell targeting vectors engineered with regions from the Dlx5-6 intergenic domain. Pan-inhibitory viral vectors are attractive because they enable ground-truth optotagging and modulation of multiple inhibitory subtypes in the same animal and, when combined with machine learning approaches, enable cell-type classifiers for NHPs. We combined in vivo anesthetized electrophysiological recordings, in vitro slice electrophysiology, and immunohistochemistry across seven rhesus macaque monkeys to assess the specificity, completeness and efficacy of three constructs in multiple sensory and higher-order association cortices. The vectors reliably restricted transgene expression to inhibitory neurons (81-97%). However, of the local GABAergic neurons only 32-64% expressed the transgene, depending on the construct. This incompleteness arose in part from uneven coverage across subtypes, with strong transgene expression in parvalbumin-positive interneurons (~60-90%), sparse expression in calbindin-positive interneurons (~1-7%), and near-complete avoidance of calretinin-positive interneurons. A construct pairing DLX2.0 with ChrimsonR was excellent for in vivo optotagging, while h56D paired with bReaChES most effectively suppressed neural activity in vivo. In the slice, activating terminals of transgene-expressing neurons optically evoked inhibitory currents in coupled pyramidal neurons confirming transsynaptic functionality of these constructs and their use for inhibitory circuit-specific synaptic assessments and manipulation. Collectively, the results provide rigorous functional characterization, and quantitative guidance for NHP researchers seeking to deploy GABAergic cell-type-specific tools in their experiments.
author_corresponding_institution: Boston University Department of Anatomy & Neurobiology

title: Multimodal longitudinal prediction of alcohol-use trajectories in adolescents and young adults: Social context, real-life social affective benefit, and fronto-striatal involvement
abstract: Escalating alcohol use during adolescence and young adulthood confers substantial risk for later substance misuse and adverse mental health outcomes, yet the factors that determine early drinking trajectories remain poorly understood. Here, we examined alcohol use across social, affective, and neural domains in a cohort of 378 community-based young drinkers using a combination of longitudinal phenotyping, ecological momentary assessment (EMA) and functional neuroimaging. Across different levels of analysis, higher baseline alcohol consumption (standard drinks per week) was associated with immediate substance-use social context, greater social-affective benefit in daily life, and heightened engagement of the fronto-striatal reward circuitry. In a one-year longitudinal follow-up, individual social-affective benefit and substance-related social environmental factors showed the strongest predictive value for drinking trajectories in a follow-up of 219 individuals after one year. Our findings identify key social and neural reward-related determinants of youth drinking behavior, informing the development of evidence-based risk detection and prevention measures.
author_corresponding_institution: Central Institute of Mental Health, Heidelberg University

title: Myelin Governs Hippocampal Network Function through the Extracellular Space it Occupies, Not Only the Axons it Insulates
abstract: Myelin, the multilamellar sheath wrapping neuronal axons, enables saltatory conduction. Beyond electrical insulation, myelin occupies volume, and therefore shapes the extracellular space (ECS) through which interstitial fluid flows and neurotransmitter diffuses. How these two roles interact is unknown. We built a multi-scale model of hippocampal CA1 coupling lattice Boltzmann simulations of ECS flow to detailed networks of reconstructed neurons and glia. Demyelination enlarged the ECS volume fraction from 28 to 43 per cent up to 43 to 70 per cent across layers, lowered tortuosity from about 1.7 to 1.4, raised effective diffusivity from 0.35 to 0.50 of free solution and shortened solute breakthrough times by roughly a third, while raising flow speed yet lowering viscous dissipation. Because transmitter concentration scales inversely with that volume, synaptic driving force fell: postsynaptic potential amplitude declined with wrap count and transmission failed entirely below four of sixteen wraps. In 200-cell networks, demyelination halved firing (pyramidal 7.9 to 4.4 Hz), rendered discharge burst-dominated, reduced band power by up to 8.7-fold and displaced the population state, which a classifier separated at 100 per cent accuracy, whereas an inflammatory glial census left every functional measure unchanged. Driving myelin continuously from intact to 12.5 per cent and back recovered the same threshold near four wraps, and firing rate and spectral power returned fully to baseline. Myelin thus governs circuit function through the space it vacates as well as the axons it insulates, with opposite consequences for clearance and for signalling, a dissociation that may matter in demyelinating disease.
author_corresponding_institution: Institute of Medical Technology, Peking University Health Science Center

title: NTAD: A longitudinal neuroimaging dataset of Alzheimer's disease pathology
abstract: We introduce the New Therapeutics in Alzheimer's Disease (NTAD) dataset, a multi-modal and longitudinal imaging dataset from 70 biomarker-positive people with early dementia or Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) due to Alzheimer's Disease (AD), assessed over 2.5 years, and 35 healthy controls assessed at baseline. The data include simultaneous magneto- and electro-encephalography (M/EEG), 3-Tesla structural and functional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), Amyloid-beta; positron emission tomography (PET), fluid proteomic biomarkers in cerebrospinal fluid and blood, and a battery of clinical and neuropsychological assessments. 11C UCB-J PET was undertaken for a subset of participants. For people with AD, assessments were repeated at approximately three weeks, 15 months, and 28 months after baseline. The data can be accessed through the Dementias Platform UK (DPUK), including pre-processed M/EEG and T1 MRI in pseudonymised BIDS format. With the pressing need to develop treatments for slowing, reversing, and preventing AD, these data provide an opportunity for identifying and validating novel biomarkers of Alzheimer's disease neurophysiology, as well as understanding its treatable pathology.

title: Neural discrimination of emotional prosody in natural sentences in 2- to 3-month-old infants using OPM-MEG
abstract: From birth, infants are sensitive to the emotional prosody of speech, yet it remains unclear when the developing brain discriminates emotions conveyed by natural spoken sentences. Here, we recorded brain activity with optically pumped magnetometer magnetoencephalography (OPM-MEG) in 15 infants aged 2-3 months while they listened to semantically neutral sentences spoken with happy or angry prosody. Natural sentences elicited robust auditory evoked responses, with prominent components at 88, 216, 380 and 1,356 ms after sentence onset and sources centred on bilateral superior and middle temporal cortex. Time-resolved multivariate pattern analysis revealed that distributed neural activity discriminated recordings spoken with happy from angry prosody 346-454 ms after the onset of the prosodically prominent word (the first word carrying a pitch peak), despite no difference in global field power between conditions. This discrimination was transient, emerged before the end of the sentence, and was carried primarily by phase-locked delta-band activity, followed by later differences in induced alpha power. Angry prosody also delayed the late auditory response by approximately 15 ms with no detectable changes in amplitude. Our findings show that cortical responses to happy and angry prosody in natural speech differ by 2-3 months of age, and demonstrate that OPM-MEG combined with time-resolved decoding can reveal the temporal, spatial and spectral organisation of early emotional-prosody processing.

title: NeuralFieldManifold: Uncovering the Manifold Geometry of Local Field Potentials
abstract: Manifold geometry has become a powerful framework for understanding how the brain organizes high-dimensional neural activity into compact, interpretable structure. To date, however, most theoretical and methodological advances in neural manifold analysis have focused on spiking activity, leaving unresolved a fundamental question: What are the geometric principles governing the dynamics of local field potentials (LFPs); population level signals reflecting integrated subthreshold and suprathreshold neural activity that are broadly integral to clinical and brain-computer interface settings. Here, we establish, analytically and empirically, that the lag-embedded dynamics of LFP signals lie on a low-dimensional K-torus, where K directly relates to sustained oscillatory modes present in the signal. Modeling LFPs as bounded autoregressive processes, we show that each oscillatory component contributes an independent circular degree of freedom, while aperiodic 1/f structure and noise contribute only geometric thickness around the manifold without altering its topology. To apply this theory to real nonstationary recordings, we introduce DeepLagField, a physics-informed network that jointly estimates time-varying AR structure and effective model order, with formal guarantees that local toroidal geometry is preserved despite non-stationary nature of neuronal processes. Persistent homology analysis on real recordings reveals topological signatures consistent with the predicted toroidal Betti numbers in primate V1 LFP, rodent hippocampal LFP, and mouse cortical EEG, with varying degrees of agreement across recordings and temporal windows. Crucially, decoding analyses across three distinct neural datasets demonstrate that these geometric structures are not merely descriptive but capture behaviorally relevant information rivaling conventional spectral features. Together, these findings establish a theoretically grounded and empirically validated geometric framework for neural field analysis, extending the manifold perspective beyond spiking activity and offering a complementary language to spectral analysis for understanding and translating population dynamics across neural modalities.

title: Noise-referenced multi-shell diffusion-weighted imaging for regional cerebrospinal fluid thermometry
abstract: We developed a multi-shell diffusion-weighted imaging approach for separate ventricular and subarachnoid cerebrospinal fluid thermometry. The approach uses measured image noise to assess agreement among temperature estimates. In 12 participants, temperature was estimated from four non-zero diffusion weightings. For each voxel, disagreement between these estimates was compared with that expected from image noise, accounting for their shared reference image. Voxels meeting this consistency criterion were retained for regional analysis. Mean diffusion-derived temperature ({+/-} SD) was 38.4 {+/-} 0.4 {degrees}C in the lateral ventricles and 36.0 {+/-} 1.1 {degrees}C in the subarachnoid space. Ventricular estimates were consistently higher than subarachnoid estimates across all participants, with a mean difference of 2.4 {+/-} 1.2 {degrees}C (95% confidence interval 1.6 -3.1 {degrees}C). This difference persisted under alternative noise models and temperature estimators. Subarachnoid estimates increased with retained voxel count; in a post hoc analysis of the six participants with the largest retained counts, ventricular estimates remained higher by 1.6 {+/-} 0.7 {degrees}C. Absolute temperature accuracy and the physiological origin of the regional difference require independent validation. This approach provides an internal consistency check for CSF thermometry and supports separate assessment of ventricular and subarachnoid temperatures.
author_corresponding_institution: The University of Newcastle, NSW, Australia

title: Norepinephrine inhibits Afferent activation of NTS Catecholamine Neurons in Mice
abstract: The nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS) integrates visceral sensory input to regulate feeding behavior, with catecholaminergic (CA) and neuropeptide Y (NPY)-expressing neurons playing key roles in energy homeostasis. Recent evidence suggests functional heterogeneity among CA-NTS neurons, including distinct subpopulations that either suppress or promote feeding. In this study, we investigated how norepinephrine (NE) modulates excitatory synaptic transmission from solitary tract (ST) afferents onto tyrosine hydroxylase-positive (TH) NTS neurons in mice. Using patch-clamp electrophysiology in horizontal brainstem slices, we found that NE inhibits ST-evoked excitatory postsynaptic currents (ST-EPSCs) in a concentration-dependent manner, with maximal effects at 10 microM and an EC of ~3.4 microM. This inhibition was mediated by alpha-adrenergic receptors and was independent of GABAA receptor activity. NE also suppressed asynchronous glutamate release and attenuated CCK-induced increase in spontaneous EPSC frequency, suggesting a presynaptic mechanism. NPY similarly reduced ST-EPSC amplitude via Y2 receptor activation, and co-application of NE and NPY produce additive or synergistic effects, even at subthreshold concentrations. Together, our results reveal a novel mechanism by which noradrenergic and peptidergic systems interact to regulate visceral sensory processing in the brainstem.

title: Oligodendrocyte precursor cell death does not contribute to lifelong population homeostasis
abstract: Oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs) proliferate and differentiate into myelinating oligodendrocytes throughout life, but it is unclear if their continuous self-renewal is balanced by cell death. We find that OPCs do not die during development or adulthood, nor during remyelination, acute systemic inflammation, or aging. These findings challenge the assumption that spontaneous OPC death is common and reveal that OPC homeostasis does not depend on programmed cell death.

title: Oligodendrocytes may provide the extra density of α-synuclein filaments from multiple system atrophy
abstract: Prion-like templated seeding of a-synuclein filaments is thought to underlie the spreading of multiple system atrophy (MSA) and other synucleinopathies through the brain. Here, we used -synuclein filaments extracted from the brains of individuals with MSA to induce seeded aggregation in undifferentiated human neuroblastoma SH-SY5Y cells, human iNeurons, mixed primary murine cortical cells and murine oligodendrocyte-enriched primary cultures, all overexpressing human -synuclein, followed by determination of the cryo-EM structures of the seeded filaments. Whereas MSA seeds comprise two protofilaments with an unidentified non-proteinaceous density located between protofilaments, seeding resulted in the formation of filaments with a single protofilament. Only the seeded structures derived from oligodendrocytes contained an extra density that resembled that of the seeds. This suggests that oligodendrocytes may provide the chemical component that is responsible for the extra density at the protofilament interface of MSA filaments. In support, the injection of MSA seeds into the striatum of transgenic mice expressing human -synuclein under the control of the oligodendrocyte-specific proteolipid protein promoter, also yielded seeded filaments with a single protofilament and a similar extra density.

title: Optimizing non-invasive assessment of gastric activity: a fully automated channel-wise pipeline for multi-electrode electrogastrography
abstract: Electrogastrography (EGG) is a non-invasive, and affordable technique for investigating gastric physiology. However, its broader adoption is hindered by low signal-to-noise ratios and the lack of standardized, objective procedures for channel-wise artifact rejection and signal quality assessment. To address these limitations, we developed a fully automated, data-driven pipeline (Gastric Signal Processing Toolbox, GSPT) for channel-wise EGG preprocessing and analysis, designed to preserve physiologically-relevant information even under high-noise conditions. GSPT exploits high-resolution time-frequency representations, to automatically identify and remove motion-related and electronic artifacts through entropy-based analysis of the signal's instantaneous energy and robust outlier detection through integration of multiple anomaly-detection strategies. The resulting signals are characterized through a channel-wise gastric fingerprint, comprising established EGG measures, such as dominant frequency, together with novel descriptors such as Renyi entropy. Channel quality relays on Monte Carlo surrogate analysis, while recording-level quality is evaluated through dominant frequency consistency across channels. GSPT further provides ridge-based estimates of instantaneous amplitude and phase and quantifies inter-channel interactions through Total Correlation, enabling the construction of a global gastric fingerprint. Validation on datasets containing controlled motion artifacts demonstrated robust signal recovery with improved signal-to-noise ratios at the dominant frequency. Artifact identification, assessed using precision and recall, was comparable or better than existing approaches. Gastric fingerprints showed high stability within subjects and across recording sessions. As a freely available, one-click MATLAB toolbox, GSPT reduces manual bias and standardizes EGG preprocessing and analysis, even in low-density recordings, potentially providing a reproducible framework for investigating gastric functions in psychological, neurological and pathological conditions.

title: Oscillatory Phase Coding Emerges in Adaptive RNNS for Flexible Working Memory
abstract: Oscillatory phase coding (OPC) is widely observed in neural systems and has been implicated in cognitive functions such as memory and sequence processing. However, its computational role and neural substrates remain largely unclear. Here, we studied OPC by training recurrent neural networks (RNNs) with adaptation to perform sequence working memory tasks with variable delays. After training, we found that OPC emerges in the RNN spontaneously: the memorized items recur at distinct phases of a shared rhythm, with oscillation amplitude encoding item identity and phase encoding serial order. Ablation studies identified three key elements required for OPC: adaptation in neural dynamics, variable delay in memory retention, and flexibility in reading out information. Neuron-type analysis revealed the emergence of content and time cells in the trained RNN, and they process item identity and sequence order separately. Recurrent connectivity analysis revealed phase-organized connections among time cells and structured connections within digit-selective content-cell groups. Inspired by these findings, we proposed a neural circuit model which reproduces OPC through interactions between content units and an adaptive time ring. Together, this study reveals how OPC arises from network structures and task demands, offers insights into the implementation and computational mechanisms of OPC in biological systems, and inspires us to develop computational models for human-like cognitive functions.

title: PHASOR: An Open-Source Pipeline for Hidden Markov Model Analysis of Stimulus-Locked Retinal Multielectrode-Array Population Activity
abstract: Multielectrode-array recordings of the retina reveal neural population activity at cellular resolution, but relating recurring population states to stimulus timing and single-unit responses requires several linked analysis steps. We present PHASOR (Population HMM Analysis of Stimulus-locked Output in the Retina), a pipeline that combines stimulus-clock alignment, Fourier-based response classification, hidden Markov modeling with Chow-Liu tree emissions, model-order selection, and state visualization. We evaluated the workflow with synthetic populations and demonstrated its use in ten ex vivo recordings from three wild-type retinas (two male, one female) and one male rd1 retina, including 2 Hz full-field sinusoidal stimulation. Across ten synthetic datasets containing seven generative states, selected model orders ranged from seven to nine, with a mean of 7.9, matching the generative count exactly in three of the ten datasets. A representative confusion matrix showed a near one-to-one correspondence between generative and decoded states, with a single additional low-occupancy state, illustrating the distinction between recovering temporal structure and recovering the exact state count. In a representative retinal recording, response classes differed in stimulus phase and contrast dependence, and decoded states differed in occupancy, dwell time, and active-unit composition. Recordings during L-AP4 application, without projected stimulation, and in a photoreceptor-degenerate rd1 retina illustrated changes in the resulting population-state descriptions. PHASOR integrates established analysis methods into a reusable workflow for relating stimulus-associated population activity to functional response classes. The selected states provide a descriptive model of population activity; their number and correspondence to biological assemblies require separate validation.

title: Pain Matters: Nociceptive signaling drives neural encoding of inflammatory responses
abstract: Pain is a cardinal sign of inflammation, constructed by the brain from peripheral nociceptive input. Yet, its role in the brain's response to inflammation remains unknown. Here, we demonstrate that nociceptive signaling is essential for the brain to represent and replay inflammatory states. Analysis of human fMRI and mouse activity mapping revealed that peripheral inflammation generates a distinct brain state. In mice, ablation of TRPV1+ sensory neurons or pharmacological analgesia disrupted this organization and prevented the insular cortex from forming retrievable immune representations. Conversely, augmenting nociceptive signaling during inflammation strengthened subsequent immune recall. These findings identify nociceptive input as a critical signal in brain-immune dialogue, enabling the encoding and retrieval of inflammatory events.

title: Paraquat Inhalation Produces Male-Biased Dopaminergic Neuron Loss and Motor Deficits in Mice: Relevance to Parkinsons Disease
abstract: Long-term exposure to paraquat (PQ), a widely used herbicide, has been linked to increased risk of Parkinsons Disease (PD) in agricultural workers and rural communities in the United States (US), findings further supported by experimental animal studies. Although banned in many countries across the globe, PQ remains widely used in the US. Inhalation of PQ has been known to induce systemic organ failure at acute concentrations. However, prolonged low-dose inhalation from agricultural spraying and pesticide drift has not been readily evaluated for its potential to contribute to neurodegenerative diseases in vivo. Instead, many experimental studies have relied on systemic routes of exposure, which do not effectively replicate the most common route of exposure to PQ in the environment. In the current study, Parkinsonian features were examined in mice that had been exposed via whole-body inhalation to PQ aerosol for either 40 or 60 days. Levels of PQ in brain were highest in olfactory bulb, followed by frontal cortex and then brainstem in both sexes. After 60 days of exposure, male-specific impairments in locomotor activity were observed, in addition to reductions in striatal dopamine, in substantia nigra tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) expression and number of TH+ dopaminergic neurons, the latter being considered the primary basis of PD, along with increased olfactory bulb -synuclein levels. As such, these studies confirm the dopaminergic neurotoxicity of inhaled PQ. These findings raise significant concerns as to the contribution of PQ exposures to the continued increase in the incidence of PD in the US.
author_corresponding_institution: University of Rochester, School of Medicine and Dentistry

title: Parkinson Disease vs Aging Features Impairments in Formation and Release of a Power Grip in Real and Pantomimed String-Pulling
abstract: Parkinson disease (PD) impairs skilled reaching tasks but less is known about its effects on rhythmic bimanual actions. We used a bimanual hand-over-hand string-pulling task that requires repeated reach, grasp, pull, push and release movements. We predicted that participants with PD would show impairment in making the rotary skilled hand movement of retrieving the string, analogous to impairments observed in single handed target reaching. Nine participants with PD (mean UPDRS-III: 24.6), 16 older adults, and 10 young adults successfully performed a real string-pulling task and then pantomimed the action. Video analyses combined optical-flow estimation of whole-body movement speed, markerless 2D pose estimation of upper-limb kinematics, and expert frame-by-frame scoring of hand and finger shaping. Machine-learning classification then identified the discriminative information carried by these multilevel movement components. Participants with PD showed lower movement speed, a smaller hand workspace, and reduced hand and finger shaping, with older adults showing intermediate values. All participants grasped the real string with a power grip, but participants with PD showed reduced rotary movements of the arm and the wrists and absent of arpeggio-like sequential finger movement during grasp and release. During pantomime, participants with PD moved faster and made larger hand movements, while grasp-related hand opening and finger sequencing was reduced or absent. The findings suggest that PD is expressed across this multicomponent movement manifold, and that the movement organization changes with task demands: real string pulling requires formation and release of a power grip, whereas pantomime does not place demands on grasping ability.

title: Path knockout: an analysis tool for connectome-driven circuit discovery
abstract: Neural circuits in the brain transform sensory information into perceptual, emotional and motor output. The connectome -- a synaptic-resolution wiring diagram of all neurons in a nervous system -- provides a neuroanatomical blueprint for identifying different circuits that mediate specific computations. However, its sheer scale and complexity pose a significant challenge in extracting functionally relevant multi-synaptic pathways. Here we established path knockout, a connectome analysis method that identifies dominant multi-synaptic pathways. Path knockout uses the input fraction of each synaptic connection as a surrogate for the probability that information transfer succeeds across that synapse and calculates approximate probability, or connection strength, that at least one path succeeds among all multi-synaptic paths between defined source and sink neuron populations. It then quantifies the importance of each interneuron by assessing the impact of its removal on the connection strength. We demonstrate that path knockout outperforms other methods for pathway analysis and identifies known and novel interneurons in the Drosophila circuits. Using path knockout, we identified a convergent circuit motif linking sexually dimorphic aggression command neurons to a shared isomorphic visual pursuit pathway. Path knockout is implemented such that it runs in minutes on a standard computer. Thus, path knockout provides a scalable and generalizable framework for connectome-driven circuit discovery.

title: Photoentrainment as Bayesian Inference: How the central circadian clock may weight and integrate the intensity and wavelength of natural light to estimate astronomical time
abstract: Synchronising with the Earth's 24-hour rotation using natural light as a timing cue presents a problem for the mammalian brain's central circadian clock. Natural light is highly variable and can take a range of values at any given time of day. For example, it fluctuates due to differences in weather conditions and across seasons. Therefore, an absolute value of light provides an uncertain indication of the time of day. Despite this uncertainty, the central clock maintains close alignment with astronomical time, and here we describe how this may be achieved computationally. We present a Bayesian model in which the clock's endogenous oscillation is used to predict the probability of observing features of light, including intensity and spectral composition, and their co-occurrence given the time of day. These predictions are drawn from a distribution of values typically experienced. When observed light falls outside the predicted range, a prediction error provides evidence that the clock may be misaligned with astronomical time. How much the clock adjusts its phase depends on the relative uncertainty associated with its internal prediction and observed light. These are combined as a weighted average according to their relative reliability, drawing the clock's updated phase towards whichever provides the more reliable estimate of astronomical time. Using natural light measurements collected over one week from 59 human observers and 100 days of environmental spectral measurements, we characterize how the variability of natural light systematically changes across the day and show how the clock may exploit this structure for circadian timekeeping. The model explains how the canonical shape of the phase response curve emerges from the relationship between light distributions and time of day, and how properties of light, including intensity and spectral composition, can be integrated according to their reliability. The central clock's synchrony to light may represent a specific instance of a general computational strategy employed by the mammalian nervous system, whereby sensory information is interpreted relative to an internally generated prediction.
author_corresponding_institution: The institute of Cognitive Neuroscience, University College London

title: Practical Identifiability of a Minimal Adaptive Learning-Gain Model for Binary Feedback: A Simulation Study
abstract: Social learning is shaped by distinct computational components--baseline beliefs (prior mean), feedback sensitivity (learning gain), and temporal uncertainty (drift)--that empirical designs rarely disentangle. We evaluate practical identifiability and predictive performance of a parsimonious four-parameter adaptive learning-gain model for binary feedback, where a latent belief about positive-outcome probability updates deterministically between observations and an internal confidence-precision state decays each trial. {sigma}, {omega}, and {lambda} are internal, model-defined variables--not validated psychological constructs. Using fixed-seed simulations, we report four findings. Joint maximum-likelihood recovery is poor: on a 24-condition grid (T=80), {sigma} and {omega} show near-zero tolerance-based recovery ([≤]0.002) across tolerances 0.3-1.0, {lambda} recovers at 0.078-0.263, and longer sequences do not improve recovery. Profile-likelihood and trade-off diagnostics show flat regions for {sigma} and {omega} and an asymmetric {lambda} profile, indicating weak practical (not structural) identifiability. A fitting-parity audit fixed a return-order bug in the fixed-gain candidate. After correction, block-level model discrimination is 0.48 (72/150) under common bounds--above chance (p<0.001)--but is driven almost entirely by Rescorla-Wagner (0.88-0.90); the adaptive filter and its nested fixed-gain restriction remain indistinguishable. Across 50 held-out datasets, the model shows no predictive advantage over an empirical-frequency baseline (paired 95% CIs span zero). Ablations show the added update components provide no consistent benefit. These results caution against interpreting individual parameter estimates from this model class in short binary-feedback designs, and specify that mechanistic claims about clinical group differences in {sigma}, {omega}, or {lambda} require graded responses, manipulated volatility, multi-context sequences, and longitudinal replication.
author_corresponding_institution: School of Psychological and Cognitive Sciences, Peking University, Beijing, China

title: Predicting cortical signal mixing in coarse-resolution fMRI: a forward-operator analysis of surface mapping and the conditional benefit of correction
abstract: Surface-based fMRI projection can mix signals from cortical locations that are close in the volume but distant along the folded cortical sheet. We constructed an anatomy- and acquisition-informed linear forward operator to estimate this mixing and evaluated a regularised surface reconstruction that inverts it. In HCP 7T geometry, the operator-predicted net far-cortex contribution to a standard surface value exceeded 5% in 4%, 10% and 22% of the group-average cortex at 1.6 mm and at emulated 2.4 and 3.2 mm resolution. Including the modelled far component improved predictions of emulated coarser maps and of real coarser StudyForrest sessions in high-leakage regions. Against finer-resolution, cross-run fMRI references, the regularised reconstruction reduced the residual error in HCP development data (n = 15) and in a pre-specified, family-independent confirmatory analysis (158 participants in 86 families). The improvement increased with a response-weighted contamination measure in HCP and in an independent 3T dataset (35 test participants), although a coarse-data-only version of the measure did not generalise to 3T, where an anatomical atlas predicted the gain at twofold coarsening. Overall performance improved at twofold, but not 1.5-fold, coarsening in the 3T sample. Ablation and data-reduction analyses were consistent with an important contribution from local deconvolution but did not uniquely identify the mechanism. Benefits were smaller or absent for multi-run averages, and no robust improvement across separately acquired sessions was established. The leakage maps characterise model-predicted, signed mixing rather than directly measured signal origins, and every gain is measured against an fMRI reference rather than against the true cortical response. Code, analysis plans and group leakage maps (7T and 3T) are provided in a public repository.

title: Pubertal timing is a critical dimension of adolescent brain vulnerability
abstract: Adolescence is a period of rapid brain development, during which biological maturational timing varies substantially between individuals. This variability may drive specific developmental vulnerabilities to adverse experiences with long-term consequences, warranting early identification of at-risk individuals. We utilized ultrasonic bone age measurements to track pubertal maturity, classifying participants by adolescent biological maturity relative to chronological age (accelerated, average, decelerated). Brain hierarchy was quantified as the irreversibility of brain signals in resting state electroencephalography, providing a brain-based method to detect vulnerability patterns. The COVID-19 pandemic presented a unique opportunity to also assess alterations in brain hierarchy following external disruption. We mapped maturity-defined trajectories and rates of hierarchical organization, and their post-pandemic deviation from expected development, capturing two distinct vulnerability forms. First, early maturing adolescents showed persistent reduction in brain hierarchy. Second, those undergoing their fastest phase of development - specifically, decelerated adolescents - showed the strongest disruption in brain hierarchy following the pandemic. These findings suggest that pubertal timing is a critical dimension of individual variation in adolescent brain development and vulnerability. They also emphasize the need for objective maturity measurements to tailor support to individual pubertal timelines, particularly given the secular trend toward earlier puberty and ongoing global ecological crises.

title: ROCK inhibitor Ripasudil reduces Alzheimer pathological proteins and enhances cellular bioenergetics
abstract: Rho-associated kinase (ROCK) inhibitors have been explored as an Alzheimer Disease (AD) therapeutic agent. In this study, we aim to determine the efficacy of a potent ROCK inhibitor, ripasudil, in impacting AD pathological protein tau in mice. The time-course study showed that ripasudil rapidly penetrated mouse brains, reaching maximal concentration half an hour post-injection. To determine the efficacy of ripasudil, we injected AppNL-G-F knock-in mice with ripasudil at 30 mg/kg and sacrificed them after three hours. We used Tandem Mass Tag labels and compared the proteomic profiles of mouse brains exposed to ripasudil to those exposed to saline. We also treated AD-patient-derived Neural Stem Cells (NSCs) with ripasudil and performed a Seahorse Mito Stress Test to evaluate their impact on mitochondrial activity. Bioinformatics analysis of the proteomic profiles revealed differentially enriched components of chromosome. The Mito Stress Test of NSCs revealed significant increases in basal oxygen consumption, ATP-linked respiration, maximal respiration, and reserve capacity oxygen consumption compared to untreated NSCs. Importantly, we found a significant reduction of Tau and pTau 396 in brains of mice treated with ripasudil. Overall, our findings highlight the feasibility and promise of ROCK inhibitor ripasudil as an AD therapeutic agent.

title: Reaction-time asymmetry covaries with shifts in hand choice in macaques
abstract: How primates choose which hand to reach with remains poorly understood. Humans prefer the hand on the target's side of the body midline, and that preference shifts with biomechanical cost and with head and gaze direction. Earlier monkey studies used only two targets, one per side, too few to fit a psychometric function. Reaction time may also reflect the choice; in humans it is longest at the point of subjective equality (PSE), the target position at which either hand is equally likely to be chosen. We measured hand choice at ten horizontal target positions in two male rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta) that chose freely on each trial. For peripheral targets, both animals used the hand on the same side of the body midline, with a well-defined transition in between. Displacing the hands, rotating the head, or displacing gaze to one side each moved the PSE toward that side. Reaction time was longest near the PSE. Hand displacement slowed the hand on the displaced side, and gaze displacement slowed the hand opposite the gaze. In every condition, the farther the PSE lay toward one side, the slower that side's hand was relative to the other. Macaque hand choice thus resembles human hand choice, making the macaque a tractable model for studying how the brain chooses a hand.

title: Real-time reorienting during episodic retrieval rescues memories from suboptimal arousal-attentional states
abstract: Successful knowledge expression varies with one's arousal-attentional (A-A) state at the moment just prior to attempting to remember. Yet, whether such states causally affect retrieval remains unclear. Here we introduce PRISM (Pupil-based Real-time Intervention System for Memory), a closed-loop paradigm that continuously monitors pupil size to track A-A states in real time and, during suboptimal states (SOS), delivers a visual reorienting cue in the moment before a retrieval attempt. In 67 participants performing a goal-directed source memory and item recognition task, we show that pupil-defined SOS just prior to retrieval impair both item recognition and source recollection relative to optimal state (OS) trials. Critically, delivering a brief visual reorienting trigger cue on SOS trials in real time rescues item memory, but not source memory, raising item memory to a level not credibly different from real-time OS trials and providing causal evidence that phasic attentional reorienting during A-A-defined suboptimal states facilitates memory access at retrieval. Offline spline-detrending analysis confirms that the A-A state-memory relationship is robust to slow physiological drift. It also shows that the trigger benefit was credible for marginally suboptimal (drift-driven) SOS trials and smaller and less certain for deeply suboptimal (drift-resistant) SOS trials, consistent with a zone-of-recoverability account, although the difference between the two SOS subtypes was not credible. Furthermore, among deeply suboptimal trials the A-A-boosting trigger cue improved memory for low-A-A SOS (i.e., pupillary constriction) but not high-A-A SOS (i.e., pupillary dilation) trials, consistent with the classic inverted-U relationship between arousal and performance, although the difference between the two directions was not credible. Together, these findings causally link phasic arousal-attentional reorienting at retrieval to memory rescue and suggest that the depth and direction of suboptimality shape whether such rescue succeeds, connecting the readiness-to-remember framework to the classic arousal-performance inverted-U relationship. Moreover, these findings provide a further foundation for adaptive closed-loop technologies that would tailor intervention to the depth and direction of momentary arousal-attentional states, facilitating memory expression in real time.

title: Reduced enteric Bdnf expression and TrkB-dependent regulation of Vip in a Mecp2-null mouse model of Rett syndrome-associated gastrointestinal dysmotility
abstract: Gastrointestinal (GI) dysmotility is a highly prevalent and clinically significant feature of Rett syndrome (RTT), yet its underlying mechanisms remain poorly defined. Here, we investigated these mechanisms of GI dysmotility in a Mecp2null mouse model of RTT. First, we observed that MeCP2 was expressed in murine myenteric ganglia, including in enteric neurons and that Mecp2null males developed maturation associated functional regression in their GI motility. In dysmotile mice, longitudinal muscle myenteric plexus tissue showed marked reductions in enteric Bdnf isoforms IV, VI, and II, whereas expression of the BDNF receptor isoforms TrkB.FL and TrkB.T1 was not significantly altered, consistent with reduced enteric BDNF TrkB signaling. Despite impaired GI motility, Mecp2null mice showed no significant changes in total enteric neuronal density, nitrergic neuronal abundance, or expression of Nos1, Chat, and Uchl1. In contrast, Vip expression was significantly reduced, while expression of VIP receptor genes: Vipr1 and Vipr2 was increased, indicating disrupted VIPergic signaling. Integration with publicly available enteric single-cell/nucleus datasets and targeted qRTPCR further suggested altered inhibitory neuronal subtype composition, with reduced Vip+ Cartpt+ signatures and increased Nfia expression, suggesting that MeCP2 loss differentially affects distinct inhibitory neuronal subpopulations. Finally, conditional loss of TrkB.FL in neural crest-derived cells reduced Vip expression without recapitulating the full Mecp2null VIPergic phenotype, indicating that impaired BDNF TrkB signaling contributes to, but does not completely explain, the GI dysmotility in this model of RTT. Together, these findings identify enteric BDNF TrkB and VIPergic dysfunction as key mechanisms underlying GI dysmotility in RTT.
author_corresponding_institution: Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center - Harvard Medical School

title: Reducing the Risk of Gradient Induced EEG Hardware Heating During Simultaneous EEG-fMRI
abstract: Simultaneous electroencephalography (EEG) and functional MRI (fMRI) has the potential to provide a more complete characterisation of brain function. Acquiring these data simultaneously requires the EEG hardware to be MR safe, since the EEG cap, amplifiers and powerpacks must be located within the MR environment. Placing them in this environment exposes them to both static and varying (radiofrequency (RF) and gradient) magnetic fields, presenting a potential heating risk. Previous studies have typically positioned the amplifiers and powerpacks outside of the bore, meaning that this risk is largely limited to the EEG cap. However, current guidelines recommend positioning the amplifiers within the bore. This reduces the distance between the EEG electrodes and amplifier, improving EEG signal quality and reducing risks of RF heating at the electrodes, but presents a potential heating risk for the amplifiers and powerpacks from the varying magnetic field gradients. In this study, we demonstrate that placing the amplifiers and powerpacks in the bore presents a significant heating risk, both at 7T and 3T. At 7T, we show that EPI sequences with a slew rate of at least 88 T/m/s resulted in significant heating of the EEG amplifiers. This heating effect could be negated by reducing the slew rate to 61 T/m/s. At 3T, we replicate the EEG amplifier heating and show that an alternative approach to reducing the gradient slew rates experience by the hardware is to increase the distance between the EEG amplifier/powerpacks and the isocentre of the magnet. Increasing the distance between the EEG hardware and MR isocentre by 30 cm mitigates the heating risk to the amplifiers and powerpacks, regardless of sequence parameters (e.g., slew rate). Therefore, whilst reducing the distance between the electrodes and amplifiers may improve EEG signal quality and reduce the potential for electrode RF heating, we show that risk of heating of hardware by gradient switching is greatly increased. This is particularly important to consider with the faster gradient slew rates available on modern MRI scanners, desired to increase spatial resolution. Experimenters must make careful decisions about hardware placement to ensure that the EEG-fMRI setup they use is safe, taking account of the varying risks that are posed by different approaches.
author_corresponding_institution: Sir Peter Mansfield Imaging Centre, School of Physics and Astronomy, University of Nottingham

title: Region-dependent regulation of Tau phosphorylation by Glycerophosphodiester Phosphodiesterase 2 in a mouse model of tauopathy
abstract: Hyperphosphorylation of Tau promotes its aggregation and neurofibrillary tangle (NFT) formation, contributing to neuronal dysfunction and neurodegeneration in diseases such as Alzheimer's Disease (AD) and AD-related dementias (ADRDs). However, the mechanisms underlying dysregulated Tau phosphorylation under pathological contexts remain unclear. Glycerophosphodiester phosphodiesterase 2 (GDE2) is a six-transmembrane enzyme that acts at the cell surface to cleave the glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI)-anchor that tethers a subclass of proteins to the membrane. Here, we show that in the PS19 tauopathy mouse model, GDE2 disruption modulates Tau phosphorylation by transiently decreasing Tau's propensity for aggregation through region-specific regulation of local kinase environments. In the cortex, GDE2 ablation in 6-month-old PS19 male mice (PS19;Gde2KO) reduces Tau phosphorylation at Serine (S)202/Threonine (T)205, T212, and S396 but increases S262 phosphorylation in the hippocampus of 6-month-old PS19;Gde2KO male and female mice. Consistent with these changes, in males, Glycogen Synthase Kinase-3  / {beta} (GSK3  / {beta}) activity is decreased in the cortex, while AKT activity is increased in both males and females in the hippocampus, with no changes in protein phosphatase 1 (PP1) and protein phosphatase 2A (PP2A) activity. Primary cortical neurons from PS19;Gde2KO animals showed reduced Tau phosphorylation at S202/T205, implying cell-autonomous roles for neuronal GDE2 in this process. GDE2 overexpression in heterologous SH-SY5Y cells increased Tau phosphorylation at S202/T205, while a catalytically inactive form of GDE2 did not, suggesting that GDE2 regulation of target GPI-anchored protein surface activity is required to modulate Tau phosphorylation. Taken together, our study identifies GDE2 as a component of the complex regulatory network that controls Tau phosphorylation in the context of tauopathy and provides insight into putative pathways relevant to Tau pathologies observed in disease.

title: Sensory neurons gate a cortical plasticity window for immune encoding
abstract: Activity-dependent plasticity allows brain circuits to encode experience, but this has been established with brief stimuli. Immune responses develop over days and are represented in the insular cortex (IC). How the cortex encodes experiences with this temporal structure is unknown. Here we show that Trpv1+ sensory neurons open a multi-day cortical plasticity window matched to the immune response. Following peripheral immune challenges, Parvalbumin-expressing inhibitory interneurons are activated first, restricting plasticity. Vasoactive intestinal peptide-expressing interneurons respond two days later, disinhibiting IC excitatory neurons. Weaker challenges trigger the first phase but not the second, and preventing the transition blocks immune encoding, whereas lowering inhibition beforehand does not. These results identify a body-to-brain mechanism that gates cortical plasticity on the timescale of slowly evolving physiological experience.

title: Sensory recurrence and convergent integration in the C. elegans connectome
abstract: The synaptic wiring of Caenorhabditis elegans has a global feed-forward architecture, from sensory to motor neurons. Yet, whole-brain optogenetic mapping shows that signals do not flow predominantly forward, and sensory neurons respond to more neurons than they drive. Where the wiring contains pathways leading back to their starting point is unclear. Here, we locate this recurrence using the feedback coefficient, derived from the Kubo-Martin-Schwinger framework for directed networks, which quantifies the proportion of walks reaching a neuron that originate from itself. The connectome has about three times more recurrence than strength-matched random networks, with the largest excess in sensory neurons, whereas random wiring places it on highly connected neurons. Along the thermotaxis pathway, this produces a recurrence gradient from thermosensory neurons to integrating interneurons. The ordering replicates in five reconstructions, including two independent adults, persists when reciprocal contacts are preserved or gap junctions removed, but vanishes with only short paths or loop counts. Convergence shows the reverse pattern, with every neuron receiving walks from fewer sources than in random wiring, especially sensory neurons. The wiring extends from a sensory periphery folding back on itself to interneurons and motor neurons integrating many sources, a candidate structural substrate for non-feed-forward signalling.

title: Socio-demographic gradients in traumatic brain injury disability, severity and nutrition: a two-level analysis of the Global Burden of Disease Study 2023 and NHANES 2011-2014
abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is among the most consequential non-fatal outcomes of trauma, yet how its burden, severity and nutritional context are patterned by socio-demographic development remains incompletely characterised. We addressed this question at two levels. Using the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) Study 2023, we quantified the socio-demographic gradients of TBI disability across the five socio-demographic index (SDI) quintiles and characterised the severity composition of the TBI disability burden, its 1990-2023 trend and its cause-specific structure. Using pooled NHANES 2011-2014, we then examined, at the individual level, how reported TBI history among US adults aged 40 years and older varied by income, education, health insurance and food security, and whether dietary differences between adults with and without a TBI history persisted after socio-economic adjustment. The age-standardised TBI disability rate was almost twice as high in the high SDI quintile as in the low SDI quintile (113.68 versus 57.55 per 100,000 in 2023), a gap essentially unchanged since 1990. Moderate or severe injuries accounted for 72.5% of the TBI disability burden in the high SDI quintile versus 84.0-84.6% in the other four quintiles, rising in every quintile between 1990 and 2023. Among US adults, reported TBI history rose with educational attainment (11.9% below high school versus 17.3% above) and was most common in very food-insecure households (23.4%; adjusted odds ratio 1.71, 95% confidence interval 1.39-2.09); income showed no unadjusted gradient but a negative association after mutual adjustment. Unadjusted dietary differences between adults with and without a TBI history largely attenuated after socio-economic adjustment, with only fibre density remaining marginally lower (-0.35 g/1,000 kcal, 95% confidence interval -0.64 to -0.06). The moderate or severe share of the disability burden is a tractable, mortality-free monitoring indicator for injury prevention, and nutritional risk among food-insecure TBI survivors warrants clinical attention.

title: Spinal Noradrenergic Overdrive Promotes Reversible Motor Unit Aging and Sarcopenia
abstract: Background Sarcopenia is characterized by progressive loss of skeletal muscle mass, strength, and physical function with aging. Motor unit degeneration is a major contributor, but the mechanisms driving age-related deterioration of motor neurons, neuromuscular junctions (NMJs), and muscle fibers remain incompletely understood. Norepinephrine (NE) regulates spinal motor neuron excitability, but its role in motor unit aging has not been established. Methods Whole-cell patch-clamp electrophysiology, optogenetics, fast-scan cyclic voltammetry, microdialysis, high-performance liquid chromatography, western blotting, and chemogenetics were used in mice aged 1-25 months. Motor neuron intrinsic properties were examined in 135 lumbar motor neurons from 81 mice. NE release dynamics, tissue content, and expression of the NE transporter (NET) and 2A-adrenergic autoreceptor were assessed in adult and aged mice. Descending spinally projecting noradrenergic neurons were selectively inhibited in aged mice using a retrograde chemogenetic approach. Results Aging produced progressive motor neuron hyperexcitability characterized by membrane depolarization, increased input resistance, elevated firing frequency, and altered action potential threshold (all P < 0.005). Optogenetically evoked endogenous NE increased motor neuron excitability by reducing action potential latency (P = 0.0001) and decreasing rheobase (P = 0.0028); these effects were prevented by 1-adrenergic receptor blockade (P = 0.0313). Aging enhanced stimulus-evoked spinal NE release, with greater responses at 20 Hz (P = 0.0223), 30 Hz (P = 0.0022), and 40 Hz (P < 0.0001). NE release elicited by stimulation of locus coeruleus and A5 noradrenergic inputs was also increased in aged mice (P = 0.0349 and P = 0.0016, respectively). Basal extracellular NE concentrations were unchanged, whereas spinal cord NE content increased (P = 0.0403). Aging reduced 2A-adrenergic receptor (P = 0.0009) and NET expression (P = 0.0046). Chemogenetic suppression of descending noradrenergic neurons in aged mice increased hindlimb muscle mass (P = 0.0111-0.0344), muscle fiber cross-sectional area (P = 0.0078-0.0467), NMJ innervation (P = 0.0210), and motor neuron soma size (P = 0.0353). Conclusions Aging promotes spinal noradrenergic overdrive characterized by increased NE storage, enhanced activity-dependent NE release, and impaired autoregulatory control. Excessive noradrenergic signaling contributes to motor neuron hyperexcitability and motor unit deterioration. Suppression of descending noradrenergic activity reverses structural features of motor neuron, NMJ, and skeletal muscle aging, identifying spinal noradrenergic signaling as a potential therapeutic target for sarcopenia.
author_corresponding_institution: Wake Forest University School of Medicine

title: Stable large-scale network architecture and structured individual variability in the awake mouse brain
abstract: Large-scale functional networks provide a scaffold for brain activity, but their population architecture and inter-individual variability remain poorly defined in the awake mouse brain. Here we introduce the Awake Mouse Connectome Project (AMCP), a population-scale multimodal MRI resource comprising 212 sex-balanced awake mice. Using this dataset, we generated high-precision in vivo tissue probability maps, derived a reproducible whole-brain functional network atlas and quantified structured variability in network connectivity across animals. The resulting atlas defined a stable large-scale architecture aligned with structural topology, while inter-individual functional connectivity variability followed organized connectional gradients rather than random dispersion. We further benchmarked the clustering-derived scaffold against conventional group independent component analysis (GICA) and release the GICA network atlas as an accompanying resource. AMCP further provides empirical scaling relationships linking sample size, scan duration and connectome precision. These analyses indicate that mean functional connectivity and functional connectivity variability have distinct sample-size requirements, providing a protocol-specific guidance for studies focused on group-average connectivity and inter-individual variability. Individualized network parcellations derived from the AMCP scaffold improved behavioural prediction relative to group-average features for selected behavioural domains, indicating functional relevance of subject-specific network architecture. Together, AMCP establishes an open dataset, tissue-template resource, clustering-derived and GICA functional atlases, and analysis toolbox for reproducible awake mouse connectomics and for translational studies linking circuit mechanisms to large-scale brain organization.
