abstract: The vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) ligand and its main receptor VEGFR2 are considered to be essential for endothelial differentiation, proliferation, sprouting and survival . Blood vessels cannot form in growing embryos or tissues when VEGF–VEGFR2 signalling is compromised in all cells . The anti-VEGF antibody, which can block angiogenesis in cancer, wound healing or ischaemic diseases, is among the most widely used antibodies in the clinic. However, vascular resistance to anti-VEGF therapy has been reported . Here we used iFlpMosaics and iSuRe –HadCre to induce and track genetic mosaics of endothelial cells (ECs) lacking VEGFR2 during the entire embryonic and postnatal development. These Vegfr2 -knockout ( Vegfr2 KO ) ECs adapted, proliferated normally and competed with wild-type cells over time, eventually forming a substantial portion of the vascular network in most organs. Vegfr2 KO ECs could not sprout during the first wave of angiogenesis in most tissues, because this process is highly VEGF-dependent and favours growth and mobilization of wild-type ECs. However, owing to their inability to respond to VEGF, Vegfr2 KO ECs became dominant in veins, which represented a long-term and continuous source of ECs for subsequent waves of VEGF-independent angiogenesis. Comparative single-cell RNA sequencing analysis of ECs with acute and long-term loss of VEGFR2 identified both common and organ-specific molecular mechanisms of adaptation and resistance to VEGF signalling loss. These included significant endothelial venousization and upregulation of ligands for VEGFR1 and VEGFR3. VEGFR1 only partially compensated for VEGFR2 loss in capillary ECs, whereas VEGFR3 compensated only in arterial ECs. Loss of the three VEGF receptors did not compromise venous growth. Notably, loss of the master regulator of venous development, NR2F2 (also known as COUP-TFII), significantly compromised expansion of Vegfr2 KO ECs. This work has implications for our understanding of the role of VEGF receptors in angiogenesis and demonstrates venousization as a mechanism of adaptation and resistance to VEGF signalling loss during angiogenesis.

abstract: High-affinity O -linked β - N -acetylglucosamine ( O -GlcNAc)-specific antibodies are crucial for the sensitive detection and functional study of O- GlcNAcylation. Here, we report the development of a nanomolar-affinity O- GlcNAc antibody named EPR19847 by using a degenerate O- GlcNAcylated peptide as the immunogen. The EPR19847 antibody can be used for O- GlcNAc detection, imaging, isolation, and chromatin immunoprecipitation. Using this antibody, O- GlcNAcylated proteins are enriched and identified in mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs). Chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by next-generation sequencing demonstrates that O- GlcNAc is enriched around the promoters of highly expressed genes, and that its genomic distribution is positively correlated with transcription-activating marks including H3K4me3, H3K9ac, and RNA polymerase II in mESCs. Further analysis suggests a high occupancy of O- GlcNAcylation within super-enhancers. We anticipate that EPR19847 will serve as a powerful tool for the highly sensitive detection and systematic functional dissection of O- GlcNAc.

abstract: Artificial intelligence is reshaping scientific discovery across diverse fields. Yet scientific AI remains constrained by data curation, which demands substantial manual effort and deep domain expertise, creating major cost and scalability barriers. Here we present the Agentic Intelligent Data Engine (AIDE), a multi-agent framework that automates data curation for scientific AI. AIDE collects, selects, and organizes data in three stages, providing an end-to-end pipeline that turns a data request into training-ready datasets. We benchmarked AIDE on 14 tasks across biomedical and chemical domains. Scientific AI models built with AIDE-curated datasets matched or outperformed those built with manually curated data, and AIDE’s fully automated preparation delivered significant gains in efficiency and data utilization without compromising quality. These findings provide consistent evidence of AIDE’s applicability across scientific domains and usage paradigms and demonstrate its potential to accelerate scientific AI development and democratize access to scientific AI.

abstract: Despite studies linking metabolism and cancer, our understanding of the metabolite network that drives metastasis remains incomplete. Through a metabolic RNAi-based screen for cell invasion, we identify alpha-aminoadipate (2-AAA), the intermediate metabolite of aminoadipic semialdehyde synthase (AASS) in the saccharopine pathway, as a common pivotal factor in metastasis of human cancers. Metabolite-protein connectivity mapping reveals that 2-AAA binds to SAE1, a crucial component of the SUMO-activating enzyme E1, and enhances SAE1 recruitment to UBA2, facilitating sumoylation. 2-AAA-mediated sumoylation of the RNA polymerase subunit POLR2A then partially promotes cancer cell invasion by inducing the expression of metastasis-promoting genes, including SPG11 and KCTD7 . Targeting AASS with cetalkonium chloride, a newly identified small molecule inhibitor against AASS, attenuates cancer cell invasion and tumor metastasis. Our study highlights the mechanism by which metastasis is mediated by metabolite-driven sumoylation and indicates AASS as an effective therapeutic target for mitigating metastatic cancer progression.

abstract: Magnetic tweezers are a popular biophysical instrument for manipulating and measuring single molecules. Most groups rely on custom-built setups tailored to specific experiments, making it challenging to implement and share software. Typically, image acquisition and hardware control are automated via LabVIEW, while real-time video processing is implemented in C + + /CUDA libraries. Live processing can eliminate the need to store raw video, enabling high throughput, fast acquisition rates, and simplified experimental workflows. However, no open-source general-purpose software framework currently unifies these capabilities for magnetic tweezers experiments. Here, we introduce MagTrack and MagScope open-source Python-based tools designed to fill this gap. MagTrack is an image-processing library that efficiently determines bead positions from magnetic-tweezers videos using CPU or GPU computation. MagScope is a comprehensive software framework offering a graphical user interface, real-time hardware control, data acquisition, and video processing. It is built on a multiprocessing architecture for responsive, high-throughput computation. Together, MagTrack and MagScope offer a fully customizable, end-to-end, open-source Python alternative to proprietary or fragmented systems, enabling laboratories to adapt and extend the framework according to their experimental needs.

abstract: Increased B cell receptor signaling pathways in patients with melanoma correlates with a favorable clinical response to a cancer vaccine expressing multiple tumor-associated antigens. Here, we utilize phage immunoprecipitation sequencing (PhIP-seq) and Rapid Extracellular Antigen Profiling (REAP) assays to analyze the autoantibody profiles of patients with melanoma from a dendritic cell vaccine trial (NCT01622933), before and after vaccination. Patients have significantly elevated breadth and titer of autoantibodies compared to healthy donors. Vaccination results in the induction of de novo autoantibodies, particularly those with a favorable clinical outcome. Reduced serum SDF1-alpha, MIP-1ß, MCP1 and increased circulating monocytes are associated with development of autoantibodies. We identify plasma autoantibody signatures separating melanoma from healthy subjects as well as clinical responders vs non-responders to vaccination treatment. These findings demonstrate the potential for autoantibodies as diagnostic and prognostic biomarkers that predict clinical outcomes in cancer.

abstract: The intestinal mucosa functions alongside trillions of commensal microbes, with immune and epithelial responses contributing to microbiota homeostasis. Both immune and nerve cells are implicated in this microbial balance, but the regulatory functions of epithelial enteroendocrine cells (EEC) are not understood well. Here we show that EEC depletion in mouse colons via Satb2-mediated Neurog3 deficiency enhances goblet cell expression of prominent antimicrobial peptides, with stronger effects in female than in male mice. Mechanistically, serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine; 5-HT) derived from enterochromaffin (EC) cells, an EEC-subtype, acts on sensory neurons to suppress the mucosal levels of calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) under physiological conditions. In the absence of local serotonin, elevated CGRP levels promote mast cell infiltration and interleukin-13 (IL-13) secretion in EEC-depleted mice and enhance antimicrobial gene expression in goblet cells. Our findings thus delineate an epithelial–neuronal–immune axis, wherein EC cells fine-tune goblet cell antimicrobial output to preserve gut microbial equilibrium.

abstract: Microproteins (typically <100 amino acids) regulate diverse cellular processes, yet their small size and low abundance make interactome mapping challenging and particularly sensitive to perturbation by conventional enzyme-based proximity-labeling tags. Here, we developed FlashID, an ultra-compact genetically encoded proximity labeling (PL) system that combines a six-amino-acid tetracysteine tag (CCXXCC, <700 Da) with the turn-on biarsenical photocatalyst FlAsH. Upon tag binding and visible-light irradiation, FlAsH generates singlet oxygen to enable spatially and temporally controlled oxidative labeling of proximal proteins. In side-by-side analyses of the bacterial microprotein AzuC, FlashID recovered the validated interactor GlpD and identified additional physiologically relevant partners that were not captured by TurboID or IP-MS under the conditions tested. FlashID also resolved compartment-specific interactomes of diverse microproteins, including RP11-469A, which we identified as a mitochondrial intermembrane protein that interacts with PHB2 to regulate proliferation. Finally, the extension of FlashID to E. coli , mammalian cells, C. elegans and Arabidopsis thaliana establishes FlashID as a complementary, minimally perturbative platform for decoding microprotein interaction networks in vivo and advancing photocatalytic proximity labeling technologies.

abstract: The intracellular delivery of therapeutic macromolecules remains a major challenge in biomedicine. Capsid-forming proteins are one promising vehicle, but to date, these have required cellular assembly or rely on fusogens for cell entry, limiting their scalability and utility. Here we reconstitute the Drosophila melanogaster Arc1 (dArc1) retroelement-derived capsid entirely from purified recombinant protein components and in vitro transcribed RNA, creating a fully defined, cell-free assembled protein nanoparticle system. We engineered the dArc1 RNA-binding domain to efficiently encapsulate both mRNA payloads and Cas9 ribonucleoproteins. We show that dArc1 capsids bind mammalian cells through a direct interaction with the surface receptor SORCS2. Leveraging this interaction, we demonstrate that intramuscular injection of dArc1 capsids carrying Cas9 gene editors achieves up to 18% exon skipping and restores dystrophin expression in muscle fibers of mdx mice, a model of Duchenne muscular dystrophy. This work demonstrates the potential of in vitro-assembled protein nanoparticles for delivery of molecular cargoes.

abstract: To advance genetic understanding of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), we conduct multi-ancestry genome-wide association studies (GWAS) meta-analyses of 63,415 cases of Europeans and East Asians, and identified 60 previously unreported susceptibility loci. Integrating multi-ancestry transcriptome-wide association studies (TWAS), cell type-specific TWAS, alternative splicing, and alternative polyadenylation analyses using RNA-sequencing data from normal colon tissues of 707 Europeans and 364 East Asians, we identify 441 candidate risk genes, including 324 not previously implicated by GWAS or TWAS, of which 291 were further supported by colocalization or summary-data-based Mendelian randomization analyses. These genes converge on pathways central to IBD pathogenesis (e.g., immune regulation), with over half showing transcriptional dysregulation supported by single-cell and spatial omics analyses. We further identify 44 druggable genes linked to 221 approved drugs or Phase II/III clinical-stage compounds. Our findings deepen the understanding of IBD genetics and provide insights for future research relevant to precision medicine for IBD.

abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a chronic inflammatory disorder driven by dysregulated immune responses. Macrophage-mediated inflammation is central to the pathology, and it is important to understand the epigenetic mechanisms involved. By screening epigenetic molecules that are differentially expressed in published human IBD datasets, we find Protein Arginine Methyltransferase 6 (PRMT6) consistently downregulated in IBD samples compared to healthy controls. Co-occurrence of Prmt6 suppression and Il1b induction within the myeloid compartment in colon biopsy samples indicates that PRMT6 limits macrophage-driven inflammation. Concordantly, Prmt6 -deficient mice exhibit increased susceptibility to both DSS- and TNBS-induced colitis, characterized by exacerbated tissue damage and systemic elevation of IL-1β. Transcriptomic profiling confirms that PRMT6 deficiency selectively upregulates Il1b among inflammatory mediators. Mechanistically, PRMT6 suppresses Il1b transcription by interacting with RBBP5 and disrupting SET1A complex assembly, thereby reducing H3K4me3 enrichment at the Il1b promoter, independently of its canonical H3R2me2a catalytic activity. Furthermore, PRMT6 is transcriptionally silenced by the NF-κB subunit p50 during inflammation. Pharmacological inhibition of p50 restores PRMT6 expression, thus protecting mice from DSS-induced colitis in a PRMT6-dependent manner. Our findings highlight PRMT6 as a pivotal epigenetic regulator of the inflammatory response and provide proof of principle for targeting the p50–PRMT6–IL-1β axis in IBD.

abstract: Translatable circular RNAs (circRNAs) have emerged as a promising alternative to conventional mRNA therapy due to their improved stability that results in a prolonged expression window. The translation of circRNAs is mainly driven by internal ribosome entry site (IRES) or IRES-like elements, which is tightly regulated by various trans -acting RNA binding proteins (RBPs). Here we develop a cell-based system to systematically screen RBPs that enhance translation of circRNAs, identifying 68 proteins as putative activators of noncanonical translation. These translation activators are involved in a broad range of biological processes including RNA processing, ribosomal biogenesis, and translation initiation. We further design a machine learning algorithm to extract common sequence features of these activators and predict more potential RBPs with translation activator activities. The newly identified and predicted activators are subsequently validated to promote the IRES-mediated circRNA translation in a context-dependent fashion. Overall, this study provides new insights into IRES-related trans -acting factors and expands the toolbox for engineered RBPs in RNA synthetic biology.

abstract: Computational and mathematical models are frequently used in the design of appropriate experimental protocols for in vitro cell differentiation assays. However, models are limited by typical monotonic dose-responses, preventing them from being used for cytokine effects that are largely non-monotonic. To address this shortcoming, we developed Uncovering Non-Monotonic Antagonistic and Synergistic Combinations (UNMASC), a mathematical model describing non-monotonic dose-response surfaces of cytokine interactions that distinguishes synergy of efficacy and potency. We demonstrate that our approach successfully recapitulates non-monotonic observed dose-response surfaces characterizing in vitro T cell progenitor differentiation. Our results show that interleukin (IL)3 and IL7 have antagonistic effects alone but are synergistic in combination. Altogether, UNMASC can aid in the efficient design of cell generation assays and extends drug interaction surfaces to a broader range of dose-responses.

abstract: Loss of proteostasis can cause protein aggregation and trigger aggrephagy, yet how these biological processes are coordinated remains unclear. Here, we showed that p62 condensates transit from a gel-like to a more liquid-like state in response to proteotoxic stress. VHL was recruited to aggresomes and colocalizes with p62, which is crucial for p62 to perform its distinct functions in aggresome formation and autophagic degradation. Mechanistically, VHL binds to p62 through its IDR1 region and increases the liquid-like properties via IDR2 region. VHL depletion or disease-associated IDR2 mutations impair p62 condensate dynamics, leading to excessive accumulation of aggregated proteins and concomitant KEAP1 sequestration/NRF2 stabilization. A chimeric peptide linking the p62 PB1 domain to VHL IDR2 recapitulates VHL’s fluidity-promoting activity and suppresses tumorigenesis and protein aggregation. Overall, our findings reveal an HIF-independent tumor-suppressive role of VHL in regulating proteostasis and suggest a new treatment for cancer through the targeting of condensate dynamics.

abstract: How transcriptional asymmetry arises in the epiblast before gastrulation remains a central question in mammalian development. Using a targeted CRISPRa screen, we identify Wt1 as a regulator of lineage-associated transcriptional programmes during formative pluripotency. Wt1 is transiently induced during formative pluripotency in vitro and in vivo, coincident with emerging lineage biases. Precocious Wt1 induction advances cells toward post-implantation identity, whereas Wt1 -deficient cells execute naïve exit but show impaired acquisition of formative and lineage-associated programmes. WT1 binds active regulatory elements together with OTX2, OCT4 and FOXO1. Comparison of Wt1 splice isoforms identifies KTS splice status as the major determinant of divergent anterior/neuroectodermal and posterior/mesodermal transcriptional programmes in vitro. In the E5.5 epiblast, Wt1 expression and splice composition align with lineage-biased states, linking isoform usage to anterior bias in vivo. Isoform-dependent programmes are conserved in human pluripotent cells. These findings identify alternative splicing as a mechanism tuning lineage-associated transcriptional bias before gastrulation.

abstract: Preprimary education is central to the global education agenda, including Sustainable Development Goal 4.2. Despite global momentum in low- and middle-income countries, cross-national evidence on long-term outcomes associated with preprimary education legislation remains limited. Here we applied a matrix-completion approach with subgroup and sensitivity analyses using 495 nationally representative surveys from 1990 to 2024, covering nearly 6.7 million women across 117 countries. Eligibility under the legislation was associated with higher educational enrolment and completion, and with more gender-egalitarian attitudes, more favourable empowerment-related behaviours and greater reproductive autonomy. For example, eligibility was associated with higher female primary-school enrolment (1.21 percentage points (pp); 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.52 to 1.91; P < 0.001) and completion (0.75 pp; 95% CI 0.24 to 1.25; P = 0.004), greater disapproval of wife-beating (1.04 pp; 95% CI 0.53 to 1.56; P < 0.001), greater participation in decisions about husbands’ earnings (3.25 pp; 95% CI 2.50 to 4.00; P < 0.001) and greater ever use of contraception (2.96 pp; 95% CI 2.33 to 3.59; P < 0.001). Eligibility under the legislation was also associated with lower rates of adolescent childbearing (−2.41 pp; 95% CI −2.67 to −2.14; P < 0.001) and child marriage (−0.43 pp; 95% CI −0.71 to −0.15; P = 0.003). These findings provide cross-national evidence directly relevant to ongoing policy discussions surrounding Sustainable Development Goal 4.2 and broader global development agendas, while emphasizing the importance of implementation capacity and equitable system expansion.

abstract: Accurate particle picking of macromolecules of diverse types, shapes and sizes in cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) is critical for understanding the molecular architecture of biological systems in their native state. Current deep learning methods have shown potential for identifying macromolecules in tomograms; however, they are vulnerable to annotation noise in the training data and to imbalanced distributions of macromolecule species. Here, to address these limitations, we developed RobPicker, a meta-learning framework that effectively mitigates these issues by automatically learning to correct label errors and by placing greater emphasis on smaller and rarer macromolecule species. In evaluations across diverse cryo-ET datasets with noisy labels and imbalanced species distributions, RobPicker substantially outperforms state-of-the-art methods, particularly in identifying small and rare macromolecules. The robustness and efficiency of RobPicker led to improved resolution in 3D density maps of protein structures, enabling high-resolution cellular structural biology analysis.

abstract: Humans can swiftly learn to recognize visual objects after minimal exposure. Integrating new information with existing knowledge requires forming enduring neuronal representations to enable future recognition. Yet, the neuronal mechanisms in the human brain underlying such rapid perceptual changes remain unclear. Here we recorded single-neuron activity in occipital cortex (OC) and medial temporal lobe (MTL) regions as participants rapidly learned to recognize degraded images. OC and MTL neurons modulated their activity to encode newly learned visual information and reshape perception. Population decoding revealed that OC neurons required additional processing time to resolve the identity of learned images, with delayed neuronal responses in the MTL. Our findings suggest that OC supports recognition after rapid learning via extensive recurrent processing, potentially involving higher-order neocortical areas, without relying on feedback from MTL. These results provide mechanistic constraints for biologically plausible models of visual recognition and few-shot visual learning.

A low-rank decoder bottleneck bounds reliability in foundation-model perturbation prediction
abstract: Foundation-model predictors of perturbation response are evaluated primarily by aggregate accuracy. Using their predictions to prioritize experiments requires assessing each prediction's reliability. We audit the state-transition (ST) decoder used in STATE across three encoders (SE-600M, scGPT, and Tahoe-x1) and four cell lines under CRISPRi. The decoder's first attention layer has a low-rank output. Projecting this output onto 4-32 fixed directions estimated from training activations preserves mean per-perturbation Pearson delta correlation (PDC). This low-rank attention bottleneck bounds the decoder's reliability by distance to training responses: PDC declines as the cosine distance from a perturbation's observed response to its nearest training response increases. We propose predicted-NN-distance, the cosine distance from a predicted response to its nearest training response, as a per-prediction confidence score. The score has a mean absolute Spearman correlation of 0.81 with PDC, close to the 0.88 obtained with the observed response. Thresholds calibrated on this score transfer across encoders and cell lines, and the score remains predictive of PDC for drug perturbations.
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026

title: A minimal E/I circuit model explains differential recovery from amblyopia under TTX and reverse occlusion
abstract: Recovery from amblyopia beyond the critical period remains a major challenge in visual neuroscience. Experimental studies show that transient inactivation of the fellow eye with tetrodotoxin (TTX) produces stronger and more persistent recovery than reverse occlusion (RO), despite both interventions reducing competition from the fellow eye. The circuit mechanisms underlying this difference remain unclear. We develop a minimal cortical circuit model combining excitatory-inhibitory population dynamics, BCM-like metaplasticity, homeostatic regulation, and eye-specific synaptic plasticity. Monocular deprivation drives the network into an amblyopic operating regime with reduced excitatory activity and fellow-eye dominance. Phase-plane and operating-regime analyses show that TTX and RO subsequently place the circuit in distinct dynamical states. TTX lowers inhibitory activity while maintaining excitatory activity above the BCM modification threshold, creating a larger plasticity-permissive regime than RO. These differences produce stronger recovery of amblyopic-eye responsiveness and greater correction of ocular dominance under TTX. A local robustness analysis across 300 perturbed parameter sets shows that the TTX advantage is not dependent on a narrowly tuned parameter choice. These results provide a mechanistic account of the differential efficacy of fellow-eye inactivation and suggest that recovery from sensory deprivation depends not only on changes in sensory input, but also on the dynamical operating regime of the cortical circuit.
comment: 24 pages, 8 figures, 3 tables. Submitted to PLOS Computational Biology

title: Bearing, heading and the perceptual geometry of collective motion
abstract: Traditional models of collective motion commonly assume that animals turn to match their neighbours' directions of travel. In the harmonic theory, decisions follow from a neural representation of direction, and a neighbour enters only as a stimulus at a bearing, the direction in which it lies. Here we show that a neighbour's spatial extent allows its orientation to enter through projection geometry alone, and the theory generates a matrix of coupling coefficients indexed by the neighbour's bearing and aspect. Responses to bearing alone form one edge of this matrix, and classical heading matching is a special case on its diagonal, one ray through a two-parameter family. Independently, an animal that responds only to neighbour position, perceived with a delay, acquires an alignment coefficient set by the slope of its distance-weighted attraction profile, so that it can align, anti-align or reverse sign. Alignment need not be a rule to be measured. In schooling fish and walking pigeons with body orientation measured independently of travel, social responses are recovered, including bearing responses in the fish. Heading excess depends on how turning is measured, appearing in the fish with forward but not centred responses and remaining unresolved in pigeons. Controls show why neither outcome identifies a direct alignment rule. In fish recordings with motion-assigned body polarity, heading-dependent structure departs from Vicsek form and fails the coefficient test for a common angular potential. Whether animals align thereby becomes a measurable question, with geometric, perceptual and behavioural origins that can be distinguished.
comment: 19 pages, 6 figures

title: Can a self-sustaining chemical network emerge due to just a few catalysts?
abstract: Understanding how self-sustaining chemical reaction networks can emerge from simple molecules is an important question in chemical approaches to the origin of life. Reflexively autocatalytic and food-generated (RAF) sets provide a mathematical framework for investigating this question. This line of research goes back to the early work of Kauffman on autocatalytic reaction networks and was subsequently developed through the probabilistic framework of Mossel and Steel. Further contributions by Hordijk, Steel, and collaborators extended the theory to more heterogeneous forms of catalysis, including reaction-dependent probabilities or power-law distributions of catalytic activity. We introduce a stochastic model that combines heterogeneous molecular catalytic activity with reaction-dependent molecule-reaction compatibility. By assigning random catalytic weights to molecules and incorporating compatibility through an explicit formulation of catalysis probabilities, our model provides a concrete and flexible setting that captures both sources of heterogeneity while remaining mathematically tractable. We establish novel and general criteria for RAF formation and nonformation. We further demonstrate that classical phase-transition criteria need not remain valid in the presence of reaction-dependent catalysis. For heavy-tailed catalytic weights, we identify and rigorously quantify an additional phase transition. In models with finite-mean catalytic weights, RAF formation and nonformation are governed by a catalytic intensity parameter. For infinite-mean weights, however, we show that RAFs may emerge with probability tending to one even when the catalytic intensity parameter tends to zero.
comment: 25 pages

title: Cell-type-specific modularity in E/I networks shapes dynamical regimes and computational capabilities
abstract: Structural modularity is a ubiquitous feature of brain networks that shapes neural dynamics and information processing. Yet excitatory and inhibitory populations can differ in their modular organization, and it remains unclear how this asymmetry affects network dynamics and computation. Here, using dynamical mean-field theory and simulations of networks performing complex temporal tasks, we show that independently tuning excitatory and inhibitory modularity controls the dynamical regimes of balanced E/I networks. In particular, such tuning can generate a dominant spectral outlier despite overall E/I balance, producing a topology-controlled transition between bulk- and low-rank-dominated regimes, with different dynamical bifurcations leading to chaos and bistability, respectively. In chaotic time-series prediction tasks, computational performance is enhanced near these dynamical boundaries, including both the onset of chaos and the transition to bistability. Favorable configurations exhibit strongly modular excitation and comparatively homogeneous inhibition, similar to what is observed in cortical connectivity.

title: CellCanon: An Agentic Cellular World Model for Prediction, Explanation, and Observation-Driven Updating
abstract: Biological discovery requires using molecular knowledge and new measurements to infer responses beyond the conditions already observed. We introduce CellCanon, the first agentic cellular world model to unify single-cell expression prediction, evidence-grounded explanation, and observation-driven updating. Its predictive core reuses condition-level biological evidence across gene-specific numerical readouts to guide single-cell expression generation. A shared world state links predictions, acquired measurements, and source-linked claims, supporting explanation and revision. On 339 held-out SciPlex3 conditions across three cell lines, CellCanon improves differential-expression AUPRC and Macro-F1 over the best baseline for each metric by 63.3% and 17.3%, respectively, and direction Macro-F1 by 7.2%. Relative to gene-wise reasoning on matched drug-cell cohorts, measured language-model token use falls by 99.77% for Predict and 98.41% for Explain. On the source-grounded benchmark, Explain correctly answers all answerable questions with supporting proofs and identifies all insufficient-evidence cases. In simulated experimental feedback, Update uses one measured source context per drug to exceed the best fine-tuned baselines in differential-expression AUPRC and Macro-F1 without changing model weights. Together, these capabilities support a cumulative account of cellular responses, with predictions and biological judgments that can be revised as evidence accumulates.
comment: 31 pages, 5 figures. Code: https://github.com/ZhaokangLiang123/CellCanon

title: Discrete Backbone Elasticity and Curvature-Dependent Torsion Statistics in Proteins
abstract: Coarse-grained models of protein conformational dynamics use $\mathrm{C}_α$ geometry to describe the probabilities of regular helices, ordered turns and disordered conformations. To test how much of this order arises from local chain elasticity, we connect discrete Hasimoto frame transport to neighboring bending mismatch, deriving a curvature-product torsion interaction and a six-parameter generalized von Mises density. Fitted on 194 chains from the ATLAS molecular dynamics database and tested on 1744 sequence-nonredundant proteins, this baseline reduces negative log-density loss from 1.490 to 1.160 nats, torsion-sign error from 12.26 to 2.15 percentage points, and helix-fraction error from 21.84 to 10.41 points. Ablations and circular-moment projections against reference generative models motivate extensions to anisotropic stiffness and two partition-function-weighted elastic states, further lowering test loss to 0.790 nats and helix error to 1.65 points. The fixed hierarchy also improves predictions across 72 trajectories of peptides $\mathrm{Fs}$ and $(\mathrm{AAQAA})_3$ and miniprotein $\mathrm{HP35}$ spanning varied starting conformations and force fields. Remaining angular errors in these trajectories are associated with atomic context at shared bends, as bend-matched peptide frames adopt opposite torsion signs with distinct hydrogen-bond patterns and a proline-containing $\mathrm{HP35}$ turn remains at negative torsion. Introducing a bilinearly coupled $\mathrm{C}_α$--$\mathrm{N}$ orientation angle largely reparameterizes the existing bend-dependent harmonics, with an empirical $L^2$ Gram projection placing 96.7\% to 99.6\% of its added coefficient-function squared norm within the original six-function span. These results link discrete Hasimoto elasticity to statistical backbone potentials and clarify the scope and limits of local $\mathrm{C}_α$ geometry.

title: Learning Time-Varying Connectomes for Stable Behavior Across Development
abstract: Neural circuits must maintain functionality to drive effective behavior while their size, topology, geometry, and intrinsic dynamics change across development. To model developing visuomotor circuits and behavior, we investigated whether a single compact generative encoding could produce functional recurrent controllers across such changes. Building on the HyperNEAT algorithm, we represented this program as a compositional pattern-producing network that received developmental time as an input to generate age-specific connectivity. The developmental substrate prescribed neuronal birth, position, sensory organization, and intrinsic time constants. We tested this approach using two geometrically distinct developmental substrates and two visuomotor tasks: optomotor responses and phototaxis. Controllers optimized at only the initial or mature substrate generally failed when evaluated at other ages. In contrast, controllers optimized across multiple developmental snapshots maintained substantially higher and more consistent performance across trained and unseen ages. Optimization at only three developmental snapshots was often sufficient to produce effective behavior across the tested developmental interval. The resulting connectomes changed substantially with age and did not converge on a single trajectory of sparsity or connection-weight statistics. Controllers also differed in whether they relied on neurons born later in development. These results demonstrate that a shared spatiotemporal time-varying connectivity program can produce recurrent neural networks that preserve behavior across substantial developmental changes. Together, these results provide a framework for studying how functional stability can emerge without requiring structural or dynamical stability.
comment: 29 pages, 6 figures

title: Mind Control of LLMs via Closed-Loop Stimulation: Out-of-Distribution Robustness
abstract: Brains and large language models need not be considered equivalent systems to reveal an interpretable commonality: both exhibit high-dimensional, nonlinear dynamics whose behavior can only be modeled imperfectly. This creates a shared challenge whenever we seek to intervene in their dynamics. A controller may either rely on a model identified around a particular operating regime and risk failure as the system moves away from that regime, or explicitly account for uncertainty and a changing internal state. Neurostimulation has confronted an analogous problem for decades. The limitations of fixed, open-loop stimulation have motivated closed-loop and state-dependent approaches that condition intervention on the ongoing state of the neural system. Inspired by this principle, we formulate LLM steering as a feedback-control problem in which the network's internal state, rather than a fixed intervention alone, determines how the system is perturbed. We further account for the mismatch between tractable dynamical models and the nonlinear transformer they approximate through robust control. As one principled realization of this framework, we develop an $H_\infty$-based steering controller that limits sensitivity to disturbances and linearization mismatches. Across multiple steering benchmarks, the controller improves performance over existing baselines, with particularly pronounced gains under out-of-distribution conditions and varying length complexities. Beyond controller performance, we introduce robust steerability, $S_{\mathrm{rob}}$, a pre-deployment measure of tolerance to dynamics mismatch; across model-task pairs, it exhibits task-specific structure and varies systematically with model scale. Beyond robust LLM steering, our measure asks not merely whether control is possible, but how much uncertainty it can survive; a principle that may span artificial and biological neural systems.

title: Modeling Gene Expression Noise: From Transcriptional Dynamics to Cell Growth and Division
abstract: Gene expression is inherently noisy, leading to substantial cell-to-cell variation in mRNA and protein levels. The telegraph model and the simpler bursty model provide good fits to single-cell count distributions and have been used extensively to understand transcriptional kinetics and estimate the kinetic parameters. However, these models all describe a static cell. Here, we review models of stochastic gene expression in growing and dividing cells which aim to understand how a cell's own life history, from its birth, through copying its genome, to its division, leaves a distinct fluctuation signature on molecule numbers. We discuss the biochemical and biophysical processes captured by these models, their analytical tractability, the concept of cyclo-stationary behavior, when this is well approximated by the steady-state of static models and how the distributions of molecular numbers measured under these conditions sensitively depend on the experimental setup. This is followed by a discussion of how these models are fitted to single-cell measurements, how biological variability can be separated from measurement noise, and which computational advances make this feasible for thousands of genes. We finish by highlighting the open problems in the field.
comment: 13 pages, 2 figures

title: PINR-ESI: Physics-Informed Self-Supervised Implicit Neural Representation Framework for EEG Extended-Source Imaging
abstract: EEG extended-source imaging aims to localize active cortical regions and characterize their spatial extent, yet supervised inverse networks typically depend on synthetic EEG-source pairs and may be sensitive to synthetic-to-real mismatch. We propose a physics-informed self-supervised implicit neural representation (INR) framework for spatial source reconstruction without paired source labels or simulation-based supervised pretraining. The lead field matrix encodes the source-to-sensor volume-conduction model and constrains the INR through agreement between predicted and measured EEG. Cortical current density is modeled as a continuous coordinate-conditioned field. A classical inverse estimate provides warm initialization and spatial constraints on source activity, while patch-integrated projection maps the field to discrete source coefficients for forward modeling. Simulations with varying noise levels, source counts, and source extents showed the clearest advantage in identifying active cortical regions, particularly for multiple and larger sources. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations using real EEG recordings from epilepsy patients and intracranial stimulation experiments further supported the feasibility of the framework for source imaging. These findings suggest the potential of physics-informed self-supervised INR for extended-source imaging.
comment: Preprint, 10 pages, 11 figures

title: Synchronized Hearts, Desynchronized Brains: A Nonlinear Dynamics Perspective for Function and Failure
abstract: Both the heart and the brain are built from electrically excitable cells, yet the emergent dynamics of these organs could not differ more. In the myocardium, a coherent traveling wave of action potentials ensures coordinated contraction; in the cerebral cortex, distributed, irregular spiking underlies efficient information processing and the generation of behavior. Here, we illuminate the principles that underlie the emergence of such distinct nonlinear dynamics using concepts from complex systems. We trace these principles across scales from ion channels and cellular action potential generation, through cellular coupling mechanisms and network architecture, to organ level dynamics and clinical phenotypes. Designed to support either synchronized waves or desynchronized information processing, the heart and the brain can thus be understood as operating on opposite sides of a synchronization phase transition. Crossing this transition implies pathological dynamics in both organs: Loss of synchrony in the heart produces arrhythmia; excess synchrony in the brain leads to epileptic seizures. We discuss how adaptation mechanisms, including plasticity, modulation, remodeling, and learning, maintain the appropriate level of (de)synchronization. Overall, we provide a unified excitable-system perspective, together with an educational notebook, to foster cross-disciplinary insights into cardiac and neural function and pathology.
comment: Irene Pellini and Simon Bauer contributed equally. Wolfram-Hubertus Zimmermann, Johannes Zierenberg, Philip Bittihn and Viola Priesemann contributed equally. Corresponding authors: johannes.zierenberg@ds.mpg.de viola.priesemann@ds.mpg.de

title: Time-Division Multiplexing: The Operational Rhythm and Temporal Organization Layer of Digital Life
abstract: Continual agents must handle urgent interaction while retaining alternatives, replaying errors, and committing safe long-term changes. A previous digital-life framework distinguishes online (busy) and offline (idle) channels, but leaves open whether these are separate programs or phases of a common process and how their operations should be ordered. Motivated by recent observations of rapidly alternating perceptual representations in primate cortex, we develop a temporal organization layer with phase-tagged micro-epochs, an observable duty cycle, independent content and resource controls, and three nested clocks separating candidate exploration from durable commitment. We give a projected duty-cycle update, state its deterministic descent guarantee and the additional noise term required for a stochastic guarantee, and specify coupled busy/idle execution contracts. Five synthetic experiments (64 seeds each) examine descent and noise, objective misalignment, gain asymmetry, resource coupling, and dropped replay logs. In the gain/noise model the best tested gain ratio is 1.55; decoupled scheduling yields 26.6% versus 11.1% success on a constructed urgent/high-load subset. A frozen-backbone Qwen3-8B prototype further checks orchestration, but its proxy outcomes are not task-benchmark evidence. The results establish a testable scheduling design and identify its conditions of validity, not machine consciousness or general-purpose agent superiority.
comment: 30 pages, 6 figures

title: A red fluorescent sensor for intensity-and lifetime imaging of cAMP in living cells
abstract: cAMP (cyclic adenosine monophosphate) is a crucial intracellular messenger involved in neuromodulation and plasticity, but more information on its spatiotemporal regulation is desirable. Here we constructed a red fluorescent indicator based on a truncated cAMP binding site derived from a regulatory PKA subunit of protozoan origin. It contains a single binding site for cAMP highly specific for cAMP over cGMP. chILI (cAMP highly-responsive Intensity and Lifetime Indicator) can be imaged as an intensity-based probe, but alternatively also offers options for fluorescence lifetime imaging. When expressed in the mouse brain using AAV-vector mediated gene transfer, it reports spontaneous and evoked cAMP transients from CA1 neurons in the hippocampus of awake mice. chILI will add valuable options for monitoring cAMP in vitro and in vivo.
author_corresponding_institution: Max-Planck-Institute for Biological Intelligence, Martinsried, Germany

title: A single day of natural daylight exposure and physical activity does not conclusively change circadian phase: A Bayesian crossover experiment
abstract: Among the environmental signals that shape human physiology, the daily light-dark cycle is the primary zeitgeber of the human circadian system. Physical activity may provide an additional non-photic time cue and frequently co-occurs with daylight in everyday life. However, their independent and combined effects on circadian phase have rarely been disentangled under naturalistic daylight conditions. In a counterbalanced mixed-design experiment, 41 healthy adults (24 women; mean age = 23.7 years, SD = 4.3) participated in up to three 40-h visits on fixed individual sleep-wake schedules. Each visit comprised an 8-h exposure beginning 1.5 h after wake to natural daylight, daylight attenuated by amber-tinted glasses, or indoor electric light (within subjects; mean photopic illuminances: 1196, 460, and 75 lx), with otherwise dim-light conditions. Participants hiked for approximately 4 h or remained sedentary (between subjects; activity indexed by median heart rate reserve [HRR]; group means: 32.7% and 2.7%). Bayesian hierarchical models used individual photopic illuminance (ActTrust 2) and median HRR to predict change in dim-light melatonin onset (DLMO; primary outcome) and exploratory outcomes (daytime and evening sleepiness, mood, and wellbeing, daytime perceived exertion, and evening psychomotor vigilance). Per standard-deviation increase in log-transformed illuminance and median HRR, estimated DLMO changes were -4.22 min (95% HDI [-10.93, 2.22]; BF = 0.70) and -6.48 min (95% HDI [-13.79, 1.27], BF = 1.56), respectively. Evidence remained inconclusive for both predictors and their interaction. Exploratory findings were largely inconclusive, practically negligible, or favoured the absence of effects. The circadian effects of a single day of natural daylight exposure, with or without physical activity, therefore remain unclear. Resolving this question may require larger samples and brighter, repeated, or habitual exposure timed to phases of greater circadian light sensitivity.
author_corresponding_institution: Psychiatric Hospital of the University of Basel

title: Active manipulation of surface orientation under directional illumination improves color discrimination
abstract: Two surfaces that appear different colors under one illumination might appear the same color under another illumination. This phenomenon is known as illuminant metamerism and is thought to limit surface color discrimination. However, real-world lighting environments are not directionally uniform. In theory, surfaces that appear the same color at one tilt might not appear the same color at another tilt where they sample a different illumination spectrum. We tested whether human observers could use this directional variation to improve surface color discrimination. Our results confirm that human color discrimination is improved when observers are able to tilt surfaces to sample directional lighting. Observer sampling motions were spatiotemporally structured and appeared to be directed towards the general lighting geometry rather than systematically maximizing color discriminating information for specific surface pairs.

title: Amnesia Induced by Suppressing the Focus of Internal Attention
abstract: Our thoughts can recede as we direct attention to the external world. This experience may reflect the suppression of thoughts about past events, future worries, or stray ideas that could otherwise disrupt focus. Such thoughts may arise spontaneously from replay mechanisms supported by the episodic memory system; hence, sustaining external focus may require suppressing these systems to stop internal distraction. Here, periods of high external focus disrupted diverse episodic content activated near in time, inducing an 'amnesic shadow'. This shadow occurred for both novel content and already formed memories and exhibited key markers of active suppression: forgetting beyond expectations from time alone, which generalised to an alternative reminder. External attention therefore automatically engages an active suppression mechanism that appears to broadly inhibit cognitive systems supporting the emergence of distracting thoughts. The findings raise the possibility that people may naturally gravitate toward activities demanding external attention, unwittingly, to regulate unwanted thoughts.
author_corresponding_institution: MRC Cognition and Brain Sciences Unit, University of Cambridge

title: An Eyewear-Based EEG Interface for Temporal-Region Monitoring and Emotion Recognition
abstract: Conventional electroencephalography (EEG) devices are often impractical for ambulatory settings due to their reliance on specialized hardware and expert operation. To address this, we developed a user-friendly eyewear-based EEG system featuring dry titanium electrodes positioned approximately 5 mm inferoposterior to the T7/T8 sites (near the ears), with metal nose pads serving as references. We evaluated the system across 103 recordings spanning five paradigms: alpha reactivity, blink-related transients, fatigue, attention, and video-elicited emotion. Following quality control, 93.2-100.0% of epochs were retained. The system demonstrated high sensitivity to ocular transients, showing significant amplitude increases during the blinking task. The emotion task yielded the most robust state-related features, with statistically significant differences in differential entropy across negative, neutral, and positive video categories, achieving balanced accuracies of 0.882 for two-class and 0.667 for three-class prediction. Despite challenges at the multiple testing correction stage, the alpha reactivity and fatigue contrast tasks were still noteworthy to some extent. The attention paradigm revealed a consistent increase in differential entropy during focused states, and the eyewear system outperformed the Muse headband in group-held-out classification. These findings provide strong evidence for the feasibility of temporal-region eyewear EEG acquisition, highlighting its potential applications in the real-world, particularly for emotion recognition.
author_corresponding_institution: Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macau Institute of CNS Regeneration, Jinan University, Guangzhou; and BIAI Laboratory, BIAI INC, Shenzhen, China.

title: An Innate Neuroprotective Reflex Activates NRF2 via Phosphorylation of p62 at Ser351 to Mitigate Traumatic Brain Injury
abstract: Rationale: The oxidative crisis in traumatic brain injury (TBI) has remained therapeutically intractable to direct antioxidant therapies. Activating nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (NRF2) offers a promising strategy, but its translation is hindered by a key question: whether TBI's depleted antioxidant reserves can accommodate canonical electrophilic activation. The diving reflex (DR) is a potential non-electrophilic alternative, but its efficacy in TBI is unknown and its natural induction is clinically impractical. This study tests whether artificial DR, induced by trigeminal nerve stimulation (TNS), can safely engage this non-electrophilic NRF2 pathway and exert a protective role in the acutely injured brain. Methods: In a rat model of severe TBI, we compared TNS-induced DR, natural DR, and exogenous calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) against the electrophilic NRF2 activator dimethyl fumarate (DMF). To define the mechanism of action, we quantified p62 phosphorylation at Ser351 (NRF2-activating) versus Ser403 (autophagy-related), alongside redox homeostasis, lesion volume, and multi-domain functional outcomes. Results: TNS-induced DR fully recapitulated the neuroprotection of natural DR, an effect mimicked by exogenous CGRP, and prevented by CGRP inhibition, confirming a shared, neuropeptide-driven mechanism. This non-electrophilic pathway operated by selectively phosphorylating p62 at Ser351, which preserved glutathione reserves, halted lipid peroxidation, and reduced chronic lesion volume. In contrast, while DMF activated NRF2, its electrophilic mechanism was associated with a further reduction in the brain's already compromised glutathione pools and increased lipid peroxidation. This mechanistic difference was functionally significant, as only the non-electrophilic approaches delivered multi-domain recovery. Conclusion: The TNS-evoked artificial DR is a mechanistically tailored strategy for activating NRF2 in acute TBI. By engaging the endogenous CGRP-p62-KEAP1 pathway, it circumvents the fundamental limitations of both passively consumed direct antioxidants and redox-costly electrophilic activators. Our findings establish a clear translational roadmap for harnessing an innate reflex as a clinically deployable therapy for hyper-oxidative states.
author_corresponding_institution: The Feinstein Institutes for Medical Research

title: Anticipatory Threat of Shock Reduces the Number of Items Reported From a Brief Visual Display: Evidence for Capacity Loss Along the Scanning Order
abstract: Background: Anticipatory anxiety impairs working memory, but whether it also limits the earliest, high-capacity stage of visual storage is unclear. We asked whether the mere expectation of an aversive electrical stimulus reduces how many items people can report from a briefly flashed display, and whether any loss is spatially uniform. Methods: Eighty-eight healthy adults aged 18-25 years were randomly allocated to a threat-of-shock condition (surface electrodes on the wrist and the instruction that a painful stimulus might be delivered; none was) or a control condition (n = 44 each). Participants viewed a 4 x 3 letter matrix for 400 ms and performed untimed written whole report. Correct recall (0-12), intrusions and the position of each reported letter were scored. Groups were compared with Welch's t test, the Mann-Whitney U test, bootstrapped effect sizes, a binomial generalised linear model and a Bayes factor; spatial effects were tested with generalised estimating equations (GEE) accounting for letters nested within participants. Results: The threat group reported fewer correct letters (3.41 +/- 1.09) than controls (4.70 +/- 1.29); Welch t(83.6) = 5.11, p < .001, Hedges' g = 1.08, 95% CI [0.70, 1.53], BF10 ~ 7,549. Intrusions did not differ (p = .376). Recall declined more steeply from left to right under threat (group x column chi2(3) = 11.24, p = .011), with losses confined to the third and fourth letters of the top row (FDR-corrected q <= .003). Conclusions: Anticipatory threat reduced the amount of information transferred from a brief display into a reportable form without increasing guessing. Intact first items and depleted later items along the habitual reading order indicate a reduced number of items read out of a rapidly decaying visual store, rather than a hemifield-specific bias. The single-trial design and the absence of a manipulation check limit mechanistic inference.

title: Automated Segmentation of the Hypothalamus: Associations of Age and Socioeconomic Status with Subunit Volumes in Cognitively Healthy Adults
abstract: Background: The hypothalamus regulates sleep-wake cycles, energy balance, and autonomic and neuroendocrine function, yet its small size and poorly contrasted boundaries have long hindered in vivo volumetry. Deep-learning segmentation now allows the hypothalamus to be divided into functionally meaningful subunits. We examined whether hypothalamic subunit volumes are associated with age and socioeconomic status (SES) in cognitively healthy adults. Methods: From the OASIS-1 cross-sectional dataset (n = 416, 18-96 years), 133 participants with a Clinical Dementia Rating of 0 and complete segmentation output were analysed (33-94 years). A FreeSurfer-based convolutional neural network, run on a cloud virtual machine, segmented five subunits per hemisphere. Volumes were normalised to estimated total intracranial volume (eTIV) and related to age and SES (Hollingshead index) using Pearson correlations with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction; partial correlations adjusted for sex (age) and for age and sex (SES) served as sensitivity analyses. Results: Older age was associated with lower normalised volume of the right posterior subunit (r = -.456, q < .001) and the left posterior subunit (r = -.274, q = .007); both associations persisted after adjustment for sex. Lower SES showed a trend towards larger left anterior-inferior volume (r = .242, uncorrected p = .005) that did not survive FDR correction (q = .053). Conclusions: Age-related volumetric differences in the healthy hypothalamus appear to be concentrated in its posterior portion, a region housing arousal-promoting circuitry. Automated subunit segmentation offers a scalable tool for studying the hypothalamus in ageing and in relation to environmental exposures; the cross-sectional associations reported here should not be interpreted as causal or as within-person change.

title: Aversive Learning Induces Context-Gated Global Reorganization of Neural Dynamics in Caenorhabditis elegans
abstract: Learning generates experience-dependent changes to the brain. However, how neurons of diverse functions and connectivity reorganize and modulate their activities to generate coherent changes while preserving essential functions is not well understood. Here, we address this question using an aversive olfactory learning paradigm whereby Caenorhabditis elegans learns to reduce its olfactory preference for pathogenic bacteria. Using functional imaging during olfactory stimulation in naive and trained animals, we show that, at brain-wide scale, cell type-by-cell type, learning induces context-gated reconfiguration of the organization of neural activity throughout the brain to alter neural responses only during bacteria-discrimination task, while leaving intact bacteria-sensing functions. We found that the context-gated encoding of learning is globally distributed across layers of the nervous system, composed of neurons carrying information of context or learning experience. In particular, aversive training modulates multiple functional connections within the nervous system, including those between sensory neurons and interneurons, as well as those among interneurons, in a context-gated manner. At the systems level, training modulates correlated activity of neural populations; we found that low-dimensional temporal patterns of population activity correlate well with locomotory gaits that express olfactory preferences. Upon training, the rotation and contraction of the low-dimensional neural manifolds shifts the brain into predisposed states for the context-gated display of learned behavior. Because animals encounter unpredictable environments in life, efficient learning about relevant cues while maintaining other functions is essential for survival. Our findings uncover network-level mechanisms that help explain how the brain reorganizes its activity patterns to both encode new experience and preserve essential functions.

title: Basal ganglia output guides decision-making by state destabilization
abstract: To execute learned behavior, the nervous system can undergo an activity-state transition between the current and the learned activity states. Here, using adult zebrafish, we show that their basal ganglia output induces such state transitions for goal-directed behavior. After learning the Go/No-go task in virtual reality, the striatal indirect pathway responds to negative values of a conditioned cue and the absence of sensory feedback by different neuronal populations. The pallidal output pathway integrates these negative value signals and then broadcasts the integrated signal to the Dc area in the pallium (fish cortex). Optogenetics and mathematical modeling suggested that this pallidal output activity uniformly destabilizes ongoing Dc activity states, thereby facilitating behavioral state transitions toward the behavioral state with the minimum pallidal output activity. This mechanism explains how pallidal output activity guides goal-directed behavior beyond potential barriers between activity states underlying different behavioral states.
author_corresponding_institution: Waseda University/RIKEN Center for Brain Science/Institute of Neuropsychiatry

title: Brain Decoding from a Deep Neural Network of Visual Memory Reveals the Maturation Trajectory of Memory Systems across Ages 3-7
abstract: Memories from the first four years of life are largely inaccessible by adulthood, yet these early experiences profoundly shape cognition throughout development. Understanding this phenomenon of infantile amnesia is critical for revealing the mechanisms of early memory development. Here, we developed a new content-based behavioral measure of memory that quantifies how closely children's memory patterns resemble those of adults, which we term the memory maturation score. Using a movie-watching fMRI dataset spanning age 3 to adulthood, we trained a cross-validated model on adults' movie-evoked brain activity to predict adult's propensity to remember each movie snippet, estimated by ResMem, a deep neural network trained to predict visual memorability. We then applied the model to each child's brain activity while viewing the same movie to assess their memory maturation (i.e., cross-decodability from adult patterns). Children exhibited adult-like neural patterns of memory around age 4, extending prior behavioral findings. Structural analyses showed that the volume of the left posterior hippocampus, but not age or total brain volume, significantly predicted children's memory maturation. Memory maturation around age 4 thus likely reflects age-related neural development of hippocampal memory systems, rather than an age increase itself. Functional searchlight analyses revealed a trajectory of memory maturation: the inferior temporal gyrus reflected mature memory-related processing from age 3 onward, the left posterior hippocampus by age 5, and higher-order regions involved in social-affective processing and multimodal integration by age 7. Together, these findings suggest that hippocampal maturation between ages 3 and 5 drives the maturation of memory patterns.

title: Chronic Sleep Disruption Activates the Transcriptional Unfolded Protein Response and Induces Compartment-Specific Proteomic Changes in Mice
abstract: Sleep disruption (SD) is associated with adverse brain health and increased risk of dementia, including Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet the pathological mechanisms underlying this association are not fully understood. Preclinical studies have shown that acute SD impairs cognition by altering vulnerable synapses (molecular composition, ultrastructure, and function). However, the cumulative effects of chronic SD on the adult brain and its vulnerable synapses, that might contribute to AD risk, remain poorly defined. Here, we investigated the impact of chronic SD on brain transcriptomic signatures and subcellular compartment-specific proteomic profiles to identify genes, proteins, and signaling pathways that might confer AD risk. Chronic SD induced a modest transcriptional stress response globally, whereas alterations were more pronounced in the synaptosomal (synapse-enriched P2 fractions) and whole-brain proteomes. Remarkably, chronic SD elicited unique proteomic alterations at the synaptic compartment were distinct from whole-brain effects, including increased proteins involved in synaptic vesicle endocytosis, regulation of dendritic spine morphogenesis, and regulation of long-term synaptic depression, compared to increased proteins involved in immune/inflammatory, glial responses and neuronal function at the whole-brain level. Consistent with the chronic SD-induced molecular signatures, we observed subtle ultrastructural changes in vulnerable CA1 hippocampal synapses, including reduced pre-synapse size and decreased synaptic vesicle density, which suggest that chronic SD modifies synaptic transmission and plasticity. Together, our findings indicate that chronic SD differentially impacts the brain and the synaptic proteome, nominating candidate therapeutic targets and signaling pathways for future mechanistic studies of chronic SD and how SD contributes to increased AD risk.

title: Clustering instantaneous phase-locking states with a rank-two Bures-Wasserstein distance
abstract: Instantaneous phase-locking (iPL) matrices, defined by the cosines of pairwise phase differences between band-limited signals, underpin widely used methods for time-resolved functional connectivity, including Leading Eigenvector Dynamics Analysis (LEiDA). Each iPL matrix has rank at most two and is fully characterized by its two nonzero eigenvalues and corresponding eigenvectors. Yet, existing methods retain different parts of this decomposition and compare them using distances that do not reflect the geometry of the underlying sample space. We show that weighting the two eigenvectors by the square roots of their eigenvalues recovers each channel's phase relative to the mean phase, and that optimal orthogonal Procrustes alignment of these weighted eigenvector pairs yields the Bures-Wasserstein distance between the corresponding iPL matrices. In EEG, where most channels oscillate nearly in phase, existing distances become insensitive to phase-lag size, whereas the Bures-Wasserstein distance preserves this sensitivity. In simulations, clustering with this distance recovered states differing in both lag size and spatial pattern that existing distances failed to distinguish.In resting-state EEG, it resolved distinct phase-gradient states that other methods merged into a single global in-phase state.

title: Concurrent metacognitive evaluation is dissociable from perceptual evidence accumulation in the parietal cortex
abstract: Adaptive behavior requires not only accumulating evidence toward a choice but also monitoring its reliability in real time. A central question is whether such concurrent uncertainty is read out directly from the circuit that accumulates perceptual evidence, or is computed by a separate process that runs alongside it. We trained two macaques on a perceptual discrimination task in which they could abandon deliberation at any moment and request assistance, so that uncertainty responses were in parallel with, rather than appended to, evidence accumulation. Behaviorally, a race between distinct perceptual and uncertainty accumulators outperformed models in which the opt-out decision was derived from the perceptual decision variable alone. To ask where the second accumulator resides, we recorded single units in the lateral intraparietal area (LIP), a canonical sensory-motor transformation area, and compared population dynamics with recurrent neural networks instantiating two architectures: one in which uncertainty is computed within the perceptual accumulator, and one in which it is computed outside and triggers the uncertainty response there. LIP exhibited all of these signatures for perceptual choices and none for uncertainty responses. Uncertainty-related activity rose late and stereotypically, lacking the coherence-scaled ramp of an accumulator, and separable from the perceptual accumulation. They are all predicted by the segregated architecture. Concurrent uncertainty is thus represented in LIP but is unlikely to be computed within LIP, indicating that metacognitive monitoring during deliberation is a dissociable operation rather than a derivative readout of the LIP perceptual circuit; its anatomical substrate is not localized here.
author_corresponding_institution: Center for Excellence in Brain Science and Intelligence, Chinese Academy of Sciences

title: Connectivity of Implicit Statistical Learning Networks is Associated with Language Impairment Severity in Post-Stroke Aphasia
abstract: Rehabilitation of language for individuals with post-stroke aphasia (PSA) requires relearning to use cognitive-linguistic skills, but little is known about how these individuals relearn, or how brain reorganization may support different types of learning. One type of learning critical to language acquisition is implicit-statistical learning (ISL), which supports robust, accurate performance with minimal conscious effort. ISL relies on brain subnetworks that include language areas as well as domain general regions (i.e., salience and cognitive control) with the latter considered less likely to be damaged in individuals with PSA. Using three brain subnetworks associated with ISL, the present study used graph theory metrics to (1) compare their functional connectivity in PSA (n = 30) relative to neurologically healthy controls (n=18), and (2) examine their relationship with aphasia severity in the PSA group. Resting-state functional connectivity was weaker for the language and salience subnetworks in PSA than controls, but not for the cognitive control subnetwork. Additionally, edges within all three networks correlated with aphasia severity, particularly between regions of the right frontal cortex, such that stronger connectivity in these ISL subnetworks were associated with milder aphasia. While it is unsurprising that the damaged left-sided brain regions in the PSA group resulted in connectivity that differed from controls, these differences were also observed in the salience subnetwork. Further, the correspondence to aphasia severity was evident in all subnetworks, highlighting that domain general ISL networks may contribute to variability in language outcomes.

title: Connectome structure constrains neural activity across scales
abstract: Connectomes can be represented at many resolutions, but coarse-graining risks discarding structure relevant to neural dynamics. Here we ask at what resolution a connectome preserves what it predicts about neural activity. In C. elegans, direct synaptic connectivity poorly predicts whether stimulating one neuron evokes a response in another. A parameter-free predictor based on paths through the connectome performs substantially better, with most predictive information carried by two-step paths and by the arrangement rather than the number of connections. Coarse-graining neurons into biological cell classes preserves these predictions despite discarding path structure, whereas random partitions degrade them. Connectivity alone identifies alternative coarse-grainings that preserve prediction down to about nine groups corresponding to nervous-system subsystems. Partitions inferred from newly hatched animals preserve adult predictions, and lineage-based partitions in Drosophila preserve path structure better than random coarse-graining. Functional prediction can therefore survive at resolutions far coarser than those required to preserve structure.

title: Conserved synaptic modifications by humanized tau through diverse isoform- and mutation-specific intracellular interactions
abstract: Mutations in the microtubule-binding protein tau are considered causal for a diverse group of neurodegenerative diseases collectively referred to as primary tauopathies. Specific tauopathies are associated with different mutations, distinct tau isoforms, manifest in unique cellular and circuit-wide patterns of degeneration, and present with specific clinical symptoms and trajectories. The mechanisms that link variations in the primary tau protein structure to distinct forms of neural circuit dysfunction remain largely unknown. Here, we created an orthogonal viral resource to systematically examine the impact of expressing humanized tau isoforms harboring different disease-relevant mutations in excitatory pyramidal cells from the mouse prelimbic cortex. We used these reagents to show that expression of mutant humanized tau (hTau) as either of two isoforms produced very similar patterns of circuit-specific synaptic disconnection on cortical projection neurons. However, mass spectrometry revealed that the interactomes of these different tau species varied markedly as functions of isoform, mutation, and subcellular location. We validated the functional relevance of increased hTau interactions with mitochondrial proteins in induced neurons differentiated from Ngn2-iPSCs expressing different hTau constructs. These results suggest different disease-relevant hTau proteins likely use distinct mechanisms to drive a highly stereotyped form of synapse loss in cortical neurons.

title: Context-dependent effects of ketamine on emotional evidence integration
abstract: Understanding others' emotions requires continuously integrating noisy affective information as emotional states change over time. Research on emotion processing, however, has thus far focused on static environments or discrete events. Here, we developed a continuous emotional evidence integration task in which participants had to track the average emotional state in a rapidly changing sequence of faces under different levels of environmental volatility. This allowed us to examine emotion integration in changing environments. In online (n=92) and in-person (n=29) cohorts, participants integrated emotional information over longer timescales in stable environments while relying more strongly on recent evidence under volatility, consistent with principles established in perceptual decision-making. We further examined whether this process was modulated by ketamine, an NMDA receptor antagonist associated with evidence integration in the perceptual domain. We conducted a double-blind, placebo-controlled, within-subject study and probed emotion integration during the post-acute period, approximately 1.5 hours after the infusion. Ketamine modulated the temporal weighting of emotional evidence, shifting the balance between recent and past information depending on environmental volatility. Together, these findings show that emotional evidence integration dynamically adapts to the statistical structure of the environment and that ketamine can further modulate this process, which may have relevance for affective disorders.

title: Contributions of Site Heterogeneity in Multi-site Brain-Phenotype Predictions
abstract: Machine learning studies of brain-phenotype associations typically summarize accuracy with a single Pearson correlation, yet in harmonized multi-site data this metric is shaped by training-set size, feature and outcome variability, and true effect heterogeneity. We analyzed structural MRI data from the Reproducible Brain Charts consortium. After preprocessing and quality control, 3486 participants from 9 sites were retained. Three training set compositions were used to understand contributions of site heterogeneity after harmonization: within-site (Local), size-downsampled multi-site (Multi-Down), and full multi-site (Multi-Full). Another site-agnostic strategy (Overall) pooled all sites into a single dataset. All strategies included the target site in the training and testing samples. These analyses separate the contribution of the site effect from that of sample size. Between-site heterogeneity was extensive (age I^2 {approx} 95%). The overall correlation of age prediction (r = 0.73) exceeded the within-site meta-analytic estimate (Multi-Full r = 0.63). The improvement of correlation in the pooled dataset was driven by a mechanical inflation from the larger outcome variance. At matched sample size, within-site training outperformed harmonized multi-site training. Increasing the multi-site training sample size did not yield a significant advantage over within-site training. The apparent advantage of cross-dataset training thus appears to reflect training-set size rather than a benefit of multi-site composition per se. The same pattern generally held for the weaker brain-p-factor signals. Together, these results indicate that between-site heterogeneity in machine learning brain-phenotype prediction persists after harmonization. We recommend reporting site-level prediction accuracy and feature dispersion and standard deviation of the outcome variable alongside any pooled estimate to improve inter-site and inter-study comparison of machine learning prediction accuracy.

title: Differential modulation of the neurocomputational signature of early and late mismatch responses to spoken words by awareness and task relevance
abstract: Mismatch responses (MMRs), including the mismatch negativity (MMN) and the P3, are a hallmark of the brains capacity to detect unexpected events. They are discussed to be generated by two main processes: adaptation and prediction error (PE). However, MMR research on underlying mechanisms has mostly relied on simple, non-linguistic stimuli such as tones, and it remains unknown how awareness and attentional conditions affect MMRs to auditory verbal stimuli, that, unlike tones, carry lexical-semantic meaning. Here, we conducted a preregistered EEG study that disentangled influences of awareness, general task-relevance of word stimuli, and specific target-relevance of word oddballs on the MMN and P3. In addition, single-trial neurocomputational models were applied to uncover the underlying generative models of the MMRs. Results show that word-related MMN and P3 were only elicited when words were task-relevant, and the P3 increased with target-relevance. Crucially, no word-related MMN emerged under inattention, in contrast to the pre-attentive MMN typically reported for tonal deviants. Neurocomputational modeling revealed that the early part of the task-relevant MMN reflects adaptation processes. PE processes generated later parts of the MMN under task-relevance, and the entire MMN under target-relevance, as well as the P3 independent of relevance conditions. This suggests that the same temporal generation pattern of adaptation and PE underlie mismatch responses to both words and tones, but that, unlike tonal MMRs, eliciting MMRs to words requires the allocation of attention. This attentional dependency may reflect the additional lexical-semantic and multi-level representational demands that spoken words impose on the auditory system.
