author_corresponding_institution: University of Munster Institute for Medical Psychology and Systems Neuroscience

title: Disentangling the effects of Anxious, Autistic and Schizotypal Traits on Perceptual Inference
abstract: Perception combines sensory information with prior knowledge, but people differ in how they do so. These differences may be associated with psychological traits; however, previous studies often focused on one trait at a time and yielded contradictory results. We measured how anxious, autistic and schizotypal traits relate to perception in two general population samples (original: n=277; replication: n=279, pre-registered). We combined tasks in which priors were either explicitly communicated or implicitly learnt with computational modelling to distinguish the decision and learning stages of perceptual inference. The three traits formed distinct but correlated dimensions. At the decision stage, higher trait anxiety was associated with more optimal choices and greater reliance on sensory information, without any alteration in the reliance on priors, whether explicit or implicit. On the other hand, state anxiety was associated with a reduced effect of sensory information on response speed. When traits were analysed separately, autistic traits showed similar associations, but these associations disappeared once anxiety was taken into account in multidimensional analyses. No other credible or consistent effects emerged for autistic or schizotypal traits, nor for learning parameters. These results highlight the importance of a multidimensional approach, including anxiety measurements, to characterise inter-individual differences in perception.
author_corresponding_institution: GHU Paris, psychiatrie et neurosciences, hopital Saint-Anne, institut de neuromodulation, 75014 Paris, France

title: Disentangling visual and motor contributions to continuous psychophysics
abstract: Continuous psychophysics measures visual function by asking observers to track a randomly moving target. Because continuous responses provide more information than traditional discrete judgements, a few minutes of tracking can estimate visual sensitivity, making the approach attractive for testing children and patients. Tracking performance is often summarized by cross-correlating the target and cursor velocities: the resulting cross-correlogram peak, lag and width index how strongly, quickly and sharply the observer responds to the target. Tracking, however, requires both seeing the target and moving the cursor towards it, so poor tracking may reflect impaired vision, impaired motor control, or both. Here, we test whether visual and motor contributions to tracking performance can be told apart. Participants tracked a target with a computer mouse while wearing glasses that simulate two levels of visual impairment, using either their dominant or their non-dominant hand. We find that both manipulations alter the cross-correlogram metrics, lowering the peak correlation and delaying and broadening the response, but in different proportions. Visual impairment mainly delays and broadens the response, and does so in proportion to each participant's loss of visual acuity. The non-dominant hand mainly lowers the peak correlation. Two signatures of motor control explain this difference: with the non-dominant hand, participants pause more often and for longer, and move more noisily between pauses, whereas visual impairment alters neither. Together, response lag, time paused and movement noise reveal whether a change in tracking is visual or motor in almost every participant. Our findings demonstrate that, given a baseline measurement, the same tracking data that measure vision can also reveal whether a change in performance reflects a change in what an individual sees or in how they move.

title: Disrupted mannosidase enzymes in C9orf72 ALS/FTD
abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is an age-related neurodegenerative disorder resulting from the loss of motor neurons in the brain and spinal cord. Neuroinflammation, induced by glial cells including microglia (MG) and astrocytes, is an acknowledged aspect of this neurodegeneration. Generating induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) neuroinflammatory models of ALS may help elucidate non-neuronal mechanisms of disease. Here, we analyze human postmortem tissue and an iPSC derived glia-crosstalk model identifying a reduction in Golgi enzymes MAN1A1 and MAN1A2 in addition to other glycan enzymes from ALS-associated microglia and astrocytes. Impaired Golgi and glycan metabolism is linked to inflammation and other related ALS disease mechanisms including impaired lysosomal proteostasis, altered extracellular matrix, disrupted secretion, and altered cell-cell signaling.

title: Disruption of theta-timescale spiking impairs learning but spares hippocampal replay
abstract: The ability to rapidly learn and retrieve salient information about new environments is critical for survival. In mammals, the hippocampus plays a crucial role in that learning. Specialized features of hippocampal population coding, including network-level theta oscillatory activity, location-specific firing of principal cells, and reactivation of experience during immobility (replay), have been implicated in rapid storage and retrieval of spatial information. Disruptions of theta and replay jointly, or replay alone, are sufficient to impair learning; however, the specific contribution of theta-associated temporal structure during locomotion remains unknown. In this study, we manipulated hippocampal spiking activity in rats specifically during locomotion by optogenetically activating septal parvalbumin-expressing GABAergic neurons. We developed a closed-loop, theta phase-specific stimulation protocol that reliably reduced theta power shortly after stimulation onset. This manipulation preserved the place codes of individual cells but disrupted the fine temporal structure of endogenous spatio-temporal representations (i.e., theta sequences) at the pairwise and population level. Theta disruption during locomotion was also sufficient to cause pronounced deficits in learning the more cognitively challenging component of a spatial alternation task, even though disruption was applied on only [~]66% of trials. Notably, network effects accompanying theta disruption were restricted to locomotor periods; we did not observe changes in replay rate, length, or content during immobility. Together, these results demonstrate the importance of the precise temporal microstructure of locomotion-associated spatial representations in the hippocampus for learning.
author_corresponding_institution: National Center for Biological Sciences, Bangalore, India

title: Dissociable Oscillatory Alpha and Aperiodic Neural Dynamics Underlie Atypical Attentional Control in Children With Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)
abstract: Children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) often have difficulty maintaining goal-directed attention when task-relevant and task-irrelevant information compete for processing resources. The present study investigated whether this difficulty reflects distinct abnormalities in demand-related attentional regulation and distractor-related neural responses. We recorded electroencephalography (EEG) signals from 45 children with ADHD and 45 typically developing (TD) children while they performed a visual detection task under low and high visual demands, with simultaneous task-irrelevant standard and deviant sounds. EEG power spectra were parameterized to separate oscillatory alpha activity from aperiodic activity, as putative indices of attentional regulation and cortical excitation/inhibition (E/I) balance, respectively. TD children showed adaptive demand-related alpha modulation, whereas children with ADHD showed an atypical alpha response pattern, including reduced frontal modulation and atypical posterior alpha enhancement; this demand-related group difference was observed in oscillatory alpha activity but not in aperiodic activity. In contrast, ADHD-related abnormalities in responses to auditory distractors were more clearly reflected in the aperiodic slope. Children with ADHD showed atypical distractor-related aperiodic modulation, suggesting reduced stability of neural background activity, potentially reflecting disrupted cortical E/I balance when irrelevant sounds had to be ignored. Furthermore, multivariate machine learning classification demonstrated that relying on these sensitive neural signatures yielded robust discrimination between children with ADHD and TD controls, with significant predictive performance emerging shortly after stimulus onset and sustaining throughout information processing. These findings suggest that oscillatory alpha activity and aperiodic neural dynamics show differential sensitivity to distinct attentional abnormalities in ADHD, with alpha oscillations primarily reflecting demand-related regulatory deficits and aperiodic activity primarily reflecting distractor-related neural instability.

title: Dissociating instructive from permissive roles of brain circuits with reversible neural activity manipulations
abstract: The brain has a remarkable capacity to recover from damage. Despite the value of such recovery, it has made determining which areas are critically involved in a specific brain function challenging. Different types of manipulations to brain tissue - from mechanical or chemical lesions to genetic ablations or pharmacological agents - often yield conflicting conclusions. In some cases, ablating a brain area causes only a temporary disruption because a downstream region can homeostatically recover from its loss of input, while in others it leads to permanent impairment due not to the damaged area per se, but because of the degeneration of distant areas. We sought to address these issues by exploiting the flexibility and reversibility of optogenetic manipulations. We applied a three-stage optogenetic approach to the mouse's primary visual cortex (V1) in a contrast detection task, beginning with intermittent silencing, followed by sustained illumination across multiple days of task-related behavior, and concluding with a return to intermittent silencing. Initially, intermittent V1 inactivation strongly impaired task performance, while during persistent multi-session inactivation, the animals' visual detection entirely recovered to pre-silencing levels. However, this recovery was itself reversible, as returning the animals to intermittent V1 inactivation reinstated the behavioral deficit. Suppressing activity in the superior colliculus (SC) concurrent with persistent V1 inactivation reversed the animals' recovery, demonstrating that SC is a key area that drives behavioral compensation in the absence of V1 function, even while under normal conditions V1 activity is crucial. These results support a scenario where primary sensory cortex is in the default circuit mice use to detect visual stimuli, but in its absence, midbrain regions can compensate for it. More generally, this temporally controllable optogenetic perturbation paradigm could be useful to adjudicate whether a brain area instructs or is accessory to a specific brain function.

title: Distinct patterns of multisensory integration underly the expression of flavor preferences and aversions in rats
abstract: Flavor is an inherently multisensory experience, combining gustatory and retronasal odor signals during consumption. Previous work has shown that rats weight taste and smell components of flavor mixture solutions to express flavor preferences. However, a comprehensive quantitative understanding of taste-smell integration is lacking. Here, we evaluated the validity of the maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) framework for explaining multisensory integration of taste and smell signals toward hedonic flavor judgments. MLE is a dominant framework for explaining multisensory integration in a wide variety of contexts, and states that components of a mixture are weighted according to their relative reliability, resulting in more reliable multisensory judgments. In our experiment, rats expressed preferences for taste, odor and taste+odor solutions in a series of two-bottle preference tests featuring an unpalatable odor component (amyl acetate), and either a palatable taste component (sucrose) or an unpalatable taste component (citric acid). Taste reliability was experimentally varied by presenting taste components at two different concentrations. Reliability of animals' preference judgements was quantified as the variance in preference across repetitions of the same conditions in the same animals. Our results confirm that preferences for mixtures featuring a palatable taste can be described as a weighted average of the component preferences where the weights depend on the relative reliability of the components-a finding that is in line with the MLE framework. However-contrary to MLE-component weighting does not increase the reliability of multisensory preference judgments themselves. In addition, preferences for taste+smell mixtures featuring an unpalatable taste follow a qualitatively different pattern: taste and smell components are combined to enhance flavor rejection judgements. These results demonstrate that the multisensory integrative principles underlying flavor preference differ from other multisensory domains and depend on the valence of the flavor components.
author_corresponding_institution: Wake Forest University School of Medicine

title: FGF signaling induces disease-associated oligodendrocyte states and drives myelin pathology
abstract: Myelin integrity is essential for normal central nervous system (CNS) function and is disrupted in neuroinflammatory and neurodegenerative disorders, including multiple sclerosis and Alzheimer's disease. In these settings, myelin-forming oligodendrocytes adopt a conserved disease-associated transcriptional state, termed disease-associated oligodendrocytes (DAOs). How DAOs arise, the signals that drive their induction, and whether they actively contribute to pathology remain poorly understood. Here we show that FGF signaling instructs mature oligodendrocytes to enter disease-associated states that are sufficient to trigger myelin pathology. By screening disease-linked secreted factors, we identify FGF1 and FGF2 as potent inducers of a DAO-like state in purified oligodendrocyte cultures, characterized by transcriptional reprogramming and myelin-membrane shedding. In vivo, activating oligodendrocyte FGF signaling is sufficient to elicit DAO programs and myelin disruption, whereas inhibiting FGF signaling suppresses DAO induction in a mouse model of multiple sclerosis. Finally, analysis of post-mortem multiple sclerosis tissue reveals a concordant DAO-like state associated with increased engagement of the FGF/FGFR axis. Collectively, these studies define a regulated mechanism of DAO formation linked to myelin disruption and position mature oligodendrocytes as active contributors to myelin pathology in CNS disease.
author_corresponding_institution: Department of Neurosurgery, Stanford University School of Medicine, Stanford, CA, USA

title: Gain Control of Peripheral Input by Core Brain Thermosensors Drives Drosophila Thermoregulation
abstract: Temperature affects all aspects of animal physiology, rendering thermoregulation critical for survival. In Drosophila larvae, well-established peripheral thermosensors detect temperature changes and mediate thermotaxis over a broad innocuous range, but how larvae seek a specific preferred body temperature within this range remains unknown. Here we show that core thermosensors in the brain (LPBT neurons) establish this setpoint by mediating warming-evoked turning at temperatures above it. LPBTs express the warmth-activated thermosensor TrpA1(A), but are not simply cell-autonomous thermosensors. Rather, sustained LPBT responses above setpoint require both peripheral thermosensory input and TRPA1-dependent thermosensing within LPBTs. TRPA1-dependent core thermosensing provides gain control that defines the homeostatic setpoint by tuning the behavioral weights of peripheral inputs. This new conception of thermal preference reveals parallels between Drosophila and mammalian thermoregulation.
author_corresponding_institution: Harvard University, Department of Physics and Center for Brain Science, Cambridge, MA, USA

title: Gut Stem Cell Secretome Therapy Promotes Durable Neuroprotection and Functional Recovery After Stroke
abstract: Background: Stroke causes rapid neuronal death and gut barrier disruption in the acute phase, with persistent cognitive-affective impairment in the chronic phase. We previously showed that transplants of intestinal epithelial stem cells ameliorated the acute and chronic impairment of stroke. The current study tested the efficacy of a cell free strategy, specifically, the secretome of intestinal epithelial stem cells. Methods: Middle aged male and female rats underwent middle cerebral artery occlusion or sham surgery and received intestinal epithelial stem cell secretome from healthy sex-matched adult or control media. Behavioral assays (social interaction, novel object recognition and Barnes maze), gut histology, markers of gut permeability, serum cytokines were performed at acute and chronic time points. Group differences were assessed by two-way ANOVA. Results: In the acute phase, vehicle-treated stroke animals displayed histopathological changes in the gut including villus blunting, loss of goblet cells, increased markers of gut permeability and elevated systemic inflammation. In the chronic phase, stroke resulted in cognitive/affective changes including social withdrawal, recognition memory and spatial memory deficits. In middle-aged males, three doses of IESC secretome treatment 4h/24h/48h after stroke restored mucosal architecture, goblet cells and dampened inflammatory cytokines in the acute phase. Cognitive and social outcomes, tested 4+ weeks after stroke, were significantly improved compared to vehicle-treated stroke animals. However, in middle-aged females treated with the same regimen of intestinal epithelial stem cell secretome, gut architecture was not restored and inflammatory cytokines remained elevated. Long term cognitive impairment was only partially improved in this group. Proteomic analysis of the secretome revealed a largely shared core of proteins between males and females with sex differences in pathway level regulation. Subsequently, another cohort of middle-aged females was administered four doses of secretome 4h/12h/24h/36h after stroke. This regimen restored gut architecture and dampened inflammatory cytokines in the acute phase, and improved long term cognitive outcomes. Conclusions: Collectively, these studies underscore the therapeutic potential of IESC secretome and the importance of tailoring post stroke therapy by demographics such as biological sex. These data further support the hypothesis that gut repair is tightly associated with long-term improvement in stroke outcomes.
author_corresponding_institution: Texas A and M University Vashisht College of Medicine

title: Homeostatic Plasticity Enables Stable, Flexible, and Tunable Assemblies
abstract: Strongly interconnected neuronal populations, called assemblies, dynamically form through synaptic plasticity mechanisms and are thought to be a substrate for memories in the brain. Many assembly formation models use Hebbian excitatory-to-excitatory plasticity, where coordinated activity strengthens recurrent structure. However, these models typically yield binary assembly outcomes: networks with either weak (no assembly) or maximally strong (assembly) connectivity. We consider networks with a combination of Hebbian excitatory-to-excitatory plasticity and inhibitory-to-excitatory synapses with plasticity that homeostatically stabilizes excitatory neuron firing at a target value. When we set excitatory-to-excitatory plasticity to be homeostatically compliant, in that potentiation and depression are balanced at the homeostatic target firing rate, we find a stable continuum of synaptic strengths, and assembly structure is no longer binary. We use a recurrent network of spiking neuron models and an associated mean-field theory to identify this continuum as a line attractor in synaptic weight space. While along the attractor, homeostasis ensures that neuronal firing rates are invariant, the dynamical response properties of the network are quite malleable, with strongly coupled networks having high gain and longer timescale responses. Using our mean-field theory we show how correlated stochastic spiking activity among the excitatory neurons can destroy the line attractor, yet this can be mitigated when correlated inputs are shared across the excitatory and inhibitory neurons. Altogether, we provide an alternative learning framework based on homeostasis, where a tunable and flexible assembly structure is possible.

title: Immersion as inference: An active inference account of induced realities and its relation to the two-competitor model
abstract: Immersive technologies are designed for a single target: the human perceptual system. Engineers of virtual and augmented reality have long recognized that a display does not have to replicate the physical world, it only has to provide the inputs that satisfy the senses at the level at which the brain samples them. This engineering intuition is, in fact, a statement about brain function. Here we develop it into a formal account of immersion within the active inference framework. We treat an induced reality (a virtual, augmented, or mixed reality, but also a book or a daydream) as a candidate generative model that competes with the model of the actual reality for the explanation of a shared sensorium and for the control of action. Immersion is then defined as the ensuant belief that the induced reality best explains the current sensory signals and supports the current perceived reality of the winning model, despite any break in immersion by Bayesian model switching driven by a high-precision prediction error that the induced model cannot absorb. Exogenous and endogenous attention, implemented as weights governing stream selection in our earlier two-competitor model, which treated attention as necessary but not sufficient for immersion, appear as two routes of precision allocation: likelihood precision of evolutionarily entrenched sensory events, and precision that follows the expected free energy of policies. Affect and motivation enter through the pragmatic and epistemic value of remaining in the induced reality and through the rate of change of free energy. We show that the two-competitor attentional focus vector and its angle are recovered from the active inference variables, and we reproduce the two scenarios of the original model, a rewarding and a fatiguing activity interrupted by a slamming door, in a minimal simulation. The account links presence, embodiment, cybersickness, and narrative absorption to a single quantity, and it yields concrete predictions for the psychophysiological assessment and closed-loop control of immersion. We discuss implications for neuroergonomic design in which the evolutionarily entrenched core of perception is non-negotiable while its experience-dependent periphery can be trained.
author_corresponding_institution: Systems Neuroscience & Neurotechnology Unit, Saarland University & htw saar

title: Inosine Triphosphate Pyrophosphatase as a Candidate Associated with White Matter Abnormalities in Chronic Heart Failure
abstract: Background: White matter hyperintensities (WMHs) are common with normal brain aging and frequently observed also in chronic heart failure (CHF). However, the relationship between CHF and white matter abnormalities and the biological factors remain unclear. We investigated WMH and associated white matter microstructural changes, such as fractional anisotropy (FA), in CHF and explored candidate molecular factors. Methods: We conducted a longitudinal prospective observation including brain T2-FLAIR magnetic resonace imaging for 32 asymptomatic Stage B (mean age 63.3{+/-}10.5 years; 25% women) and 23 symptomatic Stage C CHF patients (mean age 67.3{+/-}7.1 years; 30% women). Plasma proteomics and Mendelian randomization (MR) were used to identify candidate proteins associated with both CHF and WMH. The association of candidate proteins was further investigated using complementary analyses in CHF rats, cultured cortical neurons, and community-based genetic data in UK Biobank. Results: Global WMH volume increased more in Stage C than Stage B patients, predominantly near the anterior periventricular white matter, despite comparable cardiac indices (4,717{+/-}5,335 mm3 vs. 2,116{+/-}3,134 mm3, P=0.027). SomaScan-based proteomic analysis of plasma samples from this patient cohort revealed that 44 proteins are significantly associated with both Stage C CHF and WMH progression (P<0.05). Of these 44 proteins, two-step Mendelian randomization analysis identified inosine triphosphate pyrophosphatase (ITPA) as the only candidate protein, further supported by an association between rare variants in ITPA and FA. In CHF rats, the anterior pericallosal cortex showed decreases in myelin basic protein density and FA and an increase in ITPA expression compared to sham rats. In cultured cortical neurons, recombinant ITPA exposure reduced total axonal length. Conclusions: Symptomatic CHF was associated with WMH and impaired white matter integrity. ITPA emerged as a candidate factor across human, animal, and cellular analyses. These findings provide a basis for investgating the biological pathways linking CHF and white matter injury.

title: Insular opioid signaling and distinct claustral ensembles in hedonic feeding
abstract: Stress triggers eating that is driven by palatability rather than energy need, but how stress-related signals act on the circuits that control hedonic feeding is unclear. The claustrum, a thin sheet of neurons reciprocally connected with much of the cortex, is enriched in {kappa}-opioid receptors (KORs), the receptors for the stress-related peptide dynorphin. Here we show that a single forced swim increases palatable-food intake in mice without food restriction. Deleting or blocking claustral KOR attenuated this increase. A KOR-based sensor reported a fall in claustral opioid tone at the onset of eating. Prodynorphin (Pdyn)-expressing neurons in the anterior insular cortex (aIC) projected to the claustrum and recruited both vGAT and CaMKII-expressing claustral neurons. Single-cell imaging showed that eating engages claustral populations in distinct ways: nearly all vGAT neurons were activated, whereas KOR-Cre neurons divided into activated and suppressed subsets of similar size, with or without prior stress. vGAT responses to both sucrose and quinine grew after longer water restriction and scaled with licking, linking them to consummatory engagement rather than taste valence alone. Mice lacking Pdyn in the aIC ate more palatable food even without stress, and KOR ligands changed how mice engage with palatable food. These findings identify an insular-claustral opioid circuit through which stress can shape hedonic feeding.

title: Integrative Transcriptomic Meta-Analysis Reveals SIRT1-SNCA Correlation in Parkinson's Disease
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder that affects midbrain dopaminergic neurons without any approved therapy. Candidate molecular targets identified in one model are not always traceable across the postmortem, induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC), and cell-based systems used to study PD, which complicates clinical translation. To address this gap, we performed an integrative transcriptomic meta-analysis of 33 publicly available datasets across postmortem human brain, iPSC-derived models, and dopaminergic cell lines of PD. Differential expression and functional enrichment analyses were combined with STRING protein-protein interaction networks, followed by drug-gene interaction screening against a polyphenol panel. Overall, resveratrol was recovered in all 33 comparisons, independent of model system, tissue, and genetic background. We associated resveratrol with 30 distinct target genes, and SIRT1 was itself a recovered target in 6 comparisons spanning all three model systems. Finally, we resolved the SIRT1-SNCA relationship into four directional patterns that differed by model, inverse in postmortem brain and positive in acutely toxin-exposed cells. These findings support a candidate, context-dependent resveratrol-SIRT1 axis in PD.

title: Interpretable Machine Learning Links Group-Specific Plasma Proteomics to Regional Structural Neuroimaging in Alzheimer's Disease
abstract: Background: Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology begins years before clinical symptoms, highlighting the need for scalable biomarkers that capture biological changes across the AD continuum. Broader plasma proteomics may capture systemic processes that vary with disease stage, yet their relationship to AD-related brain neurodegeneration remains unclear. We aimed to identify plasma proteomic signatures across cognitively normal (CN), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and AD and evaluate their neuroanatomical associations. Methods: We analyzed 146 plasma analytes from 565 Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) participants (58 CN, 396 MCI, 111 AD). Group-specific proteomic signatures were identified using pairwise classification models with nested 5*5 cross-validation. SHAP quantified feature importance, with the top 15 proteins per comparison being prioritized for MRI association analysis. We analyzed 103 regional structural MRI volumes harmonized across 57 acquisition sites using ComBat. Separate ordinary least squares regression tested protein-MRI associations, adjusting for age, sex, APOE4, diagnosis, and intracranial volume, followed by Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction. Results: Classification models using proteomic data achieved AUC of 0.956 +- 0.017 for CN vs MCI, 0.963 +- 0.011 for MCI vs. AD, and 0.836 +- 0.085 for CN vs. AD. SHAP identified group-dependent proteomic signatures. No protein-MRI associations survived FDR correction for CN vs. MCI. In MCI vs. AD, higher cortisol was associated with lower left precuneus and superior parietal volumes, while higher osteopontin was associated with lower left paracentral and accumbens volumes. In CN vs. AD, higher vitronectin was associated with lower posterior corpus callosum volume. Conclusion: These findings suggest that plasma proteomics capture group-specific systemic biological signals across the AD continuum. Linking ML-prioritized plasma proteins to regional brain structure provides neuroanatomical context for blood-based biomarker discovery.

title: Intra-individual changes to peak alpha frequency map to pain perception following high frequency sensitisation of central nociceptive pathways: A test-retest reliability study
abstract: Resting-state EEG can capture cortical dynamics relevant to sensitised pain states in the absence of ongoing nociceptive engagement. However, whilst the slowing of global oscillations is evident within various chronic pain conditions, the mechanistic specificity of PAF and -band power remains uncertain. Therefore, the present study assessed these features across two identical test-retest sessions in which HFS was applied to induce the development of SHA as characterised through 128 mN MPS. Crucially, changes in -band features post-HFS were investigated. Blind source separation was also applied to identify independent sensorimotor components relevant to nociception and assess their test-retest reliability. Results demonstrated good test-retest reliability for sensor-level data at baseline, with inter-individual changes in global PAF reflecting MPS post-HFS. However, no specific regional driver of this signal was evident. Alternatively, components identified through sensorimotor template matching revealed a significant influence of -band power on MPS both at baseline and post-HFS. However, only a small number of these components genuinely localised to pre- or post-central gyri, and test-retest reliability of -band power was poor. Together, these findings indicate that resting-state EEG may be useful for tracking changes in cortical -band oscillations alongside the development of pain sensitivity. However, methods of sensorimotor component identification evidenced limited agreement and global PAF slowing could not be linked to a specific electrode grouping.

title: Investigating the dynamic relationship between anxiety and spatial memory using autonomous ecological momentary assessment
abstract: Anxiety has been extensively studied in relation to memory, yet its dynamic association with spatial episodic memory in naturalistic clinical settings remains largely unexplored. We developed an anxiety-spatial-memory EMA protocol (asm-EMA) and deployed it in 30 epilepsy patients undergoing inpatient EEG monitoring, delivering combined momentary anxiety ratings and a validated spatial memory task pseudo-randomly every 90-150 minutes across multiple days. Subject-level asm-EMA average and session-to-session variability correlated with standard neuropsychological assessments, supporting the clinical validity of the protocol. Momentary anxiety was not associated with reduced spatial memory accuracy. Higher within-person STAI-6 was associated with faster retrieval responses, but this association was attenuated after accounting for prior task exposure, suggesting that response-time effects may partly reflect task familiarity. Temporal analyses identified both gradual hospital-day change and short-term carry-over across anxiety, pain, and spatial memory measures. STAI-6 anxiety and spatial memory showed stronger hospital-day trends, whereas VAS anxiety showed the clearest carry-over from one session to the next. The asm-EMA protocol provides a feasible, autonomous framework for capturing moment-to-moment anxiety-memory dynamics in naturalistic settings.

title: Late radiation-induced brain injury is associated with functional cerebrovascular impairment without structural vessel loss in mice
abstract: Background: Radiation-induced brain injury (RIBI) is a major and often irreversible complication of cranial radiotherapy, affecting up to 90% of long-term survivors. Although cerebrovascular damage is a leading mechanistic hypothesis, whether chronic resting hypoperfusion occurs independently of structural vessel loss remains unknown. The aim of this study was to comprehensively characterize cerebrovascular, structural, and behavioral outcomes in a murine model of late RIBI to determine the primary drivers of vascular dysfunction. Methods: Adult C57BL/6 mice underwent 12 Gy whole-brain irradiation and were assessed one year later using laser speckle contrast imaging (LSCI), 7T MRI, immunohistochemistry, and behavioral testing. Results: Irradiated mice exhibited reduced pial flow velocity and flow area by LSCI, indicative of upstream cerebrovascular dysfunction, while bulk cortical tissue perfusion was preserved. This pial hypoperfusion was accompanied by cerebral atrophy, decreased T2* relaxation time and tissue iron deposition consistent with chronic microhemorrhage across multiple brain regions by MRI, blood-brain barrier disruption reflected by reduced ZO-1 and VE-cadherin expression, and increased anxiety-like behavior. Strikingly, capillary density, pericyte coverage, astrocyte endfeet, and NeuN-positive neuronal nuclei were all preserved. Conclusion: These findings demonstrate that functional vascular impairment - not structural vessel or neuronal loss - drives hypoperfusion and blood-brain barrier disruption in late RIBI. This dissociation between vascular dysfunction and rarefaction reframes the pathophysiology of RIBI and identifies endothelial dysfunction as a tractable therapeutic target for intervention.

title: Linear NeuroPaint: An Efficient Baseline for Cross-Session Neural Alignment and Inpainting
abstract: Large-scale Neuropixels recordings sample many brain areas, but no single experimental session records every area of interest. NeuroPaint, a transformer-based autoencoder, integrates such recordings by aligning area-specific latent dynamics across sessions and "inpainting" activity in unrecorded areas. Could a linear model, which would be computationally efficient and potentially more interpretable, suffice to achieve this? To address this question, we introduce Linear NeuroPaint, a linear variant of NeuroPaint, and evaluate it on two multi-area Neuropixels datasets. Linear NeuroPaint achieves strong predictive performance on recorded areas, however, it is less accurate than nonlinear models at cross-area inpainting, despite extensive hyperparameter optimization. Moreover, its parameters are not readily interpretable: incomplete cross-session alignment leads parameter-defined neuron clusters to exhibit heterogeneous response profiles. Together, these results show the limits of what a linear model can extract from multi-session recordings. Nevertheless, Linear NeuroPaint provides a computationally efficient baseline for benchmarking multi-session neural models.

title: Lipidome of Compact Myelin from Cortical Regions of the Aging Murine Brain
abstract: Age-related cognitive decline has been associated with neurodegeneration in cortical white matter tracts. The trajectory of white matter degeneration over the lifespan follows a similar pattern in humans, primates and rodents including the loss of myelin integrity and concomitant loss in myelinated axonal segments. Previous studies suggest that biochemical alterations in myelin begin to occur well prior to myelin loss. To better understand these biochemical determinants underlying white matter degeneration, we investigated the lipid composition of myelin isolated from young adult, middle-aged and aged murine brain. Compact myelin was enriched from cortical regions using a refined density centrifugation protocol and profiled the lipidome using LC-MS/MS. Over 2000 lipid species were identified, with the relative expression of 414 species changing over the age-span. The myelin lipidome from young mice was biochemically distinct compared to the aging cohorts. Aging was characterized by an overall decrease in high abundant species of glycerophospholipid and sphingolipids, including phosphocholine, phosphoethanolamine, sphingomyelin and cerebrosides. Pathway analysis by LipidSig 2.0 and lipid ontology analysis by LION/web highlighted alterations to lipid metabolism and membrane biophysical properties related to bilayer stability and organization. These data support the concept that myelin lipid compositional changes are apparent by middle age which underly structural changes in myelin at later ages. The findings provide greater insight into age-related biochemical alterations in the myelin sheath and may aid in strategies to mitigate white matter degeneration over the lifespan.

title: Locomotor activity enhances environmental representation by boosting visuo-frontal communication
abstract: During environment exploration we rapidly acquire visual information to identify targets of interest. Here, we discovered that locomotion limits how long natural scenes are viewed dur- ing free exploration. Whether the brain has developed compensatory mechanisms to ensure that sensory information is accurately transmitted to downstream areas during and after locomotion is unknown. We examined this issue by recording the spiking activity of popula- tions of neurons in visual and prefrontal cortex in conjunction with wireless recordings of oculomotor events while macaques moved freely to explore their environment or performed treadmill bipedal locomotion. The communication between visuo-frontal cortical areas was enhanced during and after locomotion to increase visual-evoked responses and population coding accuracy in prefrontal, but not visual cortical neurons. This in turn improved behav- ioral performance in a freely moving visual detection task after locomotion. Electrical stim- ulation further revealed elevated inter-areal synaptic efficacy during locomotor activity. The mechanism whereby locomotion enhances stimulus coding accuracy in prefrontal cortex and behavioral performance by increasing visuo-frontal communication is functionally beneficial during environmental exploration when incoming stimuli are rapidly changing and the win- dow for perceptual decisions is temporally restricted.

title: Loneliness as a modulator of intersubject neural alignment across social and nonsocial contexts
abstract: Loneliness is associated with cognitive biases that diverge from normative patterns of understanding and may be reflected in altered neural responses to the world. Here, we examined how loneliness modulates neural synchrony across individuals during the processing of social and nonsocial information. Using high-resolution movie-watching fMRI data (n = 178) from the Human Connectome Project, we applied intersubject correlation analyses to identify context-dependent neural signature of loneliness. Lonely individuals primarily showed more idiosyncratic responses in regions within the default mode network, visual association cortex, and amygdala during social contexts, and in reward-related circuitry during nonsocial contexts. This suggests less stereotyped processing of social information and reward in lonely individuals. In contrast, lonely individuals exhibited greater neural synchrony in the nucleus accumbens during social contexts and in somatomotor regions during nonsocial contexts. This potentially reflects shared experiences of social craving and engagement with a socially irrelevant physical environment. These effects were robust against demographic similarities, kinship, depression, and objective levels of social connection. Together, these findings identify loneliness as a modulator of intersubject neural alignment, which may contribute to shaping how individuals process and interpret different aspects of the world.

title: Matching Corticospinal and Cortical Excitability along the motor cortex: TMS-EMG-EEG study
abstract: There is still no consensus on how to choose intensities for transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS). The resting motor threshold (RMT), the intensity needed to evoke muscle contractions in the contralateral limb muscles, is a robust muscle-specific index of corticospinal excitability. RMT from one of the hand muscles is commonly used as a reference for TMS neuromodulation interventions and TMS-electroencephalography (EEG) studies. However, it only provides an indirect measure of cortical excitability, and even for the primary motor cortex (M1), we do not understand how cortical and corticospinal excitability correspond to each other. Indeed, it remains unclear whether cortical responses to TMS follow similar location-dependent patterns along the M1, and whether subthreshold stimulation can reliably engage cortical circuits relevant to motor output. Combining TMS with electromyography (EMG) and EEG, TMS-EMG-EEG, enables simultaneous assessment of corticospinal and cortical excitability to answer these questions. We investigated how cortical excitability thresholds (CETs, measured with EEG), relate to corticospinal excitability thresholds (RMTs, measured with EMG) at the hand, arm, and leg hotspots along the M1 in 24 subjects. RMTs and CETs were strongly correlated, and both increased from hand to arm to leg. CETs were generally lower than RMTs, indicating that subthreshold stimulation was enough to evoke robust early TMS evoked potentials (TEPs). Within subjects, CETs differed from the corresponding RMTs at all three M1 hotspots, and this difference increased from hand to leg representations. The findings of the present study argue against using a default hand-muscle RMT to set cortical excitability dosage along the M1 and beyond. Online TMS-EEG can enable real-time dosing and could improve stimulation precision, efficiency, and generalizability, but the site-specific variability calls for adaptive control.

title: Mechanisms of impaired cerebral hemodynamics and memory resilience differ by sex: A role for mineralocorticoid receptors in VCID
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Chronic hypertension is associated with cerebral hypoperfusion and is a primary risk factor for vascular contributions to cognitive impairment and dementia (VCID). Aldosterone, a key mediator of hypertension, causes cerebrovascular dysfunction via its mineralocorticoid receptor (MR). METHODS: The effects of MR signaling during hypertension on hemodynamics in two cognition-centric brain regions were determined in both sexes using an established model of VCID (spontaneously hypertensive rat, SHR) and MR antagonist eplerenone. Long-term and spatial working memory were tested, and absolute brain blood flow and brain oxygenation were measured in vivo in CA1 of dorsal hippocampus and medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC). RESULTS: Hypertension differentially impaired hemodynamics in a sex- and region-dependent manner. Female SHR had more pervasive hypoperfusion than males that did not affect flow-metabolism coupling. Eplerenone treatment in females restored perfusion in mPFC and hippocampus, improved working memory, but did not protect hippocampal-dependent memory. Eplerenone had no effect in male SHR, indicating the MR-dependent mechanism of VCID is sex-specific. DISCUSSION: This study advances our understanding of how chronic hypertension compromises brain blood flow, suggests that resilience of memory function differs by domain, and that efficacy of interventions depend upon sex.

title: Monoaminergic changes are associated with impaired neurogenesis along the longitudinal axis of the hippocampus in ageing and dementia
abstract: Neurogenesis persists in the adult human hippocampus and is thought to support memory and emotional regulation. Both normal ageing and Parkinson disease dementia (PDD) are associated with reduced hippocampal neurogenesis, but why this occurs and how this might change across the across the hippocampal axis remains unclear. Here, we quantified the expression of genes regulating neurogenesis from stem cell production to neuron maturation and examined their relationship with monoaminergic activity throughout the post-mortem hippocampus in young and aged individuals, as well as in individuals with PDD. DCX and MKI67 expression were markedly reduced in PDD cases throughout the hippocampus, while GFAP and GFAP{delta} were elevated in aged control individuals but not in PDD. Dopamine and serotonin levels were unchanged but reduced levels of the dopamine metabolite DOPAC, and increased levels of the serotonin metabolite 5-HIAA, were present across the hippocampal axis in PDD. Hierarchical regression analysis identified DOPAC and 5-HIAA as significant predictors of DCX and MKI67 expression independent of diagnostic group. Coupling between stem cell markers and proliferative output was preserved in the hippocampus of young controls but was absent in aged controls and in PDD. These data suggest changes in monoaminergic systems are linked to stage-specific deficits in neuronal proliferation and maturation, identifying a potential mechanistic bridge to cognitive decline in PDD.

title: Naturalistic recall preserves temporal specificity despite cortical feature reorganization
abstract: Although sensory input arrives in a largely continuous stream, recall is temporally compressed, discontinuous, and often structured as events. However, the temporal specificity of recall-related neural activity within events, and the separation and cortical organization of recalled features relative to perception, remain poorly characterized. We analyzed functional MRI data recorded during viewing and free recall of an episode of Sherlock. A data-driven alignment between viewing and recall data identified neural recapitulation of corresponding narrative events and revealed information that distinguished moments within events, particularly in the association cortex. Features ranging from low-level visual to semantic information predicted recall reinstatement. However, differences in predictive performance among feature levels became smaller during recall, and their organization along the cortical sensory-to-association gradient reversed relative to viewing. Thus, temporal specificity within events can be preserved despite substantial reorganization of feature representations across the cortex during recall.

title: Neural dynamics become significantly faster and more nonlinear at the peak of information processing
abstract: The temporal scale at which neural populations preserve stimulus information is often treated as fixed, even though population activity changes rapidly during sensory processing. Whether the information-optimal scale changes within a single stimulus-evoked episode, and what determines its evolution, remains unclear. We developed Integration-Split, a decoding-based framework that estimates the time-varying temporal resolution of population spike trains. Across four visual paradigms and throughout the mouse visual hierarchy, the optimal scale contracted after stimulus onset and subsequently re-expanded. This pattern persisted across stimulus temporal frequencies and was largely absent in a hippocampal control. The optimal scale varied inversely with stimulus decodability, reaching its finest resolution when stimulus identity was most accurately decoded. Beyond this association, independently estimating the signal-noise autocorrelation balance across candidate window widths identified the window that maximized the autocorrelation-based signal-to-noise ratio, and this optimal width closely followed the Integration-Split trajectory. Consistent with these findings, stronger nonlinear predictive structure coincided with finer optimal temporal resolution, consistent with the idea that shorter integration windows are needed to preserve informative nonlinear population structure that would otherwise be attenuated by temporal averaging. To test the functional relevance of this organization, we trained a Transformer solely to decode stimulus identity, without providing the optimal temporal-scale pattern or Integration-Split outputs. Its learned attention exhibited a similar contraction-and-recovery profile, and disrupting heads with stronger correspondence produced larger decoding deficits. Together, these findings reveal a dynamically changing, information-optimal temporal scale in population coding, shaped by the evolving balance of signal and noise autocorrelation and by nonlinear population structure, and independently recapitulated in the learned attention of a Transformer trained without temporal-scale supervision.

title: Nociceptive-evoked electroencephalography can predict inter-individual differences in high frequency induced sensitisation of central nociceptive pathways: A test-retest reliability study
abstract: Evoked-EEG can capture changes in cortical responses during experimentally induced sensitised pain states. However, the test-retest reliability of such methods requires validation. The present study applied HFS across two identical sessions in the same individuals to assess the test-retest reliability of EEG dynamics evoked by a 128mN pin-prick stimulator and single-pulse electrical stimuli before and after HFS conditioning. The value of these features for reflecting individual differences in the development of hyperalgesia was also assessed. Results demonstrate poor-to-moderate test-retest reliability and relatively wide agreement at baseline for all features, with lateralised differences often present. This was further reduced when post-HFS changes were considered. -ERD assessed from contralateral central electrodes was significantly strengthened post-HFS for both electrical and pinprick stimuli, consistent with increased sensorimotor engagement in response to hyperalgesic and non-hyperalgesic stimuli. Notably, baseline -ERD was related to the subsequent time course of SHA development. Furthermore, whilst VP magnitude displayed a significant relationship with the general intensity of perceived pain, no specificity for SHA development was evident. Alternatively, {theta}-ERS captured a general habituation effect relative to variations in reported pain intensity between sessions for both stimuli modalities. These findings indicate that evoked EEG responses may be useful for investigating individual differences in the cortical processing of acute pain and the development time course of HFS-induced sensitivity yet may not possess sufficient test-retest reliability for interventional testing.

title: One digit too many: brain rhythms and autonomic responses at the limits of working memory capacity
abstract: Physiological measures vary with working memory load, but whether they identify when demands exceed a person's working memory capacity remains unclear. We assessed neural and autonomic responses to exceeding digit span by one digit. During an adaptive digit span task, we recorded EEG, pupillometry, and photoplethysmography from 123 participants. We compared each participant's digit span (approximately 70% correct full-sequence recall) with sequences one digit longer (span+1), operationally defined as overload. Full-sequence accuracy decreased from 74.1% to 51.5%, and subjective mental demand increased. Baseline-normalized pulse wave amplitude (PWA) was lower in span+1 from the first digit through terminal retention period. PWA was lower on correctly recalled than erroneous span+1 trials. Phasic pupil responses increased across serial positions but were smaller in span+1 at late span-matched positions; responses did not differ between conditions at their final digits. Non-baseline-corrected pupil diameter was larger in span+1 before sequence onset and during terminal retention, whereas non-baseline-corrected PWA did not differ. Frontal midline theta increased with serial position and was greater during terminal retention in span+1. Alpha and beta power decreased with serial position, and differed between conditions only at late positions. Terminal beta suppression was greater on correctly recalled span+1 trials. Thus, exceeding calibrated span impaired recall without producing a common physiological breakpoint. The findings suggest that reaching this limit does not immediately lead to resource exhaustion or disengagement. Physiological responses showed shifts in timing consistent with adjustments in preparation for recall of the longer sequence, along with increased effort before and during longer sequences.

title: Organ scale Three-dimensional atlas of developing pelvic innervation for the mouse lower urinary tract.
abstract: Pelvic autonomic neurons are responsible for coordinating pelvic organ function, including storage and emptying of the urinary bladder. These neurons arise from sacral neural crest-derived progenitors which migrate to the developing urogenital sinus and undergo differentiation alongside pelvic organs, ultimately organizing into paired pelvic ganglia. To circumvent the complex morphological changes that occur during genitourinary organ development, we have optimized light sheet fluorescence microscopy imaging for three-dimensional mapping of the development and spatial distribution of pelvic autonomic neurons. To track neural crest progenitor migration, neurogenesis, and formation of mature pelvic ganglia morphology in mice, we imaged intact lower urinary tract tissue from mid-gestational to post-weaning stages at single-cell resolution. The resulting atlas identifies the precise timing and initial routes of neural crest progenitor migration, defines timing for pelvic ganglion neurogenesis, and reveals previously unrecognized neuronal cell bodies outside of the centralized pelvic ganglia structures. The analysis further highlights morphological changes to pelvic ganglion structure that occur in parallel with genitourinary maturation, including the divergence of the major pelvic ganglia and bladder-proximal accessory ganglia. This work acts as the first wholemount imaging atlas of pelvic innervation in the mouse spanning fetal and postnatal timepoints, and thus we present an informative tool for future studies of developmental neurourology and neurogenic bladder dysfunction.
author_corresponding_institution: Departments of Medicine and Cell Biology, Vanderbilt University School of Medicine

title: Physical sensorimotor contingencies facilitate learning in monkeys
abstract: Animal studies in neuroscience routinely use virtual tasks that deviate significantly from the animals' natural behavioral repertoire. This choice is often necessary for conducting careful and controlled experimentation. However, this approach raises a fundamental question: do virtual tasks expose neural computations and mechanisms associated with naturalistic tasks? In this study, we explore how naturalistic settings influence learning timescale and generalization behavior in rhesus monkeys. By training animals in a maze-solving task and comparing their behavior across two environments, we observe significant differences. Specifically, we found that a realistic setup using physical objects enabled learning that was orders of magnitude faster than the learning timescale observed in a comparable computerized virtual environment. Furthermore, we noted limited transfer of performance between the physical and virtual settings. These findings underscore the need for understanding how task environments shape learning and generalization, with potential implications for the design of future neuroscience and AI experiments.
author_corresponding_institution: 1. Biomedical Engineering, SKKU, Republic of Korea; 2. Center for Neuroscience Imaging Research, SKKU, Republic of Korea; 6. Brain Science and Engineering, SKKU

title: Presynaptic PMCA interacts with Dlg, regulating in vivo synaptic calcium in Drosophila larval NMJ
abstract: Precise regulation of presynaptic Ca2+is essential for neurotransmitter release and synaptic function. At the Drosophila larval neuromuscular junction (NMJ), the plasma membrane Ca2+-ATPase (PMCA) mediates presynaptic Ca2+; extrusion and is enriched in peri-active-zone membrane domains. Here, we investigated how PMCA distribution is regulated and contributes to synaptic function. Co-immunoprecipitation and super-resolution STED microscopy revealed that PMCA interacts and co-localizes with the MAGUK scaffold protein Discs large (Dlg) in discrete presynaptic membrane clusters. Neuronal depletion of the DlgS97 isoform disrupted PMCA clustering without substantially altering its abundance, redistributing the pump into smaller membrane puncta. Reporter assays further showed that PDZ-binding motifs in the PMCA C-terminus mediate its interaction with Dlg and are required for normal cluster formation. Electrophysiological analyses revealed that reducing either PMCA or Dlg increased spontaneous neurotransmitter release and enhanced asynchronous release following high-frequency stimulation. PMCA depletion also prolonged postsynaptic current decay during repetitive stimulation, implicating PMCA in the rapid regulation of presynaptic Ca2+; signals. Together, these findings identify Dlg as a key organizer of presynaptic PMCA and establish a link between synaptic scaffold organization and Ca2+; homeostasis in vivo. Our results demonstrate that PMCA contributes to maintaining resting presynaptic Ca2+; levels, restoring Ca2+; homeostasis after repetitive stimulation, and regulating Ca2+; dynamics following a single stimulus. These findings highlight the importance of the nanoscale organization of Ca2+; extrusion machinery in controlling neurotransmitter release at the Drosophila NMJ.

title: Rapid Detection and Initial Treatment of Life-Threatening Subdural Hematoma in a Sheep Model
abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is the leading cause of death and disability in people under 40 worldwide. There is an unmet need for detection and treatment of life-threatening TBI when computed tomography (CT) scanners and neurosurgeons are unavailable. We developed a new handheld frequency-domain multidetector infrared hemorrhage detection device. Using the new device, military pre-hospital medics required <4 minutes to detect life-threatening subdural hematoma in a sheep model. We developed a second device that allows non-neurosurgeons to safely create a burr hole and partially remove clotted subdural blood. In sheep, the treatment device reduced intracranial pressure within 20 minutes, and improved post-anesthesia blinded neurological outcomes. With human use adaptation, these devices could allow rapid detection and initial treatment of some life-threatening TBIs in challenging situations.
author_corresponding_institution: Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences

title: Recruitment of intrasegmental and propriospinal interneuron networks of forelimb motor circuitry in chronic cervical contusion spinal cord injury
abstract: Cervical spinal cord injury (SCI) disrupts descending supraspinal input and spinal networks controlling upper extremity motor function, making recovery of arm and hand function a major priority for affected individuals. The vast majority of regenerative strategies have been studied during the acute and sub-acute phases following SCI, while therapeutic testing remains limited for chronic injury, when persistent barriers significantly limit circuit remodeling. We asked whether pharmacologic enhancement of neuronal-intrinsic axon growth capacity through PTEN inhibition could promote forelimb motor recovery and circuit plasticity in a rodent model of chronic cervical SCI. Following C5 hemi-contusion, female rats underwent behavioral testing of forelimb motor function and received PTEN antagonist peptide (PAP) beginning at a chronic time point, and the trans-synaptic tracer, pseudorabies virus (PRV), was injected into ipsilesional triceps to trace forelimb-associated motor circuitry. PAP selectively improved forelimb usage during cylinder paw-preference testing, but not strength, sensorimotor, or gait-related forelimb measures. PAP increased recruitment of PRV-traced local-projecting and propriospinal interneuron networks. In addition, PAP enhanced synaptic input to these recruited propriospinal interneurons, raising the possibility that spared descending pathways may contribute to recovery through spinal relay circuits. Lastly, we mapped the supraspinal connectome providing descending input from brainstem to the lower motor neurons innervating forelimb muscle, and we determined how this connectome was impacted both by SCI and PAP. Together, these findings show that, even in chronic SCI, pharmacological PTEN inhibition can promote forelimb functional recovery and significant circuit remodeling, with spinal interneuron networks emerging as a key site of PAP-induced plasticity.
author_corresponding_institution: Sidney Kimmel Medical College at Thomas Jefferson University

title: SafeLens: A Statistically Controlled Nonlinear Machine Learning Framework for Characterizing Hidden Dynamics in Event-Locked Neural Activity
abstract: Machine learning has advanced rapidly over the past decade, yet event-locked neural activity is still analyzed predominantly with traditional statistics and linear models. While traditional linear methods provide computationally tractable statistical control for pre-selected features or trial-averaged waveforms, they miss subtle nonlinear and trial-varying neural dynamics. Nonlinear models can capture these complex patterns, but their feature reliance is opaque and notoriously difficult to threshold statistically. We introduce SafeLens (Searchlight Analysis of Fluctuation Events, Leveraging Extensive Null Sampling) to combine the power of nonlinear machine learning with the rigorous false-positive control of traditional statistical inference. At each position of a sliding window, a random forest learns to discriminate event-locked activity from interleaved resting-state neural activity using multiscale temporal derivatives. Randomized feature ablation inverts slope polarity in held-out trials to map the random forest models' reliance on specific rising versus falling excursions across the time-frequency space. SafeLens then establishes an empirical null by running the same pipeline on separate resting-state recordings, training forests to discriminate rest from rest. This empirical null translates each channel's complex nonlinear resting dynamics into a model-matched noise floor on the map's linear reliance scale, allowing a single threshold to control the family-wise error rate against the channel's own background structure rather than a summary statistic of its baseline. When we injected simulated cortico-cortical evoked potentials (CCEPs) into resting intracranial EEG recordings, SafeLens recovered ~2.5 times as many polarity-resolved deflections as trial-average thresholding and the closest data-driven method, maintaining its advantage under trial-to-trial variability while yielding ~5-11 times fewer false components, ~2-5 times lower mean boundary error, and superior single-trial latency tracking as a timing prior. In eight patients, CCEPs remained detectable above chance until 1,040 ms after stimulation, compared with 570 and 455 ms for those benchmarks. Together, these findings establish SafeLens as a novel solution for enabling nonlinear models to uncover subtle, trial-varying neural dynamics under strict statistical control.

title: Scn2a-deficient mice exhibit serotonergic dysfunction and altered behavioral responses to psilocybin
abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a prominent neurodevelopmental disorder affecting approximately 3.2% of children in the United States. Although ASD has traditionally been considered a polygenic disorder, advances in genetic testing have identified individual genes that can contribute to its development. Large-scale whole-exome sequencing has identified variants in SCN2A, which encodes the alpha subunit of the voltage-gated sodium channel Nav1.2, as a leading monogenic cause of ASD. Social deficits are a core feature of ASD, and the serotonergic system has been implicated in the regulation of social behavior. Recent studies have demonstrated that serotonergic psychedelics, such as psilocybin, can increase sociability in mouse models of ASD. However, whether underlying genetic alterations associated with ASD influence behavioral responses to psilocybin remains poorly understood. Therefore, we investigated how Scn2a deficiency affects behavioral responses to psilocybin and whether these differences are accompanied by alterations in the serotonergic system. We found that Scn2a-deficient mice exhibited differential responses to psilocybin compared to wild-type (WT) mice. Specifically, psilocybin increased sociability in Scn2a-deficient mice without affecting anxiety-like behavior, whereas WT mice exhibited decreased anxiety-like behavior without increased sociability. Further behavioral evaluation revealed a reduced head twitch response in Scn2a-deficient mice following psilocybin administration compared to WT mice. To further investigate these differences, we examined serotonin levels and receptor expression in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), a brain region implicated in social behavior and psychedelic action. Although baseline serotonin levels in the mPFC did not differ between genotypes, Scn2a-deficient mice exhibited altered serotonin receptor expression. We further characterized the serotonergic system by evaluating neuronal activity in the Dorsal Raphe Nucleus, a major source of serotonergic projections to the mPFC, and found increased spontaneous firing in Scn2a-deficient mice. Together, these findings highlight serotonergic alterations associated with SCN2A deficiency and the potential for serotonergic interventions to alleviate social deficits associated with SCN2A-related ASD.

title: Self-Other Neural Representational Distinction is Associated with Distorted Social Predictions in Social Anxiety
abstract: Background: Social anxiety (SA) is characterized by distorted negative expectations about the future. Because optimism bias is inherently comparative, the extent to which these predictions reflect a fundamental disruption in self- versus other-referential processing remains poorly understood. Methods: Across two experiments, we investigated the mechanisms underlying social predictions in SA. In Experiment 1, individuals with high (n = 52, LSAS > 65) and low SA (n = 51, LSAS < 35) rated the future likelihood of positive and negative social outcomes for themselves or for a protagonist. In Experiment 2, 35 adults spanning a continuous spectrum of SA completed the task during fMRI. Behavior was analyzed using linear mixed-effects models. Neurally, multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) quantified self-other representational distinctions, while a parametric general linear model (GLM) tracked neural sensitivity to likelihood predictions. Results: Behaviorally, higher SA was characterized by an attenuated optimism bias: individuals predicted a lower likelihood of positive outcomes, but a higher likelihood of negative outcomes, for themselves compared to others. Neurally, higher trait SA correlated with greater self-other representational distinction within the left pregenual anterior cingulate cortex (pgACC). Concurrently, the precuneus exhibited stronger parametric tracking of self-negative predictions versus others. Crucially, pgACC representational distinction during positive outcome processing significantly mediated the association between SA severity and heightened prediction-tracking in the precuneus. Conclusions: These findings offer a novel mechanistic framework, suggesting that an exaggerated neural segregation of the self from others drives hyper-vigilant, risk-sensitive social predictions in SA. This candidate circuit-level dynamic warrants further replication in clinical cohorts.

title: Sensory representation by non-equilibrium flows of neural activity at the mesoscale of cortex
abstract: We present a non-equilibrium theory of sensory perception and the mesoscale of sensory cortex. We propose that local neuron assemblies (cortical columns) toggle spontaneously between activity states (on and off) and that small populations of columns are coupled within and between areas of sensory cortex. The resulting network generates sudden, large-scale fluctuations and represents sensory inputs and perceptions by characteristic patterns of activity flows. The non-equilibrium dynamic is governed by the variational principle of maximal path entropy, or Maximum Caliber. Many current theories, by contrast, posit equilibrium dynamics and representation with activity states Our minimal model of sensory cortex describes populations of columns from two cortical areas and is fully constrained by empirical observations of `reversals' in perceived appearance, which occur spontaneously for visual, auditory, and tactile stimulation. We formalize representation by activity flows with dynamic Hamiltonian functions. Surprisingly, effective representation requires small-number fluctuations of toggling columns, as larger numbers would be dominated by hysteresis. Finally, we detail predictions for the microscale of spiking neurons that follow from on-off toggling and non-equilibrium dynamics. We conclude that the neural levels underlying perception are functionally organized in terms of activity flows. The inherent instability of non-equilibrium ensures active updating and renders all perceptions open to immediate revision. We conjecture that current theories of brain function (such as the Free Energy Principle) could be reformulated in terms of the variational principle of non-equilibrium, Maximum Caliber.

title: Serial dependence carries the action that produced the previous report
abstract: Serial dependence pulls current judgments toward the recent past, but what is carried forward is debated: the previous stimulus, the previous decision, or something about the report itself. Three magnitude-reproduction experiments separated these sources. Participants viewed dot arrays that varied independently in duration and numerosity, then reproduced the cued dimension by holding a key while a display accumulated, so that both magnitudes were produced through the same action. A response-history model partitioned the attraction into previous-stimulus and previous-response paths. The previous response predicted cross-dimensional attraction after controlling for the previous and current stimuli: a numerosity report biased the next duration judgment and vice versa (Experiment 1), also when each task used its own response key (Experiment 2). A task switch weakened this carryover without abolishing it. Experiment 3 randomized, trial by trial, whether a reported number required a long or a short key hold. The influence of a previous number on the next duration judgment changed with this mapping, showing that reported value alone did not account for carryover. Conventional stimulus-based measures showed none of this cross-task history. Serial dependence can therefore carry the trace of the action through which a previous judgment was expressed, bounded but not gated by task context.
author_corresponding_institution: Neuro-Cognitive Psychology, Department of Psychology, LMU Munich

title: Spatially resolved single-cell atlas reveals cortical glial reactivity associated with regions of neuronal growth programs in both hemispheres after stroke
abstract: Recovery after focal motor cortex stroke relies on structural remodeling of neuronal circuits in the perilesional cortex (PLC) and contralesional cortex (CLC). Although transcriptomic studies have identified distinct reactive glial states after stroke, how their spatial organization relates to processes of tissue degeneration and neuronal circuit remodeling remains poorly understood. We used a custom 347-gene Xenium spatial transcriptomics panel to profile approximately 650,000 cells across both hemispheres of male and female mice 7 days after photothrombotic stroke. We identified injury-associated myeloid populations concentrated within the infarct and reactive astrocytes enriched in the glial scar. Distinct reactive populations also extended into spared cortex, including an interferon-associated myeloid population and a reactive astrocyte population that was present in both PLC and CLC. Spatial mapping further revealed elevated neuronal growth-associated gene expression in both regions, particularly among layer 5 extratelencephalic projection neurons, which include corticospinal neurons. Intriguingly, reactive glial populations were enriched in regions exhibiting elevated neuronal growth-associated gene expression, including areas of the CLC containing axons and presynaptic terminals originating from the PLC. Together, these findings reveal a striking spatial association between reactive glial populations and neurons exhibiting elevated growth-associated gene expression and support glial-neuronal interactions as potential targets for promoting circuit remodeling and functional recovery after stroke.

title: Thalamic stereo-EEG detects sleep stages N2 and N3 with discrimination approaching scalp EEG
abstract: Sleep and epilepsy interact strongly during sleep stages N2 and N3, when synchronization of brain rhythms is increased. Sleep staging relies on scalp EEG, which is often absent or incomplete during stereo-EEG monitoring and unavailable from implanted devices, while thalamic leads are increasingly implanted for epilepsy neuromodulation. Given the role of the thalamus in spindle generation and slow oscillation dynamics, we hypothesized that thalamic channels would identify N2 and N3 (N2+N3) better than other intracranial sites. We analyzed 477 h of stereo-EEG with simultaneous scalp EEG from six adults, including 46 thalamic bipolar channels on 11 electrodes. Two classifiers were evaluated on identical channels: a random forest with hidden Markov decoding (RF + HMM) trained leave-one-participant-out, and the pretrained SleepSEEG algorithm developed without thalamic channels. The primary endpoint was discrimination of N2+N3 from other stages as classified from scalp EEG by a sleep expert. Among regions sampled in all participants, thalamic channels performed best (area under the curve [AUC] 0.94 with RF + HMM and 0.93 with SleepSEEG across whole recordings; 0.88 and 0.86 at night). With RF + HMM, thalamic channels outperformed mesial temporal and temporal neocortical channels in all six participants across whole recordings. The advantage persisted against channel-count-matched subsets and a white-matter control with both classifiers. Individual thalamic electrodes reached AUCs of 0.79-0.99 with RF + HMM (10 of 11 at least 0.89). These offline findings support thalamic N2+N3 detection and motivate real-time evaluation for sleep-targeted neuromodulation.
