Accelerating reaction network identification via frequency-domain analysis
abstract: The identification of intracellular reaction networks from single-cell data lies at the heart of many biological studies, as it can unravel key mechanisms in living organisms and provide insights for their rational engineering. However, the stochastic and nonlinear nature of these reacting systems poses significant challenges for this identification problem, making the state-of-the-art methods (e.g., particle-filtering-based approaches) computationally demanding. This paper reports a noteworthy numerical observation that for certain systems, the Fourier transform can render the likelihood of the measurement data approximately Gaussian, therefore resulting in a substantially accelerated Bayesian inference algorithm. A gene transcription example is presented to illustrate this finding and demonstrate the efficiency of {the proposed Fourier-based method}.

title: Do sEMG Foundation Models Improve Cross-Subject Generalisation?
abstract: sEMG Foundation Models aim to learn general purpose representations over diverse subjects and recording conditions that boost performance on a variety of downstream tasks. However, existing evaluations make it difficult to discern whether pretraining alone is sufficient to combat the cross-subject overfitting which makes machine learning on sEMG so challenging. We conduct a systematic evaluation of three sEMG foundation models across three gesture classification datasets under both intra-session and inter-subject splits, using three fine-tuning strategies designed to isolate the contribution of pretraining. We find that pretraining boosts performance when train and test samples are drawn from the same recording session, but this benefit largely disappears under inter-subject evaluation. In low subject count datasets, pretraining provides little to no benefit and classical ML baselines match or exceed foundation model performance.

title: Geometric Relevance Is Not Sufficient: Evaluating Focused Post-Training Supervision in Diffusion Docking
abstract: Diffusion-based molecular docking requires learning a corrective score field across a broad corruption distribution, yet individual pose errors can differ substantially in their structural consequences. This creates a post-training conflict between preserving broad score-field coverage and concentrating supervision on corrections that appear more relevant to docking geometry. Using DiffDock, a fixed-budget study compares broad continuation with torsional supervision focused on Cartesian consequence or conditional target consistency, and with a broad/focused mixture. Evaluation separates fixed score fidelity, generated-pose quality, best-of-10 sampling capacity, and confidence-selected Top-1 docking performance. At <5 Angstrom, broad continuation had the highest mean Top-1 success among trained policies, and focused or mixed supervision showed no consistent advantage under the tested budget. The starting model had better fixed score fidelity, whereas the evaluated broad-continuation model had higher mean Top-1 success with the same aggregate best-of-10 recovery. Focusing supervision on structurally consequential or more consistently specified corrections did not consistently improve returned-pose success over broad continuation.
comment: 17 pages, 5 figures; accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 AI4DD Workshop

title: How Deep is the Signal? Time-Context up to 30 Years for Colorectal Cancer Prediction in a Primary-Care EHR Model
abstract: EHR foundation models read medical events within a fixed context window, and long context has so far been measured only in tokens. How far back in time a model must look to capture the earliest predictive signal is unknown. We introduce time-context, the calendar lookback window before the prediction point, and provide, to our knowledge, the first systematic evaluation of decade-scale time-context for an EHR foundation model. We pretrained a decoder-only transformer (34.6M parameters) on 1.4B coded events from 3.6M primary-care patients in North West London and fine-tuned it to predict incident colorectal cancer under a 12-month pre-diagnostic buffer. A frozen cohort of 1,008 cases and 9,582 matched controls, all registered for at least 30 years, was evaluated at 15 nested lookback windows from 2 to 30 years, so that every truncation is compared within the same patients. Discrimination rose from an AUROC of 0.551 at 2 years to 0.590 at 18 years, then plateaued, with about 80% of the gain reached within 10 years; an XGBoost baseline converged to the same level (peak AUROC 0.589). A simulation further suggests that rotary position embeddings (RoPE) over elapsed time alias beyond about 20 years at the default base frequency, motivating a retuned $θ$. Time-context is a measurable design axis for clinical prediction models, distinct from token-context, and should be reported.
comment: Accepted at Machine Learning for Health (ML4H) 2026, Findings Track. 10 pages, 6 figures, 3 tables

title: Interpretable many-body interaction laws for collective motion from few trajectories
abstract: Models of collective motion usually reduce social interactions to pairwise forces, despite empirical evidence for many-body effects. We introduce the directional atomic cluster expansion (dACE), which adapts the atomic cluster expansion (ACE) of interatomic potentials to self-propelled agents. dACE provides a systematically improvable, exactly equivariant expansion of an agent's acceleration that splits uniquely into 1-, 2-, 3-body and higher contributions, along with a self term for the agent's own past motion that is fitted so that it does not absorb the interactions. On simulated collectives in two and three dimensions with known rules, dACE recovers the interaction law body order by body order from little data, while the neural model SocialNet, the current closest competitor, needs more data, has much larger errors on many-body or chiral rules and is restricted to 2D. On real data sets of tracked zebrafish and golden shiners, the laws learned by dACE agree better between disjoint halves of the data than SocialNet's. The learned laws are interpretable, and in the shiners the 3-body term opposes the pairwise response as neighbourhoods get dense. Finally, we show that next-step prediction accuracy mostly measures self-propulsion and noise rather than the interactions, and suggest more robust combinations of error measures for interaction learning.
comment: 19 pages, 10 figures

title: Invariance before structure: two modes of emergent compression in representation learning
abstract: Learned representations show striking invariance across biological and artificial neural networks, with different substrates and variations driven by drift, heterogeneity and initialisation. To understand this invariance, we propose Emergent Adaptive Representation Learning (EARL), a framework that distinguishes two modes of emergence in learned representations: state-space compression, where a learned representation gains predictive power over its own future beyond what the network's units can predict individually, and parameter-space compression, where networks with different micro-level parameters converge to the same representation. We formalise both as Fisher sensitivities and introduce ensemble-level information-theoretic measures for each. In a recurrent reservoir with a trained bottleneck, parameter-space compression rises within the first few epochs of training and partly independently of the task, whereas state-space compression rises about 30 epochs later and only when the network begins to learn the temporal structure of the task. These results suggest that invariance to the substrate and task-specific emergent structure are acquired in distinct phases of learning.
comment: Extended abstract, UniReps workshop at NeurIPS 2026

title: Kinetic models of a K channel with 2 stage voltage sensor activation and an opening step
abstract: The activation of a K channel with 2 voltage sensors and a separate opening step may be described by a 4 state kinetic equation. If $k_{o}$ and $k_{c}$ are the opening and closing rates, and $α$ and $β$ are the voltage sensor rates such that $k_{o}$ $\ggα,k_{c}\ggβ$ and $k_{o}$ $\gg k_{c}$, the kinetic equation may be reduced to a 3 state model where the effective backward rate from the activated-open state is $2βk_{c}/(k_{o}+k_{c})$. However, if a K channel voltage sensor activates in 2 stages, and there is a separate opening step, the occupation probabilities of the states of the channel satisfy a 10 state kinetic equation. When the time constants of the characteristic equation for each voltage sensor differ by an order of magnitude, and $k_{o}$ $\gg k_{c}$, the open state probability is proportional to $n^{2}$, where $n$ satisfies a rate equation, and the derived rates have a similar voltage dependence to the rates $α_{n}$ and $β_{n}$ from voltage clamp data.
comment: 9 pages, 9 figures

title: Leveraging deep generative modelling at the agent level in discrete-event simulations
abstract: Emulators are often invoked to facilitate parameter inference in computationally intensive agent-based simulations (ABSs). Most approaches, however, require a large sample of pre-existing outputs on which such emulators can be trained. For computationally intensive simulations, this sample can be prohibitively expensive to generate. We propose a new approach to leverage emulators at the agent level in event-based ABSs to reduce the computational requirements of the simulation itself. We demonstrate this in a computationally intensive ``multi-disease'' ABS, Thanzi La Onse, which self-consistently simulates a wide range of medical conditions in a population. By applying conditional tabular generative adversarial networks to replace the modelling of one of the simulated causes of ill health, road traffic injuries (RTIs), we are able to improve its simulation run-time by 86.6% (95% bootstrap confidence interval [85.2, 88.1]), while recovering the evolution of cause-specific mean disability adjusted life years with a 13% error, despite the low assumed incidence of fatal RTIs (~2%). Crucially, we do so while retaining the full ABS framework, and correctly recovering multi-disease dynamics. This represents a crucial step towards enabling full-model emulators for very computationally intensive simulations, and making large ABS amenable to rigorous parameter inference and a full understanding of parameter sensitivity.
comment: Accepted for publication by the Journal of The Royal Society Interface

title: Pattern selection and biomass shifts in a vegetation model with nonlocal competition and Allee activation
abstract: We study a single-species vegetation model in which a strong Allee effect acts locally and competition acts through a nonlocal kernel, and we describe the kernel with the one-parameter family of q-Gaussians, which goes from compact support to power-law tails. The local activation introduced by the Allee effect allows a finite-wavelength instability even when the Fourier transform of the kernel is positive, so Gaussian and heavy-tailed kernels can produce patterns. We derive in closed form the coefficients of the hexagonal amplitude equations and verify them against independent numerical steady states. The quadratic coefficient $Q$ results from the balance between the curvature of the local growth and the competitive inhibition at the pattern scale, and at onset its sign depends only on the fraction of the local activation that diffusion removes at the critical wavenumber. The same coefficient controls the morphology, since spots, labyrinths and gaps appear with pairwise competition only as $Q$ changes sign, and the amplitude equations predict the choice between hexagons and stripes in every simulated state in which the cubic truncation holds. It also controls the total biomass, which increases for spots and decreases for gaps.

title: PharmAgents2: Towards Autonomous End-to-End Drug Discovery
abstract: Drug discovery requires continuous scientific decision-making across a vast research space. We introduce PharmAgents2, an autonomous system for end-to-end drug discovery that combines knowledge-enhanced decision-making with organized large-scale exploration. Paper2Skill extracts transferable scientific decision knowledge from public sources and, together with expert-developed skills, supports research decisions. Self-Scaling Discovery expands exploration through parallel agents inheriting research context and decision-making capabilities across targets, scientific hypotheses, and discovery strategies. We introduce PharmAgents-Bench v0.1, comprising 121 questions across nine decision scenarios and three end-to-end tasks assessed with expert-defined process rubrics. PharmAgents2 outperforms evaluated baselines in most decision categories and achieves the highest process scores on all three end-to-end tasks. In three real-world studies, autonomous investigations generated findings subsequently supported by human-executed experiments. For LpxH, PharmAgents2 hypothesized a previously unreported allosteric site and screened compounds against it, identifying a novel inhibitor scaffold with experimentally confirmed inhibitory activity and binding. For JAK1, it prioritized a covalent inhibition strategy and nominated compounds with experimentally demonstrated activity. Starting from a known bioactive molecule, Self-Scaling Discovery explored candidate targets across the proteome and identified a new binding target, with the interaction subsequently confirmed experimentally. PharmAgents2 represents a prototype of a virtual pharmaceutical company, marking a step toward autonomous end-to-end drug discovery.

title: Reversible Dynamics, Asymmetric Actions: Parking as a Trajectory-Level Affordance
abstract: Drivers are often told to back into a tight parking space, not drive in nose first. The advice looks paradoxical, because a slow car is dynamically reversible: reverse its speed and replay the steering backward, and it retraces a feasible path. Played backward, though, reverse-in shows a car driving forward out of the space. Reverse-in and forward-in are different tasks: they share a start position but end facing opposite ways. We separate three clearances between car and obstacles. Static fit $F$ is the clearance the parked car keeps at its best acceptable destination pose. Eventual access $A_\infty$ is the clearance it can keep all the way there with unlimited corrections. Resource-bounded access $A_K$ is the clearance that survives a budget of $K$ reversals, switches between forward and reverse. They satisfy $F\ge A_\infty\ge A_K$. In one fully specified scene (one car, bay, aisle and start), a certified argument proves $A_\infty=F=0.5000$ m for both tasks. In this scene, all certified forward/reverse asymmetry therefore arises at finite $K$: it lies in how many corrections each task needs, not in the clearance either can eventually keep. With one reversal, an explicit path gives reverse-in at least $0.4410$ m clearance. A certified reachability argument caps forward-in's one-reversal clearance at $d_0<0.1720002$ m. With two reversals, forward-in gets at least $0.2833$ m. To keep a clearance strictly above any $d$ with $d_0\le d<0.2833$ m, reverse-in thus needs exactly one reversal and forward-in exactly two when both tasks move forward first. If both move in reverse first, the counts are two and three. The contrast depends on the start position (Section 4.15). Proposed experiments test whether observers distinguish fit, eventual access and budgeted access. They compare these with simpler cues, such as how the turning body sweeps, and learned manoeuvre labels.
comment: 79 pages, 15 figures

title: Same Behavior, Different Mechanism: What Finite Experiments Can Certify About Integrated Information
abstract: Interpretability, AI auditing and assessments of machine consciousness increasingly rest on mechanism-level quantities: functionals of a system's causal transition law that describe how it computes, not what it outputs. Experiments see that law only through finite, partial and noisy interventions. We ask when such a quantity is identifiable from an experiment's access, continuous in the mechanism and certifiable from finite data, and answer exactly for a deliberately demanding case - the integrated information $\varphi$ of integrated information theory - in stochastic networks of four and five units with known ground truth. Behavior can be silent: a recurrent and a feed-forward network with identical input-output laws at their response delay carry 0.28 and 0 bits, yet internal recordings separate them within 4-53 trials. Partial access can be just as blind: in our examples, units left out of a one-step recording impose precision floors of 0.30-1.02 bits that no sample size lowers, and in all-but-self parity networks, recordings of any length see several hidden units only through the product of their fidelities - a symmetry that one intervention broke in exact checks. The measure has sharp edges: because $\varphi$ selects a partition, and the cause and effect it specifies, by one criterion and reports another, infinitesimal changes of mechanism that cross an edge change it by 25-100% at 99% of the edges we found in random networks, and about 1% of surrogate models that fit interventional data almost perfectly misreport it by more than 20%. One-sided claims survive: the same data certify a lower bound on both sides of an edge, and we prove $\varphi>1.004$ bits throughout a 64-dimensional region of mechanisms and certify it from about $10^7$ controlled transitions with false-certificate probability at most $α$. Measurability is thus a design question with computable answers.
comment: 30 pages, 7 figures. Code available as ancillary files

title: Self-Supervised Learning of Local Predictive Directions as a Neural Computation
abstract: Natural sensory dynamics are globally nonlinear but often exhibit simple local geometry, with nearby trajectories evolving preferentially along a small number of predictive directions. We ask how neural circuits could discover this geometry directly from temporal experience. We introduce Local Predictive Directions (LPD), a self-supervised framework that learns local directions whose projections maximally predict near-future trajectory evolution. LPD applies past-future canonical correlation analysis to temporal differences, making the learned representation invariant to translations of the underlying state while avoiding estimation of equilibria or a global dynamical model. To represent systems with multiple predictive regimes, we introduce a non-negative similarity-matching objective, with offline and online algorithms, that partitions trajectory segments into predictive domains, each associated with a distinct local predictive direction. The online algorithm admits a natural neural-network interpretation: the resulting activities provide soft domain assignments, while synaptic weights encode the corresponding local predictive filters. On stochastic nonlinear dynamical systems, LPD recovers the local predictive geometry and partitions trajectories into distinct dynamical regimes. On naturalistic sensory streams, the online algorithm produces center-surround spatial receptive fields and ON/OFF sustained and transient temporal filters resembling those of early visual neurons. Our results suggest that predictive learning can provide a self-supervised mechanism by which neural circuits discover the local geometry of environmental dynamics and represent it in receptive fields.
comment: Marco Zenari and Xuehao Ding contributed equally

title: Static Recovery Is Not Dynamic Stability: Dynamics-Aware Benchmarking of Protein Motif Scaffolding
abstract: Protein motif scaffolding benchmarks assess whether generative models can build scaffolds around functionally important residues. Their conclusions depend on which motifs are tested and which criteria define success. Existing benchmarks typically use small hand-curated motif sets and static refolding criteria, but protein function often depends on conformational ensembles and transitions. Here, we address both benchmark scope and success criteria. We introduce BILBY-PRO, a systematically derived benchmark of structurally conserved functional motifs from PROSITE-linked experimental structures, comprising 220 cases from 174 PROSITE motif-pattern entries. Evaluating six recent scaffold-generation models reveals distinct patterns in target coverage and unique-solution yield: RFDiffusion and Proteina solve more targets, whereas ESM3 produces more unique successful scaffolds on the targets it solves. We further introduce BILBY-MD, a reference-based all-atom molecular dynamics evaluation framework. Applied to statically solved designs from the original MotifBench benchmark, it compares motif drift, scaffold drift, motif-contact preservation, and motif-dihedral free-energy landscapes against reference simulations. Of 55 statically solved model-problem pairs, 31 satisfy our MD-supported criterion and only 8 pass all checks. Compact, self-contained motifs are often MD-supported, whereas interface-like or context-dependent motifs fail more frequently. Static refolding success therefore provides useful evidence of local motif recovery but does not establish dynamical fidelity of the full scaffold. BILBY highlights three complementary axes of motif-scaffolding evaluation: target coverage, unique-solution yield, and MD-supported dynamical fidelity.
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (Evaluations & Datasets Track). 23 pages, 10 figures, including supplementary material. The first three authors contributed equally. BILBY-PRO dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/HFMI-PROFOUND/BILBY-PRO ; BILBY-MD code: https://github.com/PROFOUND-HFMI/BILBY-MD

title: 40 Hz visual stimulation increases gamma-band functional connectivity between visual, parietal and frontal regions
abstract: Visual stimulation at 40 Hz is being investigated as a non-invasive intervention for Alzheimer's disease. Its neural responses have been reported in regions beyond the visual cortex, and concurrent cognitive tasks have been shown to increase their spatial extent. However, it is unclear whether these responses reflect increased functional connectivity between regions or a common response to the stimulus, and whether a concurrent task changes this connectivity. We recorded EEG from 29 healthy young adults during Regular 40 Hz flicker and Irregular 30-50 Hz flicker, each with and without a target-counting task (2 x 2 within-participant design). Source-space connectivity between visual, parietal, and frontal regions was estimated with the debiased squared weighted phase-lag index (dWPLI). Regular stimulation increased 38-42 Hz connectivity for all three region pairs, with the largest increase between visual and parietal regions (increase in all 29 participants). The increase was specific to the stimulation frequency and was observed with two source reconstruction methods and in sensor space. The visual-parietal increase remained significant after correction for source leakage (spatial mixing between reconstructed sources) and after removal of the estimated stimulus-locked component, whereas the increases in visual-frontal and parietal-frontal connectivity did not. The concurrent task did not modulate the visual-parietal effect. For visual-frontal and parietal-frontal connectivity, the stimulation-by-ask interaction was not significant. These results show that 40 Hz visual stimulation increases gamma-band connectivity beyond the visual cortex, and much of this increase reflects a common stimulus-locked response, and connectivity beyond this response was observed mainly between visual and parietal regions.

title: A Kernel-Spectral Index for Single-Neuron Input-Output Complexity
abstract: The computational capacity of individual neurons in the brain is a central problem in computational neuroscience and an increasingly relevant link between neuroscience and AI. Recent work fitting artificial neural networks to detailed cortical pyramidal neurons showed that reproducing their millisecond-precision input-output behavior can require temporal convolutional networks with five to eight layers, suggesting that cortical neurons may function as deep computational units inside brain circuits. Yet current quantitative studies of single-neuron complexity are largely surrogate-based; consequently, the obtained results are difficult to interpret, and the process often demands massive computational resources. We introduce the Spectral Complexity Index (SCI), a white-box measure that represents presynaptic histories with an explicit kernel geometry and quantifies how many ordered spectral modes are needed to explain somatic response energy. Across 35 biophysically detailed human and mouse cortical neuron models, SCI yields a statistically significant separation of the two species, strongly agrees with the DNN-based Functional Complexity Index on these cells (Spearman correlation: {rho}=0.797), and remains stable under sampling and kernel perturbations. Additionally, compared to existing methods such as FCI, the computational cost of SCI is reduced to approximately 1/10 or less. SCI turns single-neuron complexity from a black-box surrogate property into an interpretable spectral object, enabling reproducible, fast, and efficient comparisons of neuronal computation across cells and species.

title: ACTIVATION OF THE ARYL HYDROCARBON RECEPTOR REDUCES VISCERAL HYPERSENSITIVITY IN A MOUSE MODEL OF COLITIS IN REMISSION
abstract: The aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) is expressed on gut-projecting transient receptor potential vanilloid-1 (TRPV1)+ nociceptors, but whether it has a role in regulating abdominal pain remains to be determined. Approximately 50% of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) patients experience chronic abdominal pain, even when their inflammatory disease is in remission. Previous work has shown that tryptophan metabolism to indole derivatives is reduced in IBD patients. Since microbial tryptophan metabolites (indole derivatives) serve as ligands for AhR, we hypothesized that reduced AhR activation contributes to enhanced pain sensitivity. We used a post-colitis mouse model of visceral hypersensitivity to examine the role of AhR as a mediator of nociception. AhR activation using both natural and synthetic agonists reduced visceral hypersensitivity in both male and female post-colitis mice. Conversely, pharmacological inhibition of AhR blocked the antinociceptive effects of indoles. Mechanistically, AhR activation by indole-3-pyruvic acid (IPyA) increased the transcription of the inward rectifying potassium channel Kir2.2, in TRPV1+ neurons and markedly reduced neuronal activation within the dorsal horn of the spinal cord. Metagenomic analysis revealed sex differences in indole-producing bacteria, with control males exhibiting enriched abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila and Alistipes compared to post-colitis males and female controls. These findings demonstrate that oral IPyA supplementation in post-colitis mice attenuates visceral hypersensitivity in part through activation of nociceptor AhR, providing insights that support the therapeutic targeting of AhR to treat abdominal pain in IBD patients in remission.

title: Acute nicotine exposure produces a spatially organized transcriptional response in mouse olfactory cortex
abstract: Nicotine acts on nicotinic receptors throughout the forebrain. Most molecular studies of its effects, however, have focused on reward circuitry and have used bulk tissue, which cannot show which cells respond or how responding cells are arranged relative to one another. We previously found that a single nicotine exposure activates hippocampal astrocytes through the astrocyte-expressed kinase AKT2. Here we asked which cells respond to nicotine in the anterior olfactory cortex, a cholinergic-modulated region that encodes odor associations, and whether their astrocytic surroundings change. Male mice received a single intraperitoneal injection of nicotine or saline, and coronal sections spanning the anterior olfactory nucleus, piriform cortex and adjacent isocortex were sequencing 24 h later using Visium HD. Differential expression on nucleus-based segmentation was concentrated in olfactory excitatory neurons. Pathways centered on calcium-handling, synapse-assembly and extracellular-matrix programs, together with a lasting reduction of the immediate-early gene Egr1. Within the piriform region, the response localized to a continuous population of superficial pyramidal neurons expressing Cartpt and Penk. These neurons upregulated synapse-assembly, receptor-regulation and proteoglycan programs without changes to cell-type proportions. Nicotine also reduced expression of Sparcl1, which encodes astrocyte-secreted synaptogenic protein hevin, within one cell diameter of these neurons. Our study shows that a single nicotine exposure leaves a spatially organized transcriptional program on olfactory circuitry, centered on one neuronal population and the tissue at its border. These results identify candidate cells, genes and tissue locations for testing how nicotine alters sensory cue circuits.

title: Age-specific pediatric templates improve EEG source-reconstructed biomarkers in children
abstract: EEG source reconstruction requires an anatomical head model, ideally constructed from individual magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans. In developmental studies of children and adolescents, however, MRIs are rarely available. Researchers therefore routinely rely on adult templates, such as the FreeSurfer average (fsaverage), despite substantial anatomical changes throughout development. How much this reliance on adult models biases downstream EEG biomarkers remains unclear. Here, we investigated whether age-specific pediatric templates offer a better alternative to fsaverage for EEG-derived biomarkers in children and adolescents, using individual MRI-based reconstruction as the reference. We analyzed eyes-closed resting-state EEGs from 384 Healthy Brain Network participants aged 5.5 to 17.5 years. For each participant, we tested three anatomical models: their individual MRI, an age-specific pediatric template from a series spanning ages 6-17 at one-year intervals, and the adult fsaverage template. We compared four EEG biomarkers in childhood and adolescence: absolute power, relative power, long-range temporal correlations quantified with detrended fluctuation analysis (DFA), and functional excitation-inhibition (fE/I) ratio. Pediatric templates agreed more closely with individual MRI-based biomarkers in both developmental groups and had fewer parcels with significantly different biomarker values than the adult template, except for absolute power in older adolescents. We conclude that when individual MRI is not available, age-specific pediatric templates match individual MRI-based EEG biomarker values more closely than the adult template across all four biomarkers up to approximately 12 years of age and should be the preferred choice at least up to this age.

title: An open-access neuroimaging-compatible virtual town task for assessing human spatial navigation
abstract: Spatial navigation is a cognitive skill that draws on multiple processes such as learning, decision-making and memory, which are often updated on a second-by-second timescale. However, many existing virtual paradigms designed to assay spatial navigation cannot target these processes as they unfold or are not designed for integration with concurrent neurophysiological recording. Here, we present and demonstrate our open-access task for neuroimaging: NAturalistic Virtual Assessment of Navigation (NAVAN) combining high-resolution behavioural tracking and integration with electroencephalography. We report data from this task, in which fifty-three participants completed a wayfinding navigation paradigm across twenty-four trials. Navigational efficiency improved significantly following repeated exposure to the environment, although efficiency declined across trials within each block. Self-reported spatial ability (assessed by the Santa Barbara Sense of Direction) predicted performance during early environmental exposure, suggesting concurrent validity. We demonstrated the feasibility of recording electroencephalography during the task, with in-game events streamed and aligned to the neural recording. The task provides researchers with access to detailed behavioural measures and can be adapted by modifying features such as trial number and difficulty. We also provide a step-by-step implementation guide to support reuse and customisation across experimental settings.
author_corresponding_institution: Trinity College Institute of Neuroscience, Trinity College Dublin

title: Asymmetric detection of relative speed during motion-based figure-ground segregation
abstract: Visual motion can support figure-ground segregation when a local region moves at a different speed from its background, but whether faster- and slower-than-background targets are detected equally well, and how any asymmetry depends on background speed and motion reliability remains incompletely understood. We measured relative-speed detection thresholds in four human observers using an eight-alternative forced-choice localization task. On each trial, one of eight random-dot patches at 10-degree eccentricity moved either faster or slower than a surrounding moving background. Relative-speed detection thresholds were measured with adaptive staircases at five background speeds (2.5-30 deg/s) under 100% and 60% motion coherence. In every observer, slower targets required larger relative-speed differences for detection than faster targets. This increment-decrement asymmetry was strongest at low background speeds and diminished as speed increased. Reducing motion coherence elevated thresholds overall but disproportionately impaired detection of slower targets, amplifying the asymmetry, most strongly at the lowest measurable speeds. Under 100% coherence, increment detection showed approximately Weber-like scaling from 10 to 30 deg/s, whereas under reduced coherence both increment and decrement Weber fractions decreased with increasing background speed. Relative-speed detection therefore depends on the sign of the speed difference, background speed, and motion reliability. The faster-target advantage is consistent with faster-speed weighting reported in cortical area MT and with natural-scene statistics showing that figural regions tend to move faster than their backgrounds, suggesting that relative-speed sensitivity may contribute to motion-based figure-ground segregation. More broadly, such increment-decrement asymmetries can reveal biases in how sensory signals are represented and read out.

title: Characterising cortical perturbation-recovery dynamics using TMSEEG: The Brain Dynamic Metric Toolbox
abstract: Objective: To adapt dynamical measures used in computational and experimental perturbation models to human transcranial magnetic stimulation and electroencephalography (TMS-EEG) and determine whether analysis of the extended post-stimulation trajectory reveals additional features of the cortical response to long-interval intracortical inhibition (LICI). Methods: Single pulse and paired pulse LICI TMS-EEG responses from the bilateral dorsolateral prefrontal cortex were re-analysed in 16 healthy adults. At the stimulation site, 75 single-pulse and 75 paired-pulse trials were delivered; paired pulses comprised conditioning and test stimuli separated by 100 ms. Responses from 20 frontocentral EEG channels were analysed from 50-950 ms following TMS using the open source Brain Dynamic Metric Toolbox. Perturbative Integration Latency Index (PILI) indexed cortical resilience via response energy and recovery, Autocorrelation Function Width (ACFW) captured temporal memory, and Lyapunov Exponent (LE) indicated the dynamical stability. Linear mixed-effects models examined temporal, spectral, and time-frequency effects from the measured metrics. Results: LICI altered the temporal evolution of the dynamical measures. PILI distinguished conditions in the earliest post-stimulation window before converging, whereas ACFW differences persisted across a broader early interval. LE showed weaker and less consistent discrimination. Spectral effects were most evident for ACFW, while time-frequency analyses revealed later, frequency-specific LICI effects for PILI and ACFW but not LE. Conclusions: The extended post-stimulation trajectory revealed LICI-related differences in cortical resilience and temporal memory with distinct temporal and spectral profiles, while effects on dynamical stability were less consistent. Significance: The Brain Dynamic Metric Toolbox provides a reproducible framework for quantifying perturbation-recovery dynamics in TMS-EEG and demonstrates that the extended perturbational response contains information about LICI not captured by discrete early response measures.
author_corresponding_institution: Dept. Biomedical Engineering, The University of Melbourne

title: ClearGel: a thermoresponsive hydrogel for chronic, near-millimeter two-photon imaging through the intact skull
abstract: The intact skull remains a fundamental barrier to high-resolution two-photon neuroimaging in live mice. Existing skull-clearing methods, however, cannot simultaneously provide deep cortical access, spatial selectivity, reversibility, and biological safety. Here we introduce ClearGel, a thermoresponsive hydrogel that undergoes rapid in situ gelation upon contact with the skull, confining the clearing agents to the targeted region while sustaining their release over time. ClearGel routinely enables two-photon imaging down to approximately 800 m through the intact skull-a depth statistically equivalent to open-skull windows and substantially surpassing all prior approaches. It supports user-defined clearing patterns from focal sites to whole-skull coverage, allows repeated imaging over 14 days through a reversible optical interface, and, critically, enables awake functional imaging of both neuronal Ca2+ activity and the more elusive cAMP dynamics at single-cell resolution. ClearGel requires only simple topical application-no craniotomy or skull thinning-and provides a minimally invasive, chronic-compatible optical window for longitudinal studies of cortical function in behaving mice.
author_corresponding_institution: Shenzhen Institutes of Advanced Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences

title: Common attentional mechanisms, but distinct computational dynamics, across Statistical and Reward Learning
abstract: Past experience guides attention through statistical learning (SL) and reward learning (RL). Yet, whether they do so through similar neural and computational mechanisms remains unclear. In a first EEG visual-search experiment, we tested whether RL establishes latent spatial representations, previously demonstrated for SL. Afterwards, we directly compared RL and SL in a double-session experiment. Using multivariate decoding, Experiment 1 showed that high-reward locations could be decoded before target onset following a task-irrelevant, spatially-unspecific visual perturbation. Experiment 2 revealed that SL and RL established comparable neural representations, and similarly facilitated target selection and evidence accumulation (drift-rate). However, combining Rescorla-Wagner and Drift Diffusion Model revealed slower learning-rate for RL than SL. Pupillometry further tracked spatially selective expectation violations during SL, but reflected increased arousal during RL. Together, our results reveal how the brain routes distinct computational algorithms (probability estimation versus value caching) into a unified attentional priority map.

title: Decoding and Characterizing the Intracranial Representation of Semantic Information
abstract: Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have achieved impressive performance by decoding motor and articulatory signals associated with speech production. However, considerably less is known about whether higher-level semantic representations can be decoded from human cortical activity. Demonstrating semantic decoding would advance both our understanding of language organization and the development of BCIs that rely on conceptual rather than purely articulatory information. We recorded intracranial neural activity from patients undergoing stereotactic electroencephalography (sEEG) for clinical epilepsy monitoring while they performed language tasks requiring semantic processing. High-gamma power was extracted from local field potentials and used to generate trial-level features for supervised machine-learning classification. Classification performance was evaluated using cross-validation. Semantic category information was decoded significantly above chance, with mean classification accuracy reaching 29.8% across 15 semantic categories (chance = 6.7%). These findings demonstrate that high-gamma activity contains information about conceptual category membership that can be extracted on individual trials. These results provide evidence that semantic information is accessible from intracranial population recordings and support the feasibility of semantic decoding as a complementary direction for future language BCIs. Beyond neuroprosthetic applications, this work contributes to understanding how conceptual knowledge is represented in the distributed human language network.

title: Dementia Severity Is Associated with Resting-State fMRI Network Responses to Nuisance Regression
abstract: Apparent disease effects in resting-state fMRI may be confounded by the effects of preprocessing, making it essential to understand whether nuisance removal affects patients differently across levels of clinical severity. Yet few studies directly examine whether sensitivity to preprocessing is itself clinically informative. We investigated this in 201 ADNI participants spanning normal cognition, mild cognitive impairment, and dementia. We quantified the coordinated temporal structure of the seven Yeo resting-state networks using a delay-based concentration statistic, comparing estimates after regression of 24 motion parameters and linear trends with estimates obtained after additionally removing five anatomical CompCor components. Adding these components generally reduced the measured temporal concentration, but this reduction was smaller in participants with greater dementia severity (+0.472 percentage points per CDR-SB point). In contrast, the same network measures showed little association with severity before adding CompCor. To determine whether this finding depended on how temporal trends were removed, we repeated the analysis with identical discrete cosine regressors added to both preprocessing designs. The clinical association remained similar (+0.464). Controlled simulations showed that temporal concentration increased with the strength of delayed coupling between networks, even when their individual statistical properties and instantaneous covariance remained unchanged. However, changes in observation amplitude and contamination of nuisance regressors also altered the response to preprocessing without changing the underlying neural signal. These findings suggest that disease-related differences in fMRI may partly reflect differential sensitivity to preprocessing. Systematic sensitivity analyses, including multiverse comparisons across preprocessing strategies, may therefore be essential to distinguish genuine disease effects from preprocessing-dependent associations.
author_corresponding_institution: PowerMechaniX LLC, Albuquerque, New Mexico, USA

title: Dendrite Control Theory: A Unifying Framework Bridging Neuronal Morphology And Dendritic Voltage Behavior
abstract: Control theory and dendritic computation have revolutionized their respective fields, yet they rarely converge. Here, we use control theory as a framework to reveal how dendritic morphology and synaptic input organization constrain structural resilience and energy cost. Treating diverse dendritic trees as connected network nodes, we demonstrate that the degree of structural symmetry dictates easy- versus hard-to-access control states. Notably, control inputs restricted solely to peripheral terminal branches are mathematically sufficient to govern the voltage states of the entire dendrite and soma, granting striking resilience against input loss elsewhere. Conversely, limiting input dimensionality amplifies voltage fluctuations and metabolic costs. These findings expose fundamental biophysical trade-offs between wiring cost, functional flexibility, robustness, and energy efficiency, suggesting interneurons generally exhibit higher resilience while excitatory neurons feature superior controllability. We introduce 'Dendrite Control Theory' as a rigorous engineering framework linking neuronal morphology directly to computation and robustness, offering a new neuroscience research paradigm.
author_corresponding_institution: Institute for Computational Neuroanatomy and In Silico Medicine (Anatomy II), Dr. Senckenberg Anatomy, Neuroscience Center, Goethe University Frankfurt, Frankfu

title: Disrupted sleep-wake regulation in the MCI-Park mouse model of Parkinson's Disease
abstract: Disrupted sleep has a profound adverse impact on lives of Parkinson's Disease (PD) patients and their caregivers. Sleep disturbances are exceedingly common in PD, with substantial heterogeneity in type, timing, and severity. Among the most common sleep-related symptoms reported by PD patients are insomnia, excessive daytime sleepiness, and sleep fragmentation, characterized by interruptions and decreased continuity of sleep. Alterations in brain wave activity, as measured on the electroencephalogram (EEG), also occur in PD, with changes in the pattern and relative contributions of different frequency bands of the EEG spectrum to overall EEG activity in different vigilance states consistently observed. The mechanisms underlying these PD-associated sleep-wake abnormalities are poorly understood, and they are ineffectively treated by conventional PD therapies. To help fill this gap in knowledge, a new progressive model of PD - the MCI-Park mouse- was studied. Near the transition to the parkinsonian state, these mice exhibited significantly altered sleep-wake regulation, including increased wakefulness, decreased non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep, increased sleep fragmentation, reduced rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, and altered EEG activity patterns. These sleep-wake abnormalities mirror those identified in PD patients. Thus, this model may help elucidate the circuit mechanisms underlying sleep disruption in PD and identify targets for novel therapeutic approaches.

title: Dissociating Resting-State Networks of Pedohebephilic Preference and Child Sexual Offending Using Network-Based Prediction
abstract: Pedohebephilia (P+), the sexual preference for prepubescent and early pubertal minors, regularly causes distress in those affected. While associated with child sexual offending (CSO), P+ is not a prerequisite for CSO. Limited neuroimaging studies have identified alterations associated with P+, while these may primarily reflect offending history. The correlates of P+ independent of CSO therefore remain unclear. We examined this distinction using intrinsic functional networks within a multivariate predictive framework. Using resting-state functional connectivity (rsFC) and network-based prediction (NBS-Predict), we performed pairwise classifications among non-offending pedohebephilic men (P+CSO-, n=35), pedohebephilic men with CSO (P+CSO+, n=38), and non-pedohebephilic controls without CSO (P-CSO-, n=63). Classification-relevant subnetwork nodal strength was associated post hoc with trait impulsivity within P+ groups. P+CSO- were significantly distinguished from P-CSO- (balanced accuracy [BAC]=.621, pFDR=.041), and showed reductions between default-mode hubs and temporoparietal somatomotor and ventral attention regions. P+CSO+ were also significantly distinguished from P+CSO- (BAC=.645, pFDR=.032) and yielded a smaller subnetwork centered on the substantia nigra. Against P-CSO-, P+CSO+ showed widespread reductions, particularly across subcortical, default mode, visual, limbic, and somatomotor regions (BAC=.640, pFDR=.032). Right precentral gyrus nodal strength correlated with impulsivity in P+CSO+ only (r = .57, pFDR=.024). Whole-brain rsFC contains information, distinguishing pedohebephilic preference in the absence of known CSO, while P+CSO+ show additional, more widespread network alterations involving systems implicated in action selection and behavioral regulation. These findings open new avenues for integrating pedohebephilia into broader neurobiological research frameworks.
author_corresponding_institution: Charite-Universitaetsmedizin Berlin, corporate Member of Freie Universitaet Berlin and Humboldt-Universitaet zu Berlin, Department of Psychiatry and Neuroscienc

title: Distinct computations underlie movement error parsing during implicit motor adaptation and perturbation detection
abstract: The human sensorimotor system is remarkably effective at automatically parsing total movement error into its constituent parts, the error component due to a perturbation, or externally-generated error (EGE), versus the error component due to motor noise, or internally-generated error (IGE). This implicit error parsing, and its associated perceptual processes, directly contrasts previous work showing that humans will explicitly misattribute motor errors caused by relatively large external perturbations to their own motor variability. While the combined results suggest a dissociation between perception for action---which allows for precise and automatic error parsing---and perception for conscious detection, this must be inferred across studies using different methodologies. Here, we combined a within-subjects study design and computational modeling to shed light on the principles underlying implicit adaptation to a perturbation and explicit perturbation detection. Neuro-typical adults participated in two experiments consisting of pseudo-randomized rotations during reaches to a single target, with one session requiring explicit reports after each reach of whether a perturbation was detected. Participants demonstrated a clear dissociation between implicit responses to a perturbation and explicit detection, with robust adaptation to $1\degree$ EGEs, but an inability to reliably report the presence of an EGE until it reached $\sim4\degree$. Our modeling results explain this behavioral dissociation as a consequence of the sensorimotor system applying distinct computational strategies to these behaviors. For the adaptation task, the best-fitting model assumes the participant compares proprioceptive and visual cues to detect a perturbation and corrects for a proportion of this error. For signal-detection, the best-fitting model used Bayesian causal inference in which sensory cues are optimally integrated with a prior on their cause. Combined, our study sheds light on the dichotomy between perception for action versus perception for recognition in the context of visuomotor control and adaptation.

title: Dynamic Routing on a Static Structure: Neuromodulatory Gating of Cortical Wave Propagation
abstract: Stimulus-evoked cortical responses range from tightly localized activations to spatially extended traveling waves, yet the mechanisms through which these distinct regimes are flexibly recruited remain unclear. Based on neuroanatomical and neuroimaging evidence, we hypothesize that ascending neuromodulatory systems, which deliver modulatory (gain-changing) rather than driving inputs to cortex, dynamically shape spatiotemporal propagation under a fixed anatomical backbone. To test this hypothesis, we extend an empirically grounded corticothalamic neural field model to incorporate a diffusely projecting modulatory population, parameterized on the noradrenergic (NA) arousal system of the locus coeruleus (LC) as the best-characterized case. We then examine evoked responses under transient stimulus-locked versus sustained modulation - corresponding to phasic and tonic modulation - with geometry given by distance-dependent connectivity plus additional fast-conducting non-local projections (FNPs). Transient modulation produces spatiotemporally sustained traveling waves of cortical activity, whereas sustained modulation yields temporally prolonged but spatially localized responses; without modulation, waves are weak and dissipative. The model shows that the timing and spatial pattern of modulatory engagement gate wave-onset latency and impose anisotropy, restricting stimulus propagation to modulated territories and halting it across unmodulated gaps. In the presence of FNPs, which capture contributions of long-range white matter fiber tracts in the brain, modulation also enables the rapid non-local activation of distant cortical regions required for selective long-distance routing. Our results identify patterned gain control as a parsimonious mechanism for variability in evoked dynamics, and suggest that ascending modulatory systems such as the NA system could transiently privilege specific pathways over a largely static connectome.

title: E3 Ubiquitin Ligase Highwire/Phr1 Mediates Endocytic Control of JNK Signaling in Drosophila Neurons
abstract: Endocytosis is essential for synaptic membrane retrieval and the trafficking of growth-regulatory signaling components, yet the mechanistic links between endocytic dysfunction and synaptic overgrowth have remained elusive. Here, we uncover a previously unrecognized mechanism by which endocytosis constrains synaptic growth by regulating the neuronal E3 ubiquitin ligase Highwire (Hiw/Phr1), a key negative regulator of the c-Jun N-terminal Kinase (JNK) signaling pathway. We show that loss of endocytic proteins causes Hiw/Phr1 to accumulate in the neuronal cell bodies, leading to elevated MAP3K Wallenda (Wnd)/DLK levels and hyperactivation of JNK signaling. The accumulated Hiw/Phr1 assembles into dynamic punctate structures, as revealed by their rapid and reversible dissolution with 1,6-hexanediol (1,6-HD). Acute blockade of endocytosis using a conditional temperature-sensitive dynamin mutant Shibirets similarly triggered robust Hiw accumulation at restrictive temperatures. We further demonstrate that Rab11-positive recycling endosomes are essential for proper Hiw localization and turnover, directly linking endosomal trafficking to the control of JNK signaling. Finally, we show that both the Bone Morphogenetic Protein (BMP) pathway and JNK signaling are necessary and sufficient to guide synaptic morphogenesis at the Drosophila neuromuscular junction (NMJ), thereby integrating endocytic trafficking with synaptic growth signaling. Our findings establish endocytosis as a critical regulator of Hiw/Phr1-dependent JNK signaling, with implications that extend beyond synaptic morphogenesis to axon injury and degeneration pathways.

title: Early Increases in Hippocampal Synchrony Predict Chronic Epileptiform Burden in a Temporal Lobe Epilepsy Model
abstract: Temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE), the most common focal epilepsy, is often drug-resistant and arises predominantly in the hippocampus. Disease severity is conventionally assessed by seizure frequency and duration, yet epileptiform activity outside discrete seizures may also track disease progression. Whether this activity reflects hippocampal network reorganization as part of epileptogenesis, and whether such reorganization predicts chronic severity, is unknown. Here, we combined longitudinal two-photon calcium imaging of hippocampal CA1 neurons with repeated 24-hour EEG recordings that quantified epileptiform burden in the same pilocarpine treated mice over 16 weeks. CA1 firing and synchrony rose acutely, subsided during a latent period, and increased again chronically, with synchronized firing organized into brief waves that propagated in a consistent direction. Epileptiform burden followed a similar temporal trajectory and increasingly contained electrographic seizures. CA1 synchrony correlated with epileptiform burden and stratified mice into groups with distinct neuronal and electrographic outcomes. CA1 synchrony measured within three weeks of pilocarpine induction predicted chronic epileptiform burden, identifying early hippocampal synchrony as a candidate imaging biomarker and pointing to an early window for intervention in TLE.
author_corresponding_institution: Cleveland Clinic Research, Case Western Reserve University School of Medicine

title: Evaluating State-Transition Models in Short Resting-State fMRI with Continuous-Dynamics Controls
abstract: Hidden Markov models (HMMs) are widely used to describe changes in resting-state functional MRI as transitions between a finite set of inferred brain states. However, continuously varying brain activity can produce similar apparent transitions, raising questions about their biological validity. We tested whether discrete and continuous brain dynamics could be distinguished by predicting subsequent fMRI measurements, and if temporal filtering affects this distinction. We compared hidden Markov models (HMMs) with vector autoregressive (VAR) models, which predict signals from preceding measurements without assuming discrete states. Each time point contained signals from the seven Yeo functional networks. Both models used the same preceding observations to predict the next, with accuracy measured by the log probability density assigned to the observed signals. Across 864 simulated conditions, HMMs performed better in 139/144 unfiltered discrete-state cases, whereas VAR performed better in 67/72 continuous cases. Changing only the filter during testing increased the number of continuous cases favoring HMMs from 2/72 with fixed filtering to 68/72, despite unchanged underlying dynamics. We also analyzed resting-state fMRI from 270 ADNI participants (90 cognitively normal, 90 with mild cognitive impairment, and 90 with dementia). VAR outperformed HMM in 160/184 datasets with at least 180 time points and 60/86 shorter recordings. In simulations, HMMs inferred directional state transitions even from smoothly evolving activity without discrete switching. Thus, apparent fMRI state transitions do not necessarily indicate discrete underlying dynamics. Their interpretation requires comparison with continuous models and attention to temporal filtering.
author_corresponding_institution: PowerMechaniX LLC, Albuquerque, New Mexico, USA

title: Feedback Valence, Prediction Error, and the Limits of Computational Attribution in Symptom-Related EEG
abstract: Feedback-locked electroencephalography (EEG) responses are often interpreted using model-derived prediction errors (PEs), although signed PE can be strongly coupled to feedback valence in binary-outcome tasks. We revisited a published anxiety-related EEG association using two open probabilistic-learning datasets to examine measurement reliability, predictor separability, and participant-level recovery. In the primary dataset, greater trait anxiety was associated with a larger negative-minus-positive FCz theta response among 46 participants with elevated depressive symptoms after adjustment for depression severity. The association also differed between the sampled depression-symptom groups. The feedback contrast showed useful within-session reliability, but matched delta and P3-minus-N2 analyses did not establish theta specificity. Within participants, feedback valence and signed PE were highly correlated (r = -0.964). Exact-design simulations showed that population-level model discrimination could succeed despite poor recovery of individual neural slopes. Participant-specific learning-model refits recovered overall signed PE more consistently than the within-valence variation needed to distinguish it from feedback valence. An independent dataset reproduced the FCz feedback contrast in untreated and placebo cohorts but lacked trait-anxiety scores. Adding signed PE to valence yielded a small held-out predictive improvement under one reinforcement-learning specification, with limited support across sessions and no comparable support under the dual-rate model or in placebo. Together, these findings support a symptom-related feedback EEG association while constraining its theta-specific and participant-level computational interpretation.

title: Increased activity without changes in coupling between somata and apical dendrites during visual mismatches
abstract: Leading theories of cortical function posit that sensory processing involves a comparison between top-down predictions and bottom-up sensory data. Tests of these theories have been hampered by experimental challenges related to simultaneously recording top-down and bottom-up signals in response to sensory stimuli that either do or do not match internally-generated predictions. Here, we conduct dual-plane 2-photon calcium imaging near-simultaneously from distal apical dendrites and somata of pyramidal neurons in each of 4 different regions of mouse visual cortex while the mice are presented with visual sequences that can either match or mismatch previously habituated visual stimuli. Specifically, we examine the responses in the distal apical dendrites and cell bodies of pyramidal neurons while mice view either movie clips that reverse unexpectedly or Gabor patch sequences that have orientations that do not match habituated patterns. We find that in response to unexpected reversals in natural movies, both the apical dendrites and somata show increased activity that decreases over repeated exposures, consistent with a prediction error response. However, we do not find any clear evidence for increased activity in response to mismatches in Gabor sequences, beyond possible release from adaptation effects. We additionally use volumetric images to connect dendritic and somatic compartments and examine the coupling between connected dendrites and cell bodies in layer 5 pyramidal neurons. We do not find evidence for changes in coupling in response to mismatch stimuli, either for natural movies or Gabor sequences. Our results are consistent across four regions of visual cortex. We also observe that increased responses to reversals in natural movies are stronger in layer 2/3 than layer 5 pyramidal neurons. Altogether, these data suggest that visual cortex is sensitive to deviations from previously-experienced naturalistic inputs. Our data do not suggest that this mismatch sensitivity extends to artificial stimuli, nor do they support theories of prediction error causing changes in the coupling between apical dendrites and somata.
author_corresponding_institution: Mila, Montréal, Québec,  Canada; McGill University, Montréal, Québec,  Canada

title: Individualized AI-driven Neuromodulation Selectively Enhances and Reorganizes Human Tongue Sensorimotor Networks.
abstract: Precise modulation of brain networks for tongue motor and sensory control (TMSC) is critical for neruorehabilitation. Existing neuromodulation approaches use fixed targets, ignoring individual network architecture. We present an AI-driven, individualized fMRI neuromodulation (iNM) platform adaptively targeting subject-specific TMSC networks in real-time. Using a neurofunctional twin built from each participant's anatomy and function, iNM reinforces targeted activity and suppresses competing states. Unsupervised machine learning and hidden Markov modeling showed iNM increased TMSC-state occupancy from 82% to 97% and suppressed swallow-state interference by 83%. The inferior parietal lobule emerged as a sensorimotor integration hub, with increased magnitude (d' 90.4 right, 84 left) and spatial expansion (134.8% right, 81.8% left). Cortico-subcortical connectivity strengthened 53% to 74% across motor, sensory, and attention networks and persisted into non-iNM blocks. Thus, iNM may offer precision neurorehabilitation for CNS or PNS disorders, such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and treatment-induced cranial neuropathy in head-and-neck-cancer survivors, respectively.
author_corresponding_institution: Department of Psychiatry, Baylor College of Medicine, Houston, U.S.A.; Department of Neuroscience, Baylor College of Medicine, Houston, U.S.A.; Department of Ph

title: Infant Sensory Over-Responsivity: Relations to Early Life Adversity, Emerging Behavioral Problems, and Sensory Functional Connectivity
abstract: Background. Sensory over-responsivity (SOR) in mid- to late childhood is associated with early-life adversity (ELA) and psychopathology, yet the developmental origins and timing of these relationships remain unknown. This work leverages a longitudinal pediatric dataset enriched for ELA to characterize predictors and behavioral problems associated with infant/toddler SOR. Methods. Neonatal fMRI and longitudinal behavioral data were obtained from a sample (N=399) recruited during pregnancy and enriched for social disadvantage (SD). Negative binomial regression models were used to identify pre- and neonatal risk factors for and behavioral correlates of SOR at age two (Y2). Mediation analyses tested whether Y2 SOR mediates relationships between ELA and behavioral problems at age three (Y3). Relationships between neonatal functional connectivity (FC) measures and later SOR were also computed. Results. Two forms of prenatal ELA, SD and maternal psychosocial stress (PSS), positively predicted Y2 SOR, which in turn predicted Y2 and Y3 autism and anxiety problems, greater preschool internalizing symptoms, and greater preschool separation anxiety diagnoses. Positive relationships of prenatal PSS with Y3 autism, anxiety, and internalizing problems were partially mediated by Y2 SOR. Greater neonatal FC between the cortical somatomotor hand network and bilateral thalamus was also associated with SOR at one to two years later. Conclusions. The study results demonstrate the importance of infant/toddler SOR as an early predictor of autism and anxiety behaviors in early childhood and a mediating variable that links prenatal ELA with these behavioral outcomes. Results also implicate heightened neonatal signaling in sensory circuits as an early precursor of SOR.
author_corresponding_institution: Washington University in St. Louis School of Medicine, Department of Psychiatry

title: LCN2+ Astrocytes Mark a Pro-inflammatory Astrocyte State Associated with Secondary Brain Injury After Cerebral Venous Thrombosis
abstract: Cerebral venous thrombosis (CVT) is a cerebrovascular disorder with unique pathophysiological characteristics. Although the mortality rate during the acute phase has declined in recent years, the cellular mechanisms underlying secondary brain injury and long-term neurological dysfunction after CVT remain poorly understood [1,2]. In this study, we performed single-cell RNA sequencing of brain tissues from a murine CVT model to systematically characterize the cellular landscape following CVT and identified a reactive astrocyte state characterized by high expression of Lcn2. This astrocyte subset was markedly enriched after CVT. Notably, despite the absence of significant changes in the overall proportion of astrocytes, this population exhibited enhanced inflammatory/cytokine response signatures, ferroptosis-related stress responses, and vascular-immune microenvironment remodeling programs, suggesting that the major alteration of astrocytes after CVT is driven primarily by state transition rather than cellular expansion. Pseudotime trajectory analysis further demonstrated that Lcn2+ astrocytes were predominantly localized at the late stage of the trajectory and displayed sustained upregulation of multiple inflammation- and stress-associated genes, supporting their characterization as a late-stage reactive astrocyte state under CVT conditions. Cell-cell communication analysis revealed extensive predicted interactions between this subset and myeloid cells, vascular-associated cells, as well as neuronal/synaptic populations, indicating its potential involvement in dynamic remodeling of the lesion microenvironment. Cross-model integration analysis further revealed the presence of Lcn2-high astrocytes in the middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO) model; however, their expression breadth and intensity were generally weaker than those observed in CVT, suggesting that this cellular state may represent a common reactive framework following cerebrovascular obstruction, while being particularly pronounced in CVT. Furthermore, genetic deletion of LCN2 alleviated CVT-induced brain tissue injury in vivo, providing functional evidence supporting the detrimental role of the LCN2-associated pathological state. Collectively, our study identifies a distinct Lcn2-high reactive astrocyte state after CVT that is closely associated with inflammatory amplification, ferroptosis-related stress, and microenvironmental remodeling. These findings provide new cellular insights into the mechanisms underlying secondary brain injury after CVT and highlight potential targets for therapeutic intervention.
author_corresponding_institution: Shenzhen Hospital of Southern Medical University

title: MAST1 is neuron-specific regulator of mitochondrial trafficking and abundance in human brain tissue
abstract: In human neurons, energy-demanding axonal and dendritic development requires sufficient mitochondrial distribution at distal locations, and the responsible mechanisms remain largely unknown. Here, we characterize rare de novo mutations in microtubule-associated serine/threonine kinase 1 (MAST1) in patients with multiple neurodevelopmental abnormalities, including microcephaly and thin corpus callosum. Experiments using induced pluripotent stem cell-derived telencephalic brain organoids and cortical neurons from patients and unaffected parents, as well as engineered lines demonstrate association of the MAST1 mutations with organoid growth deficits and impaired neurites. Mechanistically, the MAST1 mutations alter its interaction with mitochondria as well as mitochondrial trafficking and abundance, increasing the proportion of hyperactive mitochondria and reactive oxygen species accumulation. Exogenous wild-type MAST1 expression rescues neurite outgrowth in mutant neurons, as does prolonged treatment with creatine or N-acetyl-L-cysteine. This study identifies MAST1 as an important regulator of mitochondrial properties in human neurons and links microcephaly-associated MAST1 mutations to neuronal mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired neurites, and neuronal loss.
author_corresponding_institution: Neurobiology, Biomedical Engineering, Psychiatry departments, University of Utah, Cellular and Translational Research Core, Utah Clinical and Translational Scie

title: Multidimensional profiling of heterogeneous lateral habenula subpopulations reveals distinct responses during motivated behavior
abstract: The lateral habenula (LHb) shapes reward and aversion learning via projections to midbrain monoaminergic centers. Recent studies have demonstrated significant genetic, anatomical, and electrophysiological diversity within the LHb. However, it remains unclear how genetic or intrinsic electrophysiological characteristics relate to in vivo neuronal activity patterns. Detailed descriptions of transgenic mouse lines labeling LHb are lacking, limiting genetic access to LHb neuronal subtypes. Here we describe spatial gene expression patterns, electrophysiological characteristics, and projection targets for specific subpopulations of neurons in the LHb targeted via existing transgenic mouse lines. Furthermore, we demonstrate that two genetically defined subpopulations differentially respond to value, prediction errors, and directional movement during flexible, reward-guided behavior. These findings indicate that specific, genetically targetable, neuronal subpopulations in LHb may control discrete aspects of motivated behavior through parallel circuits targeting serotonergic and dopaminergic midbrain centers.
author_corresponding_institution: Boston University Chobanian and Avedisian School of Medicine

title: Neural representations supporting reuse of abstract structural knowledge in humans
abstract: A human ability to adapt to the dynamics of novel environments relies on abstracting and generalizing from past experiences. Previous research focused on how humans generalize from isolated sequential processes, yet we know little about mechanisms that facilitate adaptation to more complex dynamics, including those that govern much everyday experience. Here, using a novel sequence learning task based on graph factorization, coupled with simultaneous magnetoencephalography (MEG) recordings, we ask whether reuse of experiential "building blocks" is reflected in neural representations that could support inference and generalization. Behavioral results were consistent with participants decomposing task experience into subprocesses, both abstracting their dynamical structure away from their sensory specifics and reusing these in a new task environment. Neurally, this was accompanied by a learning-induced, condition-specific, increase in neural similarity among stimuli conditional on their shared structural role in abstract subprocesses across distinct task phases. Consistent with this, a complementary dynamical role decoding analysis revealed enhanced neural decodability, across experiential contexts, for stimuli that adhered to identical structural transition types, specifically when prior experience included the relevant graph structure. Decoding strength for these role representations was positively related to behavioral success in reuse of subprocess knowledge, a relationship that will require future independent replication. The findings provide neural evidence consistent with the notion that abstract role representations may contribute to the reuse of experience within new contexts.

title: Parallel descending neurons differentially encode target and looming information in the hoverfly visual system
abstract: Detecting small, fast-moving objects is crucial for behaviors such as pursuit, territorial defence, and predator avoidance. At long range, however, potential mates, rivals, and predators produce remarkably similar visual signals, potentially making them difficult to distinguish. Nevertheless, many flying insects, including the hoverfly Eristalis tenax, can respond rapidly and appropriately to these ambiguous visual cues, implying specialised neural pathways that extract behaviorally relevant information. Descending neurons link visual processing to motor output, thus transforming visual signals into behavioral actions. In E. tenax, both target selective descending neurons (TSDNs) and looming-sensitive descending neurons respond to small targets, yet their respective contributions to target processing remain unclear. Using electrophysiological recordings, we compared receptive field organization and sensitivity to target size and motion direction across these neuronal populations. Although TSDNs and looming-sensitive descending neurons differed systematically in their target coding, a subset of looming-sensitive descending neurons closely resembled TSDNs, sharing small receptive fields and sharp target tuning despite retaining sensitivity to looming stimuli. These findings reveal previously unrecognized diversity among descending neurons tuned to small targets and suggest that parallel descending pathways encode distinct information from similar visual cues. Such an organization may enable common visual inputs to support both target pursuit and the detection of approaching threats.

title: Pathology in resected areas of FDG PET hypometabolism in pediatric epilepsy patients with focal cortical dysplasia type II
abstract: Introduction: [18F]fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG-PET) frequently reveals hypometabolism extending beyond MRI-visible focal cortical dysplasia (FCD). Whether surrounding hypometabolic areas harbour pathological cells remains unclear. We compared histopathology between the lesion epicentre and surrounding hypometabolic borders in children undergoing epilepsy surgery. Methods: Fourteen children with intractable, extra-temporal focal epilepsy (mean age 9.0{+/-}5.0 years; 9 female) were retrospectively reviewed. Resections encompassed the visually-apparent MRI signal abnormalities as well as areas of surrounding FDG-PET hypometabolism when safely feasible. Multiple pathological specimens were obtained from the epicentre and surrounding hypometabolic areas. Overall, 136 specimens were analyzed: 64 epicentre (median 4{+/-}3/patient) and 72 border (median 5{+/-}4/patient). Results: Pathology was identified in 75% of epicentre specimens (59% with frank FCD (fFCD) IIa/b, 16% with dysmorphic neurons only (DNO)). Border specimens showed pathology in 62% (31% fFCD IIa/b, 31% DNO). We fitted a Bayesian logistic mixed model with pathology as outcome variable, location as predictor, and subject as a random effect. Compared to negative pathology, the log-odds of fFCD in the epicentre was 1.00 (credible interval (CI) 0.32, 1.77) and -1.25 in the border (CI -2.17, -0.40). The log-odds of DNO vs negative pathology was non-significant in both locations. Exploratory analyses did not show significant associations between pathology and degree of regional hypometabolism or volume. All patients achieved Engel Ia status at one-year follow-up with no long-term neurological deficits. Conclusion: These findings suggest a spatial difference in distribution of histopathology, with fFCD concentrated in the epicentre and DNO present in both the epicentre and hypometabolic borders. Thus, FDG-PET may be used to better detect the histopathological borders of FCD type II, and the high seizure-freedom rate presented here supports the inclusion of these surrounding hypometabolic regions in the surgical resection (when safe to do so), improving the likelihood of removing potentially epileptogenic cells.
