title: Sex differences in cell type-specific transcriptional programs and GPCR signaling in the human subgenual anterior cingulate cortex
abstract: Psychiatric conditions show marked sex differences in disease onset, symptom presentation, and response to treatments. Understanding how sex differences manifest across molecularly distinct neuronal populations in individuals without psychiatric conditions may help explain sex-dependent variation in neural circuit function and treatment response. Here, we examined molecularly distinct cell types within the subgenual anterior cingulate cortex (sgACC) of non-psychiatric subjects. Using RNA sequencing data previously generated from laser-capture microdissected neurons, we investigated sex differences in gene expression and co-expression networks in excitatory pyramidal neurons (layers 2/3 and 5/6) and somatostatin (SST)-, parvalbumin (PVALB)-, and vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP)-expressing inhibitory interneurons (N=10 males, 9 females). We identified sex differences in transcriptomic profiles, biological pathways, and co-expression network connectivity. PVALB cells showed stronger overall female transcriptional enrichment, while SST cells exhibited male-enriched transcriptional signatures. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis identified PVALB and SST modules more connected in males and females, respectively, which included hub genes involved in immune, extracellular matrix, and bioenergetic processes. Since G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are viable therapeutic targets, we examined sex differences in GPCR transcripts. Across all GPCR-cell-type combinations, CHRM2 in PVALB cells showed the second strongest sex difference (enriched in females). To test the functional relevance of this difference, we used patch-clamp electrophysiology in mouse prefrontal cortex. M2 receptor activation increased maximal firing rates in PVALB cells from female but not male mice. Collectively, our findings demonstrate cell type-specific sex differences in the sgACC corresponding to functional differences in neuromodulator signaling, with potential implications for treatment response.

title: Sex-specific gene and isoform expression characterizes hippocampal aging in rhesus macaques
abstract: Aging produces widespread transcriptomic alterations that extend beyond changes in gene expression to include changes at the isoform level. Declining splicing fidelity, including increased intron retention and aberrant isoform expression, has been proposed to contribute to cellular dysfunction; however, the extent and biological significance of isoform-specific changes in the aging brain remain poorly understood. Age-related cognitive decline has also been associated with neuroinflammation and the development of a chronic inflammatory state, or ''inflammaging,'' within the brain. Here, we used short- and long-read RNA sequencing to characterize gene- and isoform-level changes associated with hippocampal aging across sex in 24 rhesus macaques. We identified 594 age-associated differential isoform expression events, comprising both shared and sex-specific changes. Inflammatory pathways, including TNF- -- NF-{kappa}B signaling, interferon responses, and complement pathways, were enriched across both sexes. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) further identified sex-specific modules associated with inflammatory, glial, mitochondrial, and hormone-responsive processes. Notably, several age-associated changes were detected at the isoform level despite limited or absent corresponding gene-level differences, highlighting transcript-level regulation as an additional dimension of brain aging that may be overlooked by gene-level analyses. To investigate the relationship between aging and Alzheimer's disease (AD), we independently performed WGCNA on the rhesus macaque cohort and a publicly available human hippocampal AD single-nucleus RNA-sequencing dataset (GSE268609). Cross-species module preservation and gene overlap analyses identified shared genes between age-associated and AD-associated networks, with pathway enrichment implicating glial function, inflammation, and mitochondrial biology. Together, these findings highlight sex-associated differences in hippocampal transcriptomic aging, underscore the importance of isoform-level regulation, and identify shared transcriptional signatures between normal aging and AD-associated pathways.

title: Simple, static, spiking nonlinearities can account for seemingly complex interactions between visual, motor and cognitive variables in the visual cortex.
abstract: Neural activity in the visual cortex is driven by the stimulus and modulated by multiple task-related variables, including spatial attention, eye movements, and perceptual decisions. These multiple influences are each typically described as nonlinear interactions such as gain or normalization, raising the question of how these diverse signals can be combined through cellular or circuit mechanisms. Here we address this problem by examining neuronal responses in macaque visual areas V2 and V3 during a visual discrimination task that dissociates spatial attention from motor planning and microsaccadic eye movements. Using a statistical modeling framework, we show that attentional, microsaccade-related, and choice-related influences on neural activity are best explained by a simple additive stimulus-independent input modulation, which manifests as a gain via a spiking nonlinearity. In addition to explaining how interactions between variables might be accomplished mechanistically, this framework also resolves a controversy about the relationship between microsaccades and spatial attention. We find that neither microsaccade direction nor microsaccade-related neural activity accounts for attentional modulation, although these variables are often correlated, leading to apparent interactions. Thus, visual cortex can integrate sensory, motor-related, and cognitive signals through a parsimonious mechanism that preserves stable stimulus representations while supporting flexible, context-dependent modulation.

title: Social vision expands into auditory cortices of people born deaf: evidence from naturalistic film and encoding models
abstract: Comparing deaf and hearing adults provides insight into the contribution of experience to function of auditory cortical networks. We used naturalistic fMRI and voxel-wise encoding to measure information processing in auditory networks of deaf (n=24) and hearing (n=22) adults who watched a 35-minute silent animated film. Unlike simpler stimuli, naturalistic films are rich in a broad range of perceptual, affective, and social features, including motion, dynamic social interactions, and Theory of Mind. Machine vision algorithms and human coding were used to densely annotate visual and social film features. In both groups we observed a right-lateralized processing hierarchy with encoding of low-level visual features in early visual areas, social visual features along the superior temporal sulcus (STS) and Theory of Mind in temporoparietal junction. In deaf participants, auditory cortices showed enhanced encoding of a broad range of visual information, from low level motion to Theory of Mind. In higher order auditory networks, social interactions emerging as the strongest predictor of neural activity in deaf people and showed the strongest enhancement in deafness. Auditory networks of deaf adults showed systematic anatomical organization within and across hemispheres. Within the right hemisphere, higher-order auditory regions neighboring the STS preferentially responded to social visual features whereas lower-level visual features were represented broadly across the auditory hierarchy. These results suggest that proximity and connectivity principles govern anatomical expansion of information encoding in sensory loss.
author_corresponding_institution: University of Warsaw, Johns Hopkins University

title: Task structure flexibly shifts working memory formats across cortical circuits
abstract: Short-term memory in delayed-response tasks is widely attributed to choice-predictive activity in frontal cortex, maintained by discrete attractor dynamics in thalamocortical circuits. Here we ask whether this mechanism extends to tasks where cues specify goals rather than actions. We trained rats on two auditory delayed-response tasks: an egocentric task, where cues mapped to movement directions, and an allocentric task, where cues specified world-centered locations. Using electrophysiology and optogenetics, we found that the egocentric task engaged early sensorimotor transformation and prospective motor planning in secondary motor cortex (M2). The allocentric task, however, relied on a delayed sensorimotor transformation: auditory cortex carried a retrospective sensory trace, whereas M2 neither encoded choice nor was required for its maintenance during the delay. Simplifying the allocentric task to a single start position rapidly reinstated early transformation and M2 dependence within the same animals. These results demonstrate that animals flexibly select the timing of sensorimotor transformation, and that this choice determines the format and cortical locus of working memory.
author_corresponding_institution: Sainsbury Wellcome Centre, University College London

title: Taste preferences are influenced by temperature and the TRPM8 thermoreceptor
abstract: Oral temperature influences perceptual and behavioral responses to taste stimuli. Whether somatosensory processes contribute to this influence is unknown. Here we studied how stimulus temperature impacted mouse taste preferences and how these preferences were affected by the absence of TRPM8 (transient receptor potential melastatin 8). TRPM8 is a thermoreceptor supporting cool and warm temperature coding by somatosensory, including lingual trigeminal, neurons. Female and male TRPM8 gene deficient (KO) and C57BL/6J (B6) control mice (n = 69) entered thermolickometry tests that measured licking to two solutions of one taste chemical with different concentration-temperature properties across randomly interleaved brief-access (10-sec long) fluid exposure trials. Tastants were 15{degrees}C and 30{degrees}C bitter quinine (0.03 and 0.3 mM) or an appetitive sugar (sucrose or glucose, 100 and 500 mM). Mice were water-restricted or -replete during quinine and sugar tests, respectively, which were conducted separately and examined all possible concentration-temperature pairings across multiple days. Linear mixed model (LMM) analysis revealed that concentration and temperature both individually and additively affected licks emitted to quinine, with higher concentration and higher temperature (30{degrees}C) associated with the greatest reduction in quinine licks in B6 and KO mice. In contrast, LMM analysis indicated that temperature influenced licks to sugar only in KO mice, which made significantly fewer licks to higher than lower temperature sugars. Notably, KO mice also showed significantly reduced avidity to lick concentrated sugars than B6 mice. These data uncover novel roles for oral temperature and the TRPM8 thermoreceptor, and possibly its broader physiological influences, in taste preference behavior.

title: Temporal Variability in Brain Connectivity for Estimating Two-Year Clinical Severity in Mild Cognitive Impairment
abstract: Resting-state functional MRI measures coordinated activity across brain networks and may reveal early changes relevant to cognitive decline. Conventional  static functional connectivity analyses often compute time-series correlations across an entire scan, missing informative fluctuations over shorter timescales. We investigated whether these fluctuations, in fMRI scans collected at baseline, improve estimation of clinical severity two years later in mild cognitive impairment (MCI). In 48 ADNI participants with MCI, we summarized temporal variability using the standard deviation of windowed correlations between 21 pairs of brain networks. Using repeated nested cross-validation, the mean absolute error in predicting follow-up Clinical Dementia Rating Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB) was 1.62 points with clinical covariates alone, 1.66 after adding static connectivity, and 1.51 after adding connectivity variability. With additional motion covariates, the corresponding errors were 1.70, 1.73, and 1.59. Connectivity variability outperformed both conventional models in all three cross-validation repetitions, while randomized signals preserving the complete cross-spectrum did not reproduce the improvement. Perhaps surprisingly though, most of the gain occurred in participants without subsequent clinical worsening, and results were sensitive to the choice of temporal windows. These preliminary findings suggest that compact measures of connectivity variability may capture clinically relevant information beyond conventional measures of  static functional connectivity, motivating larger studies to evaluate their value for predicting future cognitive impairment.

title: Temporal stability for individual differences in both habit learning and expression
abstract: Actions transition from goal-directed to stimulus-driven habits through repetition. Individual differences in the capacity to learn and control habits are central to current models of psychopathology, which assume that overreliance on habitual control drives maladaptive behaviors. However, whether these tendencies reflect stable, trait-like cognitive processes remains unclear. We examined the temporal stability of individual differences in habit learning and expression. Across two preregistered experiments (total N = 313), we assessed stimulus-response habits using the same stimuli after one day or different stimuli after four months. Evidence for stable individual differences in habit commissions was strong and comparable across experiments, with computational modelling further supporting trait-like tendencies for habit learning and expression. Trait-like tendencies were also reflected in action automatization while practicing stimulus-response associations, which was associated with future habitual behavior. Our findings have theoretical implications for our understanding of habit formation and its role in psychopathology.

title: The C. elegans Connectome Toolbox: an open, extensible framework for multimodal connectomic data integration and analysis
abstract: The nematode C. elegans is one of the best studied model organisms in biology. Since the initial description of the C. elegans neuronal connectome by White and colleagues, numerous studies have mapped and analyzed the connectome, and released structured datasets of the connectivity, often merging and adding to previous versions. These datasets now serve as foundational resources that underpin studies into the neuronal basis of C. elegans behavior. In spite of their high utility, heterogeneity in the different datasets and their annotation conventions obscures direct comparison where discrepancies between connectomes frequently stem from differences in coverage or nomenclature rather than genuine biological disagreement. Additionally, datasets describing new connectivity modalities - contact-based (the contactome), extrasynaptic (monoaminergic and neuropeptidergic), and functional connectivity - have also recently become available. Thus, there is a need for a unified framework providing standardized access to these diverse datasets while preserving their individual provenance. Here, we present the C. elegans Connectome Toolbox, a comprehensive framework for consolidating, curating and validating historical and newly published multimodal C. elegans connectivity data. Connectome Toolbox includes an accessible online resource (https://openworm.org/ConnectomeToolbox) for interactive data exploration and is accompanied by a Python library for programmatic access. We demonstrate the utility of the toolbox through a series of analyses that illustrate how connectome data can be explored, visualized, and compared across modalities, including integration of the anatomical connectome with a comprehensive neurotransmitter atlas, and comparison with computational models of C. elegans neural circuits.

title: Traveling waves in attention networks inherit the rhythms of sensory systems
abstract: Attention emerges from coordinated activity across distributed brain regions, each with their own intrinsic rhythm: alpha (7-12Hz) in visual cortex and theta (3-7Hz) in auditory cortex. When attention is sustained on a visual location, alpha power increases over the corresponding ipsilateral hemisphere, a robust neurophysiological marker of sustained visuospatial attention named alpha lateralization. Hemispheric asymmetry during sustained attention was recently also reported for anterior-to-posterior alpha traveling waves -smooth phase shifts across the cortex. This finding suggests that traveling waves support top-down inter-areal communication within the attention network. Here we asked whether traveling waves indeed reflect top-down attention signals or are merely a byproduct of sustained visuospatial attention. We manipulated attention through different sensory modalities (auditory cueing and visual stimulation), thus engaging different sensory cortices, while maintaining the task as visual discrimination. Using electroencephalography, we tested the hypothesis that if traveling waves reflect attention signals within the network, their frequency should follow the intrinsic rhythm of the engaged sensory system: theta for auditory cueing and alpha for visual stimulation. If instead they are a byproduct of attention allocated to visual information, their frequency should remain in alpha. Our results support the former: auditory cueing led to lateralized theta traveling waves, while visual stimulation produced lateralized alpha traveling waves. Crucially, traveling-wave lateralization in both frequencies correlated with trial-by-trial alpha power lateralization. Together, attention signals appear to propagate as waves at the intrinsic rhythm of the engaged sensory system and locally modulate alpha power lateralization in task-relevant visual regions.

title: Use of Integrative Proteomic Analysis to Uncover Shared Molecular Signatures Across Distinct Forms of Hydrocephalus
abstract: Hydrocephalus is a heterogeneous disease characterized by disruption of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) dynamics and can arise from diverse etiologies, including post-hemorrhagic hydrocephalus (PHH), hydrocephalus following subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), post-infectious hydrocephalus (PIH), and idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus (iNPH). Hydrocephalus has high disease burden in pediatric and older populations and a marked increase in prevalence with advancing age. Despite this high incidence, the underpinning molecular and signaling pathway alterations remain incompletely understood. Hence CSF proteomic profiling would enable a robust and high-resolution approach for exploring disease-specific biomarkers and to discover shared molecular mechanisms underlying hydrocephalus. In this study, we performed a cross-study proteomic analysis to evaluate biomarker proteins reported across PHH, SAH, PIH, and iNPH groups. Using published proteomic datasets, we comparatively analyzed CSF proteins to investigate the differentially expressed proteins (DEPs), their common molecular signatures, and enriched biological pathways across hydrocephalus groups. Across etiologies, recurrently altered proteins were predominantly associated with inflammatory signaling (cytokine, chemokine, interleukin-(IL-17), tumor necrosis factor (TNF)), toll-like receptor (TLR) signaling, blood-brain-barrier (BBB) disruption leading to coagulation cascades, and neuronal injury responses. Hemorrhage-associated forms of hydrocephalus (PHH and SAH) demonstrated enriched coagulation and hemoglobin-related pathways, whereas infection associated forms (PIH) showed enhanced immune and inflammatory responses. iNPH exhibited alterations in proteins linked to neurodegeneration, synaptic function, and impaired CSF clearance. Interestingly, our cross-study analyses identified recurrently dysregulated proteins across hydrocephalus subtypes. Collectively, our cross-study proteomic analyses define shared and etiology-specific proteomic signatures across hydrocephalus subtypes and identify potential CSF-based biomarkers for diagnostic stratification and future precision therapeutic approaches.

abstract: Circulating concentrations of low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) and triglyceride-rich lipoproteins are leading risk factors for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease 1 . Despite several approved lipid-lowering medications, most patients fail to achieve target lipid levels under the chronic care treatment model 2,3 . Here, we describe a potential single-course treatment in which an infusion of guide RNA and mRNA encoding a CRISPR adenine base editor—encapsulated within a GalNAc–lipid nanoparticle—leads to durable, liver-selective inactivation of angiopoietin-like 3 ( ANGPTL3 ), a known driver of increased LDL-C and triglyceride concentrations. Analyses in human liver cells in vitro confirmed that the base editor introduces a DNA base-pair change at the target ANGPTL3 locus with no detectable off-target editing at any of approximately 3000 candidate sites or treatment-related structural variants. Targeted ANGPTL3 inactivation in nonhuman primates was well-tolerated and led to a > 90% mean reduction in circulating ANGPTL3 protein, with durability confirmed out to 3 years following a single dose. In mouse and nonhuman primate models of hyperlipidemia, gene inactivation was associated with reductions of approximately 40 to 50% in LDL-C and 50 to 70% in triglycerides. These results provided the scientific foundation for initiation of an ongoing first-in-human clinical trial in patients with refractory hyperlipidemia syndromes.

abstract: Structural and functional insights into the mouse hypothalamus are hampered by its small size and deep location. Here, we leverage ultra-high-field magnetic resonance imaging (UHF-MRI) at 17.2 Tesla to achieve high spatial resolution in structural, functional and neurochemical imaging of the mouse hypothalamus. From high-resolution- ex vivo anatomical data we created the MRI HypoAtlas, which improves on existing resources and reveals hypothalamic nuclei previously unresolved by MRI. Diffusion MRI and tractography mapped intra- and extra-hypothalamic pathways, facilitating circuit-level exploration without a priori assumptions. Resting-state fMRI combined with independent component analysis identified novel hypothalamic networks, demonstrating the enhanced capacity of UHF-MRI to detect deep-brain activity. ¹H-magnetic resonance spectroscopy quantified neurochemical profiles, revealing sexually dimorphic heterogeneity within the hypothalamus. Our comprehensive multimodal approach uncovered sex differences in hypothalamic anatomy, microstructure and neurochemistry, supporting the added value of these methodological advances. This integrated study offers a valuable resource for dissecting hypothalamic circuits and functions and ultimately advancing our understanding of neuroendocrine regulation, behavior and disease mechanisms, with direct translational relevance.

abstract: Patient access to nutritious food is critical for managing cardiometabolic conditions, yet barriers persist in under-resourced populations. This pilot randomized controlled trial ( N = 210) evaluated the impact of medically tailored groceries (MTG) and food resource coaching (Coach) delivered via a co-located food pantry. Participants with Type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemias, and/or hypertension were recruited from a safety-net health center and received either usual pantry support, MTG, or MTG+Coach for four months. Exploratory outcomes reported herein include self-reported diet quality, food security, and perceived health; blood pressure (BP) from electronic health records ( N = 166). Additional exploratory self-reported outcomes recommended by the funder and detailed in the supplemental materials include nutrition security, wellbeing (EQ-5D-51), loneliness, adaptive capacity, and the Cooking and Food Provisioning Action Scale. Follow-up completion was 81%. All groups improved over time in food security, diet quality, and perceived health ( P < 0.001), but baseline-adjusted analyses did not identify clear differences between MTG arms and usual pantry support for any exploratory outcome. Although descriptively larger BP reductions were observed in the intervention groups, confidence intervals were wide and adjusted between-group comparisons were not statistically significant. Further studies with standardized clinical measurement are warranted. Trial registration: This trial and protocol were submitted to ClinicalTrials.gov (Identifier: NCT06242808) on February 3 rd , 2024, prior to recruitment.

abstract: The human brain organizes visual processing into spatially structured functional clusters. Recent topographic neural networks model category-selective clusters but are limited to static images and ventral cortex. In this work, we model the topographic organization of dynamic visual representations across high-level visual cortex. We introduce a general method that spatially arranges and transforms units from a neural network onto a simulated cortical sheet. Applied to a pretrained video foundation model, the method produces spatially structured response correlations while preserving task performance and brain alignment. It captures ventral and dorsal clusters, including face-, body-, and motion-selective patches, and reflects system-level selectivity distributions for animacy, object size, and static versus dynamic content. Functional selectivity varies smoothly across both model and human tissue, suggesting predominantly general-purpose cortical processing with continuous transitions into local functional clusters. Taken together, we provide a computational framework for understanding the spatial and functional organization of high-level visual cortex.

abstract: Persistent activation of cardiac fibroblasts drives excessive extracellular matrix deposition, promoting maladaptive myocardial fibrosis, adverse remodeling, and heart failure (HF) progression. Although Adipocyte enhancer binding protein 1 (AEBP1) and Aortic carboxypeptidase-like protein (ACLP, full-length protein coded by AEBP1 ) have been implicated in pathological fibrosis across multiple organs, including the heart, its functional role in cardiac fibrosis remains unknown. Here, we demonstrate that AEBP1 is a mediator of myocardial fibrosis and adverse cardiac remodeling. Fibroblast-specific knockout or myocardial knockdown of Aebp1 significantly improves cardiac function and prevents pathological remodeling in murine models of myocardial ischemia and pressure-overload induced injury. In human myocardial tissue culture studies, ACLP overexpression induces pathological remodeling in non-failing hearts, whereas AEBP1 knockdown induces structural reverse remodeling in failing myocardium. Mechanistically, ACLP regulates the expression of MRTFB, RUNX2, SM22 and COL1A1, thereby orchestrating fibroblast activation. Collectively, these findings identify AEBP1 as a mediator of myocardial fibrosis and highlights its inhibition as a potential anti-fibrotic therapy following acute injury.

abstract: The B cells of the human immune system have evolved somatic hypermutation (SHM) mechanisms that introduce mutations at the immunoglobulin genomic loci at a significantly higher frequency than the rest of the genome thereby allowing them to evolve antibody sequences without compromising fitness due to genome-wide mutations. Inspired by these observations, here we develop a continuous directed evolution platform in human B cell lines (CODE-HB) that repurposes the SHM mechanisms to a stable, non-immunoglobulin genomic locus of the human B cell lines to continuously evolve cytosolic and surface displayed proteins with a broad mutational spectrum comprising of substitutions, deletions and insertions. Using our human B cell surface display platform and CODE-HB, we evolve neutralizing antibodies targeting avian influenza and escape variants of influenza. Given the modularity and simplicity of CODE-HB, we anticipate that this platform can be used for rapidly evolving biotechnologically relevant biomolecules directly in human cells.

abstract: A wide body of work has applied the concept of critical slowing down to estimate the stability of different Earth system components. Most of them – such as global vegetation – are inherently non-stationary, for example due to strong seasonal forcing that complicates the estimation of their resilience to external perturbations. Here, we introduce a method to account for non-stationarity in estimating the resilience of diverse synthetic and real-world systems via a regression-based formulation of the Langevin equation. Our method does not require extensive data pre-processing, is robust to gaps in the data record, and does not require regular time sampling. We further show that our method can incorporate time-varying data uncertainties, derive uncertainty bounds for stability estimates, and can be natively extended to examine spatial systems. Our method is a drop-in replacement for widely-used autocorrelation-based resilience estimates, and can be applied across diverse Earth system components.

abstract: Generalist and human-restricted Salmonella enterica serovars cause diseases ranging from gastroenteritis to typhoid fever. Using live-imaging with controlled-polarity human intestinal epithelial cell (IEC) organoids, we identify epithelial cell sensing as a pre-invasion stage of infection. The generalist serovar Typhimurium migrates toward apical but away from basolateral IEC surfaces, whereas the human-restricted serovar Typhi exhibits the opposite behavior. This polarized tropism is coordinated by signaling between the Aer and Tcp chemoreceptors. Tcp senses citrate released from apical IEC surfaces, while Aer differentially integrates this signal. A single conserved, serovar-specific residue in Aer determines whether Tcp-dependent citrate sensing promotes attraction or repulsion. This pre-invasion stage directs Salmonella to IEC surfaces permissive for invasion and contributes to distinct invasion outcomes. Our findings define a serovar-specific strategy for IEC surface recognition and provide mechanistic insight into how S . Typhimurium and S . Typhi differentially initiate interactions with the human intestinal epithelium.

abstract: The role of the hippocampus in resolving memory interference has been greatly elucidated by considering the relationship between the similarity of visual stimuli (input) and corresponding similarity of hippocampal activity patterns (output). However, these input-output functions can take surprisingly different forms. Here, we reconcile seemingly conflicting findings by considering the possibility that the hippocampus prioritizes different dimensions of visual similarity across different stages of learning. First, we generated a set of natural scene images from two visual categories and rigorously characterized visual similarity using a wide array of methods: neural networks, artificial intelligence models, and human perceptual and memory decisions. We then identified two orthogonal dimensions of visual similarity that each predicted memory interference, but that did so at distinct stages of learning. Using high-resolution fMRI, we then tested for dimension-specific input-output functions within the hippocampus. Within CA3 and dentate gyrus (CA3/DG), we show that dimensions of visual similarity were inverted (repulsion) at stages of learning when they contributed to memory interference. In contrast, CA3/DG preserved similarity when dimensions did not contribute to interference. These findings reveal that hippocampal representations of visually-similar stimuli are highly dynamic and critically depend on the dimensions of similarity that currently contribute to memory interference.

abstract: Intra-arterial tenecteplase during endovascular treatment (EVT) may increase first-pass recanalization and dissolve microcirculatory thrombi, but its efficacy and safety are uncertain. We hypothesised that this strategy would improve functional outcomes versus EVT alone. This phase 3, randomised, adaptive-enrichment, open-label, blinded-endpoint multicentre study aims to evaluate whether intra‑arterial tenecteplase improves clinical outcomes for patients with acute ischemic stroke. Patients with large‑vessel occlusion eligible for EVT within 24 hours of symptom onset were randomly assigned (1:1) to the tenecteplase group receiving intra‑arterial tenecteplase during EVT or the control group receiving EVT alone. The primary endpoint was favorable functional outcome. Of 380 randomised patients (192 in the tenecteplase group and 188 in the control group), primary outcome data were available for 190 and 186 patients, respectively. Favorable 90-day functional outcomes (modified Rankin Scale 0–2) occurred in 40.0% of the tenecteplase group versus 46.8% of the control group (unadjusted odds ratio 0.76, [95% CI 0.50–1.14], P = 0.19). This work suggests intra-arterial tenecteplase during thrombectomy did not improve 90-day functional outcomes in this population. abstract: The clinical effect of adjunctive intra-arterial tenecteplase after successful recanalization in acute basilar artery occlusion (BAO) remains uncertain. In this prospective, randomized, adaptive-enrichment, open label, blinded-end point, multi-center trial, patients with BAO within 24 h of estimated symptom onset who achieved successful reperfusion after endovascular treatment (EVT) were randomized (1:1) to intra-arterial tenecteplase ( n = 75) or control (only received standard medical therapy, n = 69). The primary efficacy outcome was independent ambulation (modified Rankin Scale 0–3) at 90 days; the primary safety outcome was symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage (sICH). The trial was stopped early due to safety concerns and lack of efficacy per Data Safety and Monitoring Committee recommendation. Among 144 randomized patients, 143 (99.3%) completed follow-up. At 90 days, independent ambulation was achieved in 40.0% of the tenecteplase group versus 50.0% in the control group (OR 0.67; 95% CI 0.34–1.29; P = 0.23). sICH occurred in 6.2% versus 4.8% (OR 1.31; 95% CI 0.28–6.89; P = 0.73). All-cause mortality at 90 days was 41.3% versus 26.5% (OR 1.96; 95% CI 0.97–4.03; P = 0.063). In this prematurely terminated trial, adjunctive intra-arterial tenecteplase did not improve functional outcomes in patients with BAO.

abstract: Dairy production is constrained by low nitrogen utilization efficiency (NUE; milk N/intake N), leading to nitrogen losses and environmental pollution. Although the rumen microbiome is central to nitrogen turnover, the role of small peptides, a critical nitrogen pool, remains poorly understood. Here, we constructed a genome-resolved atlas of predicted small-peptide metabolism and integrated high-performance chemical isotope-labeling metabolomics with metagenomics in 30 dairy cows. Among 349 detected small peptides, proline-containing dipeptides were associated with higher NUE, together with an S15 peptidyl-peptidase with Xaa–Pro dipeptide-generating activity. In vitro rumen fermentation, metatranscriptomics and targeted quantification showed that proline-dipeptide accumulation coincided with transcriptional patterns consistent with nitrogen assimilation and amino acid biosynthesis. Bacterial incubation and heterologous expression confirmed that S15.001 hydrolyzed Xaa–Pro substrates. These findings identify a microbial proline-dipeptide axis associated with NUE and provide a basis for precision nutrition strategies targeting ruminal peptide metabolism.

abstract: The epithelial barrier serves as a critical defense against bacterial invasion that is traditionally thought to be disrupted by transcriptional or proteolytic turnover of adherens junctions. Here, we reveal a striking, non-canonical mechanism of barrier failure in which the transcription factor FOXO1 mediates rapid bacteria-induced loss of barrier function independent of gene transcription or proteolysis. Using a 3D microfluidic device and an in vivo murine model, we demonstrate that bacteria or lipopolysaccharide trigger dramatic relocalization of FOXO1 to the nucleus with subsequent redistribution of E-cadherin from the membrane to the cytoplasm, resulting in an increase in epithelial leakiness. Furthermore, we found that stimulation increased FOXO1 binding to β-catenin and enhanced β-catenin Tyr654 phosphorylation, which were accompanied by disruption of the β-catenin–E-cadherin complex and destabilization of epithelial barrier integrity. Nuclear-restricted FOXO1 expression alone is sufficient to replicate bacterial effects and induce barrier failure, while cytoplasmic retention or epithelial-specific Foxo1 deletion rescues barrier function and preserves membrane-localized E-cadherin and β-catenin despite bacterial challenge. These findings define a FOXO1–β-catenin–E-cadherin spatiotemporal axis as a previously unrecognized rapid-response mechanism controlling epithelial barrier integrity.

abstract: Neutrophil extracellular trap formation is a central innate immune defence mechanism that depends on NADPH oxidase–driven reactive oxygen species production. How NADP⁺ availability is regulated during neutrophil activation remains unclear. Using integrated lipidomic, biochemical and functional analyses in human neutrophils, we identify NAD kinase, the sole enzyme responsible for NADP⁺ synthesis, as a direct lipid-regulated effector downstream of phospholipase D1. Neutrophil activation induces rapid, phospholipase D1-dependent production of phosphatidic acid and phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate, which bind and activate NAD kinase. The resulting cytosolic NADP⁺ is reduced to NADPH by the oxidative pentose phosphate pathway and consumed by NADPH oxidase during neutrophil extracellular trap formation. Pharmacological or genetic disruption of phospholipase D1 suppresses NAD kinase activity, depletes NADP⁺ and impairs neutrophil extracellular trap formation independently of direct NADPH oxidase inhibition. These findings define a lipid–metabolic axis coupling phospholipase D1-driven membrane remodelling to NADP⁺ availability and innate immune function.

abstract: Similarity of body-plan features across distant phyla provides striking testimony to the Darwinian concept of common descent throughout Metazoa. In both the cnidarian Nematostella and chordates, gastrula organizers direct the initial establishment of embryonic axes. Whether these domains share a common evolutionary origin is a fundamental question for understanding the origin of the chordate body plan. To address this question, we combine trans-species transgenesis, perturbations of signaling pathways, cross-phylum single-cell transcriptomic comparisons, and transplantation assays. We show that cis-regulatory elements that recapitulate NvBmp2/4 and NvChordin expression in Nematostella —and therefore report the endogenous cnidarian organizer regulatory environment—also drive organizer-restricted activity in chordate embryos, consistent with chordate organizer gene-regulatory logic. Moreover, we show that, as in chordates, Smad2/3-mediated signaling is active in the Nematostella organizer and is required for organizer-specific expression of NvBmp2/4 and NvChordin . Together, our data support remarkable homology between cnidarian and chordate gastrula organizers and are consistent with the idea that the cnidarian–bilaterian ancestor possessed a blastopore organizer with the potential to generate dorsal–anterior chordate fates. On this basis, we propose a scenario in which asymmetric positioning of the ancestral blastopore organizer and skewed body-axis elongation contributed to the emergence of the chordate body plan.

abstract: Associative memory, traditionally modeled by Hopfield networks, enables the retrieval of previously stored patterns from partial or noisy cues. Yet, the local computational principles which are required to enable this function remain incompletely understood. To formally characterize the local information processing in such systems, we employ a recent extension of information theory—Partial Information Decomposition. It decomposes the contribution of different inputs to an output into unique information from each input, redundant information across inputs, and synergistic information that emerges from combining different inputs. Applying this framework to individual neurons in classical Hopfield networks we find that below the memory capacity, the information in a neuron’s activity is characterized by high redundancy between the external pattern input and the internal recurrent input, while synergy and unique information are close to zero until the memory capacity is surpassed and performance drops steeply. Inspired by this observation, we use redundancy maximization at each neuron as an information-theoretic learning goal. This increases the network’s memory capacity to 1.59, a more than tenfold improvement over the 0.14 capacity of classical Hopfield networks, and also outperforming recent state-of-the-art implementations of Hopfield networks. Overall, this work establishes redundancy maximization as a design principle for associative memories and opens pathways for new associative memory models based on information-theoretic goals.

abstract: In patients with acute ischemic stroke caused by medium vessel occlusion (MeVO), intra-arterial tenecteplase may offer a targeted strategy to improve recanalization; we hypothesized that intra-arterial tenecteplase would increase successful reperfusion compared with standard care with a comparable safety profile. This phase 2, prospective, randomised, open-label, blinded-endpoint, multicentre study aims to assess the efficacy and safety of intra-arterial tenecteplase for patients with acute ischemic stroke caused by MeVO. Patients with MeVO were randomly (1:1) assigned to receive intra-arterial tenecteplase or standard care. The primary outcome was successful reperfusion of medium vessel occlusion. A total of 80 patients were randomized to either the tenecteplase group ( n = 41) or control group ( n = 39). Successful reperfusion reached 61.0% (25/41) in the tenecteplase group versus 28.2% (11/39) in the control group (unadjusted odds ratio 3.98, 95% CI 1.56-10.16; P = 0.004). Symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage within 24 h was similar between the tenecteplase and control groups. This work suggests that intra-arterial tenecteplase significantly increased the probability of successful reperfusion compared with standard care, with a comparable safety profile in this stroke population. abstract: Accurate visualization of glioblastoma is essential for guiding biopsy, resection and radiotherapy. Contrast-enhanced MRI is routine in clinical practice, yet it can miss metabolically active tumor outside areas of blood-brain barrier disruption. In a histopathology-validated cohort with 472 tissue samples of 61 patients with IDH-wildtype glioblastoma, we show that O-(2-[¹⁸F]fluoroethyl)-L-tyrosine PET ([ 18 F]FET PET) depicts tumor tissue significantly better than contrast-enhanced MRI (CE-MRI), especially in regions that show no enhancement on MRI. [ 18 F]FET PET achieves substantially higher sensitivity for tumor detection (91.2% vs 52.6%) and maintains high reliability in non-enhancing tissue (positive predictive value 98.3%), findings that are consistent across newly diagnosed and recurrent disease and in both cohorts undergoing either resection or biopsy. These results indicate that [ 18 F]FET PET complements MRI by revealing MRI-occult tumor burden. Incorporating amino acid PET into routine planning may therefore improve the accuracy of tumor visualization and, ultimately, patient management.

A Framework for SPICE MRSI Reconstruction Posterior Uncertainty Quantification
abstract: Purpose: Low-rank reconstruction methods such as SPICE substantially improve Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopic Imaging (MRSI) reconstruction quality. However, SPICE does not provide an estimate of reconstruction uncertainty. A framework for posterior uncertainty estimation in SPICE reconstruction is proposed, hereafter referred to as the framework. Theory and Methods: A Laplace approximation is used to estimate the covariance of the reconstructed spatial coefficients. This covariance is propagated through the spectral basis and spectral fitting to obtain metabolite concentration uncertainty. Matrix-free Hessian--vector products and voxel-wise conjugate-gradient estimation are used to avoid explicit construction or inversion of the full Hessian, making the method tractable. Results: Validation using repeated in vivo 7 T MRSI acquisitions showed that the estimated posterior uncertainty exhibited spatial and spectral patterns similar to those of empirical repeated-scan uncertainty. Experiments further demonstrated how spatial regularization and k-space undersampling affect the estimated uncertainty. Conclusion: The framework provides a practical framework for uncertainty quantification when using SPICE reconstruction of MRSI. It could be adapted to other regularised low-rank reconstruction methods.

title: A Mathematical Model of Reliability-Dependent Sensory Reweighting in Quiet Standing
abstract: Human quiet standing relies on vestibular, proprioceptive, and visual information whose contributions change with sensory context. Posturography characterizes this reweighting through responses to visual and support-surface perturbations, but a compact account of how sensory reliability propagates from state estimation to postural action remains incomplete. We develop a minimal quiet-standing model in which sensory reliability is encoded by channel-specific precision parameters that weight sensory prediction errors. A one-link inverted pendulum with intrinsic ankle stiffness estimates posture by minimizing an active-inference free-energy objective and selects ankle torque by minimizing the same objective under a restorative sensory goal. A fixed-point analysis predicts in closed form the perturbation-induced belief bias, each channel's state-update contribution, the steady posture, and a linear stability condition from the precisions, goal dynamics, and intrinsic stiffness. Closed-loop simulations in 115 trials matched the predicted equilibria to within 0.001degrees wherever the loop settled, and the two conditions predicted unstable diverged or drifted. Reducing an unreliable channel's precision eightfold reduced perturbation-driven posture shifts by 82%, with a matching decrease in that channel's state-update contribution; intrinsic stiffness left this reduction essentially unchanged for visual and sensory-only perturbations but bounded it for physical support tilts; a global precision reduction did not reduce the shift; and a within-trial precision switch showed belief updating, not a separate action gain, carrying the change to ankle torque. The results give a compact mathematical account of postural sensory reweighting as relative, context-selective precision control in a closed multisensory loop.

title: A biological light sheet links cellular voltage to mesoscopic brain dynamics
abstract: Membrane voltage is the fundamental currency of neural computation, yet cellular-resolution voltage imaging of large neuronal populations in vivo remains limited by trade-offs among imaging speed, field of view, and optical sectioning. We overcome this challenge by encoding a biological light sheet in the brain: Selective Plane Expression (SPress) restricts fluorescent indicator expression to a user-defined, 20-m-thick plane, suppressing background at its source. Following one-time two-photon photoactivation, SPress enables standard widefield microscopes to capture high-contrast kilohertz voltage dynamics from hundreds of densely labeled neurons across millimeter-scale cortical sheets and columns in vivo. These recordings reveal mesoscopic subthreshold waves that flexibly reorganize population-wide spike timing, together with cellularscale wavefront microstructure that preserves stereotyped local recruitment biases. By shifting optical sectioning from instrumentation to gene expression, SPress makes kilohertz cellular resolution voltage imaging accessible across mesoscopic scales.

title: A biomimetic deep encoder for auditory restoration by cortical stimulation
abstract: Cochlear and auditory brainstem implants are the primary treatments for profound deafness. However, the inherently low resolution of electrical stimulation used by these devices limits information transfer to a small number of independent stimulation channels and results in perceptual difficulties. An alternative approach is to target the auditory cortex, a brain region large enough to accommodate hundreds of stimulation channels and whose stimulation evokes sound percepts. Although modern brain interfaces offer large channel counts and spatial resolution, developing encoding algorithms capable of accurately transmitting interpretable sound information remains challenging. Here we introduce Braincodec, a deep network that optimizes both sound information transmission and the alignment of stimulation patterns with the spatial, temporal, and high-level properties of the auditory cortex neural code. Braincodec operates online and requires only a few hundred channels to transmit sufficient information for the reconstruction of natural sounds with high fidelity, a performance inaccessible to cochlear implant encoders. Moreover, mice equipped with a Braincodec-driven auditory cortical prosthesis matched the accuracy of non-implanted mice in discriminating real sounds. Braincodec therefore enables the development of high-throughput cortical neuroprosthetics with the potential to overcome the limitations of current auditory implants and provides a generic framework applicable to other sensory modalities.

title: Active eye modeling: a tool for estimating retinal image quality across the visual field in everyday life
abstract: Purpose: The "visual diet," the totality of visual experience, shapes retinal image formation and thereby refractive development, but measuring retinal image statistics during everyday behavior is challenging. Limits in mobile eye tracking, egocentric video, and full-field optical measurement leave gaps in our understanding of how environmental and behavioral factors shape image quality across the retina. Methods: We introduce active eye modeling, a computational platform combining optically validated, wide-field, accommodating eye models (Hastings et al. 2024) with realistic three-dimensional virtual environments and gaze behavior derived from human data. This approach enables systematic estimation of retinal blur across the visual field under parametrically controlled conditions, including varying viewing distances, ambient light levels, and environmental depth structure. Inputs may be simulated and/or drawn from real-world measurements: scene depth, video, and gaze/pupil recordings. Results: During simulated far work, peripheral image quality is depth-tolerant, owing to wide depth-of-field from off-axis aberrations. Near work under dim indoor lighting substantially increases peripheral blur, reducing contrast at mid and high spatial frequencies. This contrast reduction is comparable in magnitude to a moderate diffusing filter (Bangerter 0.4 strength) that affects eye growth when imposed experimentally in animal models. A consistency check with eye-tracked virtual driving confirms peripheral depth-tolerance during far work. Conclusions: Active eye modeling provides a flexible framework for investigating how visual experience shapes the retinal image, relevant to refractive development, display and lens design, and peripheral vision. Applied to common visual behaviors, the platform identifies optical conditions during indoor near work that warrant empirical investigation, complementing measurement-based approaches.

title: Altered neurodevelopment, CSF volume, and emotional reactivity following postnatal Zika virus infection in infant macaques
abstract: Although congenital Zika virus (ZIKV) syndrome is well-characterized, the neurodevelopmental consequences of postnatal infection are understudied. We used a rhesus macaque (RM) model to investigate the consequences of postnatal ZIKV infection on brain and behavior. Male and female infant RMs infected with ZIKV at 1 month of age were compared to sex-, age-, and rearing-matched controls: uninfected and treated with Poly-IC as an innate immune control. ZIKV-infected infants showed poor state control in early infancy and increased hostility during an acute stressor. They displayed sex-specific behavioral alterations during caregiver separation though attachment bonds were preserved. MRI at 3 months revealed larger total cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) volume, reduced visual processing region volumes, and sex-specific brain structural alterations: males exhibited amygdala hypertrophy, whereas females had volumetric reductions in temporal-limbic and temporal-auditory cortices. These findings indicate that postnatal ZIKV infection is associated with alterations in sensory, social and emotion-regulatory systems and in CSF volume, that may warrant long-term monitoring of exposed children.

title: An expansive internal chemosensory system in the insect abdomen implicates Gustatory Receptors in diverse aspects of interoception
abstract: Taste and olfactory receptors are gatekeepers that convey chemical information about the external environment. Their role in chemosensory systems has been extensively studied in several model system, which established their role in triggering discrete behavioral as well as physiological responses related to feeding and social interactions. Over time, cases of chemoreceptors expressed internally in organs not linked to the external chemosensory systems of taste and olfaction have been reported. Here, we present the existence of a complex internal chemosensory system in the abdomen of Drosophila melanogaster. We show that the adult fruit fly harbors a complex internal chemosensory system, composed of about 80 to 100 abdominal chemosensory neurons (ACSNs) expressing approximately 20 different Gustatory receptor (Gr) genes, including all sugar receptor and several members of the less conserved bitter receptor genes. The cells expressing specific Gr genes are stereotypically arranged along the entire circumference of the abdominal body wall, in proximity of muscle and fat layers. The ACSN fall into at least nine different subtypes based on co-expression analysis, projection trajectories into the Abdominal Ganglion (AG) and location of cell somata. Identification of different subpopulation of ASCNs expressing discrete combinations of Gr genes indicates that these receptor complexes have new, previously not considered roles in interoception, including monitoring of different nutrients, detection of cell metabolites and their byproducts and chemicals associated with pathogens.

title: Apparent sequential effects due to trial-to-trial fluctuations in decision criterion
abstract: Decision making is shaped by sequential effects, whereby preceding stimuli and responses influence current decisions. Computational models typically explain these effects by assuming that decision parameters are causally updated as a function of experimental history. Here, we challenge this assumption by showing that several hallmark sequential effects can instead emerge from slow fluctuations in the decision criterion. Using simulations based on Signal Detection Theory (SDT), we demonstrate that trial-to-trial criterion fluctuations, independent of experimental history, generate three commonly observed sequential effects: the repulsive effect of the previous stimulus (i.e., a tendency to alternate), the influence of previous response (i.e., choice history bias), and the modulation of choice history bias by previous confidence. To disentangle causal effects from effects driven by criterion fluctuations, we used the Hierarchical Model for Fluctuations in Criterion (hMFC), which simultaneously estimates both processes. Applying hMFC to 14 empirical datasets revealed that the repulsive effect of the previous stimulus was fully explained by criterion fluctuations. Accounting for criterion fluctuations also substantially altered choice history bias estimates: attractive biases disappeared in all four affected datasets, while three datasets revealed a previously masked tendency to alternate and two showed stronger alternation. In contrast, the modulation of choice history bias by previous confidence was largely unaffected by concurrent estimation of criterion fluctuations. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that criterion fluctuations account for a substantial portion of sequential effects and highlight the importance of explicitly modeling them to avoid confounded interpretations of behavioral and neuroimaging data.

title: Auditory Evoked Potentials Differ from Controls and Correlate with Aspects of Cognition in Kabuki Syndrome and Rubinstein-Taybi Syndrome
abstract: Objective Kabuki syndrome (KS) and Rubinstein-Taybi syndrome (RSTS) are two disorders caused by dysfunctional components of the epigenetic machinery and both result in intellectual disability. Mouse models of both KS and RSTS have seen reversal of cognitive impairment with epigenetic treatments. However, a great need exists for biomarkers in these disorders to improve the likelihood of successful clinical trials. This study aimed to investigate cortical auditory evoked potentials (AEPs) in KS and RSTS so that it could potentially be developed into a response biomarker in the future. Methods The amplitude of the N1-P2-N2 complex was measured for passive listening to monotonal auditory stimuli in individuals with KS, with RSTS, and typically developing controls. A standardized cognitive assessment battery was performed and specific subtests were correlated with AEP values. Results Groups differed significantly in P2, N2, and P2-N2 amplitude although RSTS was consistently more different from typically developing controls than was KS. The mid- to late-phase AEP components (P2 and N2) also correlate with cognition within and across these groups particularly with language whereas earlier components N1 and P2 correlate more with measures of executive functioning. Conclusion Late-phase components of AEPs differ in KS and RSTS from each other and from controls. KS and RSTS differ from controls in P2 and N2 amplitude in the same direction and both show a positive correlation between language and P2 amplitude and a negative correlation between language and N2 amplitude. Together they also show an association with N1 and P2 amplitude and executive functioning. Significance AEPs may turn out to be a valuable response biomarker in KS and RSTS individually and together.

title: Beyond Terrestrial Carnivores: Olfactory Bulb Anatomy in a Semi-Aquatic Mammal
abstract: The organization of the olfactory systems remains poorly understood in mustelids, particularly in lutrines adapted to semiaquatic environments. This study provides the first detailed anatomical, histological, lectin-histochemical, and immunohistochemical characterization of the main (MOB) and accessory (AOB) olfactory bulbs of the Asian small-clawed otter (Aonyx cinereus). Serial transverse and sagittal sections were examined using Nissl and Tolivia staining, a panel of lectins, and neuronal and olfactory immunohistochemical markers. Macroscopically, the olfactory bulbs were prominent and elongated, although no distinct AOB could be identified. Histologically, the MOB displayed a well-developed laminar organization, abundant mitral and tufted cells, and a clearly defined lateral olfactory tract. By contrast, the AOB was small, located dorsocaudally within the olfactory peduncle, and lacked the canonical lamination observed in many other mammals. Its identification was supported by the selective binding of Ulex europaeus agglutinin and strong Gi2 immunoreactivity in glomerular-like structures, whereas Go labeling was weak. LEA and STA labeled the superficial layers of both bulbs, while VVA and SBA recognized only scattered MOB glomeruli. Neuronal markers, including NCAM, NSE, NeuN, PGP 9.5, and {beta}-tubulin III, confirmed the neuronal nature of the AOB, while calretinin strongly labeled its glomerular structures and projection neurons. These findings reveal a marked contrast between a highly developed MOB and a small, poorly laminated but neurochemically differentiated AOB. This organization indicates that the vomeronasal pathway is retained in A. cinereus, although in a structurally reduced form, and provides a comparative basis for investigating chemosensory evolution in semiaquatic carnivorans.

title: Brief visual oddball events evoke CSF flow in the spinal canal
abstract: The measurement of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) flow with fMRI, made possible by exploiting edge artifacts of spin saturation when the bottom acquisition slice lies in a CSF reservoir, allows researchers to investigate an aspect of brain health that has been increasingly linked to cognitive aging and neurodegenerative disease via its role in glymphatic clearance. The initial demonstration of this technique used the fourth ventricle, but recent reports show it can also be done when the bottom acquisition slice lies in the spinal canal in the foramen magnum. We present a method to automatically identify the spinal canal without manual tracing, and measure CSF flow with high confidence using multi-echo acquisition to separate out BOLD-like and non-BOLD-like signal components, along with physiological regression to improve signal to noise ratio. Using these methods we found that CSF flow correlated with decreases in BOLD activity in 70 adults aged 19-76. We further found that brief, infrequent salient stimuli (visual oddballs, requiring a button press) were capable of provoking measurable CSF flow.

title: Broad Cognitive and Motivational Enhancement through M4-Selective Muscarinic Modulation
abstract: The muscarinic M4 subtype of acetylcholine receptors is part of agonist compounds considered treatment options for Schizophrenia and Alzheimers disease, but how M4-subtype selective modulation affects cognition and motivation is largely unknown due to dose-limiting side effects, a scarcity of receptor-selective compounds, and missing multi-domain assessments of cognition. Here, we surmount these constraints by utilizing a M4-selective positive allosteric modulator (PAM) to assess in nonhuman primates a broad array of endpoints spanning motivational effort control and multiple executive function domains. We found broad dose-dependent performance improvements of set shifting indexing cognitive flexibility, visual search indexing selective attention, antisaccade performance indexing inhibitory control, visuospatial maze learning, and temporal order serial object learning, while working memory span was non-systematically modulated. In addition, the M4 PAM reduced effort avoidance in an effort-based choice task documenting a pro-motivational effect. Task-composite performance scores showed pro-cognitive effects across multiple doses and an effective dose range for individual subjects in the absence of adverse dose-limiting cholinergic side effects. Together, the broad pro-cognitive and pro-motivational multi-task profile of M4 PAM modulation suggests that the M4 receptor is a master regulator of executive cognitive functioning, possibly acting on domain-general neural processes across the prefrontal-striatal circuits.

title: CD300f is required for efficient lipid handling during cuprizone-induced demyelination
abstract: Microglia play a crucial role in central nervous system homeostasis and response to demyelination, yet the mechanisms that coordinate the sensing and processing of myelin-derived lipids remain poorly understood. CD300f is a lipid-sensing innate immune receptor expressed by myeloid cells that has been implicated in tissue damage sensing, phagocytosis, and lipid metabolism. Here, we investigated the role of CD300f in the cuprizone-induced demyelination model. Using CD300f-deficient mice, we demonstrate exacerbated demyelination, increased lipid droplet accumulation, impaired microglial responses, and reduced remyelination accompanied by motor coordination deficits. Bulk RNA sequencing of the corpus callosum at the peak of demyelination revealed enrichment of homeostatic, disease-associated (DAM), and foamy microglial signatures, together with increased expression of genes involved in lysosomal function, phagocytosis, inflammation, and lipid metabolism. Notably, these transcriptional changes were associated with marked lipid droplet accumulation in microglia and enrichment of microglial states previously linked to chronic demyelinating lesions. These findings suggest that CD300f is required for efficient handling of myelin-derived lipids and for microglial metabolic adaptation during demyelination. Our study identifies CD300f as a critical regulator of microglial function and lipid homeostasis and highlights this receptor as a potential therapeutic target in demyelinating diseases.

title: Circuit and cell-type mechanisms of the spectrolaminar motif of cortical oscillations
abstract: Oscillations are a key feature of cortical activity, coordinating spike timing across areas, layers, and cell types. Recent work suggests these rhythms follow a stereotyped organization across cortical depth, the spectrolaminar (SL) motif, with higher-frequency gamma prominent in superficial layers and lower-frequency alpha/beta in deep layers, yet the mechanisms generating it remain poorly understood. Using a bio-realistic model of mouse primary visual cortex, we reproduced the SL motif and found it preserved across diverse visual stimuli. Systematic cell-type- and layer-resolved perturbations showed that the alpha/beta component was intrinsic to every layer, whereas the 50-80 Hz gamma component was predominantly generated within layer 4 (L4) and propagated network-wide through inter-laminar connections. Pvalb interneurons were the principal regulators of gamma, Sst cells shaped low-frequency power, and Vip cells controlled oscillation magnitude. The temporal properties of L4 Pvalb-to-excitatory synapses were especially influential in generating the SL motif. These models and simulation results thus offer a plausible description of circuit mechanisms underlying cortical oscillations and the SL motif and are publicly available to facilitate further studies.

title: Clinical relevance of diffusion tensor imaging-based parameters estimated with deep learning: the effect of model retraining
abstract: Deep learning (DL)-based approaches have recently become powerful tools for characterizing microstructural properties of brain tissue from diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging data. These techniques enable depicting microstructural features with significantly reduced acquisition schemes while preserving relatively high image-quality metrics compared with non-DL-based approaches. Learning-based methods have increasingly been applied to diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) and more advanced multi-compartmental biophysical models, with the potential to facilitate multiparameter analyses of brain microstructure in clinical settings. However, independently trained DL models-while maintaining image-quality properties-do not appear to preserve the statistical properties of groupwise analyses across independently trained models. In this study, we systematically evaluate the statistical properties of DL-based DTI parameters across independently trained neural networks under the same architecture to preserve group-level effects in bipolar disorder. We examine the impact of model retraining and its dependence on reducing the number of gradient directions compared with the nonlinear least-squares (NLLS) procedure. Our results show that initializing model weights randomly from a uniform distribution, while keeping the network architecture and training hyperparameters the identical in the experiment, leads to significant variation in the statistical properties of DTI measures inferred from independently trained models. The analyses showed that the true positive rate in groupwise analysis using the DL-based DTI parameters ranges from 0\% to 100\% compared with the NLLS-based analysis. As the number of gradient directions increased, the NLLS procedure yielded more stable groupwise statistical results, whereas independently trained DL models showed greater variability despite similar image-quality agreement with reference maps. The results indicate that the DTI maps retrieved from a single trained network should be treated with great caution before drawing clinical conclusions.

title: Compositional computations in the primate frontal cortex
abstract: A hallmark of intelligence is the ability to apply familiar operations to new inputs without relearning. How neural circuits carry a learned computation into states never visited during training remains unclear. Here we combined neural recordings, circuit modeling and human experiments to investigate compositional generalization. Monkeys learned to combine a start location with a displacement specified by the direction and duration of an optic-flow stimulus, then encountered novel combinations of these familiar inputs. Frontal population activity separated the computation into spatial and temporal components: start location and flow direction established the neural state, from which activity evolved along shared timing dynamics. Novel combinations elicited accurate responses when trajectories maintained this organization, whereas departures predicted systematic behavioral biases. Circuit models revealed a three-way alignment problem: input representations, recurrent dynamics and readout operations must jointly implement the required computation. Mismatches produced systematic biases that increased with distance from trained conditions. Humans exhibited similar biases when familiar sensory cues and spatial transformations were linked through an unfamiliar mapping. Together, these findings show how the coordination of reusable neural resources supports new computations, and how its disruption produces predictable failures of generalization.

title: Concussion decreases brain signal variability
abstract: Sports-related concussion represents a major public health concern, with millions of cases diagnosed annually. Despite significant methodological advances in functional brain imaging, a clinically meaningful neuroimaging biomarker of concussion has yet to be established. This may be due in part to a reliance on traditional measures. For example, approaches examining mean activation across trials reduce responses to a single measure of central tendency and therefore fail to capture important individual differences. In contrast, blood oxygenation level dependent (BOLD) variability offers a promising new approach to measuring brain function, Specifically, it captures individual differences in the temporal variability in the BOLD signal over time. Further, it is sensitive to neural, vascular, and neurovascular coupling changes that accompany concussion. We collected baseline (prior to injury) and post-concussion (within 48 hours of injury) neuroimaging data in 56 collegiate athletes. Within this longitudinal dataset, we investigated changes in BOLD variability across multiple spatial scales. In addition, we examined their relationships with self-reported symptoms and cognitive performance. As expected, symptoms increased following concussion while computerized cognitive performance declined. BOLD variability decreased from baseline to post-concussion, particularly in the somatomotor and language networks. Moreover, changes in BOLD variability were related to changes in symptom reporting and cognitive performance. Together, these findings advance our understanding of how concussion affects brain function and highlight BOLD signal variability as a promising biomarker to aid ongoing efforts to improve the diagnosis and treatment of sports-related concussion.

title: Confidence: Its Measurement, Relation to Behavior, and Neural Representation
abstract: Confidence (certainty/uncertainty about one's own decision) has attracted considerable attention in psychology, neuroscience, and artificial intelligence. Yet its relation to behavior remains unclear: Some treat confidence as a cause of behavior whereas others view it as a state controlled by environmental variables. The unobservable nature of confidence makes its measurement validation and analyses difficult. To tackle these issues, we developed a novel procedure combining a decision-making task, risk choices, and a post-task open-ended questionnaire. Point-gain/loss amounts for correct/incorrect decisions varied depending on choices between high-risk/high-return and low-risk/low-return. In the questionnaire, 90% of 16 participants reported feelings interpretable as certainty/uncertainty when making those risk choices despite no instruction about confidence, whereas 8% did so when the choices led to identical outcomes/returns. This suggests confidence is a state controlled by environmental contingencies rather than a cause of behavior. We also decoded changes in the state from electroencephalography and functional magnetic resonance imaging.

title: Cross-excitation in dorsal root ganglia redistributes coding capacity from stimulus intensity to stimulus location
abstract: The phenomenon of cross-excitation between neurons of dorsal root ganglia (DRGs) of mammals is widely known, yet its exact mechanism remains underexplored. In this work, we analyze the phenomenon as part of the signal processing performed by the body's somatosensory system. We argue that, if the mechanism is indeed as prevalent as it is reported in experimental works, it should provide a significant computational advantage. Here, we created a model network in which sensory A-type neurons are interconnected only via a chemical agent and showed that such a connection, when fitted with parameters similar to those observed in experiments, improves the stimulus-localization properties of the ganglia at the expense of intensity-encoding accuracy. Although this exchange is near-neutral in raw bits, it becomes favorable once the logarithmic compression of intensity perception - the Weber--Fechner law - is taken into account, since the sacrificed intensity capacity is largely perceptually redundant. We therefore propose that cross-excitation is not an imperfection of somatic isolation but an effective, chemically mediated pre-processing stage that sharpens spatial localization.
author_corresponding_institution: Center for Bio- and Medical Technologies

title: Curved geometry shapes the observability of hippocampal oscillations
abstract: Curved neural architectures reshape the spatial distribution of field oscillations, complicating the identification of their underlying generators. To test these principles experimentally, here we resolve the paradoxical poor expression of theta oscillations in the hilus of the folded dentate gyrus (DG), a region that otherwise exhibits some of the largest FPs in the brain. Using laminar recordings across both hippocampi and computational modeling, we show that theta is locally masked by cancellation of phase-coherent contributions. Theta generators in CA1 and DG produce volume-conducted fields that, due to the curved geometry of the DG, exhibit opposite dipolar orientations in the hilus, leading to regional cancellation. In contrast, beta and gamma generators are only weakly coordinated across hippocampal regions and therefore remain prominently expressed despite the same geometry. These results demonstrate that theta amplitude, local observability, spatial segregation and apparent translocation emerge from the interplay between geometry and temporal coherence among distributed generators, with tissue geometry acting as a spatial filter for coherent activity.

title: Deprivation of dietary fiber promotes low-grade neuroinflammation and anxiety-like behavior in mice
abstract: Background: Intestinal health is an important determinant of brain function in that an array of gut perturbants, especially those targeting microbiota, influence behavior. Fermentable dietary fiber nourishes gut microbiota and, consequently, promotes gut health. We hypothesized that depriving mice of fermentable dietary fiber would impact their brain and behavior. Methods: Male C57BL/6J mice were fed standard grain-based chow (GBC), a compositionally defined diet (CDD) which mimics macronutrient content of GBC but lacks fermentable fiber, or CDD supplemented with the fermentable fiber inulin (CDD+INU). Mice were subjected to behavioral testing 6-8 weeks later followed by analysis of the gut brain axis. Results: Relative to GBC-fed mice, CDD-fed mice exhibited low-grade gut inflammation and a reduction in open-field center exploration, signaling heightened anxiety-like behavior. CDD+INU fully reversed these abnormalities arguing they were a consequence of fiber deprivation. Analysis of the gut microbiome and serum metabolome showed that CDD+INU increased oxidative phosphorylation and immune suppressive metabolites. Flow cytometric and transcriptomic analyses of the brain revealed an array of pro-inflammatory alterations in myeloid cells, CD4+ T-cells, microglia and astrocytes in mice fed CDD but not CDD+INU. Most notably, microglia and astrocytes from mice fed CDD, but not CDD+INU, displayed reduced mitochondrial respiration and greater glycolytic activity. CDD, but not CDD+INU consumption also reduced the abundance of oligodendrocytes and neurons, and increased hippocampal pro-inflammatory gene expression. Conclusions: Deprivation of fermentable fiber results in coordinated changes in brain immune composition and glial metabolic state that is associated with increased anxiety-like behavior.

title: Developmental interactions between oscillatory and spontaneous neural activity support improvements in inhibitory control from adolescence into adulthood
abstract: Adolescence is a critical period of development marked by improvements in cognitive control driven by maturation of executive brain systems. Neural mechanisms supporting inhibitory control (the ability to suppress a prepotent response in favor of generating a goal-directed response) mature into adulthood in parallel with refinements in frequency-specific neural oscillations and broadband spontaneous activity, supporting more accurate and reliable performance on response inhibition tasks, such as the antisaccade oculomotor task. Prior work has established that the maturation of neural circuitry contributes to age-related decreases in spontaneous activity, supporting higher-fidelity transmission of task-relevant activity, such as frequency-specific neural oscillations, which are crucial for antisaccade performance.
