Using longitudinal electroencephalography (EEG) data from 146 participants (72 F, ages 10-34, 253 total sessions) collected while participants performed an antisaccade task, we sought to understand the interplay between frontal oscillatory and spontaneous activity during cognitive processing and how it supports developmental improvements in inhibitory control. We found that spontaneous activity decreased developmentally during the preparation of an inhibitory response, and that this was associated with reduced trial-to-trial variability in response latency, indicating that reductions in spontaneous activity may increase the reliability of inhibitory control processing. Furthermore, performance-related decreases in broadband spontaneous activity were associated with the suppression of preparatory high-beta oscillations in an age-dependent manner, such that this relationship became more pronounced through development. Together, these results illustrate how developmental enhancements in the coordination of frequency-specific oscillations and spontaneous activity during inhibitory response preparation support developmental improvements in inhibitory control, providing a potential mechanism through which inhibitory control becomes more accurate and reliable from adolescence into adulthood.

title: Distinct lifespan trajectories of cortical intrinsic timescales and neural oscillations
abstract: The brain integrates information over time through the persistence of neural activity, yet how this persistence changes across the human lifespan and the mechanisms underlying these changes remain unclear. Using resting-state magnetoencephalography from three independent cohorts (n = 1,156; ages 6-88 years), we systematically examined lifespan changes in neural temporal dynamics, focusing on cortical intrinsic timescales and alpha oscillatory frequency. We found that cortical intrinsic timescales shortened from approximately 29 ms in childhood to 9 ms in late adulthood, with the steepest decline occurring before age 30. This compression was reproducible across cohorts and observed in all cortical regions, while the sensory-to-association hierarchy of timescales remained preserved throughout life. By contrast, alpha frequency followed a distinct trajectory, peaking in early adulthood before declining after midlife. Individualized corticothalamic models linked timescale compression to stronger intrathalamic inhibition, whereas increased conduction delays partly accounted for alpha slowing. Further network simulations indicated that intrinsic timescales primarily reflect collective network dynamics rather than single-neuron kinetics. Together, these findings reveal distinct lifespan trajectories of neural persistence and oscillatory rhythms, implicating collective corticothalamic dynamics in the temporal organization of the human brain across development and ageing.

title: Dopamine synthesis capacity and tau pathology differentially modulate rest-to-task functional network dynamics
abstract: Optimal cognition relies on large-scale functional brain networks which balance segregation at rest with selective integration during task performance. In aging, these network dynamics are altered. We examined two prominent features of brain aging: dysregulated dopamine function and Alzheimer's disease (AD)-related pathology to examine impacts on brain network dynamics. Young adults and cognitively unimpaired older adults completed resting-state and task-based fMRI and PET imaging of dopamine synthesis capacity ([18F]fluoro-m-L-tyrosine). Older adults were classified as {beta}-amyloid negative/positive using [11C]Pittsburgh Compound-B PET(PiB- or PiB+) and underwent tau-PET scanning ([18F]flortaucipir). Greater rest-to-task network stability and task-related network segregation were associated with better subsequent memory. Compared to young adults, PiB+ older adults showed reduced network stability and both PiB+ and PiB- older adults showed reduced segregation during rest. Higher ventral striatal dopamine synthesis capacity was associated with greater stability within associative networks in young adults, but this relationship was attenuated in older adults and absent in PiB+ participants. In PiB+ older adults, higher tau burden was associated with a task-induced collapse of network segregation across large-scale networks. These findings reveal dissociable influences of dopamine and tau on rest-to-task network organization, highlighting the value of integrating neuromodulatory and pathological markers in aging research.

title: Druggable CSNK2A1-MeCP2 regulatory axis links Okur-Chung neurodevelopmental syndrome with MECP2-related disorders
abstract: The brain is exquisitely sensitive to methyl-CpG-binding protein 2 (MeCP2) abundance. Too little causes Rett syndrome (RTT), too much causes MECP2 duplication syndrome (MDS), and in both, severity tracks with the amount of functional MeCP2. Even modest deviations are detrimental, yet how MeCP2 abundance is controlled remains poorly understood. Using genome-wide CRISPR knockout screens, we identified hundreds of proteins regulating MeCP2, revealing a casein kinase 2 alpha 1 (CSNK2A1)-driven regulatory axis stabilizing MeCP2. We show this axis is druggable and therapeutically relevant, using a novel CSNK2A1 inhibitor in human cells and targeting Csnk2a1 in an MDS mouse model. We further connect CSNK2A1-MeCP2 regulatory disruption to Okur-Chung neurodevelopmental syndrome (OCNDS), caused by mutations in CSNK2A1, finding ~50% less hippocampal MeCP2 in an OCNDS mouse model. Together, these data identify a druggable regulatory axis modulating MeCP2 and implicate MeCP2 dysregulation in the molecular pathogenesis of OCNDS and potentially other neurodevelopmental disorders.

title: Early AAV9-mediated SLC9A6 gene replacement preserves cerebellar structure and motor function in the shaker rat model of Christianson syndrome
abstract: Christianson syndrome (CS) is an X-linked neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative disorder caused by SLC9A6 loss of function, resulting in NHE6 deficiency and epilepsy, intellectual disability, cerebellar atrophy, and ataxia. Following on our prior gene replacement therapeutic development, we preclinically evaluated AAV9-mediated SLC9A6 gene replacement in the context of promoter selection, dosing, and treatment timing. Intracerebroventricular delivery of neuronal-targeted gene replacement at 1 x 10^11 vector genomes (vg) produced substantial improvements in motor coordination and preserved cerebellar volume, quantified through structural MRI. Early postnatal treatment prevented the development of gait ataxia throughout the longitudinal assessment period, statistically indistinguishable from wildtype controls, with molecular analyses demonstrating restored NHE6 expression and preservation of cerebellar markers. Interestingly, later treatments at timepoints corresponding to early neurodegenerative stages yielded strong initial effects, but these effects were largely lost over time, with half-life modelling demonstrating the need for early treatment. This conflicted with more persistent motor benefit shown in prior work with an engineered capsid, suggesting the need to consider the interaction between treatment timing and capsid-specific tropism and/or persistence. Finally, we built models capable of accurately predicting motor coordination from several protein markers. These findings will impact therapeutic development for CS, with relevance across neurodevelopmental genetic disorders.

title: Emergent topological structure in spontaneous brain-organoid activity
abstract: Neural activity is widely held to organize on low-dimensional structure embedded in a high-dimensional state space. Persistent homology reads such structure directly from the pattern of pairwise correlations, without assuming in advance which variables are relevant. We apply persistent homology to microelectrode-array (MEA) recordings of spontaneous activity from human (Lancaster) and mouse (Pasca) cortical organoids, spanning 25-197 sorted units, and ask whether topological data analysis resolves structure at the node counts that neural recordings actually deliver. Building weighted networks in correlation space and characterizing them by Vietoris-Rips filtration, we find that the first homology (H1, loops) rises significantly above a rate- and population-preserving null in 14 of 18 datasets, all of which remain significant after correction for testing 18 datasets. Random removal of neural units leaves the loops largely intact. Removing the units that form the loops disrupts them more than removing equally connected units does. Topological richness grows with network size, and second homology (H2) exceeds the null only in the larger networks. These results show that persistent homology resolves structured topology in neural recordings at the scale experiments actually deliver.

title: Experience shifts value updating from synaptic plasticity to neural dynamics
abstract: Adaptive behavior requires durable value memories and rapid updating. Experience in dynamic environments accelerates value updating, but the underlying neuronal mechanisms remain unclear. Mice exposed to repeated reversals of odor-outcome contingencies acquired faster value updating at the cost of faster memory decay. Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) trained with continual plasticity revealed two routes to faster learning, one through more efficient synaptic plasticity and one through a transition to value computation by neural dynamics. Only the latter reproduced the trade-off between updating speed and memory persistence observed in mice. Consistent with this transition, inhibiting dopamine neurons at reward delivery or pharmacologically inhibiting CaMKII in the amygdala impaired initial learning but largely spared expert reversal learning. In vivo recordings in the amygdala and hippocampus revealed representations of cue value and latent context necessary for rapid value updating. Context and value signals decayed over prolonged inter-trial intervals, paralleling behavioral forgetting. Conditional deletion of CaMKIIa in Emx1-cre-expressing neurons spared initial associative learning but impaired expert reversal performance, as did freezing the recurrent weights of RNNs, suggesting distinct loci for initial value learning and meta-learning. Together, these findings reveal how experience shifts value computation from synaptic plasticity toward neural dynamics, providing a mechanistic framework for the trade-off between memory stability and behavioral flexibility.

title: Extended Pavlovian conditioned approach training and devaluation in Long-Evans rats using time-restricted feeding
abstract: Pavlovian conditioned approach (PCA) is a useful tool in studying compulsive- and addictive-like behaviors. PCA pairs a cue with reward delivery and rats typically differentiate into three phenotypes (sign-trackers, goal-trackers, and intermediates) based on behavior during the reward-paired cue presentation. Sign-trackers, who preferentially interact with the cue, are more likely to engage in compulsive behaviors and have decreased behavioral flexibility compared to goal-trackers, who preferentially interact with the food cup. However, one limitation to PCA is the use of food deprivation conditions that maintain rats at 80-90% of ad libitum weight, likely increasing stress which may bias animals towards sign-tracking behavior. Furthermore, most behavioral analysis only examines lever pressing and food cup entry, overlooking other behaviors that may better define phenotypes. In the current study male and female Long-Evans rats underwent an extended PCA training paradigm followed by satiety-induced reward devaluation under time-restricted feeding (TRF) conditions. Under TRF, rats continued to gain weight across PCA training and maintained caloric intake relative to ad libitum intake. Expanding the scope of behavioral analysis increased the proportion of ST rats in both early and late PCA training. Rats also increased the time spent interacting with the food cup during the inter-trial interval across extended PCA training. All rats were sensitive to satiety-induced reward devaluation, regardless of sex or devaluation condition. This study helps establish a PCA method optimized for Long-Evans rats with relevance for identifying PCA phenotypes contribution to dysregulated behavior in the context of chronic stress and obesity.
author_corresponding_institution: University of Cincinnati College of Medicine

title: Generalizable sex differences in functional brain organization follow the cortical hierarchy in youth
abstract: It remains unknown if sex differences in human functional connectivity follow a generalizable overarching principle. Here, we tested whether sex differences in functional connectivity during childhood and adolescence are organized along the sensorimotor-association (S-A) axis, a cortical hierarchy spanning unimodal sensorimotor to transmodal association cortex. We analyzed four large-scale, independent datasets of youth ages 5-23 years (total N = 3,355). Across datasets, males showed greater connectivity between functional networks, whereas females showed greater connectivity within networks, most prominently within the default mode network. More broadly, the sensorimotor and association ends of the S-A axis were more segregated in females and more integrated in males. This difference extended to macroscale cortical organization: the cortical hierarchy was expanded in females relative to males along the principal gradient of functional connectivity. Together, these findings identify the S-A axis as a generalizable organizing principle of sex differences in functional brain organization during youth.
author_corresponding_institution: Penn Lifespan Informatics and Neuroimaging Center (PennLINC), University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA, USA.; Department of Psychiatry, Perelman School of M

title: Graph-Based Classification of Penetrating Cortical Arteries and Veins in Whole-Mouse Vasculature Datasets
abstract: Advances in whole-brain imaging have produced large-scale vascular datasets, yet most lack artery-vein annotations. However, this is essential for quantitative analysis of whole brain vascular structure, blood flow simulation and translational cerebrovascular research. For unlabelled datasets, manual labelling is infeasible at network scale, and surface-vessel tracing is hampered by reconstruction artefacts, limiting the insights that can be gained from these datasets. Here, we focus on penetrating vessel trees, i.e. descending arteries (A) and ascending veins (V). A supervised Random Forest classifier is trained on graph-derived morphological and topological tree features, including persistent homology. Training uses datasets from two imaging modalities: Light sheet (LS) microscopy with arterial staining and two-photon (TP) micrscopy with manual labelling in smaller samples. Classification reached 96% balanced accuracy on independent TP dataset and 93% on LS datasets. Topological features alone achieved competitive accuracy without relying on diameter measurements, demonstrating cross-modality portability. Arteries exhibit larger diameters and longer inter-bifurcation segments, likely facilitating their functional task of directed blood delivery. The veins show greater branching complexity, allowing low-pressure drainage. These signatures are stable across modalities, supporting their physological relevance. The framework enables A-V label transfer to unlabelled whole-brain TP graph datasets, validated through the V:A ratio as a function of middle cerebral artery (MCA) distance. Operating on graph representations derived from any volumetric imaging modality and requiring no retraining, the approach is applicable to LS, TP, and likely other imaging platforms, providing a scalable foundation for A-V quantification, vascular topological analysis, and haemodynamic modelling.
author_corresponding_institution: ARTORG Center for Biomedical Engineering Research, University of Bern, Bern, Switzerland CH

title: Human organoid screen links transient translational modulation to progenitor progression in corticogenesis
abstract: Human pluripotent stem cell-derived models are increasingly used to recapitulate aspects of human corticogenesis, including the emergence of diverse cortical cell types and their progression through developmental states. These systems offer an opportunity to dissect the molecular mechanisms regulating transitions between cell states, but methods for perturbing them systematically at scale remain limited. Here, we developed a semi-automated culture and high-throughput arrayed screening platform for human cortical organoids. Using a library of 1,280 small molecules designed to systematically target major signaling and regulatory pathways, we screened for modulators of EOMES, which encodes for the transcription factor TBR2, and identified Emetine, an inhibitor of translation elongation, as the top hit. The effect of Emetine on cortical cell-state progression was reproduced across human pluripotent stem cell lines, non-human primate cortical organoids, and primary human cortical tissue but not broadly across translation inhibitors. Moreover, transient exposure resulted in a shift from dividing radial glia towards cortical glutamatergic neurons. Mechanistically, nascent-proteome profiling revealed an early and coordinated remodeling of newly translated proteins that preceded detectable transcriptional changes, placing translational regulation upstream of the ensuing cell-state transition. Together, these findings highlight a role for specific translational inhibitors in promoting cortical cell-state progression and establish a scalable platform for systematic perturbation and discovery in human neural organoids.
author_corresponding_institution: Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences, Stanford University School of Medicine, Stanford, CA, 94305, USA, Stanford Brain Organogenesis, Wu Tsai Neuros

title: Hyperactivity preferentially disrupts scotopic retinal circuits in the early stages of diabetic retinopathy
abstract: Diabetic retinopathy is a leading cause of blindness worldwide. In this disease, visual impairments result from neurovascular dysfunction in the retina. However, the specific retinal circuits and the mechanisms underlying their dysfunction remain unclear. Here, in mouse models of diabetes, we evaluated scotopic (night vision) and photopic (day vision) retinal circuit function in the early stages of the disease. Using a combination of immunohistochemical, behavioral and electrophysiological techniques, we show that vision impairments early in the disease are not associated with widespread degeneration of the retinal circuitry but with abnormalities localized to scotopic circuits. Specifically, we observed swelling of axon terminals in rod but not cone bipolar cells. Importantly, these abnormalities were closely linked with bipolar cell activity, as rod bipolar cells showed higher intrinsic activity than cone bipolar cells, and inducing hyperactivity in control retinas was sufficient to recapitulate the pathology in diabetic rod bipolar cells. Further, the swollen rod bipolar cell terminals exhibited an increase in oxidative stress, consistent with cellular dysfunction. In line with this notion, electrophysiological measurements demonstrated that the contrast sensitivity of retinal ganglion cells was preferentially attenuated under scotopic conditions. Finally, behavioral experiments showed that visual sensitivity under scotopic conditions was affected earlier in disease progression compared to photopic conditions. Together, these findings reveal that scotopic circuits are preferentially affected in the early stages of diabetic retinopathy and that hyperactivity is sufficient to drive these abnormalities.

title: In Vivo Network-Level Cerebrovascular Mapping Reveals the Impact of Flow Topology on Capillary Stalls After Stroke
abstract: Cerebral microvasculature is essential for brain function, but how flow and large-scale connectivity contribute to its resilience or failure remains poorly understood. To address this, we developed OMNIMap, a framework that integrates extended-focus optical coherence microscopy, learning-based segmentation and vessel-graph optimization, linking capillary flow and stalls to broader network context. Imaging over 60,000 capillaries in the mouse cortex revealed heterogeneous vascular responses to stroke, with capillary stalls, flow increases and decreases within the same networks. Divergent-to-convergent capillary subtypes had the highest stall risk. This association was not fully explained by differences in vessel structure, velocity or network position, suggesting that additional factors contribute to their vulnerability. Despite changes in individual capillary assignments after stroke, the overall proportions of capillary subtype remained largely preserved. Longitudinal mapping further showed that capillary stalls may persist until at least 7 days post-stroke. Together, these findings identify local flow topology as a marker of capillary vulnerability after stroke.

title: Increased Cognitive Load Expands, Stabilizes, and Aligns Visual Representation Across the Human Brain
abstract: Cognitive load refers to the mental effort required to perform a task. While previous research has extensively examined its detrimental effects on neural and behavioral performance, much less is known about how the brain actively adapts to heightened demands. Across two fMRI experiments involving visual n-back tasks, we identified several fundamental properties of this adaptive process. First, higher load enhanced and expanded visual representations beyond localized visual regions, leading to widespread visual coding. At the global scale, heightened load promoted cross-regional coordination by increasing representational alignment and strengthening information encoded in interregional functional connectivity patterns. Beyond facilitating stronger visual representation, increased load also reduced neural pattern variability, which led to more stable information coding. Finally, load was encoded independently of other task-relevant information as a separate brain state, supporting its overarching role in guiding visual processing. Together, these findings revealed that the brain adapts to heightened cognitive demands by globally reorganizing neural processing to support flexible cognition.

title: Individual differences reveal shared computational structure in perceptual decision-making
abstract: To discover computational mechanisms of cognition, models typically specify a fixed psychological architecture, treating individual differences as variations within a predefined parameterization. Here, we take a different approach by using the population structure of individual differences to directly drive model discovery. We develop a low-rank neural network that uses this `population geometry' to learn shared computational components and participant-specific weights from trial-level choices, allowing cross-subject variation to constrain the model's architecture. Applied to perceptual decision-making in the Bernoulli Clicks Task across primary and replication datasets, out-of-sample prediction reveals a six-dimensional representation for individual differences: two continuous dimensions of temporal evidence weighting and two of choice-outcome history dependence, alongside participant-specific side bias and signal-to-noise ratio. This low-dimensional organization replicated in an independent dataset. Together, these findings reveal that seemingly disparate decision heuristics reflect different weightings over a small set of shared computational components, and establish a principled methodology for using behavioral variability to discover the mechanistic architecture of cognition.

title: Measuring neuronal input-output operations in vivo with random access projection microscopy
abstract: Neurons transform thousands of synaptic inputs into spiking output, and understanding this transformation requires measuring many submicron synapses at millisecond timescales in vivo. Here we present SLAP2, a two-photon random access projection microscope with no per-target access time cost, yielding over 5-fold faster imaging than existing methods, and performant real-time hardware motion correction. Flexible scanning modes enable measurement of hundreds of synapses at ~200 Hz, >800 synapses volumetrically at 50-100 Hz, and compartment-resolved dendritic voltage at 2-10 kHz in behaving mice. Simultaneous dendritic glutamate and somatic calcium imaging in visual cortex pyramidal neurons revealed nonlinear input-output amplification of stimulus onset and preferred stimulus orientation responses. Amplified features are associated with spatially organized inputs and stronger trial-to-trial coupling between synaptic activity and somatic output. These measurements establish SLAP2 as a powerful tool for recording intricate patterns of subcellular fluorescence dynamics in behaving animals.
author_corresponding_institution: Allen Institute, Neural Dynamics, Seattle, WA

title: Modeling circadian rhythm splitting under chronic light and the asymmetric transition kinetics between lighting conditions
abstract: In various vertebrates, chronic light splits the single daily 24-h circadian activity bout into two 12-h behavioral components per cycle, yet the underlying mechanism remains unresolved. Here, we develop a two-lobe biophysical model of the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) to understand this phenomenon. By representing the master clock as interacting ventral core and dorsal shell populations of Kuramoto-type oscillators across bilateral lobes, we suggest that chronic light changes the excitation/inhibition (E/I) balance orchestrated by GABA, which either inhibits or excites SCN neurons. Under constant darkness, excitation dominates and provides in-phase synchronization of the populations. Under chronic light, inhibition dominates, and the ipsilateral and contralateral couplings among the core and shell populations become negative. Consequently, the shells in the left and right lobes oscillate in antiphase, producing the 12-h behavioral rhythm in downstream tissues. We suggest that this E/I balance is shifted by a light-induced change in the expression of chloride cotransporters in SCN neurons. Another key novelty is the introduction of the biologically motivated dynamics of chloride cotransporter expression, which explains the sign inversion of ipsilateral and contralateral couplings under time-varying lighting conditions. The model also reproduces the effects of unilateral SCN lesions: if one lobe is abolished, the remaining intact lobe autonomously stabilizes into a single-bout circadian output with a period comparable to that of the intact system. Finally, we compare our results with experimental data and demonstrate a close agreement.

title: Motivation-dependent communication between cortex and brainstem
abstract: Neurons in the medullary brainstem exhibit movement-related patterns of activity, but the neuronal population codes that specify distinct actions, and the mechanisms by which cortex may shape these codes as a function of motivational state, remain unclear. To explore whether coupling between cortex and medulla depends upon motivational context, we trained mice to make both pre-reward "appetitive" licks that served to trigger water availability and rapidly attenuated with satiety, and "consummatory" licks, which occur post-reward release and more slowly attenuated with satiety. Simultaneous recordings from secondary motor cortex and motor medulla revealed that medullary activity was more time-locked than cortical activity to individual licks and exhibited a phase-based population code that encoded lick direction. Correlations between cortex and medulla were stronger during appetitive licks than during consummatory licks, with causal dependency established by optogenetic intervention and supported by multi-region recurrent network models. Population codes underlying behavior shared across the central nervous system, exemplified by cortico-medullary coupling, thus may depend upon the motivational context underlying action.

title: Multi-scale place fields provide a predictive basis for hierarchical control
abstract: Hippocampal place cells typically exhibit unimodal spatial selectivity in small enclosures, but express multiple, irregularly spaced fields in environments of naturalistic scale. However, existing predictive-map theories of the hippocampus do not scale well to large environments and do not account for these heterogeneous place field characteristics. Here, we introduce the factorised hierarchical successor representation (fHSR), a predictive map that supports hierarchical control using subgoal-directed subroutines. We show that the fHSR allows efficient generalisation across tasks, scaling favourably with environmental size, and it reproduces key statistical and topological characteristics of multi-scale CA1 place cell activity in rats and bats. Analyses of experimental data further confirmed a novel prediction of the fHSR: population firing rates exhibit spatial periodicity with a characteristic wavelength independent of environmental size. These results identify the integration of hierarchical control and predictive representations as a normative principle that unifies efficient navigation with the spatial organisation of hippocampal activity.

title: Neonatal NMDA receptor blockade disrupts prefrontal cortical regulation of social affective behavior: implications for schizophrenia
abstract: Developmental N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NMDAr) hypofunction has been implicated in the pathophysiology of schizophrenia, including cognitive and emotional deficits. However, the neural circuit mechanisms linking developmental NMDAr hypofunction to social affective impairments remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated schizophrenia-related social affective dysfunction induced by neonatal exposure to the NMDAr antagonist MK-801 and examined the contribution of the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), a key hub for socio-cognitive function. Sprague-Dawley rat pups received subcutaneous injections of saline or MK-801 (MK-Low: 0.2 mg/kg; MK-High: 0.4 mg/kg) during the neonatal period. In adulthood, social affective behaviors were assessed using the Social Affective Preference (SAP) and Social Interaction (SI) tests. MK-801-treated rats, particularly the MK-High group, displayed impaired social affective responses, characterized by reduced preference for and investigation of distressed conspecifics. These impairments were ameliorated by chemogenetic inhibition of pyramidal cells in the mPFC, whereas activation of these neurons disrupted social affective behavior in naive rats. Histological analyses revealed reduced parvalbumin-positive interneuron (PVIN) density in the mPFC of MK-801-treated rats. Consistent with the involvement of PVIN dysfunction, selective activation of mPFC PVINs alleviated social affective deficits in MK-801-treated rats. These findings identify impaired PVIN-mediated inhibitory regulation within the mPFC as a circuit mechanism underlying social affective dysfunction following neonatal NMDAr blockade, providing insight into the pathophysiology of schizophrenia-related social impairments.
author_corresponding_institution: Laboratory of Psychology and Behavioral Neuroscience, University of Tsukuba

title: Network analysis of mouse brain proteomes resolves molecular and cellular endophenotypes of aging and Aβ pathology
abstract: Aging and Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology exert both shared and distinct effects on the brain, yet their relative contributions to molecular alterations remain poorly defined. Here we performed tandem mass tag proteomics across the lifespan in wild-type and 5xFAD mice and integrated these data with human brain proteomic networks to resolve aging- and amyloid-beta (A{beta}-associated molecular programs. We quantified 8,535 proteins and identified 51 co-expression modules representing neuronal, mitochondrial, glial, vascular and proteostatic pathways. Aging emerged as the predominant driver of proteomic remodeling, with widespread alterations in RNA metabolism, protein translation, and neuronal pathways occurring independently of A{beta} pathology. In contrast, A{beta} selectively modified a subset of age-dependent processes, including suppression of mitochondrial ATP biosynthetic machinery and amplification of astrocytic and microglial activation states. These key aging and disease-related molecular signatures were highly conserved in human AD brain proteomes. Together, our findings establish aging as the primary determinant of brain proteome organization while revealing specific mechanisms through which A{beta} pathology reshapes age-associated biological processes. Our results also highlight molecular mechanisms of human aging and AD pathology that can be modeled in mouse models.
author_corresponding_institution: Department of Neurology, University of Florida, Gainesville, FL, 32610, USA

title: Neural Bases for Working Memory of Natural Sound Textures
abstract: Holding sound objects in mind is critical to understanding the sound world around us. Auditory texture perception is thought to rely on extracting statistical properties of sounds over time, raising the question of how encoding duration influences subsequent maintenance of auditory texture information. We investigated this question using behavioural performance and fMRI while participants performed two delayed match-to-sample tasks: a texture discrimination and a comparison loudness discrimination task. In the texture task, participants judged whether two sequentially presented sounds belonged to the same texture type, whereas in the loudness task, participants judged whether the sounds, drawn from the same texture type, had the same loudness. Stimuli were presented for either 0.1s or 2s. Discrimination sensitivity increased with duration in both tasks, but more strongly for texture discrimination. fMRI analysis revealed distinct effects of duration on univariate and multivariate activity in the auditory cortex and medial temporal lobe (MTL) during maintenance. We found no univariate duration effect in the auditory cortex during maintenance, but multivariate patterns encoded texture category more strongly for longer stimuli, regardless of task. In contrast, MTL activity was modulated by sound duration in both tasks, but there was no effect of duration on texture category decoding. There was a task effect in MTL where multivariate patterns in posterior hippocampal and parahippocampal regions distinguished texture from loudness tasks following 2s stimuli. Together, these findings show effects of duration on sound texture representations during maintenance and that MTL representations reflect the behavioural context in which that information is maintained.

title: Neural transformation from image realism to perceived realness
abstract: Humans readily perceive whether a visual stimulus depicts something that could exist in the real world, yet the neural basis of perceived realness remains unclear. Because differences between real and unreal stimuli are ultimately expressed through visual features, realness might be expected to emerge along the ventral visual stream. Contrary to this prediction, we show that perceived-realness representations emerge in higher dorsal visual areas through a transformation of image-realism-related image-feature representations in early visual and early dorsal visual areas. fMRI revealed this representational shift toward intraparietal sulcus (IPS), with IPS patterns predicting perceived realness beyond image features and decision difficulty; source-localized MEG showed that realness coding in IPS emerged later than feature coding in early visual and dorsal visual areas. Together, these findings reveal a transformation from visual features to perceived realness along the dorsal visual stream. This representation may help guide subsequent actions and interactions with the real world.
author_corresponding_institution: National Institute of Information and Communications Technology

title: Neurons entrain and shape an intrinsic arteriole rhythm that distributes blood across the cortical mantle
abstract: The cerebral arteriole network distributes blood across cortex through branches whose diameters oscillate near a frequency fvaso ~ 0.1 Hz. We asked whether the spatiotemporal pattern of these vaso-oscillations reflects neuronal entrainment of an intrinsic vascular oscillation. Three findings support this: First, suppressing endothelial hyperpolarization left resting-state oscillations intact but weakened the vascular response to neural activity, showing that vasomotion originates within the arteriole network rather than following neuronal drive. Second, arterioles amplify sensory drive selectively rather than faithfully: neural activity near 0.1 Hz is resonantly enhanced to form a strong peak in the vascular response. Third, neuronal frequency sets spatial reach, and areas compete: when two neighboring cortical areas are driven simultaneously, the one nearer fvaso captures more vascular territory. Neurons therefore entrain an intrinsic vascular rhythm and stimulation frequency governs how vasomotion distributes blood, shapes functional brain images, and may influence interstitial fluid transport.

title: Next generation Human Neocortical Neurosolver model with biophysically realistic somatic, dendritic and synaptic dynamics
abstract: The Human Neocortical Neurosolver (HNN) is an open-source biophysical modeling tool for multiscale interpretation of human electroencephalography (EEG) and magnetoencephalography (MEG) signals. HNN's foundation is a pre-tuned canonical neocortical circuit model consisting of excitatory pyramidal neurons and inhibitory interneurons in supra- (L2/3) and infragranular (L5) layers. This model was originally developed based on studies in rodent and non-human primate cortices when dynamics of human neurons were poorly characterized. Yet recent advances in recordings from human tissue now provide unprecedented detail to update the model. Here, we present a significantly updated model for use in the HNN software, with electrophysiological properties and synaptic connections tuned to human tissue. Beyond reproducing biologically realistic somatic dynamics, the pyramidal cells simulate dendritic calcium (Ca2+) spikes in the L5 extratelencephalic-projecting (ET) neurons, and shorter dendritic spikes in the L2/3 pyramidal neurons. We demonstrate how the updated circuitry and new features in the HNN software can be used to disentangle somatic, synaptic, and dendritic contributions to human E-/MEG signatures. The model is distributed with workflows to simulate event-related responses and oscillations, and tutorials demonstrating how membrane potentials, Ca2+ dynamics, and synaptic currents can be recorded and visualized. These enhancements allow extensive model validations based on in vitro and in vivo electrophysiology, voltage and Ca2+ imaging, and provide users with novel insights on the mechanisms underlying E-/MEG signals.
author_corresponding_institution: Department of Neuroscience, Brown University, Providence, RI, USA

title: No Evidence of an Effect of a Single Mirror Visual Feedback Session on Subsequent Motor Imagery
abstract: Motor imagery (MI) and mirror therapy, based on mirror visual feedback (MVF), are recommended as adjuncts to conventional therapies for upper limb rehabilitation after stroke. Both approaches activate sensorimotor cortical networks despite the absence of overt movement, and their concurrent application has been associated with enhanced neural activation. The present study investigated whether a single session of MVF modulates subsequent kinesthetic Motor Imagery (kMI)-related neural activity. EEG data from 38 healthy participants (MVF: n = 18; sham: n = 20) were analyzed in a mixed pre-post design. Participants performed kMI before and after either an MVF or sham intervention. Analyses focused on mu-band (8-12 Hz) event-related desynchronization (ERD) and its hemispheric lateralization. Although kMI reliably elicited stronger contralateral than ipsilateral mu ERD, MVF did not significantly affect subsequent kMI-related mu ERD or its hemispheric lateralization. These findings suggest that previously reported facilitatory effects of MVF on MI may be more closely related to concurrent application than to immediate aftereffects, while potential effects of repeated MVF exposure on subsequent MI remain to be investigated. These findings provide a foundation for future studies investigating how MVF and MI can be combined to optimize upper-limb stroke rehabilitation.
author_corresponding_institution: Neurocognition and Functional Neurorehabilitation Group, Department of Psychology, University of Oldenburg, Oldenburg, Germany

title: Persistent hippocampal traces of lifelong spatial memory
abstract: Memory presents a biological paradox: the brain changes continuously, yet a brief experience can influence behavior for a lifetime. How such memories are stored in brain circuits remains unclear. Here we show that two days in a binary-tree maze leave mice with spatial memories that survive repeated 90-day absences over as much as a year. Across return visits, mice explored the maze more efficiently than when naive and resumed direct runs to a reward location sooner, both by a factor of 3. Chronic calcium imaging of the same hippocampal CA1 neurons showed that although most neurons had changed their preferred locations, the population activity at a given maze location still resembled the pattern from 90 days earlier. Furthermore, even when a neuron's place fields changed location, they tended to remain at the same branching level of the binary tree, reflecting the local geometry of the maze. In return sessions where the neural tuning for branching level was preserved more accurately, the mouse explored the environment more efficiently. Population patterns were best preserved near the reward location, and more reliable neural activity there accompanied earlier direct runs to the reward. With repeated experience, spatial representations changed less, both within a visit and across the long absences. A brief experience thus left selective hippocampal traces that survived months of absence despite drift, grew more durable with each return, and were correlated with memory in navigation behavior.

title: Personalized Prediction of Differences in fMRI Connectivity Estimates Across Preprocessing Pipelines
abstract: Longitudinal functional MRI of the human brain is valuable for tracking changes in functional connectivity (FC) associated with disease progression or treatment response. Even so, measured FC values depend on preprocessing, and nuisance regression and temporal filtering affect individuals differently. We examined whether we could use earlier scans to predict how preprocessing would affect a later scan. In 69 ADNI (Alzheimers Disease Neuroimaging Initiative) participants scanned three times, we measured how nuisance regression and filtering, alone and in sequence, changed the measured FC. A ridge regression model combined these responses with baseline FC from the third scan to predict the effect of reversing the processing order. Just four coefficients were shared across 79,800 connections. In leave-one-participant-out testing, mean squared error was 0.012, compared with 0.017 for predicting the same average response for everyone. It outperformed the best of seven alternative predictions chosen for each participant (0.013; normalized gain 0.069, 95% bootstrap interval 0.006-0.134), with lower error in 44 of 69 participants. About half the benefit of using each persons earlier responses, rather than the average across participants, came from which connections changed. This advantage persisted after accounting for acquisition variables. The ADNI-trained model reduced mean error in ten Midnight Scan Club participants without refitting. These results support using personal preprocessing history to predict changes in connectivity estimates on newly acquired scans.
author_corresponding_institution: PowerMechaniX LLC, Albuquerque, New Mexico, USA

title: Phase-locked dual-band vibration bursts strengthen anti-kindling by vibrotactile coordinated reset stimulation in a spiking network model
abstract: Parkinsons disease and related movement disorders are accompanied by pathologically synchronized neuronal activity in cortico-basal ganglia circuits. Coordinated reset (CR) stimulation was derived computationally as a means of suppressing such activity at its source, by resetting the phases of the subpopulations of a synchronized network at staggered times. Under spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP), the resulting decorrelated firing depresses excitatory coupling and establishes a weakly coupled, desynchronized state that outlasts stimulation, a process termed anti-kindling. Sustained post-stimulation benefit has been demonstrated for electrical CR stimulation in parkinsonian primates and in proof-of-concept patient studies, and vibrotactile CR (vCR) stimulation realizes the same principle non-invasively through bursts of fingertip vibration. The deployed vCR protocol employs a carrier frequency of 250 Hz, which preferentially recruits Pacinian afferents. Because Pacinian receptive fields extend substantially beyond the stimulated digit, inputs originating at adjacent fingertips converge on overlapping regions of the target population, which degrades the spatial separation on which CR depends. Here we examine whether the spectral composition of the individual burst, independent of the stimulation schedule, governs the magnitude of anti-kindling. In a Hodgkin-Huxley network with STDP, driven through a two-channel model of fast-adapting afferents, a dual-band burst superimposing a 30 Hz component on the 250 Hz carrier yielded the lowest post-stimulation coupling among eleven vCR patterns, at one third of the carriers drive power. Recruitment of focal Meissner afferents by the 30 Hz component restricts part of the drive to the stimulated subpopulation, and phase locking of that component to the burst envelope generates post-burst pauses that reset the phase of the stimulated neurons. Spectral composition therefore determines both the spatial selectivity of vCR stimulation and its capacity for phase resetting.

title: Probing EEG Foundation Model Attention Maps for Lightweight Interpretable Emotion Recognition
abstract: Foundation Models (FMs) trained on EEG signals promise subject- and dataset-independent pipelines for brain-computer interface (BCI) applications, but have yet to consistently outperform task-specific architectures, and their large representations are costly to compute and store. As a means of advancing the understanding of the Foundation Models' inner mechanisms, we propose a lightweight alternative that exploits the self-attention mechanism of REVE, a pretrained EEG FM, to derive features similar to weighted Functional Connectivity (FC) without any fine-tuning. Inspired by kernel-based FC matrices, we aggregate the raw first-layer attention weights of a single head over the full duration of dataset trials into weighted channel-to-channel adjacency matrices. These matrices replace standard encoder representation vectors as classification features, substantially reducing computational cost. We further introduce a label-free, symmetry-based criterion, motivated by the emergence of near-symmetric attention patterns in trained encoder-decoder transformers, ranking attention heads by how much discriminative information they carry. Classical machine learning classifiers are then trained on the single most informative head's attention-derived FC matrix and achieve balanced accuracy and F1 scores on the SEED-IV emotion-recognition dataset that are competitive with several fully fine-tuned state-of-the-art EEG Foundation Models, requiring at least two orders of magnitude fewer calculations than the standard use of the encoder. Subsequent cortical region analysis revealed a significant over-representation of frontal region connections by ranking the most discriminative FC matrix connectivity edges, validating our methods as consistent with prior affective-computing literature. These results suggest that interpretable, computationally inexpensive linear probing of attention maps is a viable route to deploying EEG Foundation Models in resource-constrained settings.
author_corresponding_institution: Neuroengineering and Brain-Computer Interfaces Research Infrastructure, University of Patras, 26504 Patras, Greece

title: Real-time detection of N2 and N3 sleep from scalp and intracranial EEG
abstract: Sleep rhythms such as slow oscillations and spindles arise predominantly during N2 and N3 sleep (N2+N3). Closed-loop stimulation targeting these rhythms is a promising strategy to enhance memory. Such stimulation requires online sleep stage classification. Conventional staging labels completed 30-s epochs using past and future data and cannot support online staging. We developed a causal tracker that, every 2 s, estimates the current stage from the preceding 10 s of scalp or intracranial EEG. We also evaluated a simulated rule that permits stimulation after three consecutive estimates indicating N2+N3 sleep. In six adults with drug-resistant epilepsy with simultaneous scalp EEG and stereo-EEG, real-time N2+N3 discrimination remained close to offline scoring of the same recordings (scalp AUC 0.953 versus 0.958). Thalamic channels alone reached AUC 0.934 and exceeded mesial temporal channels in every patient, and scalp plus thalamus performed best (0.967). The scalp tracker, retrained in 28 healthy adults, reached 0.976. When patients transitioned into N2+N3 sleep with stimulation initially disabled, the rule permitted stimulation within 5 min in 63-73% of transitions, with a median delay of 42-64 s among those detected. After leaving N2+N3, stimulation was disabled after a median of 19-22 s. The rule also switched on incorrectly 1.4-1.8 times per hour outside N2+N3 and remained active during 28-31% of REM in patients, compared with 2% in healthy adults. These findings show that both scalp and thalamic EEG can support real-time N2+N3 detection and inform when stimulation is permitted. Translationally, implanted thalamic leads, increasingly used for neuromodulation in epilepsy, could support sleep-stage-dependent stimulation without scalp EEG, while scalp EEG might be used for noninvasive neuromodulation. Closed-loop systems should be evaluated not only by sleep-stage classification accuracy but also by how reliably and promptly they enable and disable stimulation.
author_corresponding_institution: Department of Neurological Surgery, University of Chicago

title: Reinforcement sculpts synaptic ensembles for operant dendritic control
abstract: Reinforcement learning requires the selective modification of synapses that contribute to outcome-relevant neural activity, yet the principles underlying these selective modifications remain unclear. Here we combined longitudinal two-photon imaging of identified dendritic spines with a closed-loop optical brain-machine interface (BMI), in which activity from selected apical dendrites of layer 5 motor-cortical neurons controlled an auditory cursor, with target acquisition triggering optogenetic reinforcement. Mice learned to reliably generate the specific dendritic activity that leads to reinforcement. Learning was accompanied by selective strengthening and weakening of individual spines on reinforced dendrites. At individual synapses, the direction of plasticity depended on both the timing of activity relative to reinforced dendritic events and the pre-existing temporal organization of that activity. Furthermore, plasticity was enriched in small task-relevant synaptic groups: spines in synergistic groups were preferentially strengthened, whereas those in antagonistic groups were preferentially weakened. These changes were accompanied by the emergence of increasingly reproducible, selectively recruited, and temporally focused synaptic ensembles, and the incorporation of newly formed spines into these ensembles. Finally, blocking striatal dopamine receptor signaling impaired BMI learning and cortical synaptic reorganization of target dendrites, demonstrating a role for striatal reinforcement in cortical plasticity. Together, these findings reveal how reinforcement of specific dendritic activity sculpts synaptic ensembles that support learned operant dendritic control.

title: Robust lesion network mapping reveals symptom-specific circuits
abstract: Lesion network mapping (LNM) is a powerful tool for linking distributed brain lesions to symptom-relevant networks, but similar LNM maps across unrelated symptoms have raised concerns about its statistical validity and specificity. Here we introduce robust LNM (rLNM), a statistically principled framework that combines two complementary controls: an anatomy-preserving spatial null model to account for connectome-derived hub bias shared across symptoms, and hypothesis-driven contrasts to resolve selective specificity among related symptoms. rLNM effectively controls both false positives and negatives. Across 10 lesion datasets (384 lesions) and two task-fMRI meta-analyses (339 experiments), rLNM recovers distinct symptom-specific networks (mean r = 0.044), which show significantly reduced similarity to the connectome hub pattern (r = 0.12 vs. 0.33 in conventional LNM). In 56 patients with neurosurgical lesions, rLNM predicts postoperative language decline at the single-patient level. rLNM thus resolves these concerns and lays a unified statistical foundation for network-symptom inferenc.

title: SNAzzy: an image processing pipeline for investigating global Synchronous Network Activity
abstract: Genetically encoded fluorescent indicators are powerful tools for monitoring biological processes in live samples (Lin and Schnitzer 2016; Nakai, Ohkura, and Imoto 2001). When combined with a large field of view, a single time-lapse recording has the potential to capture many specimens, facilitating high-throughput data collection. However, this approach generates large, multidimensional datasets that are challenging to process and analyze. We present SNAzzy, a Python package for studying synchronous network activity (SNA) in Drosophila embryos via high-throughput microscopy. SNA is a hallmark of developing nervous systems (Wu, Kourdougli, and Portera-Cailliau 2024; Blankenship and Feller 2009; Akin and Zipursky 2020), often studied using genetically encoded calcium indicators to monitor neural activity in vivo. SNAzzy processes and analyzes time-lapse datasets taken from live samples using fluorescent widefield microscopy. Each dataset contains dozens of individual specimens in the same field of view and thousands of time points. The software offers individual specimen cropping for optimization of storage and processing, adaptive regions of interest for quantification of fluorescence and changes in morphology over time, a custom peak detection algorithm, and a graphical user interface for data visualization, curation, and dataset comparison. The code is available at https://github.com/ACRLab/snazzy.

title: Seed Amplification Assay-Based Detection of Alpha-Synuclein Aggregates Outperforms Immunohistochemical Analysis in the Intestinal Mucosal Biopsies of Parkinson's Disease and Multiple System Atrophy Participants
abstract: Objective: To determine whether an -synuclein (-Syn) seed amplification assay (SAA) detects seeding-competent aggregates in endoscopic mucosal biopsies, differs by gastrointestinal region, registers pathology more frequently than immunohistochemistry (IHC), and associates with Parkinson disease (PD) diagnosis, disease duration or severity. Design: This cross-sectional, proof-of-concept diagnostic accuracy study analyzed duodenum, ileum, and sigmoid biopsies from PD participants, age- and sex-matched healthy controls (HC), plus exploratory multiple system atrophy (MSA) subtypes [parkinsonian (MSA-P) and cerebellar (MSA-C)]. Ileal and sigmoid PD and HC biopsies were assessed using proteinase K-resistant phospho-Ser129 IHC. SAA positivity was evaluated against clinical and biological measures. Results: In PD, SAA detected seeding competent -Syn aggregates with high observed specificity (97.5-100%) and region-dependent sensitivity (18/37, 48.65% in ileum and 36/56, 64.29% in sigmoid). Sigmoid SAA positivity increased significantly with PD disease duration (40.00% at <5 years, 73.33% at 5-10 years, and 93.75% at >10 years), independent of motor severity, whereas ileal positivity remained stable across disease stages. In 37 paired sigmoid biopsies, SAA detected -Syn aggregates 2.8-fold more frequently than IHC. Sigmoid seeding activity was detected in all five MSA-P, but not in two MSA-C. IHC did not detect aggregates in any MSA. Conclusions: In PD, -Syn SAA detected seeding-competent -Syn aggregates in endoscopic mucosal biopsies with high observed specificity, moderate sensitivity, and approximately 2.8-fold higher detection rate than IHC in sigmoid. Positive SAA in MSA patients supports GI involvement across synucleinopathies. SAA detection in PD differed by intestinal region and disease duration, supporting further validation of intestinal SAA as a PD biomarker.

title: Sex-dependent and region-specific morphological adaptations in astrocytes following early-life stress
abstract: Astrocytes are structurally heterogeneous, with cell morphology providing a valuable readout of experi-ence-dependent plasticity. Despite this, single-cell reconstruction including complete cellular territories remains challenging to compare across brain regions and experimental groups. We used unilateral retro-orbital delivery of PHP.eB-GfaABC1D-eGFP as a practical method for sparse astrocyte labeling and ap-plied it to evaluate regional, sex, and early-life-stress comparisons in the mouse amygdala. Systemic vi-rus delivery to broadly target astrocytes across the brain produced eGFP-positive cells throughout cortex, hippocampus, hypothalamus, and amygdala with spatially isolated cells suitable for intensity projection, three-dimensional surface reconstruction, filament tracing, and Sholl analysis. In naive females, we report relatively homogenous morphological features between lateral amygdala and basal amygdala. In naive males, basal amygdala astrocytes had greater volume and a lower surface-area-to-volume ratio, while surface area, soma diameter, territory, and arborization measures did not differ significantly. Interestingly, early-life stress produced sex-specific morphological responses in the basal amygdala. Females showed increased perimeter, area, and Feret diameter without significant changes in three-dimensional volume or resolved filament measures. Males instead showed reduced surface area and volume, with no significant changes in projected territorial dimensions, soma diameter or resolved filament measures. S100{beta}-positive cell density was unchanged in the displayed regional and stress comparisons. These findings es-tablish systemic sparse eGFP labeling as an efficient route to single-cell astrocyte morphometry and re-veal a sex-dependent and region-specific dissociation between territorial expansion and three-dimensional volumetric contraction after early-life stress.
author_corresponding_institution: University of Montreal Hospital Research Centre (CRCHUM)

title: Sex-specific dynamics of activity-dependent regulation of synaptic CaMKII
abstract: Similar behavioral outcomes in males and females can mask substantial differences in the mechanisms underlying neuronal function. However, to what extent sex influences the abundance and activity-dependent changes of proteins that govern neuronal plasticity remains poorly understood. Here we investigated sex-specific regulation of calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CaMKII), an evolutionarily conserved regulator of synaptic stability and plasticity in fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster. We find that the steady state levels and activity-driven changes in CaMKII protein differ between female and male at both third instar larval neuromuscular junction (NMJ) and in adult fly mushroom body (MB). These sex-specific differences are downstream of the sex determination pathway, implicating somatic sex identity in the regulation of CaMKII abundance and its activity-dependent dynamics. Despite the differences in CaMKII levels between female and male flies, we observed no impairment of plasticity in either sex. Overall, our findings reveal sex-dependent regulation of both steady-state and activity-dependent levels of a highly conserved neuronal plasticity-associated protein across distinct neuronal contexts and development stages. These results further support the idea that females and males can achieve similar behavioral outcomes through different molecular mechanisms. Growing evidence that sexually dimorphic molecular responses contribute directly to sex differences in vulnerability to stress and disease underscores the importance of identifying these mechanisms and understanding their consequences.

title: Single-cell multi-omics identify OTP and NOVA1 as regulators of leptin action in hypothalamic feeding circuits
abstract: Leptin acts directly and indirectly on multiple neuronal populations to regulate feeding and numerous other physiologic functions. However, our understanding of how a single circulating signal coordinates diverse neuronal populations across multiple circuits is limited. To further elucidate how leptin reshapes molecular states in its direct and indirect neural targets, we combined time-resolved single-nucleus transcriptomics and chromatin accessibility profiling to map leptin-induced transcriptional and chromatin state changes across individual neurons in two key hypothalamic nuclei: the arcuate nucleus (ARC), which contains the majority of leptin receptor (LepR) neurons, and the paraventricular hypothalamic nucleus (PVH), an established downstream target of ARC LepR neurons. We found that leptin treatment of leptin-deficient ob/ob mice does not alter neuronal identity, but instead induces coordinated, cell-type-specific transcriptional and regulatory state changes that propagate hierarchically from the ARC to downstream PVH neurons. Integrating RNA velocity, cis-regulatory analysis, and cell-cell communication inference revealed that leptin modulates hypothalamic circuit architecture by selectively strengthening specific interactions while pruning broadly distributed, low-specificity signaling. Although leptin broadly activated STAT3 signaling across LepR neuronal subtypes, integrated multi-omic analyses revealed that activation of STAT3 engages distinct downstream regulatory programs in different neuronal populations, often with opposing physiological functions. Functional analyses identified the homeobox transcription factor OTP, a leptin-responsive regulator selectively induced in AGRP neurons, as a critical mediator of leptin-mediated inhibition of hunger-promoting AGRP neuronal activity and feeding. In parallel, unbiased analysis of PVH neuronal state transitions shows that NOVA1, an RNA-binding protein primarily expressed in inhibitory neurons, is regulated by leptin and alterations of NOVA1 expression bidirectionally control food intake and body weight. Together, these findings define a multi-layered regulatory framework through which leptin regulates hypothalamic feeding circuits to control energy balance.
author_corresponding_institution: Department of Anatomy and Neurobiology, University of California Irvine School of Medicine, Irvine, CA, USA

title: Striatal Value Signals Track Progress Toward a Goal During Planning
abstract: When making decisions, we often weigh immediate gains against long-term goals, and the value of the same choices can change over time. We used a novel task in which participants repeatedly chose between two cards, each with an immediate point value and an uncertain prospective value, with the latter reflecting the collection of card sets. Computational modeling showed that the prospective value captured how close participants were to completing a set. This goal gradient could be explained by both a simple progress-weighted heuristic and a forward-simulating planner. Using fMRI, we found that striatal and precuneus activity increased with the prospective value of the chosen card but not with its immediate point value. Activity in the dorsomedial and insular cortices instead increased with the value of the card given up and was highest when participants chose against the model-based value of the options. Activity in all regions of interest provides stronger support for the goal gradient rather than a full forward-planning model. These results refine the role of the valuation and cognitive control networks in goal-based decision-making.

title: Striatal cell-type-specific encoding stability and reorganization for goal-directed behavior and habit
abstract: Goal-directed decision making relies on learned action-outcome associations to allow actions to adapt when outcomes change. With repetition, behavioral control shifts toward habit, enabling more automatic action execution at the expense of flexibility. Much is unknown about how the brain learns and supports goal-directed behavior and what changes as habits form. Here, we longitudinally tracked and manipulated the activity of two major dorsomedial striatum populations, D1+ and D2/A2A+ neurons, to reveal their activity and function during goal-directed learning and habit formation. Across learning, DMS D1+ neurons stably encode instrumental actions, carry information about behavioral engagement and organization, and develop and maintain action-reward representational similarity and conjunctive activation. This persists even after behavioral control transitions to habit. In contrast, one ensemble of DMS A2A+ neurons transiently encodes actions during early learning and another slowly starts to encode actions as habits form. Both DMS D1+ and A2A+ neuronal activity mediates the learning processes underlying goal-directed control, but only DMS D1+ neurons maintain support of adaptive, goal-directed decision making. These data reveal a cell-type-specific dissociation between stable v. reorganizing striatal action representations and, independently, persistent v. transient contributions to goal-directed control.

title: Temporal Progression of Prior Precision, Surprisal, Model Updating and Tone Adaptation in Human Auditory Cortices
abstract: Auditory perception emerges from the continuous integration of incoming acoustic signals with statistical predictions, a process complemented by simpler local adaptation. Yet, how all these concurrent mechanisms unfold in time remains underexplored. Using magnetoencephalography (MEG) in participants listening to stochastic tone sequences with periodically shifting inferential statistics, we modelled the temporal, spatial, and spectral dynamics of stimulus-specific repetition suppression, surprisal, model updating, and prior precision. By concurrently tracking these computational parameters within this dynamic auditory environment, we revealed a distinct chronological hierarchy governing predictive and adaptive processing. Prior precision states - reflecting expectations - emerged earliest, followed by rapid and concurrent repetition suppression and surprisal - reflecting local acoustic attenuation and global mismatch detection. These initial dynamics culminated in subsequent, distributed model updates within fronto-parietal networks. Spectrally, these components mapped onto diverging oscillatory fingerprints, ranging from theta-alpha modulation during adaptation to beta suppression during surprisal and broad spectral dampening during precision weighting. Together, these findings demonstrate that the brain navigates uncertain auditory environments through a cascade of neural processes, where fast, local sensory gating and mismatch signals precede the hierarchical revision of internal models.

title: Temporal Structure in Resting-State fMRI under Marginal and Cross-Spectral Surrogate Controls
abstract: Resting-state functional MRI is commonly analyzed using correlations between regional signals and their frequency spectra, which characterize average connectivity and spectral properties but may miss other aspects of temporal organization. Measures of temporal complexity offer complementary information about the recurrence of signal patterns, how fluctuations vary across timescales, and signal roughness. These properties may reveal disease-related alterations in brain activity, offering opportunities for biomarker discovery and insights into mechanisms of neurological and psychiatric disorders. Here we examined sample entropy (SampEn), multifractal de-trended fluctuation analysis (MFDFA), and Higuchi curve shapes in 732 scans from 270 ADNI participants, including cognitively normal individuals, people with mild cognitive impairment, and people with dementia. Using the seven Yeo resting-state networks (Yeo-7), we compared recordings with randomized signals preserving either each networks amplitude distribution and approximate spectrum (IAAFT), or the complete cross-spectrum across networks. If these properties fully explained temporal complexity, real recordings should resemble their randomized references. We therefore counted how often each real recording was the strongest outlier among itself and 20 references. This occurred in 21.7%, 12.7%, and 44.2% of 5,124 network-visits for SampEn, MFDFA, and Higuchi, versus 5.5%, 5.1%, and 6.3% in surrogate-only controls. Cross-spectrum-preserving references yielded 39.8%, 17.5%, and 49.8%. Simulations showed that changes in sampling or signal processing, including abrupt changes in signal amplitude, can produce similar differences without changing the underlying dynamics. The measures showed repeatability across visits but did not improve retrospective prediction of changes in Clinical Dementia Rating Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB) scores. These findings identify temporal features not reproduced by the tested spectral controls and provide a basis for evaluating their potential as disease biomarkers.
author_corresponding_institution: PowerMechaniX LLC, Albuquerque, New Mexico, USA

title: The G-protein coupled receptor GPR34 maintains the homeostatic state of microglia and restrains the disease-associated microglial response in an Alzheimers disease model
abstract: Expression of the G protein coupled receptor GPR34 is highly enriched in microglia and is downregulated in various brain diseases, including Alzheimers disease (AD) and multiple sclerosis (MS). GPR34 function is poorly understood, as is its role in regulation of microglial states. Using RNA-sequencing, we find that microglia from Gpr34 knockout (KO) mouse brains exhibited a transcriptomic shift toward disease-associated microglia (DAM) and inflammatory profiles, partially resembling the microglial phenotype seen in 5xFAD AD model mice. Moreover, when Gpr34 KO mice were crossed with 5xFAD mice, the DAM transcriptional profile of microglia and glial pathology were further exacerbated beyond the already robust DAM signature driven by 5xFAD alone. This occurred without affecting amyloid plaque burden. Human stem cell-derived microglia (iMGLs) lacking GPR34 showed reduced calcium (Ca2+) and phosphorylated ERK (pERK) signaling in response to stimulation with known GPR34 agonists (lyso-phosphatidylserine (lysoPS) and myelin), as well as transcriptomic changes in immune regulation and cell proliferation related pathways. Interestingly, GPR34 KO iMGLs were selectively impaired in phagocytosis of myelin but not amyloid-B; (AB) or E. coli, and showed a diminished transcriptional response elicited by myelin. Together, these findings suggest that GPR34 is important for maintaining microglia in a homeostatic state, promotes phagocytosis of and transcriptional response to myelin, and limits microglial reactivity in neurodegenerative disease conditions.
author_corresponding_institution: The Stanley Center for Psychiatric Research, The Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard, Cambridge, MA, USA

title: Therapeutic Potential of Melatonin, Erythropoietin, and TRPV4 Antagonism in a Preclinical Model of Genetic Hydrocephalus
abstract: Symptomatic hydrocephalus is a neuropathological disorder of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) homeostasis characterized by abnormal accumulation of CSF and progressive ventricular enlargement. Current treatment relies primarily on surgical CSF diversion, which is invasive and associated with substantial rates of treatment failure and surgical revisions. Congenital hydrocephalus can be caused by genetic pathologies; for example, a point mutation in the Meckel-Gruber type 3, Tmem67, gene produces a congenital hydrocephalus phenotype in rats, characterized by progressive ventriculomegaly. Here, we evaluated a combinatorial cocktail therapeutic strategy consisting of erythropoietin (EPO), melatonin (MLT), and the transient receptor potential vanilloid 4 (TRPV4) antagonist, RN1734 (RN), in the Tmem67-- rat model of congenital hydrocephalus. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) demonstrated marked progression of ventriculomegaly in untreated Tmem67-- rats between postnatal (P) 7 and P15. RN1734 and EPO+MLT+RN1734 (triple therapy) from P7-P14 prevented further ventricular expansion. Hydrocephalus is associated with structural disruption of the periventricular white matter (WM) and ependymal lining (EL), accompanied by regionally increased TLR4 and NLRP3-associated inflammatory signaling. EPO+MLT, RN1734, or triple therapy differentially attenuated these inflammatory responses. The triple combination reduced both TLR4 and NLRP3 protein abundance within the affected periventricular region and ameliorated the structural alterations. These findings support a combined therapeutic approach that addresses ventricular pathology, inflammation and periventricular structural consequences of congenital hydrocephalus.

title: Towards an analytical framework for investigating the neurophysiological influence of social context in speech perception
abstract: Social information plays an important role in everyday speech communication, yet existing neurophysiological approaches provide limited means of isolating its contribution during naturalistic speech perception. Here, we present an analytical framework that combines the large language model (LLM) Mistral-Instruct, fine-tuned on conversational language, and temporal response functions (TRFs) to investigate the influence of social context on word-level speech processing. The framework disentangles local context (LC) from speaker-specific social context (SC) when generating LLM-derived lexical expectation measures, enabling such predictions to be generated under either matching or mismatching speaker contexts for the same speech material. This provides a direct way of isolating the contribution of social information to lexical predictions. We first show that speaker-related social context carries information about speech register and conversational role beyond that available from previous local context alone by interrogating Mistral-Instruct. We then demonstrate that lexical expectations generated from socially congruent contexts produce small but reliable improvements in EEG prediction relative to expectations generated from incongruent social contexts. These effects were observed despite identical acoustic input and neural recordings, indicating that the influence of social context on lexical expectations explains dissociable variance in neural responses to speech. Together, these findings provide a proof of concept for using LLM-derived lexical expectations to isolate and measure the influence of social context on speech processing. More broadly, the proposed framework offers a flexible approach for generating and testing hypotheses about how different forms of contextual knowledge shape neural responses during naturalistic language comprehension.

title: Tree shrews combine panoramic vision with an expanded oculomotor repertoire
abstract: Mammals differ in how they redirect gaze. Primates shift and hold gaze with rapid, precise eye movements that can be decoupled from the head. In lateral-eyed mammals studied to date, gaze is organized around the head: saccades are coupled to head rotation in freely moving animals and typically accompanied by attempted head movements even under head fixation. These observations suggest a trade-off: animals that keep a panoramic field give up the precise, eye-driven control of gaze typical of frontal-eyed animals. But because lateral eyes and head-centered gaze co-occur in every lateral-eyed species studied, it is unknown whether one follows from the other. Here we test this in the tree shrew, an arboreal mammal with laterally placed eyes. Using real-time eye tracking in head-fixed animals, we find that tree shrews saccade frequently under head fixation and that most saccades occur without detectable attempted head movement. Tree shrews make visually evoked saccades, along both the horizontal and vertical axes of the visual field, toward targets. They can also fixate on visual targets. Using widefield calcium imaging, we show that visual cortex over-represents the central visual field. Lastly, we show that extraocular muscles that move the eyes contain specialized nerve endings found in frontal-eyed species. Based on this suite of evidence, we conclude that lateral eyes do not preclude eye-driven gaze control. The two are separable dimensions of visual system design, a combination that may suit animals whose locomotion routinely points the head away from where they need to look.
author_corresponding_institution: Cornell University & Howard Hughes Medical Institute

title: Tyrosine hydroxylase deletion in Ntsr1 neurons confers resistance to diet-induced weight gain: an energy-balance analysis
abstract: High-fat diet (HFD) disrupts circadian feeding rhythms and promotes diet-induced obesity (DIO), but the neural mechanisms linking diet to energy balance remain unclear. Previously, we demonstrated that dopamine production in neurotensin receptor 1 (Ntsr1)-expressing neurons was required for HFD-induced daytime overfeeding and DIO. Here, we tested whether DIO resistance in Ntsr1Cre;Thflox conditional knockout (cKO) mice was explained by altered energy expenditure. We replicated resistance to HFD-induced weight gain and assessed food intake, indirect calorimetry, activity, body temperature, fecal energy, fecal nonesterified fatty acids, and the gut microbiome. Indirect calorimetry on standard chow diet (SCD) was confounded by reduced intake and body weight loss, whereas HFD-fed cKO mice consumed food readily and resisted weight gain. Unlike our previous study, daytime feeding was not suppressed; instead, cKO mice were slightly and variably hypophagic on HFD but not SCD. DIO resistance was not accompanied by increased energy expenditure, activity, or body temperature. Rather, cKO mice showed reduced energy expenditure and activity and lower body temperature on both diets.
